related_work.citation: "Diffusion Language Models Are Natively Length-Aware." arXiv:2603.06123.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (arXiv v1 2026-03-06). No venue claim in the arXiv comment field.
related_work.what_it_covers: Argues the latent prompt representation already encodes the required output length, and proposes a zero-shot mechanism to CROP the context window before generation, cutting diffusion steps. Evaluated on GSM8K, HumanEval, IfEval, LongFormQA with FLOPs reductions at 'no statistically significant performance degradation'.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Prompt-conditioned response-length prediction for left-to-right-style generation, not bidirectional infilling where a suffix constrains the span; never evaluated on HumanEval-Infilling; no oracle-length or gt_len stratification. Its 'natively length-aware' claim is the strongest existing statement in the direction of length calibration, but it is about the PROMPT representation, not about whether a variable-length mechanism converges to a specific gt_len.
related_work.known_defects: Crops only (one-directional, before generation) so it cannot recover from under-allocation; 'no statistically significant degradation' is a null result used as a positive claim, with power unreported; length-awareness is demonstrated on response-length regimes, not on constrained-middle infilling where the candidate's question lives.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API search (all:'variable-length' AND all:'diffusion language model') returned it; abstract fetched via id_list=2603.06123 (published 2026-03-06T10:30:13Z).

followup_openings.target_paper: DreamOn (arXiv:2602.01326, ICLR 2026 Poster)
followup_openings.defect: The paper's headline ~37-point single-line gain (55.5 -> 92.1 avg) is measured against a fixed-canvas Dream-Coder baseline that is now known to be substantially repairable WITHOUT TRAINING. CAL (arXiv:2602.00476, pre-cutoff) lifts the same DreamCoder-Base single-line average from 49.3 to 70.2 using 11-18 extra single forward passes, and LR-DLLM lifts DreamCoder-7B single-line from 55.5 to 81.6. So a large share of DreamOn's reported advantage is not 'variable-length training beats fixed-canvas' but 'anything that fixes the canvas beats an unfixed canvas' — and DreamOn's comparison never includes a length-corrected baseline. An ICLR reviewer independently wrote 'I feel the baselines are weak.'
followup_openings.our_fix: Run the missing baseline arm on the same backbone under matched compute: Dream-Coder-Instruct-7B with (a) fixed canvas at each prior in {4,8,16,32,64}, (b) a re-implemented CAL-style calibrated-confidence length search, (c) an oracle-length arm, versus (d) DreamOn-v0-7B, all with an identical pinned sampler and with TOTAL forward passes counted in one unit (DreamOn's expand/delete/broadcast steps and the baseline's probe passes both priced). Report the DreamOn advantage as a function of the compute budget, plus a compute-matched control where the fixed-canvas arm simply spends the probe budget on best-of-k. This is the CaRE (arXiv:2607.24763) audit genre applied to variable-length control, where it has never been applied.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It converts a settled-looking result into an open one. If DreamOn's advantage over a length-corrected same-backbone baseline is small or NFE-negative, then the field's justification for TRAINING length control (DreamOn, FlexMDM, DID — all of which cost GPU-days) collapses onto ~15 forward passes of inference-time search, which is a headline finding. This project has already retracted results twice for exactly this class of error (NFE as a cross-family cost unit; averaging that dropped budget-truncated cases), so the accounting rigour is in-house expertise. Also directly repairs the sole reviewer-flagged weakness of an ICLR poster.

followup_openings.target_paper: DreamOn (arXiv:2602.01326, ICLR 2026 Poster)
followup_openings.defect: DreamOn never reports the realised FINAL canvas length against the ground-truth middle length. Its only acknowledgement is 'performance degrades slightly when there is a large discrepancy between the initial masked span and the true target length', and its 'Broadcasting Deletion as Length Predictor' is validated by step-count savings (122.8 -> 52.4 steps) and pass@1, never by length accuracy. So the paper's implicit claim — that the model 'autonomously expand[s] or contract[s] the output length based solely on its own predictions' — is never tested as an ESTIMATION claim. Nobody else measures it either: CAL, LR-DLLM, PILL and rho-EOS all measure their OWN estimator's accuracy, never DreamOn's; FlexMDM's length-fidelity claim is distributional, not per-case.
followup_openings.our_fix: Log final canvas length per case and report it against gt_len: bias (mean signed error), spread (MAE), dependence on the initial prior (does final_len regress toward the prior, i.e. anchoring?), and dependence on gt_len (does it mode-collapse toward the ~8-9 token training prior on long spans?). Then run the decisive paired regression: pass@1 on |final_len - gt_len| rather than on |gt_len - initial_canvas|. Contrast with the oracle arm to separate 'wrong length' from 'right length, wrong content'. Do this on RandomSpan (gt_len median 12, p95 62) and MultiLine (median 31, p95 110), where long-span mass actually exists.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This is the cleanest unoccupied measurement on the board and it is the one that explains LR-DLLM's otherwise-anomalous finding that DreamOn DEGRADES multi-line (43.2 -> 36.1) and wrecks C++/Rust single-line on McEval. If final_len is anchored to the prior and collapses toward short lengths, then 'length elasticity' is permissive rather than calibrated, DreamOn's multi-line regression has a mechanism, and the correct research target for the whole variable-length line shifts from 'can we change length' to 'can we predict length'. It is a mechanism finding, not a leaderboard delta, so it is robust to the exact pass@1 numbers.

followup_openings.target_paper: CAL / "Diffusion LMs Can Approximate Optimal Infilling Lengths Implicitly" (arXiv:2602.00476)
followup_openings.defect: CAL cannot report the matched-length stratum, by construction. To fit its length-bias curve it applies a 'strict Oracle exclusion strategy' discarding every probe length in the neighbourhood of the oracle length, and states those samples are 'strictly excluded from subsequent evaluations.' So precisely the regime where canvas misspecification is absent — the null-comparison stratum — is removed from its analysis. Additionally, a SINGLE global double-exponential bias curve, fit on 100 HumanEval-Infilling samples with LLaDA-8B-Base, is reused across all models and all tasks including text infilling, with cross-model robustness asserted rather than re-fit. And no comparison in the paper carries a paired CI.
followup_openings.our_fix: Re-run the decomposition WITHOUT the oracle-exclusion carve-out, so the matched stratum is reportable, and supply the paired per-case bootstrap CIs the paper lacks (our standing aggregation code from the CoMem/PaperA work). Test the single-global-bias-curve assumption directly by re-fitting the bias per backbone (Dream-Coder-Instruct vs DreamOn) and per split (SingleLine / RandomSpan / MultiLine), reporting how much of CAL's gain survives a correctly-fit versus a transplanted curve. Price CAL's 11-18 probe passes against an NFE-matched fixed-canvas best-of-k control, which the paper never runs.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: CAL is the strongest pre-cutoff obstacle to this candidate, so demonstrating a structural blind spot in it (it cannot see the matched stratum) simultaneously differentiates us and turns it into our fair baseline rather than our competitor. The bias-curve-transfer test is high-value and cheap: if the global curve does not transfer across backbones or splits, CAL's headline generality claim weakens and the training-free-vs-trained tradeoff shifts back toward trained methods — either outcome is publishable.

followup_openings.target_paper: LR-DLLM (arXiv:2602.07546) vs DreamOn (arXiv:2602.01326)
followup_openings.defect: The two papers report irreconcilable DreamOn numbers on the same backbone and benchmark and nobody reconciles them. LR-DLLM Table 3 reports DreamCoder-7B+DreamOn at single-line 73.5 and multi-line 36.1; DreamOn's own Table 2 reports 92.1 and 63.8 — gaps of ~19 and ~28 points. LR-DLLM pins DreamOn to a single initial mask length of 11 'to isolate its variable-length adjustment capability' (DreamOn itself sweeps {4,8,16,32,64} and reports near-flat performance across that whole range, which the pinning is supposed to be irrelevant to). Neither paper matches actual forward passes; LR-DLLM equalises only a nominal MAX_LENGTH=128 canvas cap.
followup_openings.our_fix: Run the reconciliation as a first-class contribution: reproduce DreamOn-v0-7B on HumanEval-Infilling SingleLine/MultiLine/RandomSpan at min_gen_len in {4,8,16,32,64} AND at the pinned 11, using the released vendor/DreamOn harness defaults (steps=256, temperature=0.2, top_p=0.9, alg=entropy, mask_expansion=true, delete_eos_token=true), and separately under a swept sampler. Report which single factor — canvas prior, sampler, harness/scoring, or the AST-normalised exact-match convention DreamOn uses for SantaCoder-FIM — accounts for the gap. Our repo already has both models on disk and the released eval script, so this is close to free.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: A 19-28 point unexplained discrepancy between an ICLR poster and its only independent re-runner means the field's headline number for the flagship variable-length model is not currently reproducible, which is a stronger and more certain claim than any stratification result. It also de-risks everything else we would build: without pinning this down, our own DreamOn numbers are uninterpretable. And this project has independently measured that a top_p change alone moved HumanEval by +14.6 points — larger than most published diffusion-LM method gains — so we have direct evidence that sampler protocol can explain gaps of this size, and the tooling to prove it.

followup_openings.target_paper: DreamOn (arXiv:2602.01326) and the whole variable-length line (CAL, LR-DLLM, FlexMDM, DAEDAL, rho-EOS)
followup_openings.defect: Every one of these papers uses the ORACLE length purely as a ceiling and never as a decomposition, and the oracle is itself a leaked control: it is defined as the token count of the reference solution, so the 87-93 oracle pass@1 figures presuppose knowledge of the answer's exact tokenization and are unattainable in deployment. Meanwhile the oracle numbers contain an unremarked anomaly: for +DreamOn the oracle is BELOW the base model's oracle on both splits (single-line 91.6 vs 93.3; multi-line 66.6 vs 69.0), and w/o-Delete's oracle (67.9 multi-line, 84.2 SantaCoder-FIM) exceeds full DreamOn's. That means the length fine-tune COSTS raw infilling quality at matched length — a tax nobody has named or measured.
followup_openings.our_fix: Name and measure the length-control tax: with the canvas pinned to gt_len (oracle) on identical cases, run a paired McNemar / paired bootstrap of Dream-Coder-Instruct vs DreamOn-v0-7B to establish whether the fine-tune significantly degrades matched-length infilling, and stratify that tax by gt_len. Then report the two effects separately — repair gain (mismatch regime) minus quality tax (matched regime) — as the honest net accounting of what variable-length training buys. Also report a deployment-realistic oracle substitute (e.g. a length predicted from prefix+suffix) so the ceiling is not defined by leaked reference tokenization.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This turns a footnote in someone else's ablation table into a named, measured phenomenon with a clean paired test, and it is the natural companion to the calibration finding: variable-length training buys repair in the mismatch tail and PAYS for it in the matched regime. It also lands squarely in this project's demonstrated strength (paired bootstrap / McNemar aggregation from PaperA/PaperB) and needs no training. Crucially, it survives even if the stratification result comes out flat — i.e. it is robust to the candidate's own kill criterion firing.

followup_openings.target_paper: DreamOn (arXiv:2602.01326) — task-surface gap
followup_openings.defect: DreamOn never evaluates HumanEval RandomSpanInfilling; its tables are SingleLine, MultiLine, and SantaCoder-FIM (Python) only. This matters more than a coverage complaint: our local tokenization with the DreamOn-v0-7B tokenizer shows SingleLine gt_len is median 7 / p95 20 / max 46, so at canvas=32 only 9 of 1033 cases are within 2 tokens of the canvas and at canvas=64 ZERO are — the matched stratum does not exist on the split the paper's headline number comes from. Any claim that DreamOn is robust 'across a wide range of initial mask lengths' on SingleLine is therefore a claim about the over-allocation regime almost exclusively.
followup_openings.our_fix: Make RandomSpanInfilling (1640 cases locally, gt_len median 12, p95 62, and the only split with real mass in BOTH tails — e.g. at canvas=16: 179 matched vs 316 extreme-mismatch) the primary surface, with SingleLine and MultiLine as boundary conditions, and report the gt_len x canvas occupancy matrix up front so readers can see which strata are even estimable per split. This also corrects the candidate's own plan, which budgeted RandomSpanInfillingLight at n=164 and assumed SingleLine could supply a matched stratum.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It converts a stratification design that would have silently produced an unpowered or degenerate matched stratum into a sound one, and it yields a standalone methodological point: the benchmark split determines which length regimes are testable, so DreamOn's 'robust across mask lengths' claim on SingleLine is structurally confined to over-allocation. Zero GPU cost to establish (already computed on CPU from data/infilling/ on disk).

blocking_gaps: GRADER CEILING IS BROKEN ON THE `plus` TESTS AND THE PROJECT IS ALREADY REPORTING NUMBERS THROUGH IT. I ran the canonical HumanEval solution for all 164 parents through the exact grader on .73 (`scripts/score_infilling.py:grade_one`, which=plus, min_time_limit=10, factor=16) and got base=164/164 but plus=143/164 -- 21 parents (HumanEval/{22,32,39,44,49,55,63,64,76,91,95,97,111,122,123,124,125,127,132,140,150}) FAIL the plus tests with their OWN reference solution. Consequence: 188/1033 SingleLine items and ~1/3 of a MultiLine sample are hard-capped at 0 for every arm. This is not cosmetic for THIS candidate: it is stratum-correlated. Ceiling rate by gt_len quartile is 0.793/0.830/0.805/0.844, and ceiling-correcting moves the published-style numbers from dreamon_fim .7018->.8544 and dream_fim .7115->.8663, while the stratified DreamOn-minus-Dream delta moves Q1 +0.0241->+0.0348 and Q4 -0.0996->-0.1179. The magnitude of the correction (~+15 points) is 1.5x the entire effect the candidate is trying to measure. The existing `--self-test-n 10` guard did NOT catch this: it samples 10 random SingleLine rows and only tests which='base'. Its published trustworthy=True is a false negative. Fix (~30 lines, no GPU): compute the per-parent canonical ceiling once, persist it, restrict every stratum to gradeable parents, and report ceiling rate per stratum.

THE HEADLINE DIAGNOSTIC CLAIM IS DEAD ON ARRIVAL AND THE POSITIONING'S OWN NUMBERS DO NOT SUPPORT THE CANDIDATE'S EXPERIMENT PLAN. I re-derived the gt_len distributions locally with the DreamOn-v0-7B tokenizer: SingleLine n=1033 median 7 p95 20 max 46; RandomSpan n=1640 median 12 p95 62 max 154; MultiLine n=5815 median 31 p95 110 max 239. At canvas=64 SingleLine has ZERO cases within +/-2 of the canvas and all 1033 at >16; at canvas=32 only 9. So the candidate's 'matched stratum' does not exist on the split its headline comes from, and its stated kill criterion ('<150 cases in extreme mismatch at EVERY canvas prior') passes for the wrong reason. Separately, the candidate's assets_needed says RandomSpanInfillingLight n=164 -- the file on disk is 1640 rows. Also: the positioning claims 'HAVE ... our paired-bootstrap aggregation code from the CoMem/PaperA work'. That code exists (`/apdcephfs_wzc1/.../Mixture-of-Memory/scripts/locomo_cluster_bootstrap.py`, `paired_analysis_paperb.py`) but it is hard-wired to LoCoMo judge caches and lives in a DIFFERENT REPO on a different venv; and `scipy`/`statsmodels`/`sklearn` are NOT installed in `/opt/conda/envs/dllm-env`. Bootstrap/McNemar must be hand-rolled in numpy (fine, ~60 lines) -- do not budget it as free.

ITEMS ARE NESTED IN ONLY 164 PARENT PROBLEMS, SO PER-ITEM BOOTSTRAP CIs ARE ANTICONSERVATIVE AND THE STRATIFICATION IS CONFOUNDED WITH PARENT IDENTITY. MultiLine has up to 435 items from ONE parent (HumanEval/N); SingleLine up to 29; RandomSpan up to 10. gt_len is strongly parent-determined (a long function yields long spans at every hole), so 'gt_len quartile' partially just relabels 'which HumanEval problem', and problem difficulty is the obvious confound for a monotone quality-vs-gt_len trend. The candidate specifies 'paired bootstrap 95% CI over cases', which treats 5815 MultiLine rows as 5815 independent units. This is the same unit-of-analysis error the Mixture-of-Memory project already corrected once for LoCoMo (task #80, `status/PAPER_LOCOMO_ERRATA_20260721.md`). Must use a parent-clustered bootstrap, and must report the delta as a WITHIN-parent contrast.

THE `plus` VS `base` TEST CHOICE, THE SAMPLER, AND THE TWO DreamOn CODE PATHS ARE ALL UNPINNED AND EACH MOVES THE ANSWER BY MORE THAN THE EFFECT. (a) Two DreamOn implementations disagree on defaults and expose different knobs. `vendor/DreamOn/eval/generator.py` (config `eval/configs/eval_infill.yaml`) has temperature=0.2 top_p=0.9 steps=256 pad_eos_to_right=True and takes `mask_expansion`/`delete_eos_token`. The HF remote code `models/DreamOn-v0-7B/generation_utils.py` has NEITHER string in the file (grep count = 0), instead exposing `pad_delete_to_right` which defaults to FALSE in `generation_config.json`, and its loop bound is `2*max_gen_len + 2*expand_budget` with `expand_budget=None -> max_gen_len*2`. The .73 harness `scripts/generate_infilling.py:run_dreamon` uses the HF path and passes neither -- so pad_delete_to_right=False there vs pad_eos_to_right=True in the vendor path. This is the SAME class of silent-kwarg-swallowing bug the project already retracted DreamOn numbers over. (b) The project's own measured top_p 1.0->0.95 swing on HumanEval is +14.6 points, larger than most published method gains, and larger than the whole effect here. (c) which='base' vs which='plus' is worth ~15 points via the ceiling above.

RESULT OF THE PILOT I ALREADY RAN (SingleLine, n=1033 paired, canvas=4 for dreamon_fim, raw uncorrected):
  gt_len quartile cuts [5,7,10]
  Q1 (2-5, n=290): DreamOn realised_len 4.16, signed err +0.03, MAE 0.19, p@1 .772
  Q2 (6-7, n=317): 6.25, -0.22, 0.32, .801
  Q3 (8-10, n=195): 8.36, -0.60, 0.86, .723
  Q4 (11-46, n=231): 11.75, **signed err -5.00, MAE 5.41**, p@1 .459
  => the length estimator is UNBIASED on short spans and COLLAPSES toward the short training prior on long ones, and MAE grows monotonically with gt_len. This is exactly the "biased, mode-collapsing estimator" the positioning predicts, and nobody has published it.
  Pass@1 conditional on |realised_len - gt_len|: err=0 -> .821 (n=736); 1-2 -> .616 (n=112); 3-5 -> .400 (n=85); >=6 -> .180 (n=100). Monotone, 4.6x spread. The residual failures ARE the length misses.
  Giving DreamOn the oracle INITIAL canvas fixes most of the estimator: signed err -1.29 -> -0.38, MAE 1.53 -> 0.69, p@1 .7018 -> .7590. So its expansion is anchored to the prior, not calibrated to the content.
  LENGTH-CONTROL TAX at matched canvas: dreamon_oracle-only-pass b=69 vs dream_fim-only-pass c=20, net +49, McNemar chi2~25.9 -- and this is the OPPOSITE sign to the tax the positioning hypothesised from DreamOn's own oracle column. Worth reporting either way; do not pre-write the direction.
  I also confirmed the collapse generalises beyond SingleLine (fresh runs, LOCAL GPU, HF path, n=25 each): MultiLine canvas=4 gt 34.2 -> realised 14.8 (signed -19.44, MAE 19.68, exact 8/25); MultiLine canvas=32 -> realised 18.6 (signed -15.60, MAE 17.04); RandomSpan canvas=16 gt 30.0 -> realised 25.9 (signed -4.12, MAE 13.80, exact 3/25). The estimator is off by ~50% of the target on long spans.

ORDERED STEPS.

STEP 0 (CPU, ~2h, BLOCKING, do before anything else). Build the ceiling gate. New file `dllm_draft_104/scripts/build_infilling_ceiling.py`: for each of the 164 HumanEval parents, splice its own canonical solution and grade with `score_infilling.grade_one` under BOTH which='base' and which='plus'; write `results/infilling/ceiling.json`. Then patch `scripts/score_infilling.py` so `self_test()` (a) samples from the SPLIT ACTUALLY BEING SCORED, (b) tests both base and plus, and (c) refuses to emit unless the per-stratum gradeable count is reported. I already produced the numbers this must reproduce: base 164/164, plus 143/164, 21 named failing parents. If your run disagrees, stop -- your evalplus cache differs (mine: `/root/.cache/evalplus/fe585eb4df8c88d844eeb463ea4d0302.pkl` on .73) and every downstream number is incomparable. Decide the primary metric here and freeze it: I recommend which='base' as PRIMARY (ceiling 164/164, no correction needed, and it is what HumanEval-Infilling itself uses), with which='plus' on the 143-parent gradeable subset as the robustness leg. Report both.

STEP 1 (CPU, ~1h, zero GPU). Rerun my pilot as committed code: `scripts/analyze_infilling_calibration.py` consuming the existing `outputs/infilling_single_line/*/metrics.jsonl` + `score.json` + `ceiling.json`. Emits, per arm: signed error, MAE, exact-hit rate of realised vs gt_len, by gt_len quartile; pass@1 regressed on |realised_len - gt_len| AND on |gt_len - initial_canvas| side by side (the discriminating pair); parent-CLUSTERED paired bootstrap (B=10000, seed=1234, resample the 164 parents, hand-rolled numpy -- no scipy) for every delta; exact-binomial McNemar for the matched-canvas tax. Gate: the numbers above must reproduce to the digit, since they come from the same files.

STEP 2 (GPU, ~14 GPU-h). Protocol-pinning + reconciliation run on SingleLine, which is ALSO the deliverable that de-risks everything else. 2x2x2: {HF `diffusion_generate` path, vendor `MDMGenerator.infilling_with_expansion` path} x {pad_delete_to_right / pad_eos_to_right False, True} x {T=0.0 greedy, T=0.2/top_p=0.9 = DreamOn's published sampler}, at min_gen_len in {4,11,16} (11 = LR-DLLM's pinned value, so the 19-28 point DreamOn discrepancy between arXiv:2602.01326 Table 2 and arXiv:2602.07546 Table 3 becomes attributable). Add `mask_expansion`/`delete_eos_token` assertion: the HF path contains NEITHER string (I grepped: 0 occurrences), so any code passing them is silently no-op'ing -- assert at runtime that they are not accepted rather than trusting they were. Instrument forward passes with the existing `ForwardCostTracker`. Measured cost: SingleLine 1033 cases x 8 shards, dreamon_fim mean 0.89 s/case on H20 (from `metrics.jsonl`) = ~0.26 GPU-h per config; 12 configs ~ 3 GPU-h, x3 for LOCAL L20A being slower on this workload in my probes (2.2-4.2 s/case) and for the Dream-Coder/Qwen companion arms -> budget 14.
   Freeze ONE (path, flags, sampler) tuple as canonical here and use it for everything downstream. If Step 2 shows the DreamOn number is not stable to the sampler at the +/-15-point level, that IS the paper and you should stop and write it.

STEP 3 (GPU, ~22 GPU-h). Extend to RandomSpan (n=1640) as PRIMARY surface and MultiLine (subsample, see risk) as the long-span leg, arms {dreamon at canvas in {4,16,32}, dreamon_oracle, dream_fim at oracle canvas, qwen_fim}. Measured cost basis, all mine: MultiLine canvas=4 max_new=128 mean 3.79 s/case p95 16.5 s; canvas=32 mean 4.11 s p95 18.7 s; RandomSpan canvas=16 max_new=128 mean 9.45 s/case p95 26.8 s. Forward counts are wildly heavy-tailed (SingleLine canvas=4 max_new=64: mean 63 forwards but MAX 332, tokens_fed mean ~14k) because the HF loop bound is `2*max_gen_len + 2*expand_budget`. RandomSpan 1640 x 9.45 s / 8 GPUs = 0.54 GPU-h per arm-config; 8 arm-configs ~ 4.3 GPU-h. MultiLine at 5815 x 4 s x 6 configs / 8 = ~4.8 GPU-h if you take all of it. The 22 h is dominated by the p95 tail and by the max_new=256 leg needed so gt_len>128 (179 MultiLine cases) is not budget-truncated.
   MANDATORY: log `initial_canvas`, `realised_len`, `forward_passes`, `tokens_fed`, `expand_events`, `delete_events`, AND `hit_budget_cap` per case, and report the cap-hit rate per stratum. Retraction 3 in this project was exactly a cost average that dropped budget-truncated tasks; here, capping is gt_len-correlated by construction, so it would forge the monotone trend you are testing.

STEP 4 (CPU). Write the calibration finding as the lead: "DreamOn's expand/delete is length REPAIR that is not length CALIBRATED -- the realised length is an estimator anchored to the training prior, unbiased below ~10 tokens and collapsing to ~50% of target above, and its residual failures are concentrated exactly where the estimator misses." Stratification and the matched-canvas tax become the supporting decomposition, not the headline. Cite arXiv:2602.00476 (CAL) and arXiv:2602.07546 (LR-DLLM) as owning the |gt_len - canvas| diagnostic, and arXiv:2607.24763 (CaRE) as the compute-matching genre.

REUSE FROM WHAT IS ALREADY RUNNING ELSEWHERE, DO NOT DUPLICATE: .73's 6-arm SingleLine run IS Steps 0-1's input -- do not re-run it. .82's sampler-sensitivity audit (`bfbaef58`) is the direct evidence for Step 2's sampler leg; pull its swept-sampler numbers instead of re-sweeping. .104's Qwen2.5-Coder AR baseline supplies the AR reference and the 15G checkpoint. LOCAL/.252's Large@1024 work is unrelated; LOCAL has 7/8 GPUs free right now, .252 has 6/8 free, .73 has 8/8 free, .82 is fully busy at 99% x8.

NODE CHOICE: run Steps 2-3 on .73, where the harness, the venv (`.venv_dream`), all four checkpoints, and the evalplus ground-truth cache already sit. Doing it on LOCAL/wzc1 means porting the harness across disks (`scp -O`, .82's sftp is broken) and re-fetching Qwen2.5-Coder-7B; not worth it.
feas.risk: The single most likely outcome is a CONFOUNDED positive, not a null: a beautiful monotone "delta grows with |gt_len - canvas|" that is actually three artifacts stacked in the same direction. (1) The plus-test ceiling is stratum-correlated (0.793/0.830/0.805/0.844 by quartile) and worth ~15 points -- 1.5x the effect. (2) gt_len is largely parent-determined and MultiLine has up to 435 items from ONE HumanEval problem, so "long gt_len" partly means "hard problem", and per-item CIs on 5815 nested rows will look decisive while measuring problem difficulty. (3) Long-span cases are the ones that hit the expand budget / max_new cap, so truncation loads onto exactly the high-|gt_len - canvas| bins -- the trend can be manufactured by the harness. My probes show all three are live at effect-relevant magnitude. Secondary risk: the effect is REAL but already spoken for. CAL (arXiv:2602.00476, 2026-01-31, pre-cutoff) publishes the oracle-vs-fixed decomposition with an explicit confidence-vs-probe-length curve, and LR-DLLM (arXiv:2602.07546) already reports DreamOn helping single-line while HURTING multi-line -- so a purely diagnostic result lands as replication. The calibration measurement (realised_len vs gt_len) is the part nobody has, which is why I would make it the headline. Tertiary: the protocol may not be stable enough to support any stratified claim -- two DreamOn code paths with contradictory flag defaults, plus this project's own measured +14.6-point top_p swing, means an unpinned sampler alone can exceed the effect. Note the honest upside: even if stratification comes out flat, the calibration collapse (MultiLine gt 34.2 -> realised 14.8) and the matched-canvas paired test (McNemar chi2~25.9, and in the OPPOSITE direction to the hypothesised tax) both survive the candidate's own kill criterion.
feas.required_control:
PER-PARENT CANONICAL-SOLUTION CEILING, COMPUTED AND REPORTED PER STRATUM, WITH EVERY STRATUM RESTRICTED TO GRADEABLE PARENTS AND EVERY CI CLUSTERED ON THE 164 PARENTS.

Concretely, before any arm is scored: splice each of the 164 parents' OWN canonical solution and grade it with the identical grader/tests/timeouts; persist the verdicts; drop non-gradeable parents from the denominator; and print the gradeable count AND the budget-cap-hit rate for every (split, canvas, gt_len-bin) cell alongside the delta. Refuse to emit a stratified number for any cell whose gradeable count is below the pre-registered power floor.

This is the exact control that prevents the analogous failure, and it is not hypothetical -- I ran it and it fires. The three prior retractions were: a verifier that never compared to a reference; a pipeline stage that silently discarded its input; a cost average that dropped the expensive tasks. This candidate's version is all three at once: the grader silently caps 188/1033 SingleLine and ~1/3 of MultiLine at zero (never compares against an achievable reference), the existing `--self-test-n 10` guard reports trustworthy=True because it samples 10 rows of the wrong split and only tests which='base' (a stage that silently passes bad input), and the cap is CORRELATED WITH THE STRATIFYING VARIABLE, so the dropped/zeroed cases are precisely the expensive long-span ones (the cost-average error, transplanted onto quality). Without this control the monotone trend can be produced entirely by grader ceiling plus budget truncation, with no model behaviour involved -- and it would look like a clean, publishable, wrong result.

Two riders, both mandatory and both cheap: (a) pin and report ONE (code path, flag set, sampler) tuple, asserting at runtime that `mask_expansion`/`delete_eos_token` are rejected by the HF path rather than silently swallowed -- the HF `generation_utils.py` contains neither string; (b) report `|realised_len - gt_len|` as the primary regressor and `|gt_len - initial_canvas|` as the secondary, since only the former distinguishes "calibrated" from "merely permissive" and only the former is unoccupied in the literature.

lens.title: Execution-Grounded Remasking: Can Failing Tests Tell a Diffusion Model Which Tokens to Un-Commit?
lens.claim: Localising remasking with an execution signal (the failing-test traceback line, mapped to token spans) beats confidence-based remasking and beats random-span remasking at matched NFE on HumanEvalFix-Python. This is the one repair mechanism that is native to masked diffusion — AR must regenerate a suffix or emit a diff, whereas diffusion can un-commit exactly the implicated tokens and re-denoise them with full bidirectional context.
lens.why_now: Confidence-based remasking is now KNOWN WEAK by independent replication: arXiv:2606.12232 (2026-06-10) finds post-hoc confidence remasking (WINO) brings 'little-to-no benefit over confidence-based unmasking alone' and exacerbates diversity collapse; Corrective DLM (arXiv:2512.15596, 2025-12-17) independently shows corrective behaviour 'is not induced by conventional masked diffusion objectives' and that the model cannot distinguish correct from erroneous VISIBLE tokens. Both papers identify the same bottleneck — the model's own confidence is not an error signal — and both then reach for MORE TRAINING as the fix. Neither tries the obvious alternative: get the error signal from OUTSIDE the model, from an interpreter. The repair/edit surface is verified empty for diffusion: zero-hit arXiv queries for diffusion+program repair, +HumanEvalFix, +CanItEdit, +Defects4J, +QuixBugs, +HumanEvalPack, +'execution feedback', +diffusion LM+bug. The only paper claiming diffusion>AR on repair, arXiv:2510.04605, is not a credible preemption (CoRR-only; compares commercial Mercury-Diffusion-7B against AR-Llama3-8B, a GENERAL not code model, with no Qwen2.5-Coder control; and it cites LLaDA as arXiv:2309.12401, which is an astrophysics paper on assembly bias — a fabricated reference).
lens.experiment: HumanEvalPack Python (bigcode/humanevalpack, python split 191KB, verified HTTP 200) ships buggy_solution + declaration + test + entry_point and is FULLY SELF-CONTAINED — no docker, which matters because docker/podman are confirmed absent locally. Three arms at matched NFE and matched cumulative_model_tokens: (A) confidence-based remask top-k lowest-confidence tokens; (B) random-span remask, same token count (the control that 2606.12232's design lacked); (C) execution-grounded — run the failing test, parse the traceback line number, map to token span via our tree_sitter_python (0.26.0, installed), remask that span +/- context. Iterate up to N repair rounds. Grade pass@1 with evalplus untrusted_check (0.3.1 installed — the ONLY acceptable grader per retraction 1, never a hand-rolled did-not-raise check). Model: Dream-Coder-v0-Instruct-7B. Report per-round pass@1 and cumulative tokens so the repair curve is cost-priced. Extension if arm C wins: CanItEdit (nuprl/CanItEdit, 250KB, self-contained tests field, verified 200) for instructed multi-site edits.
lens.assets_needed: HAVE: models/Dream-Coder-v0-Instruct-7B; evalplus 0.3.1 with untrusted_check; tree_sitter 0.26.0 + tree_sitter_python for traceback-line-to-token-span mapping; scripts/refine_verifier_guided.py as the iteration skeleton (MUST be rewritten — its 'restart' policy is retraction 2, it discards the draft and regenerates from prompt, so reusing it unmodified would silently measure base Dream-Coder again); gcc/g++ present, python subprocess sandboxing already used by evalplus. DOWNLOAD: bigcode/humanevalpack python (191KB), optionally nuprl/CanItEdit (250KB). HARD BLOCKERS TO RESPECT: no docker/podman => SWE-bench/-Lite/-Verified infeasible locally; no java/javac/go/rustc/mvn/gradle => Defects4J and HumanEvalPack {java,cpp,go,rust} infeasible, so this candidate is Python-only by construction and must say so.
lens.kill_criterion: Killed if arm C (execution-grounded) does not beat arm B (random-span, matched token count) by a paired-bootstrap 95% CI excluding zero. Beating only arm A is NOT sufficient — 2606.12232 already showed A is a weak baseline, so A-only wins are uninformative. Also killed if traceback-to-token-span mapping succeeds on <60% of failures (signal too sparse to localise, in which case report the coverage number as the negative result). Pre-register N repair rounds and the remask token count before running so arms cannot be tuned differentially.
lens.builds_on: arXiv:2606.12232 (confidence remasking null result) and arXiv:2512.15596 (Corrective DLM). Both diagnose that internal confidence cannot identify erroneous visible tokens; both prescribe more post-training. We repair the shared blind spot by supplying an EXTERNAL execution signal instead, on the verified-empty repair surface. Distinguished from arXiv:2510.04605 by having a matched code-model control and a non-fabricated bibliography.

diff.differentiation_statement: No paper before 2026-05-07 uses an interpreter's positional output to decide which committed tokens a masked diffusion LM should un-commit. The remasking literature is saturated but uniformly INTERNAL: confidence thresholding (WINO, Saber), shadow tokens, leave-one-out probes, cross-chain entropy over N randomized-reveal-order chains (OSCAR), masked-context brittleness probing (CORE), learned quality heads (PRISM, RemeDi), or self-evaluation prompts that deliberately replace external verifiers (Prism, ICML 2026). Two independent papers converge on the diagnosis that these internal signals cannot identify erroneous VISIBLE tokens -- Corrective DLM (2025-12-17, pre-cutoff) on code, and Re-evaluating Confidence Remasking (2026-06-10, concurrent, ICML workshop) on generation -- and both prescribe more training. We supply the signal from outside the model instead: run the failing test, parse the traceback line, map it to a token span with tree-sitter, remask exactly that span. The nearest pipeline-shaped work, Detect-Remask-Repair (2026-06-11, concurrent), does detect-remask-repair with cost accounting and paired bootstrap, but its detector is a TRAINED faithfulness classifier and its domain is summarization with AlignScore; ours is training-free, deterministic, positional, and graded by execution. The only prior claim of diffusion > AR on repair, arXiv:2510.04605, is CoRR-only and I verified all four of its disqualifying defects from the full text: a commercial Mercury-Diffusion-7B against AR-Llama3-8B (a general, not code, model) with no code-AR control, a two-sentence implementation section with no decoding budget, unresolved metric citations, Java-only repair, and a genuinely fabricated LLaDA reference to arXiv:2309.12401 which is an astrophysics paper on assembly bias. Beyond the signal, our setting is separately differentiating: Python-only executable repair on natural buggy programs from HumanEvalPack-Fix rather than length-preserving synthetic token substitutions (Corrective DLM's CRB cannot represent insert/delete repairs, as its Limitations concede), matched-NFE AND matched-cumulative-model-token accounting in the CaRE (2026-06-04) tradition where compute-matching is shown to reverse published rankings, and pass@1 graded exclusively by evalplus untrusted_check.

followup_openings.defect: Their Takeaway 2 -- localisation is already oracle-quality and the real bottleneck is the dLLM's inability to propose a better token at the flagged position (flip-flop 75-95%) -- is measured ONLY where the erroneous token is the model's own high-confidence commitment during from-scratch generation. Their neighbourhood-expansion ablation (Appendix B.2) that would test span remasking changes two variables at once, expanding to raw +/-1/+/-2 token windows WHILE switching to the MR1 loop-guard, and uses positional windows rather than syntax-aligned spans. This is simultaneously the biggest threat to our candidate and its best opening: if their conclusion is regime-specific, our mechanism survives; if it is universal, better localisation cannot help and the candidate is dead on arrival.
followup_openings.our_fix: Port their exact flip-flop diagnostic into the REPAIR regime, where the bug is EXOGENOUS -- the buggy token was never the model's own commitment, so there is no self-consistency to pin the predictive distribution back to it. Report flip-flop rate as a PRIMARY mechanistic metric alongside pass@1, on the same instances, for confidence-remask / random-span / execution-grounded arms. Replace their +/-S positional window with contiguous tree-sitter AST-node-aligned spans, holding the loop-guard fixed so the span variable is clean. Prediction: flip-flop should be substantially lower on exogenous bugs than the 85-95% they report for Dream on self-generated errors.
followup_openings.target_paper: arXiv:2606.12232 (Re-evaluating Confidence Remasking, ICML 2026 SPIGM/AdaptFM workshop, concurrent)
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It converts our candidate from 'yet another remasking heuristic' into a scoped falsification of the field's newest negative result, and it makes the paper publishable in BOTH outcomes: either exogenous-error remasking escapes the proposal bottleneck (positive result), or the bottleneck is confirmed universal and we have established that no localisation improvement -- including a perfect one -- can rescue post-hoc remasking, which is a stronger and more useful claim than a workshop null on self-generated errors.

followup_openings.defect: Neither paper separates LOCALISATION quality from PROPOSAL quality. Corrective DLM's Algorithm 1 uses one forward pass to both score and refill, so low pass@1 is unattributable; 2606.12232's oracle is an upper bound on the MODEL's leave-one-out confidence, not a ground-truth error oracle, so 'shadow matches oracle' does not mean the true error positions were found.
followup_openings.our_fix: Add a GROUND-TRUTH ORACLE-LOCALISATION arm that neither paper has: HumanEvalPack-Fix ships buggy_solution alongside the canonical solution, so diff them to get the exact gold bug span and remask precisely that. This is a true error oracle, not a confidence oracle. Now the decomposition is complete: oracle-span vs execution-span isolates how much localisation signal the traceback actually carries, and oracle-span vs matched-count random-span isolates how much of the residual gap is proposal-side. Pre-register the remask token count so all four arms are budget-identical.
followup_openings.target_paper: arXiv:2606.12232 + arXiv:2512.15596 jointly
followup_openings.why_it_matters: The oracle arm makes the kill criterion non-fatal and the result interpretable no matter which way it falls: if oracle localisation also fails, we have measured the proposal ceiling directly on repair and quantified exactly how much headroom any localisation method (execution, confidence, learned, or perfect) could ever recover. That single number is the paper.

followup_openings.defect: Three separable defects. (a) THE HEADLINE OVERSTATES ITS OWN DATA: no chance-level baseline is reported, so 'the model cannot distinguish correct from erroneous visible tokens' rests on a top-5 hit rate of 0.59 (Dream) / 0.77-0.83 (LLaDA) which, at n_replace=1 in a ~100-token program, is roughly 12-16x chance. Confidence localises badly in absolute terms but far above chance. (b) Corruptions are type-preserving AND tokenizer-length-preserving by construction, so insert/delete and every length-changing repair is excluded -- exactly the bug class where AR's disadvantage (regenerate the suffix) would be largest, biasing the surface toward diffusion's easy case. (c) Execution is used only to FILTER benchmark instances, never as an inference-time signal, and refinement steps T in {1,2,4} are counted, never priced in NFE or cumulative tokens.
followup_openings.our_fix: (a) Report the chance floor explicitly and quote their numbers as ratios-to-chance, so our motivation is 'confidence localises weakly, not not-at-all' -- which is defensible and does not collapse if a reviewer computes the floor. (b) Use natural HumanEvalPack-Fix bugs, which are not length-preserving, and include DreamOn-v0-7B (on disk) as the length-elastic arm so insert/delete repairs are in scope rather than definitionally excluded. (c) Promote execution from instance filter to inference-time localiser, and price every arm in both NFE and cumulative_model_tokens per CaRE.
followup_openings.target_paper: arXiv:2512.15596 (Corrective Diffusion Language Models, pre-cutoff -- the one paper that could be read as preempting us)
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This is the paper a reviewer would cite to reject us. Reframing it as a repair whose flaws we name and fix -- with the chance-floor correction, the length-changing bug class they cannot represent, and execution promoted from filter to signal -- converts the closest prior art into our strongest positioning asset and yields three concrete deltas rather than one.

followup_openings.defect: DRR has NO matched random-span floor (the word 'random' appears only when describing others' work), so its gains cannot be decomposed into 'the detector found the right spans' vs 'localised editing at this budget helps wherever you edit'. Worse for the diffusion-native story, DRR reports that its framework also improves AR systems post-hoc -- which suggests the win may come from the localised-edit INTERFACE, not from bidirectional re-denoising, and it never runs the arm that separates them. OSCAR does have a random-selection localisation floor but keeps localisation internal (cross-chain entropy over N chains) and only externalises the CORRECTION via retrieved evidence.
followup_openings.our_fix: Two arms DRR and OSCAR both lack. First, matched-token random-span remasking as the mandatory floor -- already in the candidate's design and the right call. Second, and higher value: an AR-WITH-THE-SAME-LOCALISATION arm. Hand a code AR model the identical traceback-derived span as an infill/FIM instruction (Qwen2.5-Coder if obtainable; otherwise Dream-Coder-Base run left-to-right as the unidirectional control already being built on node .73) at matched cumulative tokens. That is the only experiment that separates 'the execution signal is useful to anyone' from 'diffusion is the right engine for it'.
followup_openings.target_paper: arXiv:2606.12807 (Detect, Remask, Repair, concurrent) + arXiv:2604.01624 (OSCAR, pre-cutoff)
followup_openings.why_it_matters: The candidate's central rhetorical claim -- 'AR must regenerate a suffix or emit a diff, whereas diffusion can un-commit exactly the implicated tokens' -- is currently ASSERTED, not measured. Arm D turns it into a result, forecloses the reviewer objection that DRR's own AR finding raises, and directly repairs this project's self-diagnosed meta-failure of shipping thirty diffusion evaluations with zero AR baselines.

followup_openings.defect: Both make avoiding an external verifier a stated design goal -- Prism 'replaces external verifiers with Self-Verified Feedback', PRISM 'provably learns per-token quality scores without RL or a verifier' -- and both justify it on efficiency grounds without ever pricing what an external verifier actually costs. On Python, the verifier is a subprocess: milliseconds of wall clock and ZERO forward passes. Their self-verification also inherits precisely the blind spot that 2512.15596 and 2606.12232 document, so verifier and generator share failure modes. Separately, NAVIRA (arXiv:2606.06031, concurrent) shows PRISM's inference rule couples detection and replacement in one forward pass, so erroneous tokens still condition their own regeneration.
followup_openings.our_fix: Report the interpreter's cost in the same units as the model's compute -- NFE contributed by the verifier is exactly zero, wall-clock is a measured subprocess time -- and show it against Prism-style self-verification NFE on the same tasks. Adopt NAVIRA's decoupling by construction: execute (no forward pass), remask the implicated span, THEN refill from the cleaned context in a separate pass, so no erroneous token conditions its own replacement.
followup_openings.target_paper: arXiv:2602.01842 (Prism, ICML 2026) + arXiv:2510.01384 (PRISM, ICML 2026)
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It reframes 'external signal' from an inconvenience to be engineered away into the cheapest and most reliable signal available on code, and it lets us make a quantitative rather than rhetorical argument against the design choice of two ICML 2026 papers. The zero-NFE verifier is the single most reviewer-legible number in the paper.

followup_openings.defect: CaRE's demonstration that compute-matched comparison reverses several published remasking rankings is established only on OpenWebText and LM1B with MAUVE, an open-ended-text metric. It has never been instantiated where correctness is deterministic, and it uses base models (LLaDA-8B-Base, Dream-7B-Base) whereas all published code numbers come from Instruct models.
followup_openings.our_fix: Instantiate CaRE-style accounting -- actual NFE standardised, multi-metric, stochasticity explicitly controlled -- on a pass@1-graded repair surface with Dream-Coder-v0-Instruct-7B. Report per-round pass@1 against cumulative_model_tokens as a Pareto curve, not a single-budget table. Given this project's measured sampler sensitivity (top_p 1.0 -> 0.95 moved HumanEval by +14.6 points, larger than most published diffusion-LM method gains) and its third retraction (averaging over only non-truncated tasks understated a mean cost by 2.85x/3.69x), the stochasticity control and the read-process-OR-failure_process discipline are mandatory, not optional.
followup_openings.target_paper: arXiv:2607.24763 (CaRE, concurrent) -- ally rather than obstacle
followup_openings.why_it_matters: Adopting a concurrent evaluation protocol pre-empts the strongest methodological attack on any remasking claim, and extending CaRE to the executable setting is a second, independently citable contribution that costs almost no extra compute since the arms are already budget-matched.

followup_openings.defect: Not defects in those papers but a gap in our own positioning: Tree Diffusion (2024-05-30) already couples diffusion editing of programs with observing execution results to debug them, and NARRepair (2024-06-24) already uses AST-derived dependency structure for non-autoregressive program repair. Neither appears in the candidate's builds_on. A reviewer who knows either will read 'the repair/edit surface is verified empty for diffusion' as overclaiming, and the zero-hit arXiv queries that support that phrase are all keyword-scoped to the recent dLLM vocabulary.
followup_openings.our_fix: Cite both and state the differences precisely: Tree Diffusion's execution signal is GLOBAL (rendered-output distance driving search over a graphics DSL with a small domain-specific model), so it cannot say which tokens to un-commit; ours is POSITIONAL (traceback line -> AST node -> token span) on Python with a 7B masked-diffusion LM. NARRepair uses AST structure at TRAINING time to patch NAR's independence assumption; ours uses it at INFERENCE time to convert a line number into a remask set. Reword the empty-surface claim from 'nobody has done program repair with diffusion' to the defensible and still-strong 'no masked diffusion LM has used an execution signal to choose remasking positions'.

related_work.citation: Frkovic, Jazbec, Zhang, Naesseth, Bogunovic, Nalisnick. "Re-evaluating Confidence Remasking in Masked Diffusion Language Models." arXiv:2606.12232v1.
related_work.known_defects: (1) Their own headline conclusion -- localization is fine, proposal is broken -- is established only where errors are self-generated; it is asserted as a property of masked dLLMs but measured in one regime. (2) The spatial/temporal expansion ablation that would most directly test span remasking changes two variables at once (neighborhood size AND loop-guard), so 'expansion degrades accuracy' is not cleanly attributable. (3) Workshop-scale: 2 models, one block-length pair, no code-repair surface, no random-position control at matched remask count. (4) The oracle they compute is an oracle over the MODEL's own leave-one-out confidence, i.e. an upper bound on confidence-thresholding -- it is not a ground-truth error oracle, so 'oracle-matched' does not mean 'errors were found'.
related_work.venue_status: ICML 2026 workshop (SPIGM Poster, venueid ICML.cc/2026/Workshop/SPIGM; also AdaptFM Poster, venueid ICML.cc/2026/Workshop/AdaptFM) -- verified via OpenReview api2 notes/search. NOT main-conference.

related_work.what_it_covers: Null result on post-hoc confidence remasking: WINO gives ~0.4-0.5% over Fast-dLLM at BL=32 on GSM8k/MATH-500/HumanEval/MBPP with LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-v0-Instruct-7B; gains vanish once shadow-token latency is priced in throughput. CRITICAL for us: they compute an ORACLE leave-one-out remasking confidence as an upper bound and find WINO's cheap shadow confidence MATCHES it (top-1 consistency ~100%). Takeaway 2 is therefore that localization is NOT the bottleneck -- 'the underlying dLLM fails to propose better alternative tokens at the identified positions', flip-flop rate 75-90% (LLaDA) / 85-95% (Dream). Appendix B.2 expands remasking to spatial (+/-S) and temporal (+/-T) neighbors and finds BOTH DEGRADE accuracy and do not reduce flip-flop, which they read as ruling out cascading dependencies.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Entirely from-scratch generation: the erroneous token is always the model's OWN high-confidence commitment. Never tested in a repair regime where the bug is EXOGENOUS (a buggy program handed to the model), where the proposal distribution at the flagged position has no self-commitment to be pinned to. Neighborhood expansion is +/-1/+/-2 raw token windows, never AST/syntax-aligned contiguous spans, and is confounded with a simultaneous switch to the MR1 loop-guard. No external error signal of any kind. No executable repair benchmark.

related_work.citation: Zhang, Peng, Zhang, Pan, Chrysos. "Corrective Diffusion Language Models." arXiv:2512.15596v2 (v1 2025-12-17).
related_work.known_defects: (1) THE METRIC OVERSTATES THE NEGATIVE. With n_replace=1 in a ~100-token program, a chance-level top-5 hit rate is roughly 5%; Dream's 0.59 is ~12x chance and LLaDA's 0.77-0.83 is ~16x. They report no chance baseline, so 'the model cannot distinguish correct from erroneous visible tokens' is far stronger than their own numbers support -- confidence localises poorly in ABSOLUTE terms but well above chance. Any paper (including ours) citing 2512.15596 for 'confidence is not an error signal' inherits this overstatement unless the chance floor is reported. (2) Length-preserving synthetic corruptions systematically exclude exactly the bug class where AR's disadvantage would be largest, biasing the task surface toward diffusion's easy case. (3) Localisation and correction are entangled: the same forward pass scores and refills, so low pass@1 cannot be attributed to detection vs proposal. (4) Their conclusion 'corrective behaviour is not induced by conventional MDLM objectives' is drawn from 3 models, one of which is 0.5B.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint. OpenReview api2 returns venue 'CoRR 2025', venueid OpenReview.net/Public_Article -- no conference acceptance found. (The string 'Machine Learning, ICML' in the HTML is the LaTeX keywords line of the ICML style file, not an acceptance.)
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list (v1 2025-12-17T17:04:38Z, v2 2026-01-29); full HTML arxiv.org/html/2512.15596v2 read (95k chars) incl. Sec 3 CRB construction, Table 1 numbers, Appendix A Limitations, Appendix D, Appendix G Algorithm 1; OpenReview api2 for venue.
related_work.what_it_covers: Closest pre-cutoff work on the specific claim that dLLM confidence cannot localise errors in CODE. Introduces the Code Revision Benchmark (CRB): built on HumanEval/MBPP and HumanEval+/MBPP+, applies type-preserving token-level corruptions (operator / identifier / literal substitution), and EXECUTES the corrupted program with a deterministic grader keeping only instances that fail -- so every instance has a genuine fault. Measures (a) error-token localisation as clean-vs-error confidence gap + top-1/top-5 hit rate, (b) pass@1 after confidence-threshold remask-based iterative refinement at T in {1,2,4} (Algorithm 1, Appendix G). Dream-7B-Base top-1 hit 0.076-0.094, top-5 0.57-0.61. Appendix D adds a self-revision-under-minimal-corruption control (corrupt only programs the model itself generated correctly) and still finds low pass@1 with non-monotonic gains from more refinement steps. Fix proposed = correction-aware post-training (mixture objective supervising visible incorrect tokens).
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Execution is used ONLY to filter benchmark instances -- never as an inference-time localisation signal. No external signal at all; the entire paper is internal-confidence + more training. Corruptions are type-preserving AND tokenizer-length-preserving by construction, so insert/delete and any length-changing repair is out of scope (stated in their Limitations). No natural buggy programs (no HumanEvalFix / HumanEvalPack-Fix). No random-span matched-token control. No NFE / cumulative-token cost accounting -- T in {1,2,4} is a step count, not a priced budget. No AR comparison.

related_work.citation: Zou, Horvitz, Karthick, Yu, McKeown. "Detect, Remask, Repair: Diffusion Editing for Faithful Summarization of Evolving Contexts." arXiv:2606.12807v1.
related_work.known_defects: (1) No matched random-span floor, so the reported gains cannot be decomposed into 'the detector found the right spans' vs 'localized editing at this budget helps regardless of where you edit'. (2) Their own finding that the framework also improves AR systems post-hoc undercuts any diffusion-native claim -- it suggests the win may come from the localized-edit INTERFACE rather than from bidirectional re-denoising, and they do not run the arm that would separate these. (3) Budgeted repair thresholds (repair top-25% risk on DialogSum, full budget on StreamSum) are tuned per-dataset, so the headline table mixes a tuned routing decision with the method. (4) StreamSum is LLM-synthesised, so faithfulness gains partly measure agreement with the generator pipeline.

related_work.what_it_covers: Architecturally the closest pipeline to our candidate, in a different domain. related_work.known_defects: (1) Cross-chain entropy needs N chains, so its localisation is priced at ~Nx the forward passes of a confidence method; the CDH comparison against random selection is per-position and does not charge that N. diff.sharpened_claim: On executable Python repair, an EXTERNAL execution signal is a materially better remasking localiser than any internal signal -- but localisation is not the binding constraint, and we measure both halves. Concretely, on HumanEvalPack-Fix (Python) with Dream-Coder-v0-Instruct-7B, at matched NFE AND matched cumulative_model_tokens, with the remask token count and number of repair rounds pre-registered, we run five arms: (A) confidence-based top-k remasking, (B) random-span remasking at identical token count, (C) execution-grounded remasking -- failing test, traceback line, tree-sitter AST-aligned token span, remask and re-denoise from cleaned context in a SEPARATE forward pass so no erroneous token conditions its own replacement, (D) GOLD-ORACLE span remasking from the buggy_solution-to-canonical diff, an upper bound no prior work has, and (E) a code-AR model given the identical traceback-derived span as an infill instruction at matched cumulative tokens. Alongside pass@1 (evalplus untrusted_check only) we report per-arm FLIP-FLOP RATE, importing the diagnostic from arXiv:2606.12232 into the repair regime, where the erroneous token is EXOGENOUS rather than the model's own high-confidence commitment. This yields a publishable result in every branch. If C beats B by paired-bootstrap 95% CI excluding zero, execution grounding is the first external-signal remasking policy on code and E says whether the advantage is diffusion-native or merely signal-native. If C beats B but D barely beats C, localisation is nearly saturated by the traceback and the residual gap is the proposal ceiling. If even D fails to beat B, we have shown that arXiv:2606.12232's proposal bottleneck generalises from self-generated to exogenous errors and that NO localisation method -- including a perfect one -- can rescue post-hoc remasking, which quantifies the ceiling the entire training-free remasking literature is pushing against. Traceback-to-span mapping coverage is reported as a first-class number regardless. Python-only by construction: no docker/podman, java, go, or rustc on either disk, so SWE-bench, Defects4J, and non-Python HumanEvalPack are infeasible here and we say so.

blocking_gaps: MEASURED, DECISIVE: the execution signal does not exist on this benchmark. I ran all 164 HumanEvalPack-Python buggy_solutions against their own tests (/tmp/tbaudit/audit.py, results /tmp/tbaudit/res.json). All 164 fail, but 155 fail with AssertionError raised inside the test's check() function and 3 time out -- the traceback contains ZERO frames inside the solution body. ANY traceback frame landing in the solution body: 6/164 = 3.7%. Deepest in-solution frame landing on a gold bug line (difflib buggy_solution vs canonical_solution): 3/164 = 1.8%. The candidate's OWN pre-registered kill criterion is '<60% mapping coverage => killed'. At 3.7% it is pre-killed by its own criterion before any GPU is touched. This is structural, not a parsing artifact: `failure_symptoms` in the shipped parquet is 'incorrect output' for 160/164 rows. Arm C has no input.

The obvious salvage (coverage/SBFL localisation instead of traceback lines) is ALSO below chance. I built a per-assert line tracer with subprocess isolation and SIGALRM (/tmp/tbaudit/drv.py + /tmp/tbaudit/worker.py, results /tmp/tbaudit/sbfl_res.json), n_ok=161/164. Gold bug line is executed by some test 98.1% of the time, so coverage sees it -- but Ochiai top-1 hits gold 0.373 against a measured chance floor of 0.409 (n_gold/n_exec). Ochiai is WORSE THAN RANDOM. top-3 = 0.702 but mean n_exec is only 5.6 lines, so 'top-3' is most of a 7.7-line function. Failing-only-lines hits gold 0.429 with mean 1.63 lines. No external positional signal beats chance here.

The matched-token random-span control (arm B) is brutally strong by construction, which collapses arm C's headroom. Measured on Dream-Coder tokenization: median solution body 46 tokens, median gold diff span 1 token, mean gold token fraction 0.077. Exact chance that a random K-token set contains a gold token: K=8 -> 0.395, K=16 -> 0.582, K=32 -> 0.788, K=48 -> 0.889. Any remask budget large enough to be useful already hits the bug most of the time at random, so even a perfect localiser has little room to separate from arm B on pass@1.

55.5% of the repairs are LENGTH-CHANGING in tokens (91/164; 53 need more tokens, 38 fewer; median |delta| 3, max 30), and fixed-canvas remasking on Dream-Coder cannot represent them. By bug_type this is 'excess logic' 93.5% and 'missing logic' 97.0% -- 64/164 tasks where the mechanism is structurally incapable regardless of localisation. The proposed length-elastic escape hatch is broken: `mask_expansion=True` / `delete_eos_token=True` appear NOWHERE in models/DreamOn-v0-7B/ (grep returns nothing); generation_utils.py `_prepare_generation_config` funnels them into `generation_config.update(**kwargs)`, which silently drops unknown keys, and scripts/generate_evalplus_dreamon.py:133-134 passes exactly those two dead kwargs. This repo already retracted numbers over that bug (Retraction 5).

The candidate's central rhetorical claim -- 'AR must regenerate a suffix or emit a diff, whereas diffusion can un-commit exactly the implicated tokens' -- has already been empirically undermined TWICE in this very repo, in commits landed today (git log 1170ae6, 'retractions 4 and 5'). Retraction 4: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B (architecturally identical to Dream-Coder-v0-Base-7B) scores HE+ .524 / MBPP+ .648 at 204/101 tokens_fed vs Dream-Coder-Instruct nfe512 .707/.680 at ~350,832/308,995 -- 1719x/3062x cheaper. Retraction 5: on infilling, diffusion's supposed home turf, qwen_fim .7638 at 239 tokens beats dreamon_oracle .7590 at 5827 tokens. Arm E is therefore not a nice-to-have robustness check; it is the load-bearing experiment, and the two existing measurements predict arm E wins.
