feas.risk:
The single most likely outcome is a NULL that is uninterpretable because every arm converges. Concretely: median gold span is 1 token in a 46-token body, and a random K-token set already contains a gold token with p=0.582 at K=16 and 0.788 at K=32 (measured). So at any remask budget large enough to actually repair anything, arms A, B, C and D all touch the bug on most instances and their pass@1 differences fall inside the paired-bootstrap CI. The paper then reports "no arm separates", which reads as an underpowered experiment rather than a finding, because n=164 with a ~0.05-0.15 effect has no power.

The most likely CONFOUNDED outcome is a silent budget violation masquerading as a localisation win. Arm C has an in-solution traceback frame on only 3.7% of instances, so any implementation must have a fallback. Whatever that fallback is -- last executed line, the failing assert's called line, the whole body -- it will fire on ~96% of instances, and if it widens the remask set then arm C wins purely because it un-commits MORE tokens than arm B. That reproduces this project's exact retraction pattern: a stage that silently substitutes something else for its input (Retraction 2) crossed with a cost/budget asymmetry that flatters the favoured arm (Retraction 3). A reviewer who asks "what fraction of arm C's instances used a real traceback frame, and was the token count identical to arm B on each one?" would sink the paper, and right now the answer is 3.7% and probably no.

Third risk, already half-realised: 64/164 instances need insert/delete, DreamOn's mask_expansion is a dead kwarg, and if that goes unnoticed a second time the length-elastic arm gets reported as "length-elastic" while running fixed-canvas -- the identical failure mode that forced Retraction 5 nine hours ago.
feas.required_control:
A per-instance SPAN-PROVENANCE AND BUDGET LEDGER, written for every (task, arm, round) tuple before any model call, with the run ABORTING on violation rather than logging a warning.

Each row must record: (1) which localiser branch actually fired -- one of {traceback_frame_in_solution, non_assertion_exception, timeout_stack_sample, FALLBACK_<name>} -- so "execution-grounded" can never silently mean "fallback fired"; (2) the exact remask token index set and its cardinality; (3) an assertion that |remask_set| is IDENTICAL across arms A/B/C/D for that task and round; (4) the canvas length before and after, so a length-changing arm cannot quietly buy extra capacity; (5) cumulative_model_tokens read through the union of the process AND failure_process accessors (Retraction 3's `proc()` discipline), so budget-truncated instances are never dropped from the mean; (6) pass/fail from evalplus.eval.untrusted_check ONLY, with a negative control asserting that an empty solution and an unmodified buggy_solution both score 0.000 on that task (Retraction 1's exact failure mode).

Headline reporting requirement: arm C's pass@1 must be reported TWICE -- once on the full 164 and once restricted to the instances where branch != FALLBACK_* -- and the fallback fraction (currently measured at ~96%) must appear in the same table as the pass@1. Any arm-C number quoted without its fallback fraction is inadmissible.

This is the control that prevents the analogous retraction, because all three prior ones share one shape: an intermediate stage substituted something for its declared input (hand verifier compared nothing; restart discarded the draft; the average discarded the expensive tasks) and nothing in the pipeline asserted otherwise. Here the substitution-in-waiting is the localiser fallback, and the ledger makes it impossible for arm C to be scored as execution-grounded on an instance where no execution signal existed.

lens.title: The Missing Column: Multi-Span and Random-Span Infilling as Diffusion's Uncontested Home Turf
lens.claim: Diffusion's advantage over AR-FIM grows with the number of simultaneous holes. On a k-span infilling benchmark (k=1,2,4 non-contiguous holes), AR-FIM degrades sharply because it must serialise holes and cannot condition each hole on the others' eventual contents, whereas masked diffusion fills all k jointly in one bidirectional process. If true, k-span infilling — not from-scratch generation — is the correct headline task for diffusion code models.
lens.why_now: This is the single largest verified gap. HumanEval-Infilling ships FOUR splits and every diffusion paper reports at most two: DreamOn's vendored harness hardcodes read_problems(benchmark_name='single-line') at vendor/DreamOn/eval/evaluate.py, so RandomSpanInfilling (1640 cases, 2.2MB) and RandomSpanInfillingLight (164) are simply absent from the literature, and MultiLine (5815) is reported without a multi-hole variant. arXiv query for diffusion+'multi-span' returns ZERO hits. Yet multi-hole is the exact regime where the AR/diffusion asymmetry is largest in principle — and it is the one thing DreamOn's length-elasticity machinery does not address, because k>1 is a topology problem, not a length problem. Concurrent work confirms the axis is opening (arXiv:2607.26504, 2026-07-29, 'enabling generation across non-contiguous regions' via insertion-based MDLM; arXiv:2607.22663 'Beyond Block Boundaries', 2026-06-29, on multi-block editing) — both post-date the 2026-05-07 concurrency cutoff and neither builds a k-span code benchmark.
lens.experiment: Construct k-span infilling by programmatic AST-guided hole-punching on HumanEval+ canonical solutions using tree_sitter_python: remove k non-adjacent statement-level nodes, keep everything else as two-sided context, k in {1,2,4}. This yields a controlled k-ladder on a benchmark whose evalplus grader we already trust, so a single confound (number of holes) is varied with everything else fixed — cleaner than comparing across the four heterogeneous HumanEval-Infilling splits. Also report the untouched public RandomSpanInfilling split as the external-validity anchor (the literature's missing column). Arms: DreamOn-v0-7B (native multi-mask), Dream-Coder-v0-Instruct-7B fixed-canvas, and AR-FIM Qwen2.5-Coder-7B forced to serialise holes left-to-right. Metric: pass@1 (evalplus untrusted_check) and exact-match on the held-out spans, both vs cumulative_model_tokens. Primary statistic: interaction between k and the diffusion-minus-AR delta.
lens.assets_needed: HAVE: data/evalplus/{humaneval,mbpp}_plus.jsonl and the full HumanEvalPlus-v0.1.10.jsonl locally (canonical solutions to punch holes in); tree_sitter_python for AST-level hole selection; evalplus 0.3.1; DreamOn + Dream-Coder Instruct; scaffold_coder/corruption.py already implements corruption/masking schedules and is directly reusable for hole-punching; 8 idle L20A. DOWNLOAD: HumanEval-RandomSpanInfilling (2.2MB) + Light (164 cases, already in /tmp/RandomSpanInfillingLight.jsonl) for the external anchor. MISSING AND LOAD-BEARING for the headline cross-family claim: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B (~15GB, absent from BOTH wzc1 and zwfy6). Without it, the k-ladder is still a valid within-diffusion scaling result (does DreamOn degrade with k?) but loses the 'uncontested home turf' framing. Recommend downloading it once and sharing it across candidates 1 and 4 — it is the highest-leverage missing asset in this whole lens.
lens.kill_criterion: Killed if the diffusion-minus-AR delta does NOT increase with k (no significant k x family interaction). Killed harder if diffusion degrades FASTER than AR as k grows — which is a live possibility given our own measured failure mode (Dream-Coder's unparseable-output rate was 94% at nfe16 and multi-hole may re-trigger structural collapse), and which would be a genuinely useful negative result: it would show diffusion's parallel-fill advantage is nominal rather than realised. Also killed if AST hole-punching yields <100 valid k=4 cases.
lens.builds_on: DreamOn (arXiv:2602.01326, ICLR 2026 Poster) and the HumanEval-Infilling benchmark family. Defect repaired: a hardcoded benchmark_name in the released eval harness has left two of four public splits and the entire k>1 regime unmeasured for diffusion code models, precisely where the paradigm's structural advantage should be largest.

related_work.citation: Niels Mündler, Jasper Dekoninck, Martin Vechev. "Constrained Decoding of Diffusion LLMs with Context-Free Grammars." arXiv:2508.10111. ICLR 2026 Poster (OpenReview 7Sph4KyeYO, venueid ICLR.cc/2026/Conference); earlier NeurIPS 2025 DL4C Workshop Oral (fwH661m0Kq).
related_work.venue_status: ICLR 2026 Poster — verified via OpenReview api2 search (id 7Sph4KyeYO, venueid=ICLR.cc/2026/Conference, venue='ICLR 2026 Poster'). Also DL4C@NeurIPS2025 Oral (fwH661m0Kq). arXiv v1 2025-08-13 verified via arXiv API <published>.
related_work.what_it_covers: THIS IS THE CLOSEST WORK AND THE CANDIDATE MISSED IT. It defines 'Multi-Region Infilling (mri)' as a named generation paradigm and builds exactly the k-ladder benchmark the candidate proposes: HumanEval (C++ translation), random spans removed from the canonical solution following Bavarian et al., yielding 1-mri / 2-mri / 3-mri. It reports pass@1 functional correctness AND syntactic correctness for 5 AR infilling models (StarCoder2-7B, CodeGemma-7B, DeepSeek-Coder 1.3B/6.7B/33B) across k=1,2,3, and finds exactly the monotone collapse the candidate predicts: vanilla functional correctness DeepSeek-C-6.7B 64.8 -> 29.8 -> 11.9; StarCoder2-7B 53.8 -> 20.5 -> 7.5; syntactic correctness 93.9 -> 62.0 -> 32.9. It states plainly 'No prior work supports multi-region infilling (mri) or diffusion LLM (dlm) constraining with CFGs.'
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: The load-bearing cell for our claim is EMPTY: the paper never runs any diffusion model on mri. Its separate diffusion section (LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B, DreamCoder-7B, DiffuCoder-7B, 32 steps / 256 tokens / T=0.2) uses three FROM-SCRATCH tasks — 'the model should generate the entire function specified in natural language', plus JSON and SMILES — not multi-region infilling. So the k x family interaction, which is the entire headline of our candidate, is unmeasured. Also absent: any compute/token accounting; any language other than C++; any Python/evalplus grading; any FIM-sentinel-native AR protocol.
related_work.known_defects: (1) Its AR mri protocol is a CHAT PROMPT with natural-language markers ('// region 1', '// region 2' inserted into the source, plus a stub main() and a system message asking for a ```cpp block) — NOT the models' native FIM sentinel serialisation, and it never varies the order in which regions are serialised. So 'AR degrades with k' is confounded with prompt-format brittleness at k>1. (2) No token/latency accounting on the quality axis; the only cost number is constrained-decoding overhead (67% at 1-mri -> 205% at 3-mri). (3) Severe floor effects: 3-mri functional is 4.9-12.6% for every model, leaving almost no dynamic range to detect an interaction. (4) Generation is aborted at a hard 256-token cap, so 'failures' conflate capability with budget truncation — the exact accounting error our own retraction #3 was about. (5) C++-only single-language; results may not replicate on Python where all diffusion code models are strongest. (6) Its diffusion arm is fixed at 32 steps with no NFE sweep, which our own measurements show is squarely in the regime where Dream-Coder produces unparseable output.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list=2508.10111 (v1 date, authors); ar5iv full text of 2508.10111 fetched and grepped for mri/dlm/regions/tables (Table 1 = AR x {1,2,3}-mri, Table 2 = DLM x {C++, json, smiles} from-scratch — no DLM x mri table exists anywhere in the paper); OpenReview api2 /notes/search for venue. arXiv UI full search for "multi-region infilling" returns exactly 1 result = this paper.

related_work.citation: Zirui Wu, Lin Zheng, Zhihui Xie, Jiacheng Ye, Jiahui Gao, Shansan Gong, Yansong Feng, Zhenguo Li, Wei Bi, Guorui Zhou, Lingpeng Kong. "DreamOn: Diffusion Language Models For Code Infilling Beyond Fixed-size Canvas." arXiv:2602.01326. ICLR 2026 Poster.
related_work.venue_status: ICLR 2026 Poster — verified via OpenReview api2 (id EQTPmqukiU, venueid=ICLR.cc/2026/Conference, venue='ICLR 2026 Poster', _bibtex wu2026dreamon). arXiv comment field also reads 'ICLR 2026'.
related_work.what_it_covers: Variable-length diffusion code infilling via [expand]/[delete] sentinel states. Evaluated on HumanEval-Infilling single-line + multi-line and SantaCoder-FIM(Python), vs AR baselines DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B / Seed-Coder-8B / Qwen2.5-Coder-7B. Headline: Dream-Coder-7B single-line 55.5 -> 92.1 (+DreamOn) vs Qwen2.5-Coder 92.6; multi-line 43.2 -> 63.8 vs Qwen 58.7; SantaCoder EM 59.3 -> 79.0 vs Qwen 79.8. Includes an initial-mask-length sweep (4..64) and an oracle-length row.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Every hole is a SINGLE hole: the paper's own text says it evaluates 'single-line and multi-line subsets' only. RandomSpanInfilling (1640 cases) and RandomSpanInfillingLight (164) are never touched, and k>1 is never posed. Length elasticity is orthogonal to hole topology — expand/delete cannot help when the difficulty is coordinating two holes that must agree.
related_work.known_defects: (1) The released harness hardcodes the split: vendor/DreamOn/eval/evaluate.py line 95 is literally `problems = read_problems(benchmark_name='single-line')`, verified in our local checkout — two of the four public splits are unreachable without editing the file. (2) Zero compute accounting: the mask-length sweep 4..64 changes canvas size and therefore per-step cost, but only pass@1 is reported, so 'DreamOn matches Qwen2.5-Coder' is a quality claim with no cost axis (same class of omission as reporting NFE across families). (3) OpenReview reviewer jUWCBhjtxw (rating 2, soundness 2) states 'I feel the baselines are weak — simply plugging this into a DLM will almost certainly yield improvements'; reviewer iCev1lieXF notes it is 'only evaluated on Python code infilling'. (4) Multi-line at oracle length (66.6) is BELOW +DreamOn at mask-64 (63.8)... i.e. its own oracle upper bound is nearly saturated, suggesting multi-line is close to ceiling for this method and a harder topology axis is needed to separate methods.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list=2602.01326; arXiv HTML v1 fetched and grepped (only 'single-line'/'multi-line' appear; zero hits for 'random span'/'RandomSpan'); Table 1 and Table 2 numbers extracted verbatim from the HTML; OpenReview api2 note EQTPmqukiU + its review notes; local grep of vendor/DreamOn/eval/evaluate.py confirming the hardcoded benchmark_name.

related_work.citation: Mohammad Bavarian, Heewoo Jun, Nikolas Tezak, John Schulman, Christine McLeavey, Jerry Tworek, Mark Chen. "Efficient Training of Language Models to Fill in the Middle." arXiv:2207.14255.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (arXiv only; no venue in arXiv comment field, no ICLR/NeurIPS OpenReview record found). Widely cited as the origin of RandomSpanInfilling.
related_work.what_it_covers: The paper that CREATED RandomSpanInfilling and RandomSpanInfillingLight (the candidate's 'missing column'), on top of Fried et al.'s single-line/multi-line HumanEval-Infilling splits. Establishes FIM-for-free and prescribes FIM hyperparameters.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: It explicitly and deliberately declines the k>1 regime: 'While several of these works support infilling multiple spans, we focus on the single span setting for practicality (e.g. in computer-based text generation, where the placement of cursor implies the location we want to infill).' It also declines syntactic/semantic span selection: 'we do not study syntactically or semantically motivated infilling spans'. So the AST-guided, multi-hole variant is a documented, self-declared open slot — this is the strongest textual warrant for our benchmark existing at all.
related_work.known_defects: Character-level random spans are semantics-blind (they cut mid-token/mid-expression), which is why RandomSpan requires bespoke output truncation and is the one split where post-processing is provably load-bearing. Single-span-by-construction: all four HumanEval-Infilling files have schema {prompt, suffix, canonical_solution} — verified locally, one middle per row, so k>1 CANNOT be expressed in the released format.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API + ar5iv full text of 2207.14255 (quotes above extracted verbatim, including Appendix E 'Random span infilling benchmark'); local inspection of data/infilling/HumanEval-{SingleLine,MultiLine,RandomSpan}Infilling.jsonl (1033 / 5815 / 1640 rows, single canonical_solution field each) and /tmp/RandomSpanInfillingLight.jsonl (164 rows).

related_work.citation: Dhruvesh Patel, Aishwarya Sahoo, Avinash Amballa, Tahira Naseem, Tim G. J. Rudner, Andrew McCallum. "Insertion Language Models: Sequence Generation with Arbitrary-Position Insertions." arXiv:2505.05755.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint / rejected. OpenReview: ICLR.cc/2026/Conference/Rejected_Submission (Wes9HF3ppt); also SPIGM@NeurIPS 2025 workshop (IbVGvSDFQV); CoRR 2025 (pc811uewsT). No main-conference acceptance found.
related_work.what_it_covers: The only pre-cutoff work I found that actually runs a MULTI-HOLE vs SINGLE-HOLE comparison between a masked-diffusion model and an alternative: LM1B 'single-segment' (one contiguous segment removed) vs 'multi-segment' (two or more contiguous segments removed), 3500 sequences, MDM vs ILM, metric = %change in NLL and entropy under Llama-3.2-3B. Also motivates the gap crisply: FIM-trained ARMs are 'not capable of performing arbitrary infilling, for example, filling two blanks at separate places in the sequence.'
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: No code, no execution grading, no 7B scale, and — decisively — NO AR ARM on the multi-segment leg. The k axis is binary (1 vs 2+), not a ladder, and the number of holes is never reported as a covariate.
related_work.known_defects: (1) It excludes AR models from the infilling comparison on the stated grounds that 'ARMs are not capable of performing infilling without specialized training' — which is false for FIM-pretrained code models (Bavarian 2022, and every Qwen2.5-Coder/DeepSeek-Coder/StarCoder2 checkpoint). This is the single most exploitable unfair-baseline defect in this literature: the whole diffusion-vs-AR multi-hole question is assumed away rather than measured. (2) Proxy metric: ΔNLL/Δentropy under a third-party 3B scorer, not functional correctness, so it cannot say whether the infill is *right*. (3) ~100M-parameter models on LM1B/TinyStories — no evidence the ordering survives to 7B code models. (4) 'two or more contiguous segments' pools k=2,3,4+ into one bucket, so no interaction slope can be estimated.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list=2505.05755; ar5iv full text fetched, Section 5.4 Infilling and Table 3 extracted verbatim (LM1B single-segment vs multi-segment, MDM vs ILM ΔNLL rows); OpenReview api2 search returning the ICLR 2026 Rejected_Submission and SPIGM workshop records.

related_work.citation: Marianne Arriola, Yair Schiff, Hao Phung, Aaron Gokaslan, Volodymyr Kuleshov (Kuleshov group). "Set Diffusion: Interpolating Token Orderings Between Autoregression and Diffusion for Fast and Flexible Decoding." arXiv:2607.01775. ICML 2026.
related_work.venue_status: ICML 2026 — verified via OpenReview api2 (id tN8f0dxQ9i, venueid=ICML.cc/2026/Conference, venue='ICML 2026 regular'); arXiv comment also states 'ICML 2026'. CONCURRENT (v1 2026-07-02, after the 2026-05-07 cutoff).
related_work.what_it_covers: Set diffusion over flexible-position/flexible-length token sets, generalising block diffusion, with KV-cache updates every step. Reports ROCStories 'Infill k/5' with k in {1,3} against an AR Transformer, MDLM, BD3LM, SEDD, DiffuGPT — i.e. an infilling ladder WITH an AR arm and a throughput axis. Claims 'stronger infilling performance than block diffusion'.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: The ladder is span LENGTH, not hole COUNT: appendix L.4 says 'we mask either the middle sentence or the middle three sentences', which is one CONTIGUOUS region of 1 or 3 sentences. So the topology (number of disjoint holes) is fixed at k=1 throughout. Also 110-130M params, ROUGE not execution, natural-language stories not code.
related_work.known_defects: (1) Conflates length with topology — exactly the confound our candidate is positioned to separate. (2) Diffusion throughput is reported only as a LOWER bound ('models use the maximum number of sampling steps, thus we report throughput as a lower bound'), which systematically flatters diffusion on the speed axis. (3) The AR arm actually ties or beats the proposed method at Infill 3/5 (AR R-1/2/L 18.3/1.3/13.1 vs SW-SetDLM 18.1/1.3/13.2) at 4-5x the throughput, a fact the narrative does not foreground. (4) MDLM is run without KV caching while set diffusion has it, so the speed comparison is partly an implementation artifact the authors themselves note.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list=2607.01775; ar5iv full text fetched, Table 2 and Appendix L.4 extracted verbatim; OpenReview api2 search for the ICML 2026 record.

related_work.citation: Seunggeun Kim et al. "From Interface to Inference: Eliciting Any-Order Inference from Any-Order Models." arXiv:2607.26504.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (no arXiv comment; no OpenReview record found via api2 search). CONCURRENT.
related_work.what_it_covers: Diagnoses an 'interface-inference gap' from positional uncertainty in fixed-canvas MDMs, and fine-tunes Dream-Coder-7B into a 7B FlexMDM (~1150 GPU-hours) that 'generates drafts of non-contiguous regions of the generated code', quantified by AST-walk metrics (Coverage Before Commitment). Also a 125M LatentMDM for GSM8K. Confirms the candidate's premise that the non-contiguous axis is opening.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: It is entirely about UNCONSTRAINED generation order during from-scratch synthesis, evaluated on HumanEval/HumanEval+/MBPP/MBPP+ at Pass@1/Pass@16. There is no infilling benchmark at all: zero hits in the full text for 'infilling benchmark', 'two holes', 'multiple regions', 'number of regions', 'Qwen2.5'. Non-contiguity is a measured emergent BEHAVIOUR, never an imposed task condition, and there is no AR-FIM comparison.
related_work.known_defects: (1) 'Non-contiguous' is operationalised as an internal trajectory statistic (CBC over AST siblings), not as task difficulty — so the paper cannot say whether non-contiguous capability translates into non-contiguous task performance. That gap is precisely a k-span benchmark. (2) Its headline improvement is on from-scratch generation, i.e. AR's home turf, so the structural argument is made where it is weakest. (3) 1150 GPU-hours of fine-tuning makes the comparison to un-finetuned Dream-Coder confounded by additional training. (4) 125M vs 7B split across two different tasks means neither approach is demonstrated at both scales.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list=2607.26504 (v1 2026-07-29); arXiv HTML v1 fetched (794KB) and keyword-grepped as listed; OpenReview api2 search returned no matching submission.

related_work.citation: Xingyu Mou et al. "Beyond Block Boundaries: Multi-Block Editing for Diffusion Large Language Models." arXiv:2607.22663.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (arXiv v1 2026-06-29, v2 2026-07-29 per arXiv submission history; no arXiv comment; no OpenReview record found). CONCURRENT.
related_work.what_it_covers: Identifies the 'block boundary problem' in block-diffusion dLLMs and proposes Multi-Block Editing (training-free + SFT variants) to revise decoded tokens with cross-block context. Quantifies boundary sensitivity (SCD 61.3x higher in the last quarter of a block than the first on AIME 2025). Evaluated on LLaDA2.1-Mini across 12 benchmarks, average 61.45 -> 64.24.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: 'Multi-block' is about revising already-decoded contiguous blocks during a single generation, not about conditioning on two-sided context around k user-specified holes. No infilling benchmark, no AR-FIM baseline, no k-ladder. Single model family (LLaDA2.1-Mini).
related_work.known_defects: (1) 12-benchmark average is dominated by reasoning tasks (AIME gain 13.33 pts); no infilling/editing-with-fixed-context task at all, so the 'editing' framing is not tested on actual edit tasks. (2) Training-free vs Full MBE conflates inference-time attention widening with additional SFT. (3) Single model, so the block-boundary phenomenon's generality across dLLM families is untested. (4) Throughput retention (87.3-96.7%) is measured on 4 of the 12 datasets only.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list=2607.22663 and 2607.22663v1 (v1 <published> 2026-06-29T06:24:19Z); arXiv /abs submission-history block fetched confirming [v1] 29 Jun 2026, [v2] 29 Jul 2026.

related_work.citation: Daniel Fried, Armen Aghajanyan, Jessy Lin, Sida Wang, Eric Wallace, Freda Shi, Ruiqi Zhong, Wen-tau Yih, Luke Zettlemoyer, Mike Lewis. "InCoder: A Generative Model for Code Infilling and Synthesis." arXiv:2204.05999. ICLR 2023 (notable top 25%).
related_work.venue_status: ICLR 2023 notable-top-25% — verified via OpenReview (id hQwb-lbM6EL, venueid=ICLR.cc/2023/Conference, venue='ICLR 2023 notable top 25%'). arXiv v3 comment: 'ICLR 2023. v3: camera-ready'.
related_work.what_it_covers: Origin of the HumanEval-Infilling single-line/multi-line splits and of causal-masked multi-region infilling. Appendix B.2 gives the exact k>1 serialisation protocol: '[A; <Mask:0>; C; <Mask:1>; E; <Mask:2>]' and states 'infill the masks IN ORDER, appending the appropriate <Mask:k> sentinel tokens to signal the start of generation for the next span'. Its Variable Name Prediction task masks ALL occurrences of a name at once (a genuine multi-hole task with a correctness metric: 18.4 L2R-single / 23.5 L2R-rerank / 30.6 causal-masked infilling).
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Multi-region infilling is described in an appendix as an inference capability and demonstrated qualitatively (Figure 1, imports example); it is never turned into a graded k-ladder with pass@1. Variable renaming is the one multi-hole quantitative task, but there k is data-determined (occurrence count), not a controlled factor, the answer is a single shared string (so holes are trivially coupled by copying), and prediction is aggregated by majority vote across masks — which is a k-hole task that *avoids* the joint-coordination difficulty rather than measuring it. Pre-dates all diffusion coders.
related_work.known_defects: (1) The canonical AR multi-hole protocol is sequential-in-order-only; nobody has ever tested whether serialisation ORDER matters, so 'AR must serialise' has never been separated from 'AR must serialise left-to-right'. That is a cheap, high-value control we can add. (2) Variable-renaming majority-vote aggregation deliberately collapses k independent predictions into one, so the paper's own multi-hole number does not measure joint consistency across holes. (3) 6.7B dense model, 2048-token context, Python-centric.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list=2204.05999; ar5iv full text fetched, Appendix B.2 multi-mask serialisation and Section 4.4 Variable Name Prediction + Table 4 extracted verbatim; OpenReview search for the ICLR 2023 venueid.

related_work.citation: Linyuan Gong, Sida Wang, Mostafa Elhoushi, Alvin Cheung. "Evaluation of LLMs on Syntax-Aware Code Fill-in-the-Middle Tasks" (SAFIM). arXiv:2403.04814. ICML 2024 Oral.
related_work.venue_status: ICML 2024 Oral — verified via OpenReview (id jKYyFbH8ap, venueid=ICML.cc/2024/Conference, venue='ICML 2024 Oral'); arXiv comment also states 'ICML 2024 Oral'.
related_work.what_it_covers: 17,720-example multi-language syntax-aware FIM benchmark (algorithm block, control flow, API call completion) with syntax-aware post-processing and 15 LLMs, sourced post-April-2022 to limit contamination. The reference point for 'AST-guided hole selection' as a benchmark-construction methodology.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Every SAFIM task is a single syntactic hole. No k>1 condition, no diffusion models (predates them), no cost axis.
related_work.known_defects: Per-task-type bespoke truncation rules (one line / match ground-truth structure / after first closing paren) mean the metric is entangled with the post-processor — a construct-validity issue that becomes acute at k>1 where a model can bleed one hole's content into another's. Also single-hole-by-construction, so it cannot be reused directly.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list=2403.04814 (abstract, comment); OpenReview api2 search for the ICML 2024 Oral record.

related_work.citation: Linyuan Gong, Alvin Cheung, Mostafa Elhoushi, Sida Wang. "Structure-Aware Fill-in-the-Middle Pretraining for Code" (AST-FIM + Real-FIM-Eval). arXiv:2506.00204.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint / CoRR 2025 — OpenReview api2 returns only dblp.org/journals/CORR/2025 (id dDMSyS7MD3); no conference venueid found. arXiv comment: '14 pages' only.
related_work.what_it_covers: AST-guided masking of complete syntactic structures for FIM PRETRAINING (the exact hole-selection mechanism our candidate proposes for eval), plus Real-FIM-Eval derived from 30k+ GitHub commits across 12 languages. Shows AST-FIM beats random-character FIM by up to 5 pts.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: AST-guided masking is used as a training-data transform, and evaluation is on standard single-hole FIM benchmarks. No k-ladder, no diffusion arm, no report of how many holes a real commit spans (even though the 30k-commit corpus would trivially support that statistic).
related_work.known_defects: (1) Real-FIM-Eval is derived from real commits, which frequently touch multiple disjoint regions — yet the benchmark keeps a single infill region, discarding exactly the multi-hunk structure its own data source contains. Recovering that would be a strong external-validity anchor and it is left on the table. (2) 5-pt gains at 1B/8B without cost accounting. (3) The masking policy is AST-node-based but never checks whether the removed node's siblings/parents remain resolvable, which is the crux at k>1.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list=2506.00204 (abstract, comment); OpenReview api2 search returning only the CoRR 2025 record.

related_work.citation: Wasi Uddin Ahmad et al. "Planning-Aware Code Infilling via Horizon-Length Prediction" (HLP). arXiv:2410.03103.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (no arXiv comment; no conference record surfaced). Unverified beyond arXiv.
related_work.what_it_covers: Argues next-token prediction over reordered FIM sequences under-trains planning w.r.t. distant right context, and adds a horizon-length prediction objective; up to 24% relative FIM gains across model families/sizes at file and repo level, no inference cost.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Single-hole FIM throughout. Never asks whether horizon-length prediction, which is defined for one middle, extends to k middles whose lengths are jointly unknown — arguably the natural AR-side counter-method to our claim, and it is untested at k>1.
related_work.known_defects: The AR-side weakness our candidate attributes to serialisation may be substantially a horizon/length-planning weakness, which HLP already partly fixes. Our design must therefore include an AR arm that is not naively disadvantaged, or explicitly bound the claim to standard FIM-trained checkpoints.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list=2410.03103 abstract; no venue claim made.

related_work.citation: Wonjun Kang et al. (title as listed) "From Output to Evaluation: Does Raw Instruction-Tuned Code LLMs Output Suffice for Fill-in-the-Middle Code Generation?" arXiv:2505.18789.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint ('Work in progress' per arXiv comment; no OpenReview record found).
related_work.what_it_covers: IMPORTANT CORRECTION TO THE CANDIDATE'S PREMISE: this paper DOES report the RandomSpan split. It evaluates Qwen2.5-Coder 7B/14B/32B (base and instruct, plus fine-tuned) on all three HumanEval-Infilling tasks — columns SL / ML / RS — plus SAFIM, and tabulates the truncation rule for each ('Random-span: truncate output if overlaps with prefix and suffix').
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: AR-only; no diffusion model, and no k>1. So the candidate's 'missing column' is real but must be scoped precisely: RandomSpan is missing for DIFFUSION models, not from the literature as a whole.
related_work.known_defects: Its central finding is a direct threat to any RandomSpan-based headline: post-processing remains NECESSARY when the middle is a random span, even for strong instruct models, whereas it becomes unnecessary for complete-line middles. Any diffusion-vs-AR RandomSpan comparison therefore has a stopping-rule fairness problem — diffusion fills a fixed canvas and cannot over-generate the same way, so 'truncate if overlaps with prefix/suffix' is not a paradigm-neutral rule. We must report both raw and post-processed numbers and make the stopping rule explicit, or the comparison is not interpretable.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list=2505.18789; ar5iv full text fetched, Table 1 (truncation rules) and Table 2 (SL/ML/RS columns) extracted verbatim.

related_work.citation: Hechang Niu et al. "Diffusion LMs Can Approximate Optimal Infilling Lengths Implicitly" (CAL). arXiv:2602.00476.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (no arXiv comment, no OpenReview record found).
related_work.what_it_covers: Training-free calibrated adaptive length search for diffusion infilling; +47.7% Pass@1 over fixed-length baselines on HumanEval-Infilling for LLaDA-8B(Base/Instruct), DiffuCoder-7B-Base, DreamCoder-Base-7B. Reports an oracle-length table showing fixed-length sensitivity (e.g. DreamCoder-Base 24.0/55.6/63.2/54.3 at L=4/8/16/32 vs oracle 88.1).
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Explicitly 'Single-Line and Multi-Line tasks' only — zero hits for 'random span'/'RandomSpan' in the full text. Also no AR baseline at all (no Qwen2.5-Coder), and no k>1. Confirms that as of 2026-01 the diffusion infilling literature is still entirely single-hole.
related_work.known_defects: (1) No AR arm whatsoever, so it cannot speak to the cross-family question. (2) The length-search probes cost extra forward passes but the paper reports overhead only qualitatively ('modest'), with no NFE accounting — so the +47.7% is not on a matched-compute basis. diff.differentiation_statement: The candidate's premise needs one correction that actually strengthens it: the k-span code-infilling benchmark is NOT unbuilt. Mündler, Dekoninck & Vechev (arXiv:2508.10111, v1 2025-08-13, ICLR 2026 Poster) named the paradigm "multi-region infilling (mri)", constructed it on HumanEval by removing random spans following Bavarian et al., and published a clean 1-mri/2-mri/3-mri ladder showing exactly the monotone AR collapse the candidate predicts (DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B functional 64.8 -> 29.8 -> 11.9; syntax 93.9 -> 62.0 -> 32.9 across five AR models). Our zero-hit searches for "multi-span" missed it purely on terminology; "multi-region infilling" returns it as the single hit. This does not kill the candidate — it converts it from a benchmark-construction paper into a much better-defended interaction paper, because the one thing 2508.10111 never does is run a diffusion model on mri: its diffusion section (LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B, DreamCoder-7B, DiffuCoder-7B at 32 steps) evaluates FROM-SCRATCH C++/JSON/SMILES generation, so the diffusion x k cell — the entire content of our headline — is empty, and no paper anywhere fills it. Our differentiation is therefore fourfold and each part is independently sufficient. (i) Family: we supply the missing diffusion column on a k-ladder, which is the first measurement of the k x family interaction; every diffusion infilling paper to date is single-hole by construction (DreamOn's released harness literally hardcodes read_problems(benchmark_name='single-line') at vendor/DreamOn/eval/evaluate.py:95, verified in our checkout; CAL reports zero hits for "random span"). (ii) Protocol fairness: 2508.10111's AR arm at k>1 uses natural-language "// region 1 / // region 2" markers inside a chat prompt with a stub main(), never the models' native FIM sentinels, and never varies serialisation order — so its "AR degrades with k" is confounded with prompt-format brittleness. InCoder's canonical multi-mask protocol (Appendix B.2) fills masks strictly in order, and nobody has ever tested whether order matters. We run three AR conditions (native-FIM sequential, native-FIM permuted, chat region-marker) so the serialisation penalty is separated from the format penalty. (iii) Cost accounting: no paper on this axis reports quality against tokens — 2508.10111 reports only constrained-decoding overhead, DreamOn sweeps mask length 4..64 with no cost column, Set Diffusion reports diffusion throughput as an explicit lower bound. We report pass@1 versus cumulative_model_tokens, which is where our repo's three retractions taught us the real claims live. (iv) Topology vs length: Set Diffusion's "Infill k/5" (concurrent, ICML 2026) varies the LENGTH of one contiguous middle, not the NUMBER of disjoint holes; we hold total masked tokens fixed while varying k, so topology is isolated from the length-elasticity axis that DreamOn and CAL already own. Setting differences add further separation: Python + evalplus untrusted_check (2508.10111 is C++-only, with 3-mri functional pinned at 4.9-12.6% i.e. near-floor with almost no dynamic range) and a 256-token abort that conflates capability with budget truncation.

followup_openings.target_paper: Mündler, Dekoninck & Vechev, "Constrained Decoding of Diffusion LLMs with Context-Free Grammars", arXiv:2508.10111 (ICLR 2026 Poster; v1 2025-08-13)
followup_openings.defect: The paper introduces the mri (multi-region infilling) paradigm and the k=1,2,3 ladder, and separately evaluates four diffusion LLMs — but never crosses the two. Its diffusion tasks are from-scratch C++/JSON/SMILES generation ('the model should generate the entire function specified in natural language'), so there is no diffusion x mri table anywhere in the paper. The whole point of the mri paradigm is that out-of-order generation should shine there, and that hypothesis is left untested by the very paper that formalises both halves.
followup_openings.our_fix: Fill the missing cell directly, reusing their paradigm name and citing them as the source of the k-ladder: run DreamOn-v0-7B (native multi-mask), Dream-Coder-v0-Instruct-7B (fixed canvas), and an AR-FIM arm on a matched k in {1,2,4} ladder, and report the k x family interaction as the primary statistic. Because the AR half of the table already exists and replicates in a second community (HUNK4J, arXiv:2506.04418, shows the same decline with hunk count on real Java defects), our contribution reduces to one clean measurement rather than a whole benchmark build — the cheapest possible path to a main-conference claim.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: The single most-asked question about masked diffusion — does bidirectional joint filling actually beat serialised AR editing — currently has exactly one supporting citation in the code domain (arXiv:2510.04605), and that citation compares a commercial diffusion code model against general-purpose AR-Llama3-8B with no code-specialised AR control, making it unidentifiable. Filling this cell settles a load-bearing empirical question with a defensible control.

followup_openings.target_paper: Mündler et al., arXiv:2508.10111 — AR multi-region prompting protocol (Figure 4)
followup_openings.defect: At k>1 the AR arm is prompted with natural-language region markers injected into the source ('// region 1', '// region 2') plus an appended stub main() and a chat system message, rather than the models' native FIM sentinels. The five AR models evaluated (StarCoder2, CodeGemma, DeepSeek-Coder family) are all FIM-pretrained and have dedicated prefix/suffix/middle tokens which are simply not used at k>1. Serialisation ORDER is also never varied — InCoder's canonical protocol (arXiv:2204.05999 Appendix B.2) fills masks strictly in order, and no paper has ever asked whether order matters. So the reported AR collapse (64.8 -> 11.9 functional) may be substantially a prompt-format and ordering artifact rather than an intrinsic serialisation cost.
followup_openings.our_fix: Three AR conditions on the identical hole specs: (a) native-FIM sentinel serialisation, holes filled left-to-right per InCoder B.2; (b) native-FIM with permuted hole order (and, for k=2, both orders, giving a within-item paired test); (c) the chat region-marker format as an exact replication of theirs. If (a) and (b) recover most of the k=1 -> k=4 loss, the field's 'AR must serialise' story is a prompting artifact — a genuinely useful negative result. If they do not, our interaction claim rests on a fair AR baseline no reviewer can attack. Also add an HLP-style right-context-planning check (arXiv:2410.03103) so we cannot be accused of using a naively disadvantaged AR arm.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This is the exact defect class that produced our own three retractions (a measurement whose baseline was doing something other than advertised). It converts the weakest link in our claim into a contribution, and it is nearly free — it is a prompt-construction variant on the same generations.

followup_openings.target_paper: Mündler et al., arXiv:2508.10111 — cost accounting and truncation
followup_openings.defect: Quality is reported without any token or latency axis (the only cost number is constrained-decoding overhead, 67% at 1-mri rising to 205% at 3-mri), and generation is hard-aborted at 256 tokens with aborts scored as failures. Their own Figure 3(a) shows a task failing because 'the model exceeds the token limit of 256 tokens as it generates large amounts of unnecessary code' — so at higher k, 'AR is worse' is partly 'AR ran out of budget', with the most expensive items scored as zeros.
followup_openings.our_fix: Report pass@1 against cumulative_model_tokens for every arm and every k, and report the abort/truncation rate per cell separately so capability and budget are never conflated. Sweep the AR budget so its curve is measured at its own asymptote, and sweep diffusion NFE (our repo has the ladder: HE+ .000 at nfe16 up to .707 at nfe512, saturating exactly there) so neither family is evaluated at a single arbitrary compute point (2508.10111 fixes diffusion at 32 steps, which our own data show is deep in the unparseable-output regime).
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This is our repo's hard-won lesson stated as a contribution: our retraction #3 understated scaffold Large's cost 2.85x/3.69x by dropping exactly the budget-truncated tasks. A k-ladder where cost grows with k is a trap for precisely that error, and being the paper that gets it right is a durable differentiator — it also gives us the quality-compute frontier framing that already survived three falsifiability tests in this project.

followup_openings.target_paper: Patel et al., "Insertion Language Models", arXiv:2505.05755 (ICLR 2026 Rejected_Submission; SPIGM@NeurIPS 2025)
followup_openings.defect: It runs the only pre-cutoff single-hole vs multi-hole diffusion comparison (LM1B single-segment vs multi-segment, MDM vs ILM) but EXCLUDES autoregressive models from the infilling evaluation entirely, on the stated grounds that 'ARMs are not capable of performing infilling without specialized training'. That is false for every FIM-pretrained code model since Bavarian et al. 2022. The cross-family multi-hole question is thus assumed away rather than measured. Compounding this: the metric is %change in NLL/entropy under a third-party Llama-3.2-3B scorer, not correctness; scale is ~100M; and k=2,3,4+ are pooled into one 'multi-segment' bucket so no slope is estimable.
followup_openings.our_fix: Re-pose their multi-segment vs single-segment contrast with (i) an FIM-trained AR arm included, (ii) execution-based grading via evalplus untrusted_check instead of a proxy NLL, (iii) 7B rather than 100M models, and (iv) k as a graded ladder {1,2,4} rather than a binary bucket. Cite them as having identified the phenomenon and us as having measured it fairly.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This is the cleanest unfair-baseline repair available on the whole axis, and it directly supplies our differentiation statement's strongest sentence: the one prior paper that compared families on multi-hole infilling disqualified the comparison family by assumption.

followup_openings.target_paper: Arriola et al., "Set Diffusion", arXiv:2607.01775 (ICML 2026; CONCURRENT, v1 2026-07-02)
followup_openings.defect: Its 'Infill k/5' ladder varies the LENGTH of a single contiguous middle (appendix L.4: 'we mask either the middle sentence or the middle three sentences'), not the NUMBER of disjoint holes, so hole topology is fixed at k=1 while being presented as a k-ladder. Separately, diffusion throughput is reported only as a lower bound because 'models use the maximum number of sampling steps', which structurally flatters diffusion on the speed axis, and its AR arm actually ties/beats the proposed method at Infill 3/5 (AR R-1/2/L 18.3/1.3/13.1 vs SW-SetDLM 18.1/1.3/13.2) at 4-5x throughput — a fact the narrative does not foreground.
followup_openings.our_fix: Design the ladder as a 2D grid: k holes in {1,2,4} CROSSED with total masked tokens held constant, so span length and hole count are orthogonal factors and the interaction of interest cannot be re-explained as a length effect. Report diffusion cost as measured tokens/NFE, not as a bound. This also cleanly separates our axis from DreamOn's and CAL's, both of which own the length-elasticity axis.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It pre-empts the single most likely reviewer objection ('isn't this just that more masked tokens is harder?'), and it makes the topology-vs-length distinction — which is the conceptual core of why k>1 is not solvable by DreamOn's expand/delete machinery — an experimental fact rather than an argument.

followup_openings.target_paper: Wu et al., "DreamOn", arXiv:2602.01326 (ICLR 2026 Poster) — released eval harness
followup_openings.defect: vendor/DreamOn/eval/evaluate.py line 95 hardcodes `problems = read_problems(benchmark_name='single-line')`, verified in our local checkout, so two of the four public HumanEval-Infilling splits are unreachable without editing the harness. RandomSpanInfilling (1640 cases) and RandomSpanInfillingLight (164) are consequently unmeasured for every diffusion code model — CAL (arXiv:2602.00476) independently confirms this, with zero occurrences of 'random span' in its text. DreamOn also reports no compute accounting despite sweeping canvas size 4..64, and its own oracle-length multi-line upper bound (66.6) sits BELOW its mask-64 result (63.8), indicating multi-line is near-saturated for this method.
followup_openings.our_fix: Patch the harness to parameterise the split, then report the untouched public RandomSpanInfilling / RandomSpanInfillingLight for diffusion models as our external-validity anchor alongside the synthetic k-ladder — with the stopping-rule caveat handled explicitly (see next item). Add the cost column DreamOn omits, so 'DreamOn matches Qwen2.5-Coder' becomes a statement on the quality-compute plane rather than a bare pass@1 comparison.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: A one-line defect in a released ICLR harness has left a public split unmeasured for an entire model family; documenting and repairing that is a concrete, verifiable community contribution, and RandomSpan's harder, semantics-blind spans give us headroom that multi-line no longer has.

followup_openings.target_paper: Kang et al. (as listed), "From Output to Evaluation ... Fill-in-the-Middle", arXiv:2505.18789
followup_openings.defect: This paper corrects our own framing (RandomSpan IS reported for AR — it tabulates SL/ML/RS for Qwen2.5-Coder 7B/14B/32B) and simultaneously identifies a metric-validity trap for us: post-processing remains NECESSARY on RandomSpan even for strong instruct models, while becoming unnecessary for complete-line middles. The benchmark's RandomSpan rule is 'truncate output if overlaps with prefix and suffix' — a rule written for over-generating AR decoders. A fixed-canvas diffusion model cannot over-generate the same way, so this truncation rule is not paradigm-neutral and quietly advantages one family.
followup_openings.our_fix: Scope the 'missing column' claim precisely to diffusion models rather than to the literature. Report every RandomSpan number BOTH raw and post-processed, state the stopping rule for each family explicitly, and make the AST-guided synthetic ladder (where hole boundaries are syntactic and the correct span is unambiguous) the primary evidence, with RandomSpan as a secondary anchor whose protocol asymmetry is disclosed.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: Ignoring this would reproduce our retraction #1 (a grader that scored the wrong thing) at benchmark scale. Handling it explicitly turns a hidden threat into a methodological contribution: the first paradigm-neutral stopping-rule specification for cross-family infilling evaluation.

followup_openings.target_paper: Bavarian et al., arXiv:2207.14255 and Gong et al., AST-FIM/Real-FIM-Eval, arXiv:2506.00204
followup_openings.defect: Bavarian et al. explicitly decline the regime — 'While several of these works support infilling multiple spans, we focus on the single span setting for practicality' — and also decline syntactic span selection ('we do not study syntactically or semantically motivated infilling spans'). AST-FIM then supplies exactly the AST-guided masking machinery, and builds Real-FIM-Eval from 30,000+ real GitHub commits, but still keeps a single infill region per example, discarding the multi-region structure its own corpus contains. Neither reports the distribution of how many disjoint regions a real code edit spans.
followup_openings.our_fix: Position the AST-guided k-span construction as the union of two documented, self-declared open slots (multi-span from Bavarian, AST-guided selection from AST-FIM), and add the missing empirical prior: measure the distribution of disjoint edit regions per commit from a public commit corpus to justify the k in {1,2,4} range on external grounds rather than convenience. This gives the benchmark an ecological-validity argument that neither prior work provides.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It answers 'why these k values?' with data rather than taste, and it lets us cite the two most authoritative FIM papers as having explicitly deferred exactly what we do — the strongest possible framing for a benchmark contribution whose construction otherwise overlaps 2508.10111.

diff.sharpened_claim: Reposition from "we build the missing k-span benchmark" to "we measure the k x family interaction that the paper which built the k-span benchmark left empty, on a protocol that survives the fairness objections its AR arm does not." Concretely: Mündler et al. (arXiv:2508.10111, ICLR 2026) established multi-region infilling (mri) and showed AR code models collapse monotonically with hole count k on HumanEval (DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B pass@1 64.8 -> 29.8 -> 11.9 for k=1,2,3), but evaluated diffusion LLMs only on from-scratch generation, leaving the diffusion x k cell empty; no paper has filled it. We measure it on a Python, evalplus-graded, AST-guided ladder with k in {1,2,4} CROSSED with total-masked-tokens held constant (separating hole topology from the span-length axis that DreamOn and CAL already own), reporting pass@1 against cumulative_model_tokens with per-cell truncation rates disclosed. The AR arm is run in three protocols — native-FIM sentinel serialisation in InCoder order, native-FIM with permuted hole order, and the chat region-marker format used by 2508.10111 — so an intrinsic serialisation cost is distinguished from prompt-format brittleness and from ordering choice. Primary statistic: the k x family interaction on the quality-compute plane. Three outcomes are all publishable and pre-registered: diffusion's advantage grows with k (the paradigm's structural claim finally has evidence, and k-span infilling, not from-scratch generation, is the right headline task for diffusion code models); the interaction is null (diffusion's parallel-fill advantage is nominal, not realised — and the field's belief to the contrary rests on a single CoRR-only paper, arXiv:2510.04605, that compares a diffusion code model against a general-purpose AR model); or AR's apparent k-collapse largely disappears under native-FIM serialisation with permuted order, in which case the published AR degradation is a prompting artifact and the correct contribution is that repair.

ALREADY-BUILT WORK THE CANDIDATE PROPOSES TO BUILD: scripts/generate_evalplus_ar.py (482 lines) already implements the exact cost accounting listed as a differentiator -- a real forward_pre_hook measuring forward_passes / tokens_fed / attended_context_sum, with analytic cross-check and an explicit docstring caveat that it is not a FLOP count. scripts/test_multiregion.py already contains a working 2-hole mutually-dependent Dream infilling probe. The hardcode at vendor/DreamOn/eval/evaluate.py:95 (problems = read_problems(benchmark_name='single-line')) is real and confirmed. MEASURED CONFOUND, the real threat to the headline: diffusion's exact-match-to-gold rate RISES with k (.633 at k=1 -> .792 at k=2 -> .833 at k=4).
