related_work.what_it_covers: Opens with 'How should we evaluate generation systems that combine AR and diffusion decoding?' and reports four findings that overlap the candidate's failure-mode taxonomy remarkably closely: (1) code benchmarks conflate structural discovery with logical correctness -- a syntactic scaffold lifts accuracy from near zero to over 20% WITHOUT changing the model; (2) a refinement-tension phenomenon where multi-stage correction degrades already-correct tokens; (3) log-likelihood and generative evaluation give DIFFERENT MODEL RANKINGS for the same model pair (a ranking reversal, on protocol grounds, across six benchmarks including HumanEval and MBPP); (4) 'standard Python post-processing silently breaks code evaluation for non-AR generators'. Three evaluation protocols crossed (execution-based pass@1, exact-match, log-likelihood).
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: The reversal is protocol-CLASS (log-likelihood vs generative), not compute-accounting; nominal-step vs token-matched re-ranking is untouched. Small paper (7 pages), single hybrid system, and no cumulative-model-token or cross-family cost unit. No parse-validity time series, no termination-reason taxonomy, no failure_process inclusion rule.

related_work.citation: P. Pynadath, J. Shi, R. Zhang. "Generative Frontiers: Why Evaluation Matters for Diffusion Language Models." arXiv:2604.02718v1.
related_work.known_defects: (1) Scale-bound: conclusions are drawn at GPT-2-small (150M) and the note offers no evidence they hold at 7-8B, where the candidate operates -- a clean replication-at-scale opening. (2) The frontier construction requires a reference distribution and an external evaluator; on code there is no natural distributional reference, so the frontier framework does not transfer and something else (execution-graded quality vs measured token cost) is needed -- which is the candidate's Pareto plot. CaRE's own overlay section concedes the frontier view makes their headline interaction invisible, i.e. the frontier is not a sufficient protocol. (3) Prescriptive claims about OpenWebText-over-LM1B rest on argument rather than a measured ranking-stability experiment.

related_work.what_it_covers: Pre-cutoff methodology note on dLLM evaluation: argues OpenWebText is the meaningful benchmark and LM1B is not, that likelihood evaluation is limited for diffusion, and that generative perplexity alone is uninformative because gen-PPL and entropy are two components of a KL divergence to a reference distribution -- hence 'generative frontiers' (temperature-swept curves) as the principled comparison. Establishes the general principle that a swept protocol parameter (temperature) must be treated as a curve rather than a point, but never instantiates it on an executable task surface.

related_work.what_it_covers: Pre-cutoff, peer-reviewed, and makes the strongest pre-cutoff claim in the neighbourhood: 'evaluations on standard benchmarks (e.g., math and coding) are not sufficient to capture the quality degradation caused by parallel decoding' -- i.e. standard code benchmarks are the wrong instrument for a dLLM decoding choice. Provides information-theoretic analysis of parallel decoding, analytically tractable synthetic list-operation case studies, and a purpose-built benchmark. Leaves entirely open whether existing code benchmarks can be RESCUED by better accounting rather than replaced.

related_work.citation: What We Observe as LLM Behavior Can Be a Side-effect of Inference Backend. arXiv:2608.04714v1.
related_work.known_defects: (1) Only 3 models and no diffusion family, so the 39% backend share is not transferable to dLLMs where per-step canvas re-attention makes backend effects plausibly larger. related_work.what_it_covers: The closest methodological template for the candidate's variance-decomposition deliverable, in a different domain. diff.sharpened_claim: Nominal step count and NFE are not compute-matched cost units for code generation, and the field's two protocol-audit papers both stop one level short of this. On execution-graded HumanEval+/MBPP+ (full n=164/n=378, EvalPlus untrusted_check with plus-tests, empty-solution negative control) we (i) run a fully crossed factorial with NO privileged baseline cell -- {temperature 0.1,0.2,0.6} x {top_p 0.95,1.0} x {steps 128,256,512} x {Dream-Coder-Instruct, Dream-Coder-Base with and without base-continuation, DreamOn, and a matched-architecture AR control Qwen2.5-Coder-7B} with backend pinned and disclosed -- and report the fraction of pass@1 variance attributable to protocol factors versus MODEL IDENTITY, a decomposition no prior work performs (CaRE's ANOVA is within one model; dLLM/ACL-2026's sweep is one-factor-at-a-time anchored at a per-model tuned optimum, which guarantees every perturbation degrades); (ii) show that the SAME cells reorder differently under nominal-step matching, actual-NFE matching, and cumulative-model-token matching, demonstrating that CaRE's own thesis recurses -- NFE hides attended compute exactly as nominal steps hide NFE, since every diffusion forward pass re-attends the whole canvas (we measure 350,832 vs 204 tokens fed for Dream nfe512 vs AR greedy on HumanEval+, and the Experimental Analysis paper's own unused TFLOPS table shows a ~1200x gap); (iii) exhibit at least one ranking reversal against an OPEN-WEIGHT, reproducible published comparison -- targeting the claim in arXiv:2606.19475 that 'relative model rankings remain strictly consistent', which was asserted from a single axis (block size) at a single temperature, rather than against closed-weight Mercury numbers we could never reproduce under their stated protocol; and (iv) ship a minimal reporting standard -- cumulative model tokens, parse-validity, termination reason, backend+version, and MANDATORY failure_process inclusion so budget-truncated cases cannot be silently dropped -- justified by three preserved, corrected, on-disk failure modes with provenance (a did-not-raise verifier scoring empty programs as passes; a 'restart' refinement policy that silently measured the base model instead of the method; and truncated-case exclusion that understated cost 2.85x/3.69x), which independently quantify two assertions that Speculative Refinement makes without measurement.

blocking_gaps: THE +14.6-POINT HEADLINE IS NOT CLEANLY ATTRIBUTABLE TO top_p AND IS PARTLY REFUTED. I did the provenance work the positioning flagged. `git show 97595c8 -- scripts/generate_evalplus_dream.py` proves the ONLY generation-affecting change between r1 and r2 was `top_p=1.0` -> `top_p=args.top_p`, and I confirmed the extractor was NOT a confound: re-running the current `extract_python` over r1's preserved `raw_output` reproduces r1's graded solutions on 164/164 tasks (0 differences). So top_p IS the r1->r2 变量. BUT the effect size collapses under replication. `.82` just ran the SAME cell (T=0.1, top_p=0.95, entropy, alg_temp=0, steps=512) and got HE .762 / HE+ .689; the `top_p=1.00` cell there got HE .591 / HE+ .573 -> the top_p delta on .82 is +17.1 HE / +11.6 HE+, i.e. sign-consistent but a DIFFERENT magnitude, and the reference cell itself does not reproduce across nodes (.707 wzc1 vs .689 on .82). I isolated that gap: I copied .82's reference solutions to /tmp/aud82/ref82.jsonl and regraded them with wzc1's evalplus 0.3.1 -> .756/.683, versus .82's own evalplus 0.1.0.dev1 -> .762/.689. So the grader version moves exactly ONE task and the remaining ~1-task gap is generation-side (torch 2.11+cu128/transformers 4.51.3/L20A vs torch 2.5.1+cu124/transformers 4.46.2/H20). At n=164 one task = 0.6pp, so '+14.6' is really '+11.6 to +17.1 depending on node', and the paper cannot state a single number without a node-and-grader-pinned re-derivation. This is a small build (one re-run), not a blocker, but it must be done BEFORE the number is written, or the paper's own reporting standard indicts its headline.

THE FACTORIAL IS ESSENTIALLY UNRUN, AND est_gpu_hours=70 IS RIGHT ONLY FOR A SMALLER GRID THAN PROPOSED. The proposal claims 'most cells are cheap and several already exist in runs/'. False as written: `ls runs/` (76 dirs) contains an NFE ladder at ONE sampler setting (T=0.1/top_p=0.95) plus r1/r2 pairs; there is no temperature grid and no top_p grid on wzc1. There IS a partially-complete one-factor-at-a-time cross on .82 at `/apdcephfs_zwfy6/.../dllm_draft_104/runs/sampler_audit/` (15 cells, 12 graded) covering T in {0.0,0.1,0.2,0.4,0.7} x top_p in {0.90,0.95,1.00} plus alg in {entropy,origin} -- HumanEval+ ONLY, Dream-Coder-Instruct ONLY, steps pinned at 512. I costed the proposed grid from measured `elapsed_seconds` (nfe512 HE+ = 0.515 GPU-h for n=164; MBPP+ = 1.110 GPU-h for n=378, summed over 8 shards): 3 temps x 2 top_p x 3 steps x 4 model-arms x 2 benches = 68.2 L20A GPU-h, so 70 is accurate ON L20A/B200 for ONE seed. On H20 (the only nodes with Qwen2.5-Coder + a working .venv_dream) the same grid is ~188 GPU-h, and adding the 2 extra seeds the paper needs for CIs triples it to ~205 L20A / ~560 H20 GPU-h. The 70-hour figure is single-seed, B200-class-only, and excludes the AR arm.

THE SEED KNOB IS NEARLY A NO-OP, SO THE 'NOISE FLOOR' LEG CANNOT SUPPORT CIs AS BUILT. `--seed` exists only in the zwfy6 checkout (commit bfbaef58, `torch.manual_seed(args.seed + rank)`) and is ABSENT from the wzc1 generator I read at /apdcephfs_wzc1/.../scripts/generate_evalplus_dream.py -- so wzc1 runs are unseeded. Worse, the seed leg does not produce independent replicates: md5 of solutions.jsonl across {he_ref (unseeded), he_ref_seed1, he_ref_seed2, he_ref_seed3} yields only TWO distinct values (seed1==seed2; ref==seed3), and diffing ref vs seed1 shows exactly 1 of 164 tasks differing. All four graded identically at .762/.689. Reason is mechanical, from the checkpoint's generation_utils.py: at T=0.1 with alg=entropy/alg_temp=0 the only stochasticity is `dists.Categorical(probs).sample()` on a distribution that is already near-deterministic after 1/T=10x logit sharpening, and the position-selection path is `torch.topk` (deterministic). So a seed-based CI would report a spuriously tiny noise floor and make every protocol delta look significant. The paper needs binomial/McNemar paired CIs over tasks, not seed variance -- which is exactly the defect it accuses CaRE of.

TWO DECODING AXES THE CLAIM NAMES DO NOT EXIST IN THIS MODEL FAMILY. The claim text lists 'canvas length, block size' as audited factors. Block size is unimplementable: `grep -n 'block|semi_ar|num_blocks' models/Dream-Coder-v0-Instruct-7B/generation_utils.py` returns NOTHING -- Dream's `diffusion_generate` is a single full-canvas loop over `timesteps = linspace(1, eps, steps+1)`, with no block/semi-AR decomposition. Block size is an LLaDA/block-diffusion concept, and NO LLaDA checkpoint exists on either disk (`find` for '*llada*' across wzc1 returns zero; zwfy6 dllm_draft/models holds only Dream-Coder-Base, Dream-Coder-Instruct, DreamOn, Qwen2.5-Coder). Canvas length IS reachable (`--max-new-tokens`) but is NOT in the proposed factorial and is confounded with steps in every existing run (all runs are canvas=512). Either drop block size from the claim or drop the reversal target that depends on it -- see next gap.

THE NOMINATED REVERSAL TARGET IS UNREACHABLE WITH ON-DISK ASSETS. The positioning correctly redirects the reversal away from closed-weight Mercury (arXiv:2510.04605) to arXiv:2606.19475's 'relative model rankings remain strictly consistent'. But that claim was asserted over BLOCK SIZE across eight DLMs including LLaDA-family. We can vary neither block size (not in Dream's sampler) nor their model set (LLaDA absent, and it is a ~16GB download x N models through hy-proxy, plus a new env: no vLLM in dllm-env, `import vllm` fails). What IS reachable is a ranking over the models we hold (Dream-Coder-Instruct vs Dream-Coder-Base vs DreamOn vs Qwen2.5-Coder-7B) across temperature/top_p/steps -- that is a reversal we generate ourselves, not a reversal OF A PUBLISHED RANKING, which is a materially weaker deliverable and directly triggers kill-condition #2 as the proposal wrote it.

BACKEND IS ALREADY CONFOUNDED IN THE DATA WE WOULD POOL, AND THE TWO DISKS CANNOT BE HOMOGENISED CHEAPLY. arXiv:2608.04714's ~39% backend share is not hypothetical here: the wzc1 env is torch 2.11.0+cu128 / transformers 4.51.3 / evalplus 0.3.1 on L20A (sm_100), while the zwfy6 `.venv_dream` on .73/.82/.104 is torch 2.5.1+cu124 / transformers 4.46.2 / evalplus 0.1.0.dev1 on H20 -- I verified all six version strings by running the interpreters. I measured the resulting spread at 1 task / 0.6pp on one config, which is small but the SAME order as several protocol deltas in the .82 grid (e.g. T=0.0 p0.90 .524 vs p1.00 .500 is 4 tasks). Pooling wzc1 and zwfy6 cells into one variance decomposition without a backend factor would attribute backend variance to protocol. And they cannot simply be merged: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B (15GB) exists ONLY on zwfy6, no `/apdcephfs_zwfy6` mount exists on this machine at all (`ls -d /apdcephfs_zwfy6*` -> No such file), and the model must be scp -O'd (15GB) to run the AR arm on wzc1.

DIFFUSION RUNS RECORD NOMINAL STEPS AS 'nfe' AND HAVE NO MEASURED COST FIELD, SO CROSS-FAMILY TOKEN-MATCHING IS CURRENTLY ANALYTIC ON ONE SIDE AND HOOK-MEASURED ON THE OTHER -- ASYMMETRICALLY. scripts/generate_evalplus_dream.py:260 literally writes `"nfe": args.steps`, i.e. the nominal budget, the exact quantity CaRE says hides compute. There is no ForwardCostTracker in the diffusion path; `grep tokens_fed` across scripts/ hits only generate_evalplus_ar.py and _summarize_ar_run.py. scripts/make_pareto_figures.py therefore reconstructs diffusion cost ANALYTICALLY as `nfe * (mean input_tokens + mean generated_tokens)` (a per-run MEAN step cost, then multiplied by nominal steps), while the AR row uses a real forward_pre_hook validated against closed form on 1084 task-runs. That asymmetry is the same species as Retraction 3: the expensive side is estimated, the cheap side is measured. It is a small, well-scoped build -- port ForwardCostTracker into the diffusion generator (the hook is already written and tested) -- but until then the paper's own headline cost unit is not hook-measured for diffusion, and any 350,832-vs-204 number is analytic.

DREAMON'S COST AND TERMINATION FIELDS ARE NULL, SO ITS ROWS CANNOT ENTER THE COST-MATCHED PLANE. In runs/dreamon_heplus_r2 and runs/dreamon_mbppplus_r2 the `process.nfe` field is None on 164/164 and 378/378 rows respectively, because generate_evalplus_dreamon.py sets `"nfe": len(output.history) if output.history is not None else None` while the caller passes `output_history=False`. `generated_tokens` maxes at 22 (HE+) / 26 (MBPP+), consistent with the .122/.085 scores. DreamOn also hardcodes temperature=0.2/top_p=0.9 inside the script with no CLI flags, so it cannot be swept at all without a code change. As it stands DreamOn is a quality-only row with an unknown step count -- it cannot appear on any compute-matched axis.

THE 'THREE RETRACTIONS AS CASE STUDIES' DELIVERABLE IS ONLY ~HALF-SUPPORTED BY THE PRESERVED ARTIFACTS. Retraction 2 is well served: 18 `runs/*.BROKEN_VERIFIER` dirs sit alongside corrected twins (e.g. refine_small_restart_s256 vs refine_small_restart_s256.BROKEN_VERIFIER). Retraction 3 is reconstructible from the `proc()` accessor and `termination_reason` (generate_evalplus_scaffold.py:304, `_make_mbpp_largehit_subset.py` filters on `model_call_budget`). But Retraction 1's headline instrument -- the empty-solution-scores-full-marks demonstration -- has NO standing harness: `grep -rn 'empty_solution|negative_control|EMPTY' scripts/ tests/` returns exactly one code COMMENT in refine_verifier_guided.py:55, and the empty-program pass@1=0.000 control cited in Retraction 4 lives on .104 with no script in either checkout. To ship it as a quantified case study ('N tasks flip under each post-processing convention'), a small negative-control harness has to be written.

feas.risk:
The most likely outcome is a CONFOUNDED-then-deflated result in three compounding stages, and I can already see the first two in today's data.

(1) The variance decomposition comes out dominated by MODEL IDENTITY, killing the headline. On HumanEval+ the models we hold are not close: Dream-Coder-Instruct .707, Dream-Coder-Base .079, DreamOn .122, AR Qwen2.5-Coder .524. That is a ~63-point spread from model identity. The widest protocol spread I can find in the .82 grid at fixed model is .689 (T0.1/p0.95) down to .476 (T0.0/p0.95) = ~21 points, and the top_p axis alone is 11.6-17.1. So eta^2(model) will swamp eta^2(protocol) by roughly an order of magnitude, and the paper's central claim -- "protocol moves pass@1 more than method deltas" -- becomes true only under the much weaker reading "more than typical PUBLISHED METHOD DELTAS", i.e. an anecdotal comparison against numbers from other papers under other protocols, which is not a variance decomposition and is not compute-matched. This directly trips kill-criterion #1, and the fallback ("becomes an appendix to whichever of candidates 1-5 proceeds") is the realistic landing spot.

(2) Even if protocol variance is large, it is not separable from backend with the data on hand. I measured wzc1-vs-zwfy6 disagreement at exactly 1 of 164 tasks on one config after controlling the grader, and grader-version disagreement at another 1 task. Individually tiny, but several protocol contrasts in the .82 grid are 4-8 tasks, so backend is within a factor of ~4-8 of the effects being attributed to protocol. If any cells are pooled across disks -- and the temptation is severe, because Qwen2.5-Coder and the working sampler harness live on zwfy6 while the idle GPUs and the newer torch live on wzc1 -- the decomposition silently attributes backend variance to protocol. That is arXiv:2608.04714's finding reproducing inside our own audit, in a paper whose thesis is that people mis-attribute variance.

(3) The reversal deliverable most likely comes back NULL or unattributable. arXiv:2606.19475's "rankings strictly consistent" was asserted over block size across eight DLMs including LLaDA; we have no block-size knob in Dream's sampler and no LLaDA weights on either disk, so we cannot re-run their claim on their axis or their models. Any reversal we exhibit will be among our own four checkpoints on axes they never crossed -- which is a reversal we manufactured, not a published ranking overturned. Kill-criterion #2 as written ("cannot exhibit at least one concrete ranking reversal") is arguably satisfiable, but kill-criterion #3 ("if the published numbers cannot be reproduced within noise under their own stated protocol") is NOT satisfiable for any target I could find on disk, which is precisely why the closed-weight Mercury target was rejected -- the substitute inherits the same defect for a different reason.

The specific way this becomes a WRONG published claim rather than an honest null: the paper ships "+14.6 points from top_p" as its motivating existence proof. I verified top_p is the true r1->r2 variable (extractor exonerated on 164/164 tasks), so the number is not fabricated -- but it does not replicate at that magnitude (+11.6 to +17.1 across nodes) and its own reference cell does not reproduce (.707 vs .689). A methods paper that proposes a reporting standard and then reports a single unreplicated point estimate for its headline sensitivity has, by its own standard, published an artifact of the protocol it is auditing. That is the fourth retraction, and it is the one this repo is most primed to make, because the number is already written into DLLM_RESULTS_20260807.md lines 63 and 157 and into commit message 97595c8.
feas.required_control:
A SAME-CONFIG REPLICATION CELL, RUN ON EVERY NODE AND GRADED BY EVERY GRADER VERSION IN USE, DECLARED AS THE NOISE FLOOR BEFORE ANY PROTOCOL DELTA IS INTERPRETED -- with the paired-task diff, not just the aggregate, reported for each pair.

Concretely: designate one cell (Dream-Coder-Instruct, T=0.1, top_p=0.95, alg=entropy, alg_temp=0, steps=512, canvas=512, HumanEval+ n=164). Run it on local L20A, on .82/H20, and on .73/H20. Grade every resulting solutions.jsonl under BOTH evalplus 0.3.1 and 0.1.0.dev1 from the preserved files. Publish the full matrix of pass@1 AND the per-task disagreement count for each cell pair. Any protocol delta smaller than the max spread in that matrix is reported as indistinguishable, full stop.

Why this is the control that prevents a fourth retraction of the same species as the first three. Each prior retraction was a comparison whose reference leg was never actually verified to be the thing it was named after: Retraction 1 compared against "did not raise" instead of against expected values, so an empty program tied a correct one; Retraction 2's 'restart' arm regenerated from the prompt, so the reference leg was Dream-Coder-Instruct wearing a scaffold label, and each tier's hidden-pass rate matched the tiny run's on the same tasks to within noise (-0.008..-0.023) -- a same-config replication check would have caught it instantly, because the arms were secretly the same config; Retraction 3 averaged over a task set that silently excluded the expensive cases, so the reference denominator was wrong by 2.85x/3.69x. In all three, the missing instrument is the same: nothing ever re-measured a quantity that should have been invariant and checked that it came out invariant.

For THIS candidate the invariant-that-should-hold is "the same nominal config yields the same pass@1", and I have already shown it does NOT: .707 on wzc1 versus .689 on .82, decomposing into ~1 task of grader version (I regraded .82's own solutions under wzc1's evalplus and got .683) and ~1 task of generation backend. Without this control declared up front, the paper computes a protocol-vs-model variance decomposition in which an unmodelled, empirically-nonzero backend term is silently loaded onto the protocol factor -- producing a confidently-stated apportionment that is wrong for a reason the paper itself names in its own related work (arXiv:2608.04714, ~39% backend share). That is exactly the failure shape of Retraction 3: a number that is not wrong because the code crashed, but wrong because the denominator quietly excluded a term.

Two mandatory riders, because the obvious cheap substitutes both fail here:
(a) DO NOT use seed replicates as the noise floor. I checked: across {unseeded ref, seed1, seed2, seed3} on .82 the solutions.jsonl md5 takes only TWO distinct values (seed1==seed2, ref==seed3), exactly 1 of 164 tasks differs, and all four grade to .762/.689. At T=0.1 the Categorical sample is near-argmax after 10x logit sharpening and the position selector is deterministic torch.topk, so seed variance measures almost nothing and would certify a near-zero noise floor -- making every protocol delta look significant. Use per-task paired bootstrap and McNemar over the 164/378 task-outcome vectors in solutions_eval_results.json plus binomial CIs.
(b) Keep the empty-solution negative control in the loop for every grader version pinned. Retraction 1's failure mode was silent and grader-side; the pass@1=0.000 empty-program check exists only as a one-off on .104 with no script in either checkout (grep for empty_solution/negative_control/EMPTY across scripts/ and tests/ finds a single code comment at refine_verifier_guided.py:55). A ~30-line harness asserting empty-solution pass@1 == 0.000 under each pinned evalplus version must run alongside the replication matrix, or the "single trusted grader" premise is itself untested.

lens.title: Cost-Unit Inversion: The Choice of Cost Axis, Not the Method, Decides the Diffusion-LM Efficiency Frontier
lens.claim: For masked diffusion LMs, the Pareto frontier of quality vs. cost is not a property of the method but of the cost unit: the SAME set of measured configurations yields disjoint, non-overlapping frontiers under (a) tokens-processed, (b) wall-clock latency, and (c) FLOPs. Concretely, on HumanEval+ our structural runtime is 25.1x cheaper than vanilla nfe512 in tokens processed (13,980 vs 350,832) yet is simultaneously 1.71x SLOWER (19.38s vs 11.31s) and 0.53 worse in pass@1 -- i.e. it owns the token-cost frontier while being strictly Pareto-DOMINATED under wall-clock. Any diffusion-LM efficiency claim that reports one unit is therefore unfalsifiable without the others.
lens.why_now: The 2025-2026 dLLM efficiency literature is exploding (Fast-dLLM, dKV-Cache, Elastic-Cache 2510.14973, dInfer 2510.08666, FOCUS 2601.23278, BlockServe 2607.08930, DiLaServe 2606.29094, Sangam 2607.04206) and each picks its own unit: NFE, tokens/s at batch 1, or throughput at large batch. CaRE (2607.24763, 2026-06-04, CONCURRENT) is the first attempt to standardize -- and it standardizes precisely the unit we can PROVE is unfair across families, and does so on MAUVE/OpenWebText rather than executable pass@1. We already hold the falsifying measurement in hand.
lens.experiment: All quantities are already logged per-task in runs/*/metrics.rank*.jsonl (elapsed_seconds, peak_memory_gib, cumulative_model_tokens, nfe) across 11 HE+ and 11 MBPP+ configurations -- so the core result exists TODAY at zero GPU cost. Deliverable: (1) recompute the frontier under 4 units (tokens processed, wall-clock, analytic prefill-FLOPs = calls x seq_len^2 attention + seq_len x params, peak memory) for Dream-Coder-Instruct nfe{16,32,64,128,256,512,1024} + scaffold {tiny,small,medium,large} on HE+/MBPP+, and report the frontier membership set per unit (measured: tokens-frontier = {scaffold tiny, small, medium, vanilla nfe256, nfe512}; seconds-frontier on HE+ = {nfe16, nfe64, nfe128, nfe256, nfe512} -- scaffold vanishes entirely). (2) Add the missing controlled axis: re-run the 7-point NFE sweep at batch in {1,2,4,8,16,32} to show the ordering moves again with batch. (3) Publish a cost-reporting checklist + the per-task telemetry as an artifact. Mandatory self-falsification section: our own prior 'structural runtime owns the low-cost frontier' claim survives ONLY under tokens and is retracted under wall-clock.
lens.assets_needed: HAVE: all 22 run dirs with per-task elapsed_seconds + peak_memory_gib + cumulative_model_tokens (verified present); models/Dream-Coder-v0-Instruct-7B; models/Scaffold-v0-stage1-7B; data/evalplus/*; evalplus 0.3.1; 8x L20A. MISSING/FLAG: (a) no vLLM or SGLang in /opt/conda/envs/dllm-env (pip list shows only torch 2.11 + transformers 4.51.3), so any AR-side throughput number would be unfairly slow -- either install a real serving stack or scope the paper to diffusion-vs-diffusion; (b) batch>1 path in scripts/generate_evalplus_dream.py is currently one-task-per-forward and must be batched; (c) L20A-only results need one replication on .252 (B200) or .73 (H20) to show the inversion is not hardware-specific.
lens.kill_criterion: Falsified if the frontier membership set is identical under all cost units after adding per-request fixed overhead correctly (i.e. if the inversion is an artifact of our 0.589s measured per-request fixed cost rather than a real per-call arithmetic-intensity gap). Also killed if, once batching is implemented, scaffold's per-call latency drops to parity with vanilla's 22.1 ms/call -- that would mean the 302.4 ms/call we measured is a harness artifact, not a roofline property. Quantitative bar: the inversion must persist with >=2x separation on both HE+ and MBPP+ and on >=2 GPU types.
lens.builds_on: Follow-up on 'Beyond Next-Token Prediction: A Performance Characterization of Diffusion versus Autoregressive Language Models' (arXiv:2510.04146, 2025-10-05, NOT concurrent -- the closest prior audit). It establishes arithmetic intensity + batching + block-decoding scaling, but three defects we repair: (i) it profiles performance WITHOUT an iso-quality control, so it never shows a frontier reversing; (ii) it never reconciles cost units across model families, which is exactly where we measured a 3.1x tokens/call gap co-occurring with a 13.7x ms/call gap (43x utilization gap); (iii) it does not use executable correctness (pass@1) as the quality axis. Differentiation from CaRE (concurrent): CaRE standardizes NFE; we show NFE and tokens are BOTH insufficient and that wall-clock reverses the ranking. Differentiation from 'Diffusion Language Models: An Experimental Analysis' (2606.19475, 2026-06-17, CONCURRENT): broad quality+efficiency survey, but no cost-unit reconciliation and no demonstrated frontier inversion.

related_work.citation: Dehghani, Tay, Arnab, Beyer, Vaswani. "The Efficiency Misnomer." arXiv:2110.12894; ICLR 2022.
related_work.venue_status: ICLR 2022 (Conference and Workshop Papers) — verified via DBLP API, which lists both the 2022 ICLR entry and the 2021 CoRR preprint. OpenReview api2 search did not surface it (returned unrelated hits), so venue rests on DBLP.
related_work.what_it_covers: The canonical statement of the general thesis: common cost indicators (params, FLOPs, throughput, latency) are assumed correlated but can contradict each other; incomplete reporting yields misleading efficiency conclusions. Demonstrates contradictory rankings across indicators for vision/NLP Transformers and proposes reporting multiple indicators.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Entirely pre-diffusion, pre-iterative-decoding. All models are single-forward-pass; there is no notion of NFE, denoising steps, or a decode loop whose per-call sequence length differs between methods. No executable-correctness quality axis. No demonstration that the *Pareto frontier membership set* (as opposed to a scalar ranking) becomes disjoint. No per-task telemetry artifact.
related_work.known_defects: Contradictions are shown as ranking flips on scalar comparisons, not as disjoint frontier-membership sets over a swept configuration family; no formal criterion for when an indicator is admissible; no treatment of aggregation estimator (mean vs median vs paired) as an independent source of flips, which our data shows is as large as the unit choice itself.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv abs page (proxy curl, citation_title + submission-history v1 2021-10-25, v2 2022-03-16); DBLP publ API for venue.

related_work.citation: Kim et al. (submitter Minseo Kim). "Beyond Next-Token Prediction: A Performance Characterization of Diffusion versus Autoregressive Language Models." arXiv:2510.04146.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (CoRR only) — DBLP lists it as 2025 CoRR with no conference entry; no OpenReview record found via api2 title search. v1 2025-10-05, v2 2025-12-15.
related_work.what_it_covers: The closest prior systems audit. Theory + empirical profiling of ARM vs DLM: arithmetic intensity, failure to scale with context, block-wise decoding decoupling intensity from sequence length, batched inference (ARMs benefit more from batch parallelism), and the conclusion that step reduction is the key lever for DLM latency.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: No iso-quality control — it profiles cost surfaces without a downstream-accuracy axis, so it can never exhibit a frontier reversing. No cross-family reconciliation of cost units (it does not ask what happens if you re-plot the same configs under tokens vs seconds vs FLOPs). Quality is absent entirely, so executable correctness (pass@1) is untested. No structured/non-flat-canvas decoder in scope.
related_work.known_defects: (i) Absence of a quality axis means every claim is about the cost surface alone, and the paper's own recommendation ('reduce sampling steps') is untested against the quality cost of doing so — precisely the trade our NFE sweep measures (nfe512→256 costs .152 pass@1 on HE+). (ii) Batching conclusions are drawn on the profiling harness rather than a production serving stack, the same defect Speculative Decoding: Performance or Illusion? documents for SD. (iii) Single hardware generation, so the arithmetic-intensity conclusions are asserted rather than shown to be roofline-invariant.

related_work.citation: Chakraborty et al. "CaRE: Compute-aware Remasking Evaluation Protocol for Masked Diffusion Language Models." arXiv:2607.24763.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint. arXiv v1 timestamp Thu, 4 Jun 2026 22:21:08 UTC, citation_date 2026/06/04, single version, comments field 'updated version'. No OpenReview record under this title (api2 exact-title search returned only an unrelated SPIGM/AdaptFM workshop paper). NOTE: the arXiv identifier prefix 2607 is inconsistent with a June-4 v1 date; I could not resolve which is authoritative, but both readings are on/after 2026-05-07 so concurrency is unaffected.
related_work.what_it_covers: The direct competitor for the standardization framing: audits 7 MDLM remasking strategies on LLaDA-8B-Base and Dream-7B-Base by standardizing *actual* NFE, enforcing multi-metric reporting, and controlling stochasticity; finds temperature explains most MAUVE variance and that compute-matched comparison reverses several published rankings. Releases protocol + 12-model leaderboard (150M–8B).
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: It standardizes on NFE — the single unit our measurement shows is inadmissible across decoder families, because scaffold's per-call sequence is ~186–332 tokens vs vanilla's 685-token flat canvas (a 2–3.7x tokens/call gap) while per-call latency differs by up to 13.7x. CaRE is also diffusion-vs-diffusion within one flat-canvas decoder family, on MAUVE/OpenWebText/LM1B — no executable correctness, no wall-clock or FLOPs axis, and no frontier-membership analysis.
related_work.known_defects: (i) NFE-only compute matching silently assumes all methods pay the same cost per function evaluation; this is false the moment the canvas length or the attended prefix differs between arms, which our runs measure directly. (ii) MAUVE as the primary quality metric is itself a contested construct and is temperature-confounded, which the paper reports but then continues to rank on. (iii) 'Compute-matched comparisons reverse several published rankings' is demonstrated only under their one unit, so the reversal is not shown to be stable under a second unit — the exact hole our result fills.

diff.differentiation_statement: Nothing in the literature makes this claim in this setting, and the two papers that come closest each leave the exact hole we fill. The Efficiency Misnomer (ICLR 2022) established the general thesis — cost indicators can contradict each other — but for single-forward-pass vision/NLP models, where there is no denoising loop, no NFE, and no per-call sequence-length asymmetry between methods; it shows scalar ranking flips, not disjoint Pareto-frontier membership sets. arXiv:2510.04146 (2025-10-05, the closest prior dLLM systems audit, CoRR-only) profiles the AR-vs-DLM cost surface with no quality axis at all, so it structurally cannot exhibit a frontier reversal, and it never re-plots a fixed configuration set under alternative units. CaRE (concurrent, 2026-06-04) is the only attempt to standardize dLLM compute reporting, and it standardizes on NFE within a single flat-canvas decoder family, scored by MAUVE on OpenWebText/LM1B — whereas our measurement shows NFE is inadmissible the moment the attended sequence per call differs between arms (we measure 186–332 tokens/call for a structured runtime against a 685-token flat canvas, a 2–3.7x tokens/call gap co-occurring with a per-call latency gap of up to 13.7x). The concurrent IJCAI-ECAI 2026 survey (2026-07-14) proposes a latency-decomposition framework precisely because these factors "are often conflated in existing benchmarks", but supplies guidelines without a falsification experiment. Our differentiators are therefore concrete and stackable: (1) executable correctness (evalplus pass@1+, n=164/378) as the quality axis rather than MAUVE or no quality axis at all; (2) two structurally different decoder families — flat-canvas diffusion and a typed-AST structural runtime — rather than variants of one; (3) frontier *membership sets* per unit as the reported object, not scalar rankings; (4) a matched Plain-SFT control (same base checkpoint, split, corruption weighting, trainer, scaffold machinery removed) that reaches the frontier at zero points, which no cost-unit paper has; and (5) released per-task telemetry (elapsed_seconds, peak_memory_gib, cumulative_model_tokens, nfe across 22 run directories) so the re-accounting is auditable rather than asserted. The genre precedent a reviewer will invoke is Speculative Decoding: Performance or Illusion? (2025-12-31), which is a different acceleration family and a different confounder (prototype-vs-production, batch size); we are the diffusion-side, cost-unit analogue, and we should cite it as the template we are extending rather than pretend it does not exist.

followup_openings.target_paper: CaRE: Compute-aware Remasking Evaluation Protocol (arXiv:2607.24763, concurrent 2026-06-04)
followup_openings.defect: CaRE standardizes on "actual NFE" as the compute unit, which assumes every function evaluation costs the same. That assumption fails whenever arms differ in attended sequence per call. Our telemetry measures the failure directly: a structured runtime attends 186-332 tokens/call while vanilla re-attends a 685-token flat canvas every step, so NFE-matching hands the structured arm a 2-3.7x free multiplier. CaRE's headline finding ("compute-matched comparisons reverse several published strategy rankings") is thus demonstrated under one unit and never shown stable under a second.
followup_openings.our_fix: Re-run CaRE's own protocol logic on our configuration set under four units (tokens processed, wall-clock, analytic prefill-FLOPs, peak memory) and report the frontier-membership set per unit. Show that NFE-matching and token-matching give different winners, so the fix to "incompatible settings" is not a better single unit but mandatory multi-unit frontier reporting. Because CaRE is concurrent, this is a citable extension, not a competition.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It converts our result from "a measurement we happen to have" into the missing validity test for the field's first standardization proposal, and it inherits CaRE's framing and audience.

followup_openings.target_paper: Accelerating Masked Diffusion LLMs: A Survey (arXiv:2607.12829, IJCAI-ECAI 2026 Survey Track, concurrent 2026-07-14)
followup_openings.defect: The survey proposes a unified latency-decomposition framework explicitly to disentangle factors "often conflated in existing benchmarks", and closes with reproducible-benchmarking guidelines — but as a survey it supplies no experiment in which following the guidelines overturns a conclusion. Guidelines with no falsification case are exactly as unfalsifiable as the benchmarks they critique.
followup_openings.our_fix: Supply the missing empirical case study: instantiate their decomposition on our 22 measured configurations, and exhibit at least one concrete conclusion (our own prior "structural runtime owns the low-cost frontier") that survives under one unit and is retracted under another. Publish the per-task telemetry as the artifact their guidelines call for.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: A survey-track framework plus a paper that validates it is a natural citation pair; we become the reference implementation of a framework an accepted venue already blessed, which is far cheaper than establishing the framing ourselves.

followup_openings.target_paper: Beyond Next-Token Prediction (arXiv:2510.04146, 2025-10-05, not concurrent)
followup_openings.defect: Three repairable defects, as the candidate states, and the first is the load-bearing one: the paper profiles cost with no quality axis, so its central prescription — "reducing the number of sampling steps is key for open-source DLMs to achieve lower latency relative to ARMs" — is never priced against the quality it destroys. It also draws batching conclusions from a profiling harness rather than a production engine, and never reconciles cost units across families.
followup_openings.our_fix: Price their prescription. Our NFE sweep is exactly the experiment they omit: nfe512->256 buys 1.85x lower latency and costs .152 pass@1 on HumanEval+ (.707->.555); nfe512->128 buys 3.2x and costs .567 (->.140); nfe512->1024 buys nothing at all (exactly 0 gain, so the step-count lever is already saturated at their recommended operating point). Add the iso-quality control they lack and report the step-reduction lever as a frontier, not a direction.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This is the single strongest and cheapest repair available: it is pre-cutoff prior art (so it genuinely preempts nothing), it is CoRR-only (so it is not entrenched), and the fix requires zero new GPU hours because the sweep already exists.

followup_openings.target_paper: FOCUS (arXiv:2601.23278, ICML 2026, verified via OpenReview venueid ICML.cc/2026/Conference)
followup_openings.defect: FOCUS accelerates by evicting non-decodable tokens on the fly, which reduces attended tokens per call. That is a mechanism whose reported benefit is intrinsically unit-sensitive: a tokens-processed or NFE accounting credits the eviction while charging nothing for the eviction bookkeeping, which is paid in wall-clock. The abstract shows no evidence the gains were checked at multiple batch sizes or on a second GPU family.
followup_openings.our_fix: Add FOCUS (and the two canonical accelerators it builds on, Fast-dLLM 2505.22618 and dKV-Cache 2505.15781) as arms in the multi-unit re-accounting, using dInfer (2510.08666) as the standardized substrate so the comparison is not harness-limited. Report per-unit frontier membership for each.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: Re-auditing an ICML-accepted acceleration system under a unit its authors did not report is the highest-visibility version of this paper, and it converts our thesis from a claim about our own arms into a claim about the field's published results.

followup_openings.target_paper: Our own candidate as written (self-repair, highest priority)
followup_openings.defect: I recomputed the headline from the run directories and found three problems that a reviewer would find first. (1) SIGN FLIP ACROSS BENCHMARKS: on MBPP+ the structural runtime is FASTER, not slower — scaffold medium 5.382s vs vanilla nfe512 10.573s, a 1.97x speedup, while tokens are 43.7x cheaper (7,080 vs 309,248). The claimed inversion holds on HumanEval+ (19.379s vs 11.306s = 1.71x slower) and reverses on MBPP+. The candidate's own kill criterion demands ">=2x separation on both HE+ and MBPP+" in the stated direction, and the existing data already violates it. (2) MEAN-VS-TAIL ARTIFACT: the HE+ inversion is carried by a heavy tail, not the typical task. Paired per-task, scaffold medium is faster on 84/164 tasks (51.2%) and the median paired ratio is 0.965 — statistical parity; the top-10 slowest tasks carry 24% of scaffold's total time. For scaffold Large the mean is 54.62s but the median is 3.42s, and 11 error/budget-capped tasks consume 190k-251k tokens each; excluding capped tasks the mean falls to 10.41s and ms/call from 523 to 182. (3) ESTIMATOR-DEPENDENT PER-CALL GAP: the 302.4 ms/call figure is a ratio-of-means; median-of-ratios is 212.5 (medium HE+), 71.9 (large HE+), 19.6-20.7 (MBPP+) — i.e. the "13.7x ms/call gap vs vanilla's 22.1 ms/call" ranges from ~13.7x to ~0.9x depending purely on the estimator. Vanilla is estimator-insensitive (22.1 by all three), which makes the asymmetry look like a method property when it is partly an aggregation choice.
followup_openings.our_fix: Promote the aggregation estimator to a FOURTH axis alongside the three cost units, and make the benchmark sign flip the centrepiece rather than an embarrassment. The sharpened thesis becomes strictly stronger: frontier membership is jointly determined by (unit, estimator, benchmark), and we can demonstrate all three flips on one measured configuration set — including a case where the same two systems trade places between HumanEval+ and MBPP+ under the same unit. Report mean, median, and paired per-task distributions for every cell; state capped-task handling explicitly (this is the same failure class as the candidate's own retraction #3, so pre-empting it is mandatory); and restate the kill criterion in terms of "at least one frontier-membership disagreement that survives all three estimators" rather than a fixed >=2x latency gap in a fixed direction.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: As written, a reviewer who recomputes from the released telemetry retracts the headline in one afternoon: the MBPP+ number goes the other way and the HE+ median is parity. Reframed, the same data supports a broader and more defensible claim, and the estimator axis is novel relative to every paper found — CaRE controls stochasticity, the Eval-Illusion paper controls prompt template, BlockServe engineers the tail away, but nobody treats mean-vs-median-vs-paired aggregation over a heavy-tailed decode workload as a conclusion-flipping variable.

followup_openings.target_paper: BlockServe (2607.08930, concurrent) + DiLaServe (2606.29094, concurrent) + Sangam (2607.04206, concurrent)
followup_openings.defect: All three are batch/serving-side and all three report throughput or SLO attainment — units that hide the quality axis entirely (SLO can be attained by degrading confidence thresholds). BlockServe additionally documents "convergence heterogeneity" causing stragglers and tail latency, and treats it purely as a scheduling defect to engineer away.
followup_openings.our_fix: Use convergence heterogeneity as evidence rather than as a bug: it is the mechanism that predicts our batch>1 ordering will move, and it is the same heavy-tail structure that makes our mean-based HE+ latency misleading. Run the 7-point NFE sweep at batch in {1,2,4,8,16,32} (requires batching the currently one-task-per-forward path in scripts/generate_evalplus_dream.py) and show the frontier membership set changing with batch as a fourth flip, citing BlockServe for the mechanism. Scope the AR-side comparison out unless a real serving stack (dInfer, or vLLM for the AR arm) is installed — our env has only torch 2.11 + transformers 4.51.3, so any AR throughput number would be unfairly slow and is a reviewer trap.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It makes the batch leg mechanistically motivated by concurrent work instead of an arbitrary sweep, and it pre-empts the strongest systems objection ("your batch-1 numbers are meaningless") which is exactly what sank the prototype-based SD evaluations.

diff.sharpened_claim: For masked diffusion LMs, quality-vs-cost Pareto frontier membership is not a property of the method but a joint artifact of three reporting choices — the cost unit, the aggregation estimator, and the benchmark — and we demonstrate all three flips on a single, already-measured set of 22 configurations (Dream-Coder-Instruct nfe{16..1024} plus a typed-AST structural runtime at four capacity tiers, plus a matched Plain-SFT control) scored by executable correctness (evalplus pass@1+, n=164/378). (1) UNIT: on HumanEval+ the structural runtime is 25.1x cheaper in tokens processed (13,980 vs 350,720) yet 1.71x slower in mean wall-clock (19.38s vs 11.31s), so it holds the token frontier while being Pareto-dominated under seconds; the tokens-frontier is {tiny, small, medium, nfe256, nfe512} while the HE+ seconds-frontier is {nfe16, nfe64, nfe128, nfe256, nfe512} and the structural arm vanishes entirely. (2) ESTIMATOR: that same wall-clock inversion is carried by the tail, not the typical task — paired per-task the structural arm is faster on 84/164 tasks with a median ratio of 0.965 (parity), the top-10 slowest tasks carry 24% of its total time, and the per-call latency gap vs vanilla's estimator-invariant 22.1 ms/call ranges from 13.7x (ratio-of-means) to ~0.9x (median-of-ratios) depending only on how one averages. (3) BENCHMARK: the inversion changes sign across task surfaces — on MBPP+ the structural runtime is simultaneously 43.7x cheaper in tokens (7,080 vs 309,248) AND 1.97x faster in wall-clock (5.38s vs 10.57s), so the same two systems trade Pareto places between two code benchmarks under an unchanged unit. Consequently any diffusion-LM efficiency claim reporting one unit, one estimator, and one benchmark is unfalsifiable, and we retract our own prior claim that the structural runtime "owns the low-cost frontier" as holding only under tokens-processed with mean aggregation on HumanEval+. We deliver the four-unit frontier-membership tables (tokens, wall-clock, analytic prefill-FLOPs, peak memory) x three estimators x two benchmarks, a batch in {1,2,4,8,16,32} leg motivated by the convergence heterogeneity that BlockServe documents, a >=2-GPU-family replication, a cost-reporting checklist, and the per-task telemetry (elapsed_seconds, peak_memory_gib, cumulative_model_tokens, nfe) as a released artifact.

feas.risk: The overwhelmingly likely outcome is a NULL that reads as a self-inflicted bug report. Once shape bucketing lands, per-call latency across the two families converges to 1.24x (measured), and per-call cost becomes a near-monotone function of attended sequence length — 11.1 ms at 195 tok, 11.2 at 218, 11.6 at 332, 16.4 at 685. At that point wall-clock is roughly tokens-processed times a nearly constant ms/token, the seconds-frontier collapses onto the tokens-frontier, and all three advertised flips (unit, estimator, benchmark) evaporate simultaneously. The paper's thesis degrades from "the cost axis decides the frontier" to "our harness had a dynamic-shape recompilation pathology, and after fixing it the axes agree" — true, useful internally, and not a main-conference systems result. The second failure mode is confounding rather than nullity: if the team remeasures without fixing the 8-way co-tenancy AND without n>=3 identical-config replicates, any residual inversion is indistinguishable from scheduler noise, given that my own 40-call vanilla arm spanned median 16.8 to p90 36.7 ms on a contended node — a 2.2x spread that is larger than most of the effects being claimed. Third, subtler: the surviving heavy tail will be partly artifactual, because the number of distinct shapes a task visits scales with its number of model calls, so shape-recompile cost and genuine structural difficulty are collinear in the current data and cannot be separated post hoc.
feas.required_control: COST-AXIS VALIDITY CALIBRATION, run per arm, gating entry into any frontier table. For every configuration, measure the same work twice: (a) in the production harness, and (b) in an isolated single-task probe on an idle GPU with warmup discarded and shapes pre-warmed, at matched sequence length. Publish both, and require agreement within a pre-registered tolerance before that arm's number is allowed to appear on a Pareto axis. Any arm failing the check is reported as HARNESS-LIMITED, never as "Pareto-dominated". This is the exact control that would have caught the present failure: in-harness scaffold showed 302 ms/call while the isolated probe at the same 195-332 token lengths shows 11.1-11.6 ms — a 26x discrepancy that no amount of re-averaging the existing telemetry could reveal, because the pollution is inside the number being averaged. Two mandatory sub-clauses. (1) Log and release per-FORWARD (shape, milliseconds) pairs, not per-task scalars. The per-call distribution is bimodal (12 ms vs 2000 ms); reporting any single statistic over a bimodal cost distribution is structurally identical to retraction 3, where a mean over a mixture silently dropped the expensive mode. (2) A replicate is only a replicate if the sampler arguments are byte-identical. r1 vs r2 differ by `--top-p 0.95` and were about to be reported as run-to-run variance while actually differing by .12 in pass@1. This maps onto all three prior retractions: retraction 1 compared nothing and called it a pass; retraction 2 let a stage discard its input and still labelled the output with the input's name; retraction 3 averaged over a mixture and dropped the costly mode. The common root is that no arm was ever required to prove its reported number measures the thing the label claims. This control makes that proof a precondition for publication.

lens.title: The Parallelism Is Never Measured Where the Quality Is: Diffusion Code LMs Report Headline Accuracy at a Definitionally Sequential Operating Point
lens.claim: Masked diffusion code LMs are sold on parallel decoding, but their published headline-quality operating point sets steps == canvas length, which under the reference cosine/linear transfer schedule commits ~1 token per model call -- i.e. ZERO parallelism, and strictly more expensive than autoregressive decoding (a full bidirectional re-attention of prompt+canvas per token instead of one cached incremental forward). Moreover, raising steps ABOVE canvas length is not merely diminishing but definitionally wasted: we compute that steps=1024 on a 512-token canvas spends 514/1024 (50.2%) of steps committing exactly zero tokens, and we measure that it costs 2.14x the wall-clock of steps=512 to produce output that is 99.4% (HE+) / 99.5% (MBPP+) BYTE-IDENTICAL.
lens.why_now: Upstream Dream-Coder's own eval script (vendor/Dream-Coder/instruct/code_eval/evalplus/eval.sh) uses `--max_new_tokens 768 --diffusion_steps 768`, and our reproduction that MATCHES its published numbers (HE+ .707, MBPP+ .680, MBPP +1.1 over paper) uses steps=512=canvas. So the entire quality-vs-AR comparison in this literature is conducted at the one setting where the parallelism advantage is exactly 1.0x. Meanwhile a large 2026 acceleration literature reports speedups relative to this same inflated baseline, which mechanically inflates every published speedup factor.
lens.experiment: Three legs, all cheap and mostly already done. (1) SCHEDULE AUDIT (no GPU): from models/Dream-Coder-v0-Instruct-7B/generation_utils.py lines 406-439, the transfer count is int(num_mask*(1-s/t)) with timesteps=linspace(1,eps,steps+1); simulate commits-per-step for steps in {16..2048} x canvas in {256,512,768,1024} and tabulate (useful steps, zero-commit steps, step at which the canvas closes). Measured already: steps=512 -> commit trajectory [0,1,1,1,...,2], i.e. 1 tok/call; steps=1024 -> 514 zero-commit steps; steps=2048 -> 1539 (75.1%). (2) IDENTITY CHECK (done): 163/164 and 376/378 solutions byte-identical between steps=512 and steps=1024 -- so the 'exact 0.0 quality gain at 512->1024' we previously reported is not a model plateau but a schedule no-op, and must be rewritten as such. (3) DECOUPLING GRID (the new measurement): sweep steps in {32,64,128,256,512} x canvas in {256,512,768} independently, reporting pass@1, mean tokens committed per call, wall-clock, and unparseable rate -- yielding the first quality-vs-actual-parallelism curve for a diffusion code LM, and identifying the largest steps<canvas setting that retains .707/.680.
lens.assets_needed: HAVE: models/Dream-Coder-v0-Instruct-7B/generation_utils.py (schedule source, read and verified); vendor/Dream-Coder upstream eval.sh proving the steps==canvas convention is upstream and not ours; all 14 existing NFE-sweep run dirs; solutions.jsonl for the byte-identity check (done); scripts/generate_evalplus_dream.py already exposes --steps and --max-new-tokens separately, so leg (3) needs no new code. MISSING/FLAG: replication on a second checkpoint family is needed to claim generality -- LLaDA-8B-Instruct and DiffuCoder-7B are NOT on either disk (checked wzc1 models/ and dllm_draft/models/, and zwfy6) and would need a proxied HuggingFace download.
lens.kill_criterion: Killed if leg (3) shows that steps<canvas materially degrades quality at every setting -- i.e. if .707/.680 genuinely REQUIRES 1-token-per-call, then 'sequential at the quality point' is an unavoidable property of the model rather than an unexamined convention, and the paper becomes a much weaker note. Specifically: if no (steps, canvas) pair with steps <= canvas/2 reaches within 0.02 of .707 on HE+, the reformulation dies. Also killed if the byte-identity is an artifact of greedy-ish sampling at T=0.1 rather than schedule no-ops (control: repeat at T=0.7, where identity should break but the zero-commit step count must not).
lens.builds_on: Nearest neighbour is 'Neither Parallel Nor Sequential: How DiffusionGemma Actually Commits Tokens' (arXiv:2606.14620, 2026-06-12, CONCURRENT -- does not preempt). It instruments commit ORDER on DiffusionGemma 26B and independently notes commitment 'finishes in a short late burst well inside the step budget', which corroborates our no-op finding on a different model. Differences: it studies decoding ORDER and its measurement artifacts, not cost accounting; it does not connect the burst to the steps>=canvas convention, does not show byte-identical outputs across step budgets, and does not audit the benchmark recipe under which headline accuracy is published. Our contribution is the accounting consequence: every speedup reported against a steps==canvas baseline is inflated by a factor we can compute exactly from the schedule.

diff.sharpened_claim: The reference cosine/linear mask-transfer schedule shipped with Dream-family masked diffusion code LMs makes the number of denoising steps a *nominal* rather than an *effective* compute knob, and the community's headline-quality convention (steps == canvas length, upstream `--max_new_tokens 768 --diffusion_steps 768`) sits exactly at the degenerate end of that mapping. We prove this by arithmetic, not by fitting: because the per-step transfer count is `int(num_masked * (1 - s/t))` with `t` on `linspace(1, eps, steps+1)`, the schedule commits ceil-1 token per model call whenever steps == canvas, and for steps > canvas it emits a computable number of *strictly zero-commit* steps -- 514/1024 (50.2%) at canvas=512, 1539/2048 (75.1%), and 770/1024 (75.2%) at canvas=256 -- which we verify are true no-ops by showing 163/164 (HE+) and 376/378 (MBPP+) outputs are BYTE-IDENTICAL between steps=512 and steps=1024 while wall-clock rises 2.14x/2.18x. The consequence is an accounting correction, and it cuts in a direction that is uncomfortable for us as well as for the field: (i) since the loop has no KV cache and no early exit, the published headline point is *strictly more expensive per token* than autoregressive decoding, so the field's flagship quality numbers are obtained at parallelism exactly 1.0x; (ii) any acceleration paper that reports speedup against a steps==canvas (or worse, steps>canvas) baseline inherits a multiplicative inflation factor we can compute in closed form from the schedule alone, with no GPU; and (iii) our own previously-reported "exact 0.0 quality gain from 512->1024 steps" must be retracted and rewritten -- it was never a model saturation plateau, it is a schedule no-op. We further show the quality end of the curve genuinely *requires* the sequential point on this checkpoint: at fixed canvas=512, pass@1+ falls .707 -> .555 -> .140 at steps 512 -> 256 -> 128 (HE+) and .680 -> .545 -> .233 (MBPP+), i.e. no steps <= canvas/2 setting comes within 0.02 of the headline. So the contribution is not "you can get the same quality cheaper"; it is that the headline operating point is definitionally non-parallel, that this is a property of the *reference schedule* (which allocates its transfer mass so that the last-mile tokens each get their own full forward pass) rather than an inevitability of masked diffusion, and that the baseline convention silently inflates a whole 2026 speedup literature.
diff.differentiation_statement: The closest works divide cleanly into (a) pre-cutoff papers that touch the step-count knob but frame it as a model property, and (b) concurrent papers that audit dLLM evaluation but not this convention. On (a): DiffuCoder (arXiv v1 2025-06-25, ICLR 2026 Poster) is the one genuine pre-cutoff overlap -- its Figure 11 / Appx C.3 measures exactly steps=L vs steps=L/2 on HumanEval/HumanEval+/MBPP/MBPP+, states "1x means the default setting where decoding timesteps are equal to the sequence length", and reports drops of -9.4% to -30.6%. Crucially, DiffuCoder interprets that drop as a *model* property ("AR-ness"), using it as a diagnostic of how non-autoregressive a checkpoint has become and as a target for RL to improve; it never asks whether the 1x point itself is a sensible baseline, never computes the schedule's commits-per-call, never identifies zero-commit steps, and never observes that steps>L is a no-op. Our claim is the complementary and strictly stronger one: the 1x point is *definitionally* one-token-per-call under the shipped schedule, so DiffuCoder's "1x" is not a parallel baseline at all but a sequential one that is more expensive per token than AR (no KV cache, full bidirectional re-attention of prompt+canvas each call, verified by reading the generate loop) -- which reframes their own -9.4%..-30.6% numbers as the cost of buying *any* parallelism at all rather than as a checkpoint-quality signal. On (b): CaRE (v1 2026-06-04, concurrent; the OpenReview-visible variant "Re-evaluating Confidence Remasking in Masked Diffusion Language Models" is an ICML 2026 SPIGM/AdaptFM workshop poster) standardises *actual NFE* across remasking strategies and shows compute-matched comparison reverses published rankings -- but it audits remasking strategies on OpenWebText/LM1B with MAUVE, i.e. a different object (which sampler wins), a different task surface (open-ended LM, not verifier-graded code), and a different lever (it equalises NFE rather than exposing that NFE overstates work); it never treats steps>canvas as arithmetic waste. The DiffusionGemma commit-order paper (2606.14620, v1 2026-06-12, concurrent) independently observes commitment "finishing in a short late burst well inside the step budget" on a different model family, which corroborates us, but its subject is decoding ORDER and the measurement artifacts that manufacture spurious order results; it makes no cost claim and no baseline-inflation claim. Fast-dLLM (v1 2025-05-28, ICLR 2026 Poster) is the origin of the practice we critique -- it correctly notes open dLLMs lag AR "due to the lack of KV Cache" and reports up to 27.6x throughput, but its baseline is precisely the uncached steps==canvas configuration, so it is a *target* of our accounting correction, not prior art for it. SureLock (2602.06412, ICLR 2026 Poster) and the length-aware cropping work (2603.06123) both attack dLLM compute waste but along orthogonal axes -- redundant recomputation at *already-committed positions*, and an oversized *canvas* for short responses respectively -- neither notices that the *step axis* itself contains provably empty steps at the field's default setting. Beyond the differentiation, our sharpest reviewer-facing move is that the correction is adversarial to our own prior claim: we retract "exact 0.0 gain at 512->1024 is a saturation plateau" and replace it with "it is a schedule no-op, and we can predict the exact number of wasted steps before running anything."

followup_openings.target_paper: Fast-dLLM: Training-free Acceleration of Diffusion LLM by Enabling KV Cache and Parallel Decoding (arXiv:2505.22618, v1 2025-05-28; ICLR 2026 Poster per OpenReview venueid ICLR.cc/2026/Conference)
followup_openings.defect: Headline "up to 27.6x throughput" is measured against the vanilla open-weight dLLM sampler at the steps==canvas convention with no KV cache. Under the reference schedule that baseline commits ~1 token per full bidirectional forward pass over prompt+canvas, so it is a *sequential-and-uncached* reference, i.e. slower per token than plain AR decoding. The speedup factor therefore conflates two very different wins -- (i) removing an accounting artifact that nobody should have paid for, and (ii) genuine algorithmic parallelism -- and the paper never decomposes them. The problem compounds if any measurement used steps>canvas, where a computable fraction of steps commit exactly zero tokens (50.2% at steps=1024/canvas=512).
followup_openings.our_fix: Publish a closed-form schedule audit that converts any (steps, canvas) baseline spec into (useful steps, zero-commit steps, mean tokens committed per model call), then re-express Fast-dLLM-class speedups against a *schedule-corrected* reference: the smallest steps that still closes the canvas at the same quality. Report the correction as an explicit multiplicative deflator per paper. This needs zero GPU and zero reimplementation -- only the baseline's declared steps and canvas, both always reported.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It retroactively re-scales the headline number of essentially every 2026 dLLM acceleration paper (we found 30+ in a single arXiv query, including Fast-dLLM++, dInfer, BlockBatch, LEAP, DAWN, Optimus, PSD, Polestar). Reviewers can apply the deflator themselves from the reported config, which makes it a durable evaluation-hygiene contribution rather than a one-off measurement.

followup_openings.target_paper: DiffuCoder: Understanding and Improving Masked Diffusion Models for Code Generation (arXiv:2506.20639, v1 2025-06-25; ICLR 2026 Poster per OpenReview)
followup_openings.defect: DiffuCoder's Figure 11 / Appx C.3 attributes the pass@1 drop when halving steps ("1x" -> "2x", -9.4% to -30.6% on HumanEval/+/MBPP/+) to the checkpoint's "AR-ness", treating it as a model property that RL can improve. But the 1x baseline is `timesteps == sequence length`, which under the shipped `int(num_mask*(1-s/t))` transfer rule commits ~1 token per call by construction. So a large part of the measured drop is the schedule's fixed cost of granting any parallelism at all, not the model's causal bias -- the metric is confounded with the sampler's allocation rule. The paper also never separates steps from canvas: `sequence length` is used both as the canvas and as the step count, so 1x/2x changes two things at once when generations are shorter than the canvas.
followup_openings.our_fix: Run the 2-D decoupling grid the literature never ran: steps x canvas independently (steps in {32,64,128,256,512} x canvas in {256,512,768}), reporting pass@1+ AND mean tokens-committed-per-call AND wall-clock AND unparseable rate per cell. That factorises "drop from halving steps" into a schedule component (predictable from the transfer arithmetic alone, model-free) and a residual model component -- the latter being the only part that deserves the name AR-ness. Our existing canvas-512 runs already pin one column of the grid (steps 16/32/64/128/256/1024), so the marginal cost is the canvas 256 and 768 columns. We should also state plainly that our own data *reproduces* DiffuCoder's qualitative finding (HE+ .707 -> .555 at steps=canvas/2, a -0.152 drop inside their -9.4%..-30.6% band), so this is a reinterpretation of a real effect, not a contradiction of it.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: AR-ness is now used as a training-time target (coupled-GRPO explicitly optimises for a smaller drop at 2x). If a chunk of the drop is schedule arithmetic rather than model causality, then RL objectives tuned to shrink it are partly optimising against a sampler constant, and the metric needs a schedule-free redefinition before it can guide training.

followup_openings.target_paper: CaRE: Compute-aware Remasking Evaluation Protocol for Masked Diffusion Language Models (arXiv:2607.24763, v1 2026-06-04, CONCURRENT; workshop variant "Re-evaluating Confidence Remasking..." = ICML 2026 SPIGM + AdaptFM Poster per OpenReview)
followup_openings.defect: CaRE standardises *actual NFE* and shows compute-matched comparison reverses published remasking rankings -- but it stops one level short. NFE counts model calls; it does not count *productive* model calls. Under the reference schedule a nontrivial fraction of calls commit zero tokens, so two configurations can be NFE-matched while differing in useful work. CaRE also evaluates on OpenWebText/LM1B with MAUVE, a metric with no notion of task success, and (by its own account) one where temperature explains most of the variance -- so it cannot say whether the compute-accounting problem changes any *capability* conclusion. Finally its object is remasking strategy choice, not the benchmark recipe under which headline accuracy is published.
followup_openings.our_fix: Extend NFE-matching to *effective*-NFE-matching: report zero-commit-step count and mean tokens/call alongside NFE, so a compute-matched comparison is also a work-matched one. Then instantiate it where CaRE cannot -- on verifier-graded code (EvalPlus HumanEval+/MBPP+, pass@1+ via evalplus untrusted_check, n=164/378), which has an unambiguous correctness signal instead of MAUVE, and on the exact upstream-shipped recipe (Dream-Coder `--max_new_tokens 768 --diffusion_steps 768`) rather than a synthetic step grid. Cite CaRE as concurrent and converging, and position ours as the capability-benchmark + effective-work complement.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: CaRE establishes that MDLM evaluation conflates compute with algorithm; we establish that the compute unit itself (NFE) is inflated by the default schedule, and that the inflation is exactly computable. Together these close the loop from "rankings are incomparable" to "here is the closed-form correction, and here is what it does to a task-success metric."

followup_openings.target_paper: Neither Parallel Nor Sequential: How DiffusionGemma Actually Commits Tokens (arXiv:2606.14620, v1 2026-06-12, CONCURRENT -- verified on arXiv abs page, citation_date 2026/06/12, no venue comment)
followup_openings.defect: Reports that commitment "finish[es] in a short late burst well inside the step budget" on DiffusionGemma 26B and that task accuracy matches its AR Gemma-4 sibling, but treats the late burst purely as a decoding-ORDER observation. It never asks what the steps *outside* the burst cost, never connects the burst to the steps>=canvas convention that produced its step budget, never demonstrates the strongest possible evidence of no-op-ness (byte-identical outputs across step budgets), and never draws the cost conclusion that "accuracy matches AR" was obtained while spending more compute per token than AR.
followup_openings.our_fix: Supply the cost half they left on the table, and make the no-op claim falsifiable rather than inferential: byte-identity of outputs across steps=512 vs 1024 (163/164 HE+, 376/378 MBPP+) with 2.14x/2.18x measured wall-clock, plus the arithmetic that predicts the exact zero-commit count before any run. Also add the sampling control they lack -- repeat at T=0.7 where byte-identity must break while the zero-commit step count must not, separating "identical because near-greedy" from "identical because the steps were empty". Cite them as independent corroboration on a second model family, which strengthens both papers.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: Their model is a 26B MoE built on Gemma 4; ours is a 7B dense Qwen2.5-Coder-derived masked diffusion LM. Two families showing the same late-burst/no-op structure turns a single-checkpoint curiosity into a property of the reference schedule family, which is what licenses the field-wide accounting correction.

followup_openings.target_paper: Stopping Computation for Converged Tokens in Masked Diffusion-LM Decoding (SureLock, arXiv:2602.06412, v1 2026-02-06; ICLR 2026 Poster per OpenReview venueid ICLR.cc/2026/Conference) and Diffusion Language Models Are Natively Length-Aware (arXiv:2603.06123, v1 2026-03-06)
followup_openings.defect: Both correctly identify dLLM compute waste but on axes orthogonal to the one that dominates at the published operating point. SureLock removes redundant recomputation at *already-committed positions* (30-50% algorithmic FLOP saving on LLaDA-8B); the length-aware work crops an oversized *canvas* for short responses. Neither notices that the *step axis* contains provably empty steps under the default schedule, so both measure their savings relative to a baseline that already contains a free, zero-quality-cost reduction. SureLock's savings in particular are reported "relative to the same sampler without locking", i.e. relative to the inflated reference.
followup_openings.our_fix: Add the missing third axis and show the three are composable and orderable: (steps) schedule waste -> (canvas) length waste -> (positions) recomputation waste. Report each method's saving relative to a schedule-corrected baseline, and check whether the position-locking win survives once the empty steps are removed -- there is a real possibility that locking's benefit is concentrated in exactly the late, low-commit steps that should not have been run at all, in which case its 30-50% is partly double-counting our correction.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: If the three waste axes are not disentangled, the field will stack methods whose reported savings overlap, and aggregate claims will exceed the true headroom. Establishing the ordering (remove empty steps first, since it is free and needs no method) gives subsequent acceleration work a principled reference point.

followup_openings.target_paper: Our own prior result: "exactly 0 pass@1+ gain from steps 512 -> 1024" (dllm_draft/DLLM_RESULTS_20260807.md lines 170-171, 186; runs/dream_instruct_{heplus,mbppplus}_nfe1024)
followup_openings.defect: We reported this as a model *saturation plateau* ("饱和点一致"). It is not. It is a schedule no-op: at canvas=512, steps=1024 spends 514 steps (50.2%) committing exactly zero tokens, so 1024 and 512 are running the same productive trajectory. The correct reading was available for free from the transfer arithmetic. This is the same class of error as our three logged retractions (fake verifier, refinement 'restart' policy discarding the draft, averaging only over non-truncated tasks): treating an artifact of the measurement apparatus as a property of the model. A related self-audit finding: our existing 14-run NFE sweep held canvas fixed at 512 for *every* nfe in {16,32,64,128,256,1024} (verified from process.generated_tokens across all metrics.rank*.jsonl), which means the sweep was already a steps-only sweep at fixed canvas -- so it silently answers the kill_criterion, and it fails it.
followup_openings.our_fix: Retract and rewrite the plateau claim in the paper as a schedule no-op, with the arithmetic and the byte-identity evidence. Simultaneously downgrade the candidate's kill_criterion, which is already falsified by data on disk: no steps <= canvas/2 point comes within 0.02 of .707 (steps=256/canvas=512 gives HE+ .555, MBPP+ .545; steps=128 gives .140/.233). Therefore do NOT frame the paper as "the same quality is available with real parallelism" -- that is false on this checkpoint. Frame it as "the headline point is definitionally sequential, the excess beyond canvas is computably empty, and the quality-vs-effective-parallelism curve is steep", which is true, measured, and still a main-conference accounting result. Keep the T=0.7 control to rule out near-greedy-induced identity.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: Shipping the candidate with its stated kill_criterion intact would have us assert a claim our own data refutes. Reframing pre-emptively converts a fatal reviewer objection into a demonstrated self-correction, and the surviving claim is the one that is unscooped anyway.

related_work.citation: Apple / Wang et al., "DiffuCoder: Understanding and Improving Masked Diffusion Models for Code Generation", arXiv:2506.20639
related_work.venue_status: ICLR 2026 Poster. Verified via OpenReview api2 /notes/search: returns two records for this title, one venue="CoRR 2025" venueid=dblp.org/journals/CORR/2025 and one venue="ICLR 2026 Poster" venueid=ICLR.cc/2026/Conference. arXiv v1 date 2025-06-25 from citation_date meta tag on abs page.
related_work.what_it_covers: THE key pre-cutoff overlap. Trains a 7B masked diffusion code LM on 130B code tokens and systematically studies its denoising behaviour. Introduces local/global "AR-ness" metrics. Explicitly documents the convention we critique: "Both models use a maximum sequence length and diffusion timesteps of 512" and "1x means the default setting where decoding timesteps are equal to the sequence length while 2x means 1/2 fewer steps which will result in 2x speedup." Figure 11 / Appx C.3 measures pass@1 on HumanEval, HumanEval+, MBPP, MBPP+ at 1x vs 2x for several checkpoints, reporting drops of -9.4% to -30.6%, and argues coupled-GRPO reduces AR-ness so the 2x drop shrinks.

Never computes commits-per-model-call for the schedule; never identifies that steps==L implies ~1 token/call by construction; never examines steps>L at all, hence never finds zero-commit steps; never notes that the uncached bidirectional forward makes the 1x point more expensive per token than AR; never separates the step axis from the canvas axis (both are "sequence length"); no wall-clock or byte-identity analysis; no claim about baseline-induced inflation of others' reported speedups.
related_work.known_defects: (1) The AR-ness construct is confounded with the sampler's transfer-allocation rule: part of the 1x->2x drop is the schedule's fixed price for granting any parallelism, not the checkpoint's causal bias -- yet AR-ness is then used as an RL optimisation target (coupled-GRPO), so training may be partly optimising against a sampler constant. (2) steps and canvas are varied together (both = "sequence length"), so 1x/2x changes two variables at once whenever generations are shorter than the canvas. (3) Speedup is asserted definitionally ("1/2 fewer steps which will result in 2x speedup") from step counts, with no wall-clock measurement and no accounting for absence of KV cache. (4) Only two step points (L, L/2) -- no curve, so no way to locate where the quality cliff actually is. (5) GRPO rollouts used diffusion timesteps 256 while eval used 512, a train/eval sampler mismatch that is never controlled.
