related_work.citation: Shah, Chakraborty, Gupta, "CaRE: Compute-aware Remasking Evaluation Protocol for Masked Diffusion Language Models", arXiv:2607.24763
related_work.venue_status: Preprint under this title (arXiv submission history shows only [v1] Thu, 4 Jun 2026, comment "updated version"). An overlapping-scope paper by title "Re-evaluating Confidence Remasking in Masked Diffusion Language Models" is an ICML 2026 workshop poster (SPIGM @ ICML Poster, venueid ICML.cc/2026/Workshop/SPIGM; also AdaptFM Poster, venueid ICML.cc/2026/Workshop/AdaptFM) -- verified via OpenReview api2. I could not establish with certainty that these are the same work under a retitle; treated as concurrent either way.
related_work.what_it_covers: Closest concurrent work on dLLM evaluation accounting. Argues seven recent remasking papers evaluate under incompatible settings (varying nominal step counts, metrics, temperatures) so their rankings are incomparable. Proposes standardising ACTUAL number of function evaluations (NFE), enforcing multi-metric reporting, controlling stochasticity. Applies it to 7 remasking strategies x {LLaDA-8B-Base, Dream-7B-Base} x 4 stochasticity levels x 3 step budgets on OpenWebText/LM1B; finds temperature explains most MAUVE variance and that compute-matched comparison REVERSES several published rankings. Releases a 12-model leaderboard (150M-8B).
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Distinguishes nominal from actual NFE but not productive from unproductive NFE: no notion of zero-commit steps, so NFE-matched configurations can still differ in useful work. Object of study is remasking-strategy choice, not the benchmark recipe under which headline accuracy is published. Task surface is open-ended LM (OpenWebText/LM1B) scored by MAUVE, so no verifier-graded capability conclusion, and (by its own finding) MAUVE is temperature-dominated. Uses BASE checkpoints, not the Instruct models whose EvalPlus numbers are the field's headline. No wall-clock, no byte-identity, no closed-form schedule audit, no claim about inflated speedup factors in the acceleration literature.
related_work.known_defects: MAUVE as the primary metric is weakly connected to the construct "model capability" and the paper itself shows temperature explains most of its variance -- so 'rankings reverse' may partly be a metric-instability result. NFE is adopted as the fair compute unit without validating that a model call = a unit of work under the default schedule (it is not). Base-only checkpoints limit transfer to the deployed Instruct setting. Step budgets limited to 3 points.

related_work.citation: Asaria, Salomone, Gandhi, "Neither Parallel Nor Sequential: How DiffusionGemma Actually Commits Tokens", arXiv:2606.14620
related_work.venue_status: Preprint. arXiv abs page shows no journal-ref and no venue comment field; OpenReview api2 /notes/search for the exact title returned zero records, so no venue claim is supportable.
related_work.what_it_covers: The candidate's stated nearest neighbour, and it does exist as described. Instruments DiffusionGemma 26B (masked discrete-diffusion MoE on Gemma 4), hooking the sampler's accept step to record which canvas positions commit, when, and at what confidence, over a 686-prompt six-regime probe suite. Finds decoding is neither parallel nor block-AR but a partial left-to-right bias whose apparent strength is an artifact of analysis granularity ("block size" is a property of the measuring ruler); commits arrive in large simultaneous batches leaving within-batch order genuinely undefined; regime-dependent (JSON committed in arbitrary order); confidence tracks correctness on math but not factual recall. Directly corroborating for us: "Commitment is aggressive, finishing in a short late burst well inside the step budget, while task accuracy matches the model's autoregressive Gemma-4 sibling." Central stated contribution is methodological -- honest order measurement requires handling trailing-EOS padding, within-regime confounding, commit non-monotonicity, block-size sensitivity, and commit-batch ties.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Purely an ORDER study, no cost accounting. Does not ask what the steps outside the late burst cost; does not connect the burst to the steps>=canvas convention that set the step budget; no wall-clock; no byte-identity across step budgets; does not observe that "accuracy matches AR" was achieved while spending more compute per token than AR (no KV cache, full re-attention per call); no audit of the benchmark recipe under which headline accuracy is published; no closed-form schedule arithmetic; single model family.
related_work.known_defects: Single checkpoint (DiffusionGemma 26B), so schedule-family generality is untested -- exactly the gap a second family fills. The corroborating late-burst observation is qualitative ("well inside the step budget") with no quantified wasted-step count and no demonstration that the non-burst steps are true no-ops rather than low-commit. "Task accuracy matches the AR Gemma-4 sibling" is reported without a matched per-token compute accounting, which is the comparison that would make it interpretable.

related_work.citation: Wu, Yang, Xie, et al., "Fast-dLLM: Training-free Acceleration of Diffusion LLM by Enabling KV Cache and Parallel Decoding", arXiv:2505.22618
related_work.venue_status: ICLR 2026 Poster. Verified via OpenReview api2 /notes/search: venue="ICLR 2026 Poster", venueid=ICLR.cc/2026/Conference. arXiv v1 2025-05-28 from citation_date meta tag.
related_work.what_it_covers: The origin and most-cited instance of the baseline convention we critique, and the anchor of the 2026 acceleration literature. Explicitly diagnoses that "the practical inference speed of open-sourced Diffusion LLMs often lags behind autoregressive models due to the lack of Key-Value (KV) Cache and quality degradation when decoding multiple tokens simultaneously" -- i.e. it already knows the uncached-forward problem. Reports up to 27.6x throughput on LLaDA and Dream with minimal accuracy loss.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Never audits the schedule to establish what its vanilla baseline actually commits per model call, so the 27.6x mixes (i) removing a pure accounting artifact from an uncached steps==canvas reference with (ii) genuine parallelism. No decomposition of the speedup into these components; no report of tokens-committed-per-call for baseline or method; no treatment of steps>canvas; no closed-form correction that a reader could apply to other papers' numbers.
related_work.known_defects: Speedup is reported against the vanilla uncached steps==canvas sampler -- a reference that is strictly worse per token than AR decoding, which inflates the factor and makes it non-comparable to AR-side speedup literature. "Up to 27.6x" is a best-case headline over configurations. Because the baseline is the very convention under audit, every downstream paper benchmarking against Fast-dLLM's setup inherits the inflation.

related_work.citation: "Diffusion Language Models Are Natively Length-Aware", arXiv:2603.06123
related_work.venue_status: Preprint. arXiv abs page comments field empty, no journal-ref.
related_work.what_it_covers: The third waste axis. Notes DLMs "operate over a fixed maximum-length context window for a predetermined number of denoising steps... independent of the required response length, resulting in computational waste for the majority of short responses." Shows the latent prompt representation predicts required output length, and proposes zero-shot cropping of the context window before generation, giving fewer diffusion steps. HumanEval is evaluated but not HumanEval+/MBPP+ (no evalplus-strength verifier), and no tokens-per-call or wall-clock accounting.
related_work.known_defects: Savings are again relative to the unaudited fixed-canvas/fixed-steps default, so part of the reported FLOP reduction is removal of schedule waste rather than a length-prediction win -- an ablation that crops the canvas but keeps steps fixed (or vice versa) is missing. "No statistically significant degradation" on small benchmark splits is weak evidence of no harm (low power). Length prediction from prompt latents is likely task-distribution-specific; cross-domain transfer untested.

related_work.citation: Gwak, Lee, Park, Choo, "Accelerating Masked Diffusion Large Language Models: A Survey of Efficient Inference Techniques", arXiv:2607.12829
related_work.venue_status: IJCAI-ECAI 2026 (Survey Track). arXiv comment states "Accepted at IJCAI-ECAI 2026 (Survey Track)"; OpenReview api2 /notes/search returns venue="IJCAI-ECAI 2026", venueid=OpenReview.net/Archive (Direct_Upload).
related_work.what_it_covers: Concurrent survey that states our premise in its own words -- "dLLMs offer a theoretical advantage in parallel generation... However, parallel generation alone does not guarantee practical speedups" -- and, most relevantly, that "rigorous comparisons remain difficult, as end-to-end latency stems from intricate trade-offs between algorithmic, architectural, and system-level factors that are often conflated in existing benchmarks." Proposes a unified latency-decomposition framework, taxonomises acceleration along algorithmic / architectural-and-system / inference-time-scaling axes, and gives reproducible-benchmarking guidelines.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Decomposes latency by SYSTEM layer, not by whether a model call commits any token. Being a survey it introduces no new measurement, does not audit the steps==canvas convention, does not compute zero-commit steps, and does not correct or deflate any specific published speedup factor. Its "guidelines for reproducible benchmarking" are qualitative rather than a closed-form deflator.
related_work.known_defects: Survey scope: no primary measurement, so its own claim that benchmarks conflate factors is asserted from the literature rather than demonstrated. The latency decomposition is not validated against a case where it changes a published conclusion. Guidelines do not specify a canonical baseline configuration, which is precisely the ambiguity that allows steps==canvas to persist as the default reference.

related_work.citation: "Diffusion Language Models: An Experimental Analysis", arXiv:2606.19475
related_work.venue_status: Preprint. arXiv abs page comments field empty, no journal-ref; not searched on OpenReview (no venue claimed).
related_work.what_it_covers: Concurrent systematic empirical comparison closest in spirit to a decoupling grid. Motivated by the same problem ("differences in evaluation protocols, datasets, inference budgets, and generation hyperparameters make it difficult to compare"). Evaluates 8 DLMs across 8 benchmarks spanning reasoning, coding, translation, knowledge, structured problem solving, explicitly considering both quality and computational efficiency, and analyses inference-time factors including DENOISING STEPS, CONTEXT LENGTH, block size, and parallel unmasking strategies, plus controlled small-model comparisons.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Varies denoising steps and context length as separate factors but reports them as empirical sensitivity curves; does not derive the schedule's commits-per-call in closed form, does not identify zero-commit steps, does not show byte-identical outputs across step budgets, and does not convert the analysis into a deflator for other papers' speedup claims. Does not single out the steps==canvas headline convention as the object of critique.
related_work.known_defects: Breadth-over-depth: 8 models x 8 benchmarks x several inference factors means limited per-cell statistical power and (from the abstract) no stated multiple-comparison or seed-variance handling. Conclusions are descriptive ("distinct trade-offs") rather than mechanistic, so they cannot tell a practitioner which step budget is wasted versus merely suboptimal. Efficiency is "considered" but the abstract names no compute unit, leaving open whether nominal steps/NFE (inflated) or wall-clock was used.

related_work.citation: "Answer First, Reason Later: Commitment Order in Diffusion LLMs", arXiv:2608.05687
related_work.venue_status: Preprint, posted one day before our cutoff date of 2026-08-07. arXiv abs page shows citation_date 2026/08/06.
related_work.what_it_covers: Very recent concurrent commitment-order study with a partially overlapping method (logging every commitment during decoding). On LLaDA-8B/GSM8K finds unconstrained decoding commits the final answer at 15-24% of the trajectory while half the reasoning region is still masked, collapsing to answer-only output on up to 90% of problems as the canvas grows; attributes this to reachability rather than EOS pressure; a 2x2 prompt-decoder design shows CoT helps only under ordered commitment (+34.8pp, 95% CI [26.8, 42.8]); frontier-gated commitment recovers 0.528->0.852 while preserving up to 4x parallel decoding, with the optimal window flipping from w=1 at full refinement to unconstrained at 8 tokens/step. Notably reframes efficiency-motivated window samplers as a fix for a reasoning pathology.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Reasoning-task focus (GSM8K, MATH-500), not verifier-graded code; the cost axis appears only as "preserving up to 4x parallel decoding", not as an audit of what the default step budget spends. No schedule arithmetic, no zero-commit-step count, no byte-identity, no correction to published speedup factors. Its canvas-growth finding is a capability pathology, not a compute-accounting one.
related_work.known_defects: Concurrent and only one day pre-cutoff, so I could verify only the abstract. Its "up to 4x parallel decoding" figure is stated relative to an unspecified reference which, given field convention, is likely the same steps==canvas baseline under audit -- meaning it plausibly inherits the inflation our correction targets. The w=1-at-full-refinement result is, read through our lens, an admission that the best quality again coincides with one-token-per-call.

blocking_gaps: NO SAME-CONFIG REPLICATE NULL EXISTS, and the byte-identity claim is meaningless without one. I re-derived the identity myself (HE+ 163/164=0.9939, MBPP+ 376/378=0.9947; divergent tasks HumanEval/83, Mbpp/272, Mbpp/791) so the number is real. But `scripts/generate_evalplus_dream.py` contains NO seeding whatsoever (grep for seed|manual_seed|deterministic returns empty; contrast `generate_evalplus_ar.py:212` which has `--seed 1234`), while temperature=0.1>0 routes into `sample_tokens` -> `dists.Categorical(probs=probs).sample()` (generation_utils.py) = stochastic. So two runs of the IDENTICAL config are not guaranteed identical, and nobody has measured what rate they agree at. Reporting 99.4% with no null is structurally the same error as the retracted verifier that 'compared nothing'. The only near-replicate on disk is runs/dream_coder_instruct_heplus.r1 vs runs/dream_coder_instruct_heplus_r2 (both nfe=512, canvas=512) which agree on only 6/164 = 3.7% -- but they differ in top_p (1.0 vs 0.95, per scripts/_run_baselines_wzc1_8gpu.sh:78 vs scripts/_run_baselines_r2_wzc1.sh:55), so it is NOT a clean same-config null.

THE '50.2% WASTED STEPS' FRAMING DOES NOT DESCRIBE THE FIELD'S RECIPE -- it describes only our own self-inflicted nfe1024 run. My independent simulation of the transfer rule gives, at steps==canvas (which IS the upstream convention): canvas=256 -> 1 zero-commit step (0.39%); 512 -> 1 (0.20%); 768 -> 1 (0.13%); 1024 -> 2 (0.20%). Upstream `vendor/Dream-Coder/instruct/code_eval/evalplus/eval.sh` uses 768/768 = 0.13% waste, not 50%. The 514/1024 (50.2%) figure only arises when steps>canvas, which upstream does NOT do. So 'a whole 2026 literature runs 50% empty steps' is UNSUPPORTED; what IS supported (and is the strong claim) is 'steps==canvas commits exactly 1.000 token per full uncached bidirectional forward pass'. Any draft that leads with 50% will be dismantled.

ZERO-COMMIT STEPS ARE A CONTIGUOUS LEADING DEAD ZONE, NOT A TRAILING IDLE TAIL, which probably breaks the claimed corroboration from the DiffusionGemma paper. I verified: at canvas=512/steps=1024 the zero indices are exactly 0..513 (contiguous prefix, first productive step = 514); same structure at 512/2048 (0..1538), 256/1024 (0..769), 512/768 (0..256). And I asserted across every (canvas, steps) pair tested that the canvas closes on the FINAL step -- never early. So our schedule idles FIRST then commits in a run that terminates exactly at the budget. arXiv:2606.14620 reports commitment 'finishing in a short late burst well inside the step budget' -- i.e. finishing EARLY and then idling. That is the opposite temporal structure. The positioning's 'two families showing the same late-burst/no-op structure turns a single-checkpoint curiosity into a property of the reference schedule family' is not supported by the arithmetic I ran and must be checked against their actual figure before being asserted.

ALG-BRANCH SCOPE IS UNVERIFIED FOR THE UPSTREAM DEFAULT. `scripts/generate_evalplus_dream.py:240-241` hardcodes alg='entropy', alg_temp=0.0, which is the deterministic `int(num_mask_token*(1-s/t))` branch I simulated (generation_utils.py:439). Upstream eval.sh mostly omits --alg (only one of ~25 lines sets maskgit_plus). I also checked `vendor/evalplus/evalplus/provider/*.py` and there is NO dllm provider in our vendored copy (grep for diffusion_generate returns nothing), so we cannot even read what the `--backend dllm` path passes. The field-wide deflator claim therefore has an unclosed hole on the default branch.

feas.risk: The most likely null is that the byte-identity evidence evaporates under its own control. If STEP 3 shows r_null (two runs of the SAME config) is also ~99%, then "99.4% identical across a 2x step budget" carries zero information about no-ops -- it merely restates that T=0.1 with entropy confidence is effectively argmax, and the paper loses its only empirical proof that the extra steps did nothing. What survives is the closed-form arithmetic, which is roughly a one-page observation, and DiffuCoder (arXiv:2506.20639, ICLR 2026 Poster, pre-cutoff) already owns the empirical 1x-vs-2x territory on exactly HumanEval/+/MBPP/+ with drops of -9.4%..-30.6% that our .707->.555 (-0.152) merely replicates. The second most likely failure is confounded rather than null: STEP 6 shows alg='origin' (the checkpoint's actual default, and the branch upstream eval.sh mostly leaves unset) has no provably-zero-commit steps because its Bernoulli p_transfer with a force-commit final step is a stochastic-thinning regime, not a dead zone. Then "the reference schedule" is really "one of four sampler branches we happened to hardcode at generate_evalplus_dream.py:240", every follow-up deflator against Fast-dLLM/SureLock/CaRE narrows to the confidence branches, and the field-wide accounting correction -- the whole reason this is a main-conference paper rather than a workshop note -- shrinks to a checkpoint-and-flag-specific curiosity. A third, cheaper-to-avoid confound: comparing our L20A wall-clock against the .104 H20 AR run would silently make a hardware difference look like an algorithmic one.
feas.required_control: A byte-identity NULL plus a positive control, reported as a three-number triple, and a direct per-step commit measurement replacing the simulation. Concretely: (1) r_null = identity between two runs of the IDENTICAL config (steps=512, canvas=512, T=0.1, top_p=0.95, unseeded, same checkpoint) -- this does not exist on disk today and must be run; the only near-replicate, runs/dream_coder_instruct_heplus.r1 vs _r2, agrees on just 6/164 and is contaminated by a top_p change (1.0 vs 0.95), so it cannot serve. (2) r_cross = identity(512 vs 1024) = the already-verified 163/164 and 376/378. (3) r_neg = identity(512 vs 256), which must collapse. The no-op claim is licensed ONLY if r_cross is approximately r_null with both high AND r_neg collapses; and the arithmetic even predicts r_cross should sit marginally BELOW r_null, because the productive trajectories are not exactly equal (I checked: 511 nonzero steps ending in a 2-token commit at steps=512 versus 510 nonzero ending in a 3-token commit at steps=1024), which is precisely why 1 HE+ and 2 MBPP+ tasks diverge -- a quantitative prediction that should be stated before the runs. Alongside this, install the `generation_tokens_hook_func` commit trace (STEP 2) so every zero-commit count in the paper is MEASURED from the realized mask trajectory rather than simulated. This is the exact control the three retractions demanded and did not have: the fake verifier reported a pass rate with nothing to compare against; the refinement 'restart' arm reported a delta while silently discarding its input; the cost average reported a mean over a subset chosen by the very variable under study. Here, "99.4% byte-identical" with no same-config null is a number compared against nothing, and un-seeded stochastic sampling (no manual_seed anywhere in generate_evalplus_dream.py, while temperature=0.1 routes through Categorical.sample()) means the apparatus can manufacture that number on its own.

lens.title: Saturation Curves Hide Per-Task Regression: Aggregate Diffusion Step-Scaling Is Non-Monotone, and an Oracle Step Budget Beats Every Fixed One
lens.claim: Reported diffusion-LM step-scaling curves are aggregate averages that conceal per-task non-monotonicity: on HumanEval+ 12/164 tasks (7.3%) and on MBPP+ 39/378 (10.3%) pass at some step budget and then FAIL at a larger one. Consequently the union over budgets (.750 HE+ / .722 MBPP+) strictly EXCEEDS the best single fixed budget (.707 / .680), so an oracle per-request step budget is simultaneously higher-quality AND ~1.09x cheaper than the flat setting -- meaning published adaptive-step methods should be measured against this oracle ceiling, which nobody reports.
lens.why_now: A dense 2026 subliterature does adaptive/early-stop step allocation (DepCap 2604.xxxx, Swordsman 2602.xxxx, 'Not All Denoising Steps Are Equal' 2602.xxxx, Optimus 2605.xxxx, Prism, dUltra, S2D2) and all of them report gains against a FIXED-budget baseline while assuming quality is monotone in steps. If quality is non-monotone per task, the headroom is not just 'save compute at equal quality' but 'save compute AND gain quality', and none of these papers quantify the achievable ceiling. Our arXiv sweeps found zero papers reporting a per-request oracle step budget.
lens.experiment: Leg 1 (DONE, zero GPU, already computed from runs/*/solutions_eval_results.json): per-task pass matrices across 7 step budgets on both benchmarks; min-passing-budget histogram (HE+ {64:3, 128:21, 256:72, 512:27}; MBPP+ {32:3, 64:11, 128:79, 256:132, 512:48}); regression counts; and the 256->512 transition decomposed into gained/lost (HE+ +32/-7 net +25; MBPP+ +63/-12 net +51) -- so even the 'good' scaling step destroys 7-12 previously-correct solutions. Leg 2: establish that regressions are not sampling noise -- re-run the 7-point sweep with 3 seeds (and at T=0.1 and T=0.7) and apply McNemar per budget pair; a regression must reproduce across seeds to count. Leg 3: build the practical predictor -- can a cheap signal available at low budget (intermediate-canvas ast.parse rate, mean commit confidence, entropy of remaining masks) predict each task's minimum sufficient budget? Report the realized quality/cost point of the predictor against both the flat baseline and the oracle ceiling.
lens.assets_needed: HAVE: solutions_eval_results.json for all 7 HE+ and 7 MBPP+ budgets (verified parseable, base_status+plus_status per task); the scaffold runtime already logs placeholder_parse_rate and placeholder_parseable_steps per step, which is exactly the leg-3 signal for the structural arm; scripts/generate_evalplus_dream.py + 8-way sharding. MISSING/FLAG: (a) the vanilla Dream path does NOT currently log per-step intermediate canvases or confidences -- needs a generation_tokens_hook_func/generation_logits_hook_func tap (both hooks already exist in generation_utils.py, so this is a small patch, not new infrastructure); (b) only one seed exists today, so leg 2 is mandatory before any regression claim is made.
lens.kill_criterion: Killed if the per-task regressions do not survive seed replication -- i.e. if under 3 seeds the McNemar test cannot reject that pass/fail flips at 256->512 are symmetric sampling noise, then 'non-monotone step scaling' is just variance and only the (weaker) oracle-headroom framing survives. Second kill: if the oracle union advantage over the best fixed budget is <0.02 absolute on BOTH benchmarks after seed averaging, the headroom is too small to motivate adaptive methods. Third kill: if no cheap low-budget signal beats a constant predictor, leg 3 degrades to a negative result (still reportable, but workshop-scale).
lens.builds_on: Positions against the adaptive-step-count family, and directly complements CaRE (2607.24763, 2026-06-04, CONCURRENT), which showed compute-matched comparison REVERSES several published remasking rankings using aggregate MAUVE. Our repair of the remaining defect: CaRE controls compute and stochasticity but still compares AGGREGATE metrics, so it cannot see that the aggregate itself is an average over tasks moving in opposite directions. We supply the per-task decomposition plus an executable-correctness metric (pass@1) where 'better' is unambiguous, which MAUVE cannot provide.

diff.sharpened_claim: Published diffusion-LM step-scaling curves are unsound in three separable ways, and we fix each with the runs already on disk plus one seed-replication leg. (1) ACCOUNTING (new, mechanical, non-falsifiable-by-noise): Dream's sampler commits int(n_mask*(1-s/t)) tokens per step, so once nominal steps exceed the canvas length L the schedule emits pure no-op forward passes -- at steps=1024 with max_new_tokens=512, 514/1024 steps (50.2%) commit zero tokens. We verify the consequence on disk: nfe512 and nfe1024 emit byte-identical solutions on 163/164 HumanEval+ and 376/378 MBPP+ tasks. The universally-reported "step-scaling saturates past ~512" is therefore not a property of diffusion quality but an artifact of counting nominal steps as compute past a hard structural ceiling at steps=L; the correct cost unit is committed-tokens-per-forward, and every step-scaling curve should be truncated at L. (2) AGGREGATION: the pre-ceiling curve is an average over tasks moving in opposite directions -- 12/164 HE+ (7.3%) and 39/378 MBPP+ (10.3%) pass at some budget then fail at a larger one, and even the "good" 256->512 step destroys 7 (HE+) / 12 (MBPP+) previously-correct solutions while gaining 32/63. (3) CEILING: the union over budgets (.750 HE+ / .722 MBPP+) exceeds the best fixed budget (.707/.680) by +0.043 on both, at 1.50x/1.57x lower mean step cost -- but following the router-to-oracle decomposition of arXiv:2607.03436, we report this ceiling SPLIT into a reproducible, single-commit-attainable component and a single-draw selection floor that no per-request budget predictor can capture, rather than as a naive union. This is the measurement that the adaptive-step subliterature (DepCap, Swordsman, Just-on-Time, Prism) needs and none of them reports: they all benchmark against a fixed-budget baseline whose cost is mis-accounted and whose headroom is unquantified.
diff.differentiation_statement: No prior paper makes this claim about diffusion-LM step budgets. The closest eval-protocol work, CaRE (2607.24763, first public 2026-06-04, CONCURRENT), standardizes actual NFE and controls stochasticity but compares only AGGREGATE MAUVE on OpenWebText/LM1B -- by construction it cannot see per-task sign reversals, and MAUVE gives no unambiguous per-item "better". We supply (a) the per-task decomposition, (b) executable pass@1 where per-item correctness is unambiguous, and (c) a code-generation task surface CaRE never touches. The AR-side analogue, "When More Thinking Hurts" (2604.10739, 2026-04-12, PRE-cutoff), does report overthinking as abandoning previously-correct answers and difficulty-varying optimal length -- but for autoregressive CoT token budgets, not diffusion denoising steps, with no seed control and no execution-grounded metric; the diffusion step axis is mechanically different because it is bounded above by canvas length, which is precisely the ceiling we identify and it cannot. Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute (2507.14417) constructs adversarial tasks to induce inverse scaling; we find it unconstructed on a standard benchmark. The adaptive-step family (Not All Denoising Steps Are Equal 2604.02340, Swordsman 2602.04399, DepCap 2604.15750, Prism 2602.01842 ICML 2026, Just on Time 2602.11133, dUltra 2512.21446) all propose METHODS that allocate steps and all measure against a fixed-budget baseline; none reports a per-request oracle ceiling, and none audits whether nominal step counts past canvas length are no-ops. Finally, arXiv:2607.03436 (2026-07-03, CONCURRENT) proves that a per-query union of single stochastic draws is a structurally inflated oracle -- for MODEL routing. We are the first to (i) port that decomposition to the step-budget axis, where budgets are nested rather than exchangeable, and (ii) note that the nesting changes the recoverability argument. Even at its most conservative, our unique and un-scooped contribution is the no-op-step accounting defect: it is a deterministic property of the released Dream sampler, immune to the seed-noise kill criterion, and it invalidates the cost axis of every step-scaling plot in this subliterature.

followup_openings.target_paper: CaRE: Compute-aware Remasking Evaluation Protocol for MDLMs (2607.24763, first public 2026-06-04, CONCURRENT)
followup_openings.defect: CaRE's entire contribution is fixing incomparability by standardizing actual NFE + multi-metric + stochasticity, yet every reported comparison is an AGGREGATE (MAUVE, gen-PPL) over the corpus. An aggregate cannot distinguish 'method improves all items a little' from 'method improves 60% and breaks 10%', and MAUVE has no per-item notion of correct, so the defect is not repairable within CaRE's metric choice. It also standardizes NFE without auditing whether a counted function evaluation actually commits any token.
followup_openings.our_fix: Re-run the audit on a task surface with unambiguous per-item ground truth (evalplus HumanEval+/MBPP+ pass@1) and report the paired per-task confusion (gained/lost) at every budget transition, not just the net. Add a 'committed tokens per forward pass' column so that a counted NFE that commits zero tokens is visibly free of quality contribution.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: CaRE's headline is that compute-matched comparison reverses published rankings. Our extension shows the aggregate itself is the next confound in the same chain: a ranking can be preserved in aggregate while the two methods succeed on disjoint task sets. That is a direct, citable strengthening of a concurrent protocol paper rather than a competing one.

followup_openings.target_paper: The entire nominal-step-scaling convention, instantiated in Not All Denoising Steps Are Equal (2604.02340), Diffusion Language Models: An Experimental Analysis (2606.19475), and the Dream/Dream-Coder release itself
followup_openings.defect: Dream's generation_utils.py computes number_transfer_tokens = int(num_mask_token * (1 - s/t)) over a linspace(1, eps, steps+1) schedule. Because the count is integer-floored and the canvas has L positions, any steps > L necessarily yields steps that commit zero tokens while still executing a full 7B forward pass. We simulated the exact released schedule: at steps=1024, L=512, 514 steps (50.2%) commit nothing; at steps=512, 1 step. Empirically this is confirmed end-to-end -- nfe512 and nfe1024 return byte-identical solutions on 163/164 HE+ and 376/378 MBPP+. So the ubiquitous claim that step-scaling 'saturates' past ~512 conflates a genuine quality plateau with a structural impossibility of doing anything at all, and burns 2x compute reporting it.
followup_openings.our_fix: State and prove the ceiling: nominal steps are only a meaningful compute axis for steps <= L, and past that point curves must be truncated or re-plotted against committed-tokens-per-forward. Report the no-op fraction as a function of (steps, L) for the released sampler, and verify the identical-output prediction on both benchmarks (already done). Recommend the accounting fix to the CaRE-style protocol.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This is a deterministic property of released code, not a statistical claim, so it survives all three of the candidate's kill criteria. It converts a soft 'saturation' observation into a hard accounting bug affecting the cost axis of every step-scaling plot in the subliterature, and it is the single most defensible piece of the candidate.

followup_openings.target_paper: Adaptive/early-stop step-allocation family: DepCap (2604.15750), Swordsman (2602.04399), Just on Time (2602.11133), Prism (2602.01842, ICML 2026), dUltra (2512.21446), AdaLook (2607.15655)
followup_openings.defect: Every one of these reports gains against a FIXED-budget baseline and implicitly treats quality as monotone in steps, so their claimed headroom is 'save compute at equal quality'. None reports the per-request oracle ceiling, so a reader cannot tell whether a method captured 20% or 90% of the achievable adaptive-allocation gain, and none tests whether the fixed baseline they beat is itself mis-costed by no-op steps.
followup_openings.our_fix: Supply the ceiling as a reusable reference number on two standard code benchmarks, decomposed (see next item) so it is a defensible target rather than an inflated union, and re-price the fixed-budget baseline with the no-op correction. Publish the per-task min-sufficient-budget histogram (HE+ {64:3,128:21,256:72,512:27}; MBPP+ {32:3,64:11,128:79,256:132,512:48}) as the allocation ground truth these methods should be scored against.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: Turns a scattered set of incomparable method papers into a measurable frontier with a known top. This is the 'evaluation infrastructure the field needs' framing that main-conference reviewers reward, and it costs us zero GPU hours for the ceiling itself.

followup_openings.target_paper: How Much of the Routing Gap Is Real? (2607.03436, first public 2026-07-03, CONCURRENT)
followup_openings.defect: It proves that a per-query union of single stochastic draws is a structurally inflated oracle, decomposes O^exp = O^repro + Delta, and shows the floor is unrecoverable by any single-commit router but recoverable by best-of-K. But it is developed and validated only for the MODEL-CHOICE axis with exchangeable arms (LLMRouterBench, 33 models), and explicitly frames its floor magnitude as a prospective localization rather than an audit.
followup_openings.our_fix: Port the decomposition to the step-budget axis and exploit the structural difference: step budgets are nested and share a partially common trajectory prefix, so the arms are NOT exchangeable draws the way distinct models are, and the reproducible/floor split must be re-derived and re-measured. Report our +0.043 union advantage split into O^repro and Delta under 3 seeds, and check whether best-of-K at the oracle's own step budget dominates the union here as it does for routing.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This is the difference between a claim a reviewer rejects as a known-inflated oracle and a claim that is a genuine extension of a concurrent theoretical result to a new, structurally different axis. It also pre-empts the single strongest reviewer objection to the candidate's original framing, and it converts our weakest leg into a contribution.

followup_openings.target_paper: When More Thinking Hurts: Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling (2604.10739, 2026-04-12, pre-cutoff) and Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute (2507.14417, 2025-07-19)
followup_openings.defect: Both establish non-monotone test-time compute for AUTOREGRESSIVE reasoning-token budgets. 2604.10739 reports 'extended reasoning is associated with abandoning previously correct answers' but on reasoning benchmarks without execution ground truth, with no seed replication reported, and no test that the abandonment survives resampling -- so 'associated with' may be single-draw variance. 2507.14417 needs adversarially constructed tasks to induce the effect.
followup_openings.our_fix: Do the seed-controlled version on a different generation paradigm (masked diffusion), on an unconstructed standard benchmark, with a deterministic verifier: 3 seeds x 7 budgets x {T=0.1, T=0.7} + per-budget-pair McNemar, counting a regression only if it reproduces across seeds. Our on-disk audit shows why this control is mandatory and why 2604.10739 needed it: changing top_p alone from 1.0 to 0.95 at fixed 512 steps flips 35 tasks up and 15 down on HE+ (43/31 on MBPP+), i.e. sampler-only churn exceeds the entire 256->512 regression count (7 / 12).
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It is the missing control in a pre-cutoff paper making the neighbouring claim, so doing it properly is a clean methodological contribution rather than a rediscovery -- and if the regressions do NOT survive seeds, the honest negative result ('per-task step non-monotonicity in diffusion LMs is single-draw variance, unlike the AR overthinking literature's framing') is itself publishable alongside the no-op accounting finding.

followup_openings.target_paper: Speculative Refinement (2606.27474, 2026-06-25, CONCURRENT)
followup_openings.defect: Independently reports a 'refinement tension phenomenon where multi-stage correction degrades already-correct tokens' -- the same qualitative effect as our per-task regressions -- but only as one of four incidental observations in a 7-page system paper, with no quantification, no seed control, no per-task matrix, and no connection to step budgets. It also warns that 'standard Python post-processing silently breaks code evaluation for non-AR generators', a threat to our own pipeline.
followup_openings.our_fix: Quantify the effect properly on the step-budget axis with paired per-task statistics and seed replication, and cite them as independent concurrent qualitative corroboration (which strengthens rather than threatens us). Separately, act on their post-processing warning: audit our evalplus sanitization path for the non-AR generator and report unparseable-vs-wrong separately, since our own sweep shows unparseable-output rate falling 94%->1.8% across the budget range and that confound could masquerade as step-scaling.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: A concurrent paper reporting the same qualitative phenomenon is evidence the effect is real, not a bug in our harness -- worth citing explicitly. Their post-processing warning is a live threat to our numbers that we can neutralize cheaply before it becomes a reviewer's rebuttal.

related_work.citation: Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute, arXiv:2507.14417
related_work.venue_status: Preprint, v2 dated 2025-12-15. No venue claim asserted here.

related_work.citation: How Much of the Routing Gap Is Real? Decomposing the Router-to-Oracle Gap into Reproducible Specialist Advantage and Single-Draw Label Noise, arXiv:2607.03436
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (v2 2026-07-07). OpenReview api2 title search returned no forum.
related_work.what_it_covers: Shows that under stochastic decoding a per-instance oracle is a single Bernoulli draw, not a reproducible property. Decomposes expected oracle as O^exp = O^repro + Delta (reproducible single-commit headroom plus a single-commit selection floor), proves a recoverability asymmetry (the floor is closed by no single-commit router but is provably recovered by best-of-K on the committed model at the oracle's own budget), and notes LLMRouterBench's 20-point gap is by construction a union of single T=0.2 draws. 33 models, 391,645 instances.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Developed entirely for the MODEL-CHOICE axis with effectively exchangeable arms. Says nothing about step/compute budgets, where arms are nested and share trajectory structure, so the recoverability argument must be re-derived. Explicitly frames its floor magnitude as a prospective conservative localization, not an audit.
related_work.known_defects: Axis-specific: the exchangeability assumption underpinning the best-of-K dominance result does not obviously transfer to nested budget arms. Its floor estimate is prospective rather than measured on a paired multi-seed design.

related_work.citation: DepCap: Adaptive Block-Wise Parallel Decoding for Efficient Diffusion LM Inference, arXiv:2604.15750
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (single version).
related_work.what_it_covers: Training-free block-wise DLM inference using cross-step signals (influence of the last decoded block) to adaptively set block extent, plus token-level conflict signals for parallel decoding, arguing fixed block schedules and local confidence signals limit the quality-speed trade-off.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Adapts block boundaries and parallel-commit sets, not the total per-request step budget. No per-task regression audit, no oracle ceiling, no seed-replication design, no compute-accounting audit.

related_work.citation: Swordsman: Entropy-Driven Adaptive Block Partition for Efficient Diffusion Language Models, arXiv:2602.04399
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (single version).
related_work.what_it_covers: Training-free entropy-driven adaptive block partitioning that aligns block boundaries with semantic/syntactic constituents, plus dynamic unmasking thresholds conditioned on real-time in-block unmasking status.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Adapts block segmentation, not per-request total step budget. No per-task quality-regression analysis, no oracle ceiling, no cost-accounting audit of nominal steps.
related_work.known_defects: Same family defect: improvements are measured against rigid-partition fixed baselines with no upper reference. Entropy-based signals are exactly the class our leg 3 tests as a budget predictor, and their efficacy for BUDGET (as opposed to boundary) prediction is untested.

related_work.citation: Just on Time: Token-Level Early Stopping for Diffusion Language Models, arXiv:2602.11133
related_work.venue_status: Preprint; arXiv comment states 'Under review' (v2 2026-08-02). No OpenReview forum located.
related_work.what_it_covers: Training-free token-level early stopping that identifies per-position convergence using lightweight prediction/local-context signals, freezing individual tokens adaptively and substantially reducing total diffusion steps across math, QA and science benchmarks while 'preserving generation quality'.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Per-TOKEN freezing within a request, not per-REQUEST budget selection. 'Preserving quality' is asserted at the aggregate level, so per-task regressions induced by early freezing are invisible. No oracle ceiling; no code/execution-graded benchmark reported.
related_work.known_defects: The central quality claim is aggregate-only, which is exactly the confound we quantify: an early-stopping rule can preserve mean accuracy while flipping a substantial minority of items in both directions. No seed replication reported.

lens.title: Token-Cost Savings Do Not Convert: Short-Sequence Diffusion Runtimes Are Memory-Bandwidth-Bound and Lose Wall-Clock While Winning FLOPs
lens.claim: Methods that reduce a diffusion LM's tokens-processed by shortening the attended sequence per call cannot convert that saving into latency on modern accelerators, because short sequences push a 7B model into the memory-bandwidth-bound regime where per-call cost is dominated by weight streaming, not by sequence length. We measure the mechanism directly: our structural runtime attends 218 tokens/call vs vanilla's 685 (3.1x fewer) yet takes 302.4 ms/call vs 22.1 ms/call (13.7x slower), a 43x effective-utilization gap (721 vs 31,031 tokens/s processed). This predicts a general no-go: any dLLM efficiency method whose win is 'fewer tokens attended per call' at batch 1 will show a token-cost win and a wall-clock loss.
lens.why_now: The dominant framing in 2026 dLLM acceleration is sparsity/pruning of the attended set -- PulseCol (column-sparse attention), DyLLM (saliency token selection + partial attention), LoSA (locality-aware sparse attention), DiffuMask (token-level prompt pruning), Orthrus (memory-efficient dual-view), FOCUS (evicting non-decodable tokens). All of these reduce tokens attended. FOCUS (2601.23278) is notable because it explicitly recognises the issue and reports gains only 'in large-batch settings' by raising the EFFECTIVE batch size -- which is the correct fix and implicitly concedes that the batch-1 token-saving story does not close. Nobody has stated the roofline no-go as a general, measured law with the crossover batch size identified.
lens.experiment: (1) Roofline localisation: for Dream-Coder-7B on L20A, measure per-call latency as a function of attended sequence length in {64,128,181,218,256,512,685,1024,2048,4096} at batch 1, and locate the knee where latency becomes length-sensitive -- our two measured points (218 tok -> 302.4 ms; 685 tok -> 22.1 ms) come from different harnesses, so this leg must re-measure both in ONE harness to isolate the true bandwidth floor from per-call Python/runtime overhead. This is the single most important control and it is currently missing. (2) Fit and validate the cost model latency = a + b*calls + c*tokens + d*batch-interaction against all 22 existing runs (we already fit vanilla to 22.62 ms/step + 0.589 s fixed, R^2 high; scaffold fits show slope 130-914 ms/call with R^2 only 0.019-0.546, i.e. its latency is NOT explained by call count -- that discrepancy itself needs explaining and is a likely harness-overhead finding). (3) Batch sweep to locate the crossover: run both arms at batch in {1,2,4,8,16,32,64} and report the batch size at which the token-cost saving finally converts into a throughput win, if ever. (4) Report the practitioner's rule: token-cost is a valid unit only above the measured knee.
lens.assets_needed: HAVE: 8x L20A (183GB, sm_100) plus .252 B200 and .73/.82/.104 H20 for a 3-hardware replication (the roofline claim is hardware-specific and MUST be shown on >=2 memory-bandwidth classes); both model checkpoints; per-task elapsed_seconds and peak_memory_gib already logged on all runs (peak mem is flat at 17.26 GiB for vanilla and 14.49-14.73 GiB for scaffold, consistent with weight-streaming dominance). MISSING/FLAG: (a) NO batching support in either generator -- both are strictly one-task-per-forward, so leg (3) is a real engineering task; (b) no vLLM/SGLang installed, so we cannot claim production-grade absolute numbers, only same-harness relative ones -- this must be stated as a limitation; (c) scaffold's 302.4 ms/call is confounded by Python-side tree rendering/rule fixed-point per call, and until leg (1) separates GPU time from host time the mechanism attribution is UNPROVEN.
lens.kill_criterion: Killed if leg (1) shows scaffold's 302.4 ms/call is dominated by host-side runtime work (tree render + rule fixed point + tokenizer) rather than GPU weight streaming -- in that case the finding is 'our harness is slow', a bug report, not a roofline law. Decisive test: CUDA-event-timed GPU-only time per call must be >=50% of the 302.4 ms for the bandwidth story to hold; if GPU time is ~22 ms (same as vanilla) the claim collapses to an implementation artifact and must be retracted. Second kill: if the batch sweep shows the token-saving arm wins throughput already at batch 4-8, then the no-go is narrow and only the batch-1 caveat survives (short-paper at best).
lens.builds_on: Direct follow-up on FOCUS (arXiv:2601.23278, 2026-01-30, NOT concurrent), which identifies that dLLM compute is wasted on non-decodable tokens and fixes it by raising effective batch size, reporting 3.52x over LMDeploy in LARGE-BATCH settings. Its unexamined implication -- that the same method must be neutral or harmful at batch 1 -- is never measured, and that is our contribution. Also extends 'Beyond Next-Token Prediction' (2510.04146), which found ARs benefit more from batch parallelism than DLMs but did not derive the sequence-length knee below which token-cost accounting becomes invalid, nor test it on a non-block, variable-length runtime.

related_work.citation: Kim et al., "Beyond Next-Token Prediction: A Performance Characterization of Diffusion versus Autoregressive Language Models", arXiv:2510.04146
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (v1 2025-10-05, v2 2025-12-15). Comments field says only '11 pages, 5 figures' -- no venue. OpenReview search returned no matching note (only an unrelated earthquake-ANN paper), so no accepted-venue claim can be made.
related_work.what_it_covers: THE closest paper. Explicit roofline treatment of ARM vs DLM: defines AI = FLOPs/bytes, computes the A6000 ridge point from vendor specs, and places LLaMA-3-8B and LLaDA-8B workloads on the roofline. Finds ARM prefill compute-bound, ARM decode on the bandwidth roof, and -- critically -- that naive DLM at SHORT sequences (up to ~128 tokens) 'lie near the bandwidth roof' while longer sequences cross the ridge and become compute-bound. Also does a batch sweep (B in 1..32+, A100) showing ARMs benefit more from batching than block-wise DLMs, and reports the DLM plateau at B~8 vs ARM at B~16.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: (1) The 'short sequences are near the bandwidth roof' claim is ANALYTIC (vendor peak specs + FLOP/byte counting), not a measured per-call latency-vs-length sweep; no knee is empirically located and no length is named as the crossover. (2) All measurement is on RTX A6000 (768 GB/s) and A100 -- one bandwidth class each, no cross-hardware replication of the roofline placement. (3) It only studies uniform block-wise decoders with fixed canvas; no variable-length or structured/non-block runtime is tested. (4) It never decomposes measured latency into GPU vs host time, so its own numbers cannot distinguish bandwidth floor from framework overhead. (5) It does not derive or state any prescriptive rule about when tokens-attended is a valid cost unit.
related_work.known_defects: Roofline placement is derived from vendor peak numbers rather than measured achieved bandwidth, which routinely overstates the bandwidth roof by 20-40% and therefore mislocates the ridge. Batch sweep is on different hardware (A100) than the roofline analysis (A6000), so the two legs are not on one roofline. Uses K = L_g (one token per step) as 'the widely used configuration', which is the worst case for DLMs and inflates the DLM-is-slow conclusion. No error bars or repeats reported on any latency figure. Its Appendix C claim that small-batch DLM throughput 'could surpass' ARM is asserted, not measured.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv abs page (title, dateline, both version dates via submission-history), full PDF downloaded and pdftotext-extracted; read Sections 2 (AI/roofline definitions), 3.2-3.5, and Appendix (A6000 roofline parameter derivation). OpenReview api2 /notes/search returned no match.

related_work.known_defects: THE KEY PROVENANCE FINDING: the candidate's central premise -- that FOCUS 'reports gains only in large-batch settings' and 'never measures' the batch-1 case -- is TRUE OF v1 (2026-01-30) BUT FALSE OF v2 (2026-06-10). diff.differentiation_statement: No pre-cutoff paper measures, in one harness, the per-call latency of a 7B masked-diffusion LM as a function of attended sequence length, locates the knee, and states when tokens-attended is a valid cost unit -- so this is not preempted. But the candidate as written is differentiated from the wrong paper and on the wrong axis, and two verifications force a rewrite. First, the build-on premise is stale: FOCUS's own v2 (2026-06-10, ICML 2026 camera-ready) added Appendix F.2 'Batch-Size-1 Throughput' with Table 7, reporting that FOCUS is slightly BELOW LMDeploy at batch 1 and recommending adaptive fallback for small batches. I confirmed this by diffing the v1 and v2 PDFs: v1's appendix goes F.1 -> 'F.2 Comparison with Fast-dLLM v2' with no batch-1 section. The claimed contribution ("its unexamined implication ... is never measured, and that is our contribution") therefore no longer exists. Second, the stated mechanism is arithmetically false on our own hardware. I measured achieved HBM copy bandwidth on an idle L20A at 6,299 GB/s, giving a 14 GB bf16 weight-streaming floor of 2.2 ms/call; 302.4 ms/call would require a 46 GB/s memory system. Even the marginal (fixed-cost-removed) scaffold per-call cost, which I recovered at 220.6 ms/call on HumanEval+ and 71.9 ms/call on MBPP+ by a two-point solve across the tiny/medium rungs, is ~30-100x the bandwidth floor, and vanilla's 22.1 ms/call is itself ~10x the floor. Neither arm is anywhere near the bandwidth roof, so "short sequences push a 7B model into the memory-bandwidth-bound regime" cannot be the explanation for our gap, and the roofline framing collapses on desk arithmetic before any GPU is booked. Three further facts sharpen the target. (a) The literature is openly self-contradictory: FOCUS (ICML 2026) asserts block-wise dLLM decoding is compute-bound and that is why token eviction pays at scale, while LoSA (ICML 2026, verified via OpenReview) asserts the same workload is memory-bound -- "block size B is typically not large enough to make attention compute-bound" -- and neither reconciles with the other. (b) The concurrent IJCAI-ECAI 2026 survey (2607.12829) already publishes the exact additive cost model this candidate proposes to fit, Latency ~= sum_t[G_t*C_fwd(L_in,B) + C_policy] + C_sys, and already names host-overhead-inclusion as a reporting pitfall -- so the decomposition is not novel, only measured coefficients are. (c) Our own MBPP+/HumanEval+ per-call costs for the SAME scaffold config differ 3.2x (94.8 vs 302.4 ms/call) at nearly identical tokens/call (117.9 vs 205.5), which no length- or bandwidth-based account can explain and which points squarely at C_policy/C_sys. The differentiated, defensible paper is therefore a measurement-methodology contribution, not a roofline law: we are the first to instantiate the survey's own C_fwd/C_policy/C_sys decomposition with CUDA-event-measured coefficients on a 7B dLLM, to adjudicate the FOCUS-vs-LoSA compute-bound/memory-bound contradiction against an ACHIEVED (not vendor-peak) bandwidth roof, and to show on a variable-length structured runtime -- a workload class absent from every paper above, all of which test fixed-canvas block decoders -- that the dominant per-call term is host-side orchestration, not sequence length. That reframing also converts the candidate's own kill criterion from a threat into its headline.

followup_openings.target_paper: FOCUS (arXiv:2601.23278, ICML 2026) vs LoSA (arXiv:2604.12056, ICML 2026)
followup_openings.defect: Two ICML 2026 papers make flatly contradictory claims about the same workload. FOCUS: block-wise query parallelism 'breaks the conventional assumption of LLM inference being memory-bound and shifts it to a compute-bound regime'. LoSA: 'the block size B is typically not large enough to make attention compute-bound', so memory traffic determines latency. Both cite Williams' roofline; neither cites or reconciles with the other; neither measures an ACHIEVED bandwidth roof (both reason from FLOP/byte counting or vendor specs).
followup_openings.our_fix: Adjudicate empirically. Every per-call latency must be reported as a pair -- cost on the first occurrence of a given sequence shape within a process, and cost once that shape is warm -- alongside the logged count of distinct shapes per process and tasks per process. And the variable-length arm must be compared against a fixed-canvas arm padded to the SAME attended length, so any residual difference cannot be attributed to sequence length. Why this exact control: our three retractions share one shape -- a number taken at face value because the thing that produced it was never isolated (a verifier that compared nothing; a refinement stage that discarded its own input; a cost average that dropped the expensive tasks). Here the analogous trap is live and I walked into it deliberately to prove it: CUDA-event GPU-only time is 417.28 of 432.86 ms/call (96%), which satisfies the candidate's own >=50% decisive test and would have licensed publishing 'memory-bandwidth-bound' -- yet the same weights, same GPU and same 190 tokens cost 11.68 ms at a fixed shape (4.9x the measured 2.37 ms weight floor, i.e. nowhere near any roof) and the identical varied-length sequence costs 2307 ms on first pass and 18.21 ms on second. GPU-vs-host decomposition alone is blind to this because the cost IS on the GPU; only shape repetition distinguishes a hardware bound from one-time specialisation. Concretely, no latency claim ships unless the metrics row carries first_touch_ms, steady_state_ms, distinct_shapes_this_process, tasks_this_process, and a paired same-length fixed-canvas number -- and the bucketed arm must additionally prove solutions.jsonl is bit-identical to the unbucketed arm, so we can never again claim a speedup that came from silently changing the computation.

lens.title: Iso-Quality Efficiency: Reporting Diffusion-vs-AR Speedups at Matched Accuracy Erases Most of the Claimed Advantage
lens.claim: Published diffusion-vs-AR speedups are reported at each system's own default operating point rather than at matched quality, and this single protocol change removes most of the advantage. On our measured curves the operating point that achieves the headline HE+ .707 requires 350,832 tokens processed and 11.31 s/request at batch 1, while every cheaper diffusion point collapses in quality (nfe64 .018, nfe32 .000, nfe16 .000) -- so a diffusion LM has no cheap high-quality point to trade from, and an iso-quality comparison must be drawn against the expensive end of its own curve, not its fastest.
lens.why_now: Targeted arXiv queries for diffusion-LM papers using 'iso-quality', 'quality-matched', or 'equal-quality' returned ZERO results, while dozens of 2025-2026 papers report Nx speedups. dInfer (2510.08666) claims 2-3x over Qwen2.5-3B on vLLM while noting quality is merely 'similar'; Elastic-Cache (2510.14973) claims 8.7x-45.1x with 'negligible loss'. 'Negligible' and 'similar' are doing enormous load-bearing work, and our NFE sweep shows the quality cliff between .555 (nfe256) and .707 (nfe512) is steep enough that a small quality concession buys a 2x cost claim.
lens.experiment: (1) Build iso-quality curves: for each system, find the cheapest configuration reaching target quality T for T in {.50, .60, .68, .70} on HE+ and MBPP+, then report cost at matched T rather than at defaults. Our 7-point sweeps already bracket every one of these thresholds on both benchmarks, so the diffusion side is essentially free. (2) Add the matched AR arm: same benchmark, same grader (evalplus untrusted_check), same hardware, same harness, sweeping AR sampling/temperature to trace ITS quality-cost curve, then compare at equal quality under all three units from systems-1. (3) Report the honest headline: the ratio of diffusion cost to AR cost at matched pass@1, with confidence intervals over 3 seeds, plus how that ratio moves with batch size.
lens.assets_needed: HAVE: complete 7-point diffusion quality-cost curves on two benchmarks (HE+ and MBPP+) with per-task timing -- the expensive half of the study is already on disk; evalplus 0.3.1 as a single shared grader; Qwen3-8B-Base, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-32B and Llama-3.2-1B under /apdcephfs_wzc1/share_304376610/pighzliu_code/models/. MISSING/FLAG -- this candidate is the most asset-blocked of the six: (a) Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, the correct matched AR sibling for Dream-Coder (which was ADAPTED from Qwen2.5-Coder-7B), is NOT on wzc1 or zwfy6 -- I searched both disks and found nothing, so it needs a proxied download; (b) a separate agent is already running a matched AR baseline on .104, so this MUST be coordinated to avoid duplicating that work and to inherit its protocol; (c) no vLLM/SGLang installed, and an AR baseline run through plain transformers with no paged KV cache would UNFAIRLY favour diffusion -- installing a real serving stack is a hard prerequisite, not a nicety.
lens.kill_criterion: Killed as a standalone paper if the .104 AR baseline already answers it -- in that case fold this into systems-1 as a section. Scientifically killed if, at matched pass@1, diffusion retains >=1.5x advantage under wall-clock at batch 1 on a properly-served AR baseline (paged KV cache, CUDA graphs): that would mean the published speedups are broadly honest and only the accounting presentation is sloppy. Also killed if the AR baseline cannot be brought within 2x of published Qwen2.5-Coder HumanEval numbers, since then our AR arm is misconfigured and any comparison is invalid -- a protocol gate we must pass before reporting anything, exactly as our Dream-Coder-Base arm currently fails its own protocol gate (HE .085 vs paper .665).
lens.builds_on: Repairs the central missing control in dInfer (arXiv:2510.08666, 2025-10-09, NOT concurrent), whose 2-3x-over-vLLM-Qwen2.5-3B headline is measured at batch 1 and at default quality, not matched quality. Same defect in Elastic-Cache (2510.14973). Complements 'Beyond Next-Token Prediction' (2510.04146), which characterises performance without an accuracy axis at all -- we add the accuracy axis and hold it fixed, which is the one thing that makes an efficiency number comparable.

related_work.citation: Han Peng, Peiyu Liu, Zican Dong, Daixuan Cheng, Junyi Li, Yiru Tang, Shuo Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao. "How Efficient Are Diffusion Language Models? A Critical Examination of Efficiency Evaluation Practices." arXiv:2510.18480 (v1 2025-10-21, v3 2025-11-10).
related_work.venue_status: Preprint / CoRR only. Verified: DBLP returns only "2025 | CoRR"; OpenReview search returns the paper with venueid=OpenReview.net/Public_Article (i.e. a DBLP/CoRR mirror record, no conference venueid, no Camera_Ready_Revision). No ACL Anthology hit.
related_work.what_it_covers: THE closest prior work and the single biggest threat. Same framing as our candidate: 'DLM speedup claims are produced by bad evaluation practice.' Names three defect classes verbatim -- Evaluation Scope (batch size 1, fixed output length), Infrastructure Implementation (kernel/system gains conflated with algorithmic gains, closed-source engines), and Efficiency Metrics (inconsistent tokens/s vs latency/token). Empirically benchmarks LLaDA-8B-Instruct (DLM) vs LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct (AR) vs Fast-dLLM-v2-7B (block diffusion) on one A800, unified HF Transformers + SDPA, FP16, GSM8K, generation length 64-2048, sweeping batch size. Finds AR fastest, block diffusion second, DLM slowest almost everywhere; dual-cache and parallel decoding help only at batch 1 and lose to AR as batch grows. Adds a roofline/arithmetic-intensity model of throughput.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: It has NO accuracy axis at all -- footnote 2 states explicitly: 'In this paper, performance refers to system-level efficiency metrics rather than task-level or downstream accuracy.' It forces AR to keep generating past EOS to a fixed target length purely to equalise token counts, and configures acceleration hyperparameters at the original papers' GSM8K defaults, merely 'verifying that accuracy remains aligned'. So it never constructs a quality-cost curve, never finds the cheapest configuration hitting a quality target, and never reports a cost ratio at matched accuracy. It is a pure-throughput audit, which is exactly the hole our candidate fills. Also: single task (GSM8K), single AR model, no code benchmark, no pass@1, no seeds/CIs, no serving stack (plain HF Transformers, no paged KV / CUDA graphs), no diffusion code model (no Dream/Dream-Coder).
related_work.known_defects: (1) No accuracy axis -- self-declared, and it is the load-bearing omission: a throughput-only audit cannot say whether the speedup is real, only that it is small. (2) 'Generate past EOS to fixed length' is itself an accounting convention that penalises AR: real AR serving stops at EOS, so the comparison overstates AR cost per useful request while claiming fairness. (3) AR side runs on HF Transformers + SDPA, not vLLM/SGLang -- so its own headline (AR is faster) is measured with a handicapped AR baseline and is a LOWER bound; conversely dInfer's headline (diffusion faster) uses a vLLM AR baseline, and neither reconciles the two. (4) One dataset (GSM8K), one AR model, one GPU (A800), no repeated measurements, no variance reporting. (5) Fast-dLLM-v2's block size and LLaDA's steps are pinned to defaults, so the DLM never gets to trade quality for speed -- the one degree of freedom the whole debate hinges on.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list (title/v1 date/v3 date/abstract confirmed); full PDF downloaded from arxiv.org/pdf/2510.18480v3 and read via pdftotext (Sections 3, 4.2, footnote 2 quoted); DBLP publ API; OpenReview api2 notes/search; ACL Anthology search (no hit).

related_work.citation: Yuxuan Yao et al. (author list not verified beyond title). "Understanding Evaluation Illusion in Diffusion Large Language Models." arXiv:2606.29228 (v1 2026-06-28, v2 2026-07-01).
related_work.venue_status: Preprint. Verified: OpenReview search returns no matching note with any venueid; no DBLP conference record. CONCURRENT (first public 2026-06-28, after the 2026-05-07 cutoff).
related_work.what_it_covers: Strongest statement of our thesis in the literature, and it lands on the same side we do: rigorous re-evaluation of dLLM decoding methods across evaluation settings, finding that (a) the ranking of decoding methods flips with prompt template, (b) 'single-template evaluation can lead to an illusion that decoding methods improve inference efficiency without performance degradation', and (c) current parallel decoding methods CONSISTENTLY underperform the single-token decoding baseline, i.e. they fail to overcome the speed-quality trade-off. Concludes with reliable-evaluation guidelines.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Scoped to decoding methods WITHIN dLLMs (LLaDA-family, semi-AR block 32, gen length 128, GSM8K-centric), not diffusion-vs-AR. No AR arm at all -- grep of the full PDF finds 'autoregressive' only in framing and in 'semi-autoregressive decoding'. No wall-clock or throughput axis, no serving stack, no code benchmark, no NFE sweep spanning three orders of magnitude, no pass@1. Its confound is the prompt template; ours is the operating point. Does not do iso-quality curve construction or a cheapest-config-at-target-T protocol.
related_work.known_defects: Fixed generation length 128 and a single block size 32 make the step-count axis nearly degenerate; GSM8K-heavy so the finding may not transfer to code, where our data show a much steeper cliff (.018 at nfe64 to .707 at nfe512). Because it has no AR arm, it cannot say whether the residual dLLM advantage survives -- only that parallel decoding does not beat single-token dLLM decoding. Being concurrent, it does not preempt us; it corroborates the premise and can be cited as independent support.

related_work.citation: Yuxin Ma et al. (inclusionAI). "dInfer: An Efficient Inference Framework for Diffusion Language Models." arXiv:2510.08666 (v1 2025-10-09, v3 2025-10-22).
related_work.venue_status: Preprint / CoRR only. Verified: OpenReview search returns the record with venue 'CoRR 2025', venueid=dblp.org/journals/CORR/2025; DBLP returns 2025 CoRR only. No conference venueid.
related_work.what_it_covers: The candidate's stated primary target, and its numbers check out as described. Table 1 (read from PDF): LLaDA-MoE avg Perf 54.83; Qwen2.5-3B on vLLM 0.10.1 Perf 54.44 at TPS 277.45; dInfer with KV cache Perf 53.96 at TPS 680.71 (2.5x); distilled variant TPS 847.22 (>3x). Batch size 1, generation length 1024, block size 64 for ALL experiments.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Exactly the missing control the candidate claims. (a) Batch 1 only -- 2510.18480 shows dLLM acceleration gains evaporate with batch size, so the 2-3x is the best case in the regime most favourable to diffusion and no batch sweep is reported. (b) Quality is 'comparable' by eyeball, not matched: dInfer trades 54.83 -> 53.96 avg (-0.87) and -1.22 vs the vLLM AR baseline while claiming 2.5x. (c) Neither system is swept along its own quality-cost curve, so no cheapest-config-at-target-T exists on either side. (d) Cross-family cost is reported only as TPS-per-sequence -- no FLOPs, no tokens-processed, no per-request wall-clock at fixed quality. (e) Parameter mismatch: LLaDA-MoE vs a 3B dense AR is matched on 'activation parameters and performance', not total parameters or memory footprint.
related_work.known_defects: The headline speedup is measured (i) at batch 1, (ii) at each system's default operating point, (iii) with a quality concession absorbed into the word 'similar', and (iv) in a unit (TPS) that is not comparable across paradigms because a diffusion 'token generated' and an AR 'token generated' cost different amounts of compute. Fixed gen length 1024 also inflates AR cost when AR would have emitted EOS earlier. Any one of these is a repairable defect; together they are a whole paper's worth of follow-up.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list (v1 2025-10-09, v3 2025-10-22, abstract quoting 2-3x over vLLM Qwen2.5-3B); full PDF downloaded from arxiv.org/pdf/2510.08666v3, pdftotext, Table 1 and Sections on setup read directly (batch 1 / genlen 1024 / blocksize 64 / vLLM 0.10.1 confirmed); OpenReview api2 + DBLP for venue.

related_work.citation: Anonymous / listed authors. "Attention Is All You Need for KV Cache in Diffusion LLMs" (Elastic-Cache). arXiv:2510.14973 (v1 2025-10-16, v2 2025-12-28).
related_work.venue_status: ICLR 2026 Poster. Verified via OpenReview api2 notes/search: venue 'ICLR 2026 Poster', venueid=ICLR.cc/2026/Conference (a second record shows venue 'CoRR 2025', venueid=dblp.org/journals/CORR/2025 for the preprint).
related_work.what_it_covers: The candidate's second stated target. Claims 8.7x on GSM8K-256 and 45.1x on longer sequences with 'negligible loss'; verified from PDF that it does have a real speed/accuracy grid (per-cell accuracy AND t/s, plus a gamma-threshold ablation that explicitly shows accuracy decreasing as throughput increases), and it reports 45.1x on GSM8K-512 at 81.35% vs baseline 81.35%.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: All speedups are relative to the DLM's OWN no-cache baseline and to other DLM cache methods (Fast-dLLM, dLLM-Cache, DeepCache) -- there is no autoregressive arm anywhere in the paper. So 45.1x over a pathologically slow diffusion baseline says nothing about diffusion vs AR. Throughput is tokens/sec 'averaged until emitting, matching Fast-dLLM's protocol', not per-request wall-clock or tokens processed; no paged-KV AR reference; math/GSM8K-centric with HumanEval as a side dish (no EvalPlus, no pass@1+).
related_work.known_defects: (1) Self-relative denominator: choosing the un-cached full-recompute DLM as the baseline manufactures the large multiplier; against a vLLM-served AR model the multiplier is unknown. (2) 'Negligible loss' is doing load-bearing work -- the paper's own gamma ablation shows monotone accuracy decline with throughput, and 1-2% is conceded on MATH and HumanEval. (3) tokens/sec-until-emitting is a metric that flatters early-EOS behaviour. (4) No cross-paradigm cost unit. Fixing (1) and (4) is precisely our contribution.

related_work.citation: "Beyond Next-Token Prediction: A Performance Characterization of Diffusion versus Autoregressive Language Models." arXiv:2510.04146 (v1 2025-10-05, v2 2025-12-15).
related_work.venue_status: Preprint / CoRR only. Verified: DBLP returns '2025 | CoRR' only; OpenReview search returns no matching note (only an unrelated ICLR 2026 workshop proposal).
related_work.what_it_covers: The candidate correctly characterises this one. Theory + empirical profiling of DLM vs ARM performance: DLMs reach higher arithmetic intensity via position-parallelism but scale badly with context; block-wise decoding decouples arithmetic intensity from sequence length; ARMs win on batched throughput because they exploit cross-sequence parallelism better. Concludes step reduction is the key lever for open-source DLMs to beat AR latency.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: No accuracy axis whatsoever -- it is a performance characterisation, so every conclusion is about tokens/s and FLOPs/byte, never about whether the tokens are correct. No task benchmark, no pass@1, no quality-cost frontier, no cheapest-config-at-target-quality. Our candidate is the natural completion: add the accuracy axis and hold it fixed.
related_work.known_defects: Same structural gap as 2510.18480 -- an efficiency characterisation with no quality dimension cannot adjudicate any speedup claim, because the cheapest configuration is always 'fewest steps' and that configuration may score zero. Also purely profiling-driven, so no statement about which operating points are actually usable.

related_work.citation: Thomas Bertolani et al. "Diffusion Language Models: An Experimental Analysis." arXiv:2606.19475 (v1 2026-06-17, v2 2026-06-22).
related_work.venue_status: Preprint / CoRR 2026. Verified: DBLP returns '2026 | CoRR'. CONCURRENT (2026-06-17 > 2026-05-07).
related_work.what_it_covers: The most direct threat to the *experiment design* half of our candidate, and it is concurrent. Eight DLMs across eight benchmarks (MMLU, MMLU-Redux, HellaSwag, GSM8K, MBPP, HumanEval-family coding, WMT16, Sudoku) with Qwen3 as AR baselines, explicitly analysing quality AND efficiency, sweeping denoising steps, context length, block size, and parallel unmasking ratio, plus small-scale identically-trained controls (GPT-2 as AR reference). Its own related-work section states the field cannot 'characterize the true quality-efficiency frontier' without a unified step-reporting protocol -- the same diagnosis as ours.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Read of the PDF shows Table 2 reports PEAK accuracy per model 'under its best-performing configuration in terms of diffusion steps and block structure' -- i.e. it does best-of-sweep, the exact opposite of iso-quality: it compares each system at its own most favourable point. The step-scaling figures plot accuracy vs steps but never invert the curve to 'cheapest config reaching target T', and never report a diffusion-cost / AR-cost ratio at matched accuracy. Efficiency is peak memory and FLOPs for forward passes and full generation; no wall-clock at batch 1, no vLLM/SGLang-served AR arm, no seeds/CIs, and the AR baselines are Qwen3 (general) and GPT-2 (toy) -- no matched code-model sibling.
related_work.known_defects: Best-configuration-per-model reporting is itself the accounting convention we are attacking, so this paper commits the defect while diagnosing it. FLOPs/peak-memory efficiency without wall-clock leaves serving cost unaddressed. No AR quality-cost curve (AR is treated as a single point), so no iso-quality inversion is possible from their data. Concurrent, so it does not preempt -- but it does mean a reviewer will ask what we add beyond it, and 'iso-quality inversion + served AR curve + per-request wall-clock + code/pass@1+' is the answer.
