diff.differentiation_statement: Two pre-cutoff papers audit diffusion-LM efficiency claims (2510.18480, 2510.04146) and both explicitly refuse the accuracy axis -- 2510.18480 says so in a footnote ("performance refers to system-level efficiency metrics rather than task-level or downstream accuracy"), and 2510.04146 is a pure performance characterisation. One concurrent paper (2606.19475, 2026-06-17) does sweep denoising steps against accuracy, but reports each model's PEAK accuracy "under its best-performing configuration", which is the best-of-sweep convention we are attacking rather than an iso-quality comparison; a second concurrent paper (2606.29228, 2026-06-28) shows parallel decoding never beats single-token dLLM decoding, but has no AR arm and no wall-clock. So nobody, before or after the cutoff, has performed the specific inversion this candidate proposes: fix a quality target T, find the CHEAPEST configuration of each system that reaches T, and report the diffusion/AR cost ratio at matched T. Our differentiation is four-fold and each leg is independently sufficient. (1) Direction of the operation: prior work plots accuracy as a function of budget; we invert the curve and read off budget as a function of accuracy, which is the only form in which an efficiency number is comparable across paradigms. (2) Task surface and grader: the entire audit literature is GSM8K-centric with generation lengths of 128-1024; ours is execution-verified code (HumanEval+/MBPP+ under a single shared evalplus 0.3.1 untrusted_check), where our measured cliff is far steeper than anything in the math literature -- pass@1+ goes .018 (nfe64) to .555 (nfe256) to .707 (nfe512) with exactly zero gain from 512 to 1024, so the high-quality end is reachable only at the expensive extreme of the diffusion curve and there is no cheap high-quality point to trade from. (3) Cost accounting: we report tokens processed, per-request wall-clock, and (per systems-1) multiple units, versus prior work's tokens-per-second-per-sequence (dInfer) or tokens-per-second-until-emitting (Elastic-Cache), neither of which is commensurable across a paradigm where one "generated token" costs a different amount of compute on each side. (4) Baseline symmetry: 2510.18480 runs its AR arm on plain HF Transformers + SDPA and concludes AR wins, while dInfer runs its AR arm on vLLM and concludes diffusion wins -- these two results have never been reconciled, and our design (a properly served AR baseline WITH its own quality-cost sweep, so both sides are curves rather than points) is the missing experiment that adjudicates between them. Finally, our own three published retractions -- especially the NFE-as-cross-family-cost-unit error and the metric-averaging error that understated a mean cost 2.85x by silently dropping budget-truncated tasks -- give us a first-hand, documented account of exactly how these accounting mistakes are made, which is unusual credibility for a methodology paper.

followup_openings.target_paper: How Efficient Are Diffusion Language Models? A Critical Examination of Efficiency Evaluation Practices (arXiv:2510.18480, 2025-10-21, NOT concurrent)
followup_openings.defect: Self-declared absence of any accuracy axis (footnote 2: 'performance refers to system-level efficiency metrics rather than task-level or downstream accuracy'). It pins LLaDA's steps and Fast-dLLM-v2's block size to the original papers' GSM8K defaults, merely 'verifying that accuracy remains aligned', so the DLM is never allowed to trade quality for speed -- the single degree of freedom the whole diffusion-vs-AR debate hinges on. Consequently its central conclusion ('AR is faster') is unfalsifiable in the direction that matters: a DLM could be slower at its default and still faster at matched quality, or vice versa, and the paper cannot tell.
followup_openings.our_fix: Take their exact three-way design (DLM / AR / block diffusion, one node, one framework, FP16, batch sweep) and add the missing axis: for each system sweep its own quality knob (denoising steps / block size / AR temperature-top_p) and report the cheapest configuration reaching pass@1+ targets T in {.50, .60, .68, .70} on HE+ and MBPP+, then the diffusion/AR cost ratio at each matched T with 3-seed CIs. Our 7-point NFE sweep already brackets every threshold on both benchmarks, so the diffusion half of this is on disk. Also drop their generate-past-EOS convention in favour of reporting both EOS-respecting and fixed-length accounting, since forcing AR past EOS silently penalises the AR side.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This converts a throughput-only audit into a decision-relevant one. Under their protocol nobody can answer 'if I need pass@1 of .70, which paradigm is cheaper?' -- which is the only question a practitioner asks. It also resolves the standing contradiction between their AR-wins result (HF Transformers AR) and dInfer's diffusion-wins result (vLLM AR), because our design makes both sides curves rather than points.

followup_openings.target_paper: dInfer (arXiv:2510.08666, 2025-10-09, NOT concurrent)
followup_openings.defect: The 2-3x-over-vLLM headline is measured at batch size 1, generation length 1024, block size 64 for every experiment, at each system's default operating point, with a quality concession (LLaDA-MoE 54.83 -> dInfer 53.96, vs Qwen2.5-3B/vLLM 54.44) absorbed into the word 'comparable'. Cost is reported only as tokens-per-second-per-sequence, a unit that is not commensurable across paradigms. And 2510.18480 independently shows that dLLM acceleration gains shrink monotonically with batch size and eventually invert -- so batch 1 is the single most favourable regime for the claim and no batch sweep is reported.
followup_openings.our_fix: Re-report the same comparison as a cost ratio at matched accuracy, under three units (tokens processed, per-request wall-clock, FLOPs), swept over batch size {1, 4, 16, 64}. Concretely: fix avg accuracy at 54.44 (the vLLM AR point) and ask what dInfer configuration reaches it and what it costs, rather than accepting 53.96 as 'similar'. Report the batch size at which the advantage crosses 1.0x -- prior work says one exists but nobody has published the crossing point for a properly served AR baseline.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: A 2-3x claim that holds only at batch 1 and only with a -1.2-point quality concession is a very different engineering fact from a 2-3x claim that survives matched quality and realistic batching. Publishing the crossover batch size gives the field a single number that determines whether diffusion serving is deployable, and it is currently absent from the literature.

followup_openings.target_paper: Elastic-Cache / Attention Is All You Need for KV Cache in Diffusion LLMs (arXiv:2510.14973, 2025-10-16, ICLR 2026 Poster -- NOT concurrent)
followup_openings.defect: The 8.7x/45.1x multipliers are entirely self-relative: every speedup is against the DLM's own no-cache full-recompute baseline or against other DLM cache methods (Fast-dLLM, dLLM-Cache, DeepCache). Full-PDF read confirms there is no autoregressive arm anywhere in the paper. Its own gamma-threshold ablation shows accuracy declining monotonically as throughput rises, and 1-2% is conceded on MATH and HumanEval, yet the abstract says 'negligible loss'. Throughput is 'tokens/sec averaged until emitting', a metric that flatters early-EOS behaviour.
followup_openings.our_fix: Recompute their speedup with an external denominator: a paged-KV, CUDA-graph-served AR sibling at matched pass@1+, measured as per-request wall-clock rather than tokens/sec-until-emitting. Simultaneously turn their gamma ablation into a proper quality-cost curve and read off the cheapest gamma reaching each target T, so the accuracy concession is priced instead of adjectivised. Predicted outcome: 45x collapses to a small single-digit or sub-1x factor once the denominator is a real serving stack.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: Choosing the un-cached DLM as the denominator manufactures arbitrarily large multipliers -- 45x over a pathological baseline conveys no deployment information. Establishing the convention that cross-paradigm speedups require an externally-served denominator at matched quality is a reusable methodological contribution, and this ICLR 2026 paper is the cleanest possible illustration.

followup_openings.target_paper: Diffusion Language Models: An Experimental Analysis (arXiv:2606.19475, 2026-06-17, CONCURRENT)
followup_openings.defect: It correctly diagnoses that the field 'cannot characterize the true quality-efficiency frontier' without unified step reporting, then commits the very convention it diagnoses: Table 2 reports each model's PEAK accuracy 'under its best-performing configuration in terms of diffusion steps and block structure' -- best-of-sweep, i.e. every system evaluated at its own most favourable point. Efficiency is peak memory and FLOPs, with no per-request wall-clock and no served AR baseline; the AR side (Qwen3, and GPT-2 in the small-scale controls) is a single point rather than a curve, so their data cannot be inverted to an iso-quality ratio even in principle.
followup_openings.our_fix: Perform the inversion they set up but did not execute: same style of step/block sweep, but report cheapest-config-at-target-T and the diffusion/AR cost ratio at matched T, with the AR side swept along its own quality-cost curve (sampling temperature/top_p, and a matched code-model sibling rather than a general-purpose AR model) under a real serving stack, with per-request wall-clock alongside FLOPs and 3-seed CIs. Add execution-verified code metrics (EvalPlus pass@1+) where the cliff is steepest.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This is a concurrent paper, so it does not preempt us, but it is the work a reviewer will most want distinguished. Framing our contribution as 'they built the sweep and reported peaks; we invert the sweep and report matched-quality ratios' is a crisp, defensible delta, and it also demonstrates that best-of-sweep reporting is pervasive enough to appear even in a paper whose stated purpose is to fix reporting.

followup_openings.target_paper: Efficient-DLM (arXiv:2512.14067, 2025-12-16, ICML 2026 -- NOT concurrent)
followup_openings.defect: Claims BOTH higher accuracy and higher throughput (+5.4%/+2.7% accuracy at 4.5x/2.7x throughput vs Dream 7B and Qwen3 4B), which if taken at face value falsifies any blanket 'speedups vanish at iso-quality' thesis. But it compares single points, not curves, and the AR comparison is size-mismatched (8B dLM vs Qwen3 4B) with no FLOP- or memory-matched control and no quality-cost sweep on either side.
followup_openings.our_fix: Include Efficient-DLM as a deliberate adversarial case in the iso-quality frontier and report the result honestly whichever way it falls: apply the same cheapest-config-at-target-T protocol with a size-and-memory-matched AR sibling. If the 2.7x survives matched quality and matched footprint, that is a genuine positive existence result -- 'careful accounting shrinks most claims but this one is real' -- which is a far stronger and more publishable paper than a uniformly deflationary one.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: Pre-registering the strongest counterexample immunises the paper against the fatal 'you only audited the weak claims' rebuttal, and makes the kill criterion meaningful rather than rhetorical. It also converts a threat into a contribution: the field currently has no way to tell which of the dozens of Nx claims are real, and a protocol that certifies one is more useful than one that only debunks.

followup_openings.target_paper: On Evaluating Performance of LLM Inference Serving Systems (arXiv:2507.09019, 2025-07-11) + The Efficiency Misnomer (arXiv:2110.12894, ICLR 2022)
followup_openings.defect: Both are checklists or taxonomies without a quantitative demonstration in the diffusion-LM setting. 2507.09019 names 'baseline comparisons that conflate engineering effort with algorithmic novelty' as an anti-pattern -- which is exactly dInfer's vLLM-vs-dInfer confound and 2510.18480's HF-Transformers-AR handicap -- but never re-runs a published claim to show by how much it moves. The Efficiency Misnomer establishes that cost indicators contradict each other, but pre-dates any paradigm where the practitioner turns a continuous quality-cost knob at inference time.
followup_openings.our_fix: Make our paper the quantitative instantiation: take specific published multipliers (dInfer 2-3x, Elastic-Cache 8.7x/45.1x, Planned Diffusion 1.27-1.81x, Efficient-DLM 2.7x) and report what each becomes under (a) matched quality, (b) three cost units, (c) a batch sweep, (d) a properly served AR denominator -- i.e. a table of 'as published' vs 'as re-accounted'. Cite The Efficiency Misnomer as the source of the multi-unit requirement and 2507.09019 as the source of the baseline-fairness requirement, and adopt Planned Diffusion (1.3-1.8x with a stated 0.87-5.4% quality cost) as the positive control for what an honestly-accounted claim looks like.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: A published-vs-re-accounted table is the single most citable artifact this direction can produce, and it inherits legitimacy from an ICLR paper's framework rather than asserting a new one. It also gives the field a reusable protocol rather than a one-off audit, which is what lifts this from a workshop note to a main-conference methodology contribution.

diff.sharpened_claim: Every published diffusion-vs-AR efficiency comparison reports cost at each system's own operating point -- either its default (dInfer, Elastic-Cache) or its best-of-sweep peak (2606.19475) -- and the two pre-cutoff audits that question these claims (2510.18480, 2510.04146) both explicitly omit the accuracy axis, with 2510.18480 stating so in a footnote. We supply the missing inversion: fix a quality target T, find the CHEAPEST configuration of each system reaching T, and report the diffusion/AR cost ratio at matched T under three commensurable units (tokens processed, per-request wall-clock, FLOPs), swept over batch size, on execution-verified code (HumanEval+/MBPP+, single shared evalplus 0.3.1 grader) rather than the GSM8K-at-length-128 setting the entire audit literature inhabits. Our measured curves make the code setting the decisive one: Dream-Coder-Instruct-7B's pass@1+ is .000/.000 at nfe16/32, .018 at nfe64, .555 at nfe256, .707 at nfe512, and exactly .707 again at nfe1024 -- a cliff far steeper than anything reported on math, with the unparseable-output rate falling 94% to 1.8% across it. So a diffusion code LM has NO cheap high-quality operating point to trade from, and any iso-quality comparison must be drawn against the expensive end of its own curve, not its fastest. The deliverable is a published-vs-re-accounted table covering dInfer (2-3x), Elastic-Cache (8.7x/45.1x), Planned Diffusion (1.27-1.81x, our positive control because it already prices its 0.87-5.4% quality cost), and Efficient-DLM (2.7x at higher accuracy, our pre-registered adversarial case), quantitatively instantiating The Efficiency Misnomer's multi-unit requirement and arXiv:2507.09019's baseline-fairness checklist in a setting neither anticipated. Secondary contribution, which resolves a standing contradiction: 2510.18480 concludes AR wins with an HF-Transformers AR arm while dInfer concludes diffusion wins with a vLLM AR arm, and nobody has reconciled them -- we do, by making both sides curves under one served stack, and we report the batch size at which the advantage crosses 1.0x.

Read the Efficient-DLM PDF first; the positioning report admits it never did, so its batch/engine/genlen protocol is currently unverified and must not be characterised until read.
feas.risk: See risk field above.
feas.required_control:
TWO controls, both mandatory, each mapped to a specific past retraction.

CONTROL A -- THE PROTOCOL-SYMMETRY DIFF (prevents retraction 2's failure mode: a pipeline stage that silently discarded its input, so the arm you thought you measured was not the arm you measured). Before ANY iso-quality cell is written, dump the full resolved protocol for every arm and diff them field by field, then publish the diff as a table in the paper. The AR script already writes protocol.json (generate_evalplus_ar.py, rank 0); the diffusion script does NOT -- add the equivalent dump. Assert equality on: chat_template on/off, base_continuation, add_bos_token, instruct-vs-base checkpoint lineage, stop_strings, max_new_tokens/canvas L, temperature, top_p, seed, grader version, GPU MODEL, and number of concurrent processes per GPU. Any inequality must either be eliminated or printed in the caption of every table it touches. This control is what catches the live instruct-vs-base confound (Dream INSTRUCT + chat ON vs Qwen BASE + raw continuation) and the live L20A-vs-H20 split, both of which are currently invisible in the summary markdown and both of which would have shipped. It also catches the r1/r2 trap: those two differ by top_p (1.0 vs 0.95, one passed --top-p and one relied on the default), so treating them as a seed replicate -- which the 21% "spread" invites -- would mislabel a sampler ablation as measurement noise.

CONTROL B -- MEASURED-VS-ANALYTIC COST AGREEMENT ON THE DIFFUSION ARM, PER TASK (prevents retraction 3's failure mode: a cost average that dropped the expensive tasks, understating a mean 2.85x; and retraction 1's: a verifier that compared nothing). The AR arm already has this: a forward_pre_hook measures cost, a closed form predicts it, and the run asserts they match (measured_matches_analytic: true, inconsistent_task_ids: []). The diffusion arm has no such instrumentation -- its cost is a pure identity nfe*(P+L). Port ForwardCostTracker onto Dream and assert per-task agreement, and require that every cost aggregate report n alongside the mean plus a hard assertion that n equals the full benchmark size (164 / 378), with truncated/budget-hit/errored tasks INCLUDED at their true cost rather than dropped. Additionally: compute every per-task cost from that task's own input_tokens (77..430, giving 301568..482304 at nfe512) and never from the run-mean scalar 350,832 -- reusing the mean as a per-task value is precisely how a cost average silently loses its tail. Without Control B the load-bearing 350,832 is an assumption about the decoder, not a measurement of it, on the exact axis the paper's thesis is about.

lens.title: Tail-Aware Cost Accounting: Truncated Requests Are Systematically the Most Expensive, and Dropping Them Understates Cost by up to 3.7x
lens.claim: Cost averages in generation-with-budget systems are silently conditioned on successful termination, and because budget-truncated requests are precisely the most expensive ones, this understates the true mean cost by a large and method-dependent factor. We measured 2.85x (HumanEval+) and 3.69x (MBPP+) understatement for the arm with the heaviest tail, versus only 0.93-1.15x for six other arms -- so the bias is not a constant offset but actively reorders methods, and it removed a configuration from the frontier once corrected. We further show budget-doubling does not fix the tail: 512->1024 model calls moved the truncation rate only ~1pp (10.4% -> 9.2%).
lens.why_now: Every 2026 dLLM serving paper (BlockServe 2607.08930 on convergence heterogeneity and stragglers, DiLaServe 2606.29094 on SLO attainment, Sangam 2607.04206 on deficit scheduling, Optimus 2605.xxxx on elastic decoding) is fundamentally about the request tail -- yet the offline evaluation literature those systems are optimising against reports mean cost over completed requests. The serving community has discovered the tail matters while the evaluation community still averages it away. This is also our own Retraction 3, so we can write it with full first-person evidence of how the error arises and how it is caught.
lens.experiment: Mostly analysis over data on disk. (1) Formalise the estimator bias: define proc() over the union of process and failure_process telemetry, and show that the conventional completed-only mean is E[cost | terminated], deriving conditions under which it is downward-biased. (2) Empirical magnitude across all 8 scaffold arms x 2 benchmarks: report per-arm (completed-only mean, all-request mean, ratio, n dropped, coverage) -- measured ratios 2.85x/3.69x for Large vs 0.93-1.15x elsewhere, with 17/164 and 35/378 requests dropped. (3) Show frontier reordering: the corrected accounting moves scaffold Large OFF the Pareto frontier on both benchmarks, converting our earlier 'Large plateaus vs Medium' into 'Large is strictly dominated' (same-or-worse quality at 2.5x/3.0x cost). (4) Budget-doubling falsification (already run): Large@512 147/164 resolved with 17 truncations vs Large@1024 with truncation rate ~9.2%, confirming the tail is intrinsic, not a budget artifact. (5) Report the recommended reporting standard: cost distributions with p50/p95/p99 and explicit field coverage, plus tail-latency percentiles -- we already have per-task p95 wall-clock showing scaffold Large at 261.27s vs a 3.42s median, a 76x intra-arm spread that no mean can represent.
lens.assets_needed: HAVE everything needed for legs 1-5: 8 scaffold run dirs x 2 benchmarks with process/failure_process split and termination_reason per task; the Large@1024 falsifiability run (HE+ complete, MBPP+ still in flight on all 8 local GPUs as PIDs 335200-335207 -- do NOT disturb); scripts/make_pareto_figures.py already patched with a unified proc() accessor and a field_coverage() reporter (commit 8451e93); per-task elapsed_seconds enabling latency percentiles. MISSING/FLAG: (a) MBPP+ Large@1024 must finish before the budget-doubling leg is complete on both benchmarks; (b) to generalise beyond our own runtime we need one external system with a comparable truncation mode -- a max-token-capped AR baseline or a block-diffusion early-exit arm -- otherwise the finding reads as specific to our harness rather than a general accounting hazard, which is the main threat to this candidate's reach.
lens.kill_criterion: Killed as a standalone contribution if a survey of recent dLLM/serving papers shows they already report all-request cost with explicit coverage (i.e. the hazard is hypothetical): I would need to check ~15 papers' evaluation sections and find that >=80% already handle truncation correctly. Killed as a general claim if the bias magnitude does not reproduce on any system other than ours -- i.e. if only our scaffold runtime has a heavy enough tail for the conditioning to matter, then this is an errata note, not a methods paper. Quantitative bar for 'matters': the corrected accounting must change frontier membership or method ranking in at least one external setting, not just ours.
lens.builds_on: Generalises our own Retraction 3 into a reusable estimator critique, and connects it to the serving-side tail literature (BlockServe 2607.08930 and DiLaServe 2606.29094, both CONCURRENT, both centred on straggler/convergence heterogeneity) which independently confirms tails dominate real cost. The opening those papers leave: they fix the tail in the SERVING layer while offline evaluations continue to report tail-truncated means, so system gains and benchmark costs are measured in mutually incompatible units. Note this candidate is the most defensive of the six -- its natural home is a section of systems-1 plus a reproducibility/artifact track submission, not a standalone flagship.

diff.sharpened_claim: Budget-truncated requests are the most expensive requests, so the near-universal convention of averaging cost over completed requests is a *survivorship-conditioned* estimator E[cost | terminated] whose bias is (a) large, (b) arm-dependent, and (c) order-reversing. On our 8-arm x 2-benchmark scaffold corpus we measure per-arm bias ratios spanning 0.95x-7.18x: 2.85x/3.69x for the heavy-tail arm at model_call_budget=512 versus 0.95-1.15x for five other arms. Two consequences are new relative to the candidate as filed and are the strongest form of the claim: (1) the bias *reverses pairwise cost orderings*, not just inflates magnitudes -- under completed-only accounting scaffold-Large looks CHEAPER than scaffold-Medium (0.88x HE+, 0.83x MBPP+) whereas under union accounting it is 2.48x/3.05x MORE expensive, a sign flip in both benchmarks that converts "Large plateaus" into "Large is strictly dominated"; and (2) the bias GROWS with the compute budget rather than shrinking -- doubling model_call_budget 512->1024 moves the truncation rate only ~1-2pp (10.4%->10.4% HE+, 9.3%->8.5% MBPP+) while the bias ratio rises 2.85x->5.32x (HE+) and 3.69x->7.18x (MBPP+), so raising the budget makes completed-only accounting *more* misleading, not less. This inverts the natural intuition that a generous budget is a safe substitute for correct accounting, and it means the hazard is worst exactly in the generous-budget regime that Cost-of-Pass-style economic frameworks and dLLM efficiency papers evaluate in. We give the estimator, a coverage-reporting protocol (union-of-{process, failure_process} accessor, explicit n-dropped and field-coverage, p50/p95/p99 and termination_reason breakdown), and evidence that the hazard is invisible to a reader: our own AR-baseline summarizer independently reproduced the same `if row.get("process")` filter, i.e. the bug is a convergent default, not a one-off slip.
diff.differentiation_statement: The closest prior work partitions cleanly into three families, none of which makes our claim. (1) Cost-aware evaluation frameworks -- Cost-of-Pass (2504.13359, ICLR 2026 Poster, first public 2025-04, so PRE-cutoff) and AI Agents That Matter (2407.01502, TMLR) -- argue that accuracy must be reported jointly with cost and build economic frontiers over cost-accuracy pairs. They establish the *axis*; they are silent on the *estimator* used to populate it, and Cost-of-Pass's expected-cost-per-correct-solution is in fact a construction where the conditioning-on-termination hazard bites hardest. Our contribution is orthogonal and downstream: given that you have decided to report cost, which sample do you average over. (2) Efficiency-reporting critiques -- The Efficiency Misnomer (2110.12894) shows cost indicators (FLOPs, params, latency) disagree and urges multi-indicator reporting; CaRE (2607.24763, CONCURRENT, 2026-06) shows MDLM remasking rankings reverse under compute-matched NFE and that temperature dominates MAUVE variance. Both are *cross-indicator* / *cross-configuration* critiques: they hold the sample fixed and vary the metric or the compute setting. Ours is a *within-indicator, within-configuration* critique: fix the indicator and the budget, and the choice of denominator alone reverses the ordering. CaRE is also the nearest neighbour in spirit and in subfield (MDLM eval protocol audit) and, notably, standardises NFE without addressing what happens to requests that exhaust the step budget -- which is precisely our hazard, so we are a complement it invites rather than a duplicate. (3) Serving-side tail work -- BlockServe (2607.08930), DiLaServe (2606.29094), Sangam (2607.04206), all CONCURRENT (2026-06/07) -- treats convergence heterogeneity, stragglers and tail latency as first-class in the *scheduler*, and thereby independently corroborates that the tail dominates real dLLM cost; but each measures throughput/SLO on the serving side while the offline numbers those systems are optimising toward are still tail-truncated means. We name and quantify that unit mismatch. Finally, the canonical statistical machinery for exactly this problem exists but in a different community and for a different purpose: right-censored runtime handling in algorithm configuration (Bayesian Optimization With Censored Response Data, 1310.1947) and the SAT/planning community's PAR10 convention deliberately impute a penalty for capped runs. That is strong support for our framing -- the LLM-evaluation community has re-encountered a hazard that solver benchmarking solved two decades ago and codified in its default metric -- and it is a positioning asset, not prior art, because no one has ported the censoring correction to generation-with-budget LLM cost reporting or shown it flips method rankings there. Reviewer-facing one-liner: prior work fixed the cost *axis* (Cost-of-Pass), the cost *indicator* (Efficiency Misnomer), the cost *budget* (CaRE), and the *scheduler* (BlockServe/DiLaServe/Sangam); nobody fixed the cost *denominator*, and we show the denominator alone reverses orderings and gets worse with a larger budget.

Latency: scaffold_large_heplus median 3.42s, p95 261.27s, max 889.32s -- the candidate's "261.27s vs 3.42s median, 76x" reproduces exactly. THREE FINDINGS I ADDED that are NOT in the candidate as filed and that materially strengthen it: (i) the pairwise sign flip -- completed-only Large/Medium cost ratio is 0.88x (HE+) and 0.83x (MBPP+), union is 2.48x and 3.05x, so the bias reverses the ordering rather than merely inflating it; (ii) the bias ratio GROWS with budget -- scaffold_large_heplus_budget1024 ratio 5.32x and scaffold_large_mbppplus_budget1024 ratio 7.18x, versus 2.85x/3.69x at budget 512, so budget-doubling makes the accounting error worse; (iii) the convergent-default evidence -- scripts/_summarize_ar_run.py line ~44 independently reintroduces `ok = [row for row in metrics if row.get("process")]` and computes every cost stat over `ok`, i.e. the AR baseline written by a different agent after Retraction 3 has the same bug, which is much better evidence that this is a systematic hazard than a single self-report. CORRECTIONS to the candidate's own text: (a) it says MBPP+ Large@1024 is "still in flight on 8 local GPUs (PIDs 335200-335207)" -- that run has LANDED, runs/scaffold_large_mbppplus_budget1024 has n=333 records (28 truncations, 8.5%), so the budget-doubling leg is complete on BOTH benchmarks and the "MISSING (a)" flag is stale; note n=333 not 378, so the arm is 45 tasks short of full coverage and any cross-arm comparison at 1024 must be restricted to the shared 333 task_ids or explicitly flagged. (b) The candidate's truncation-rate figure "10.4% -> 9.2%" is a cross-benchmark blend; per-benchmark the correct numbers are HE+ 10.4%->10.4% (17/164 both) and MBPP+ 9.3%->8.5% (35/378 -> 28/333). So "corrected accounting moves scaffold Large off the Pareto frontier" is no longer interesting, because AR removed the whole scaffold family from the frontier first. Leg 3 must be reframed as the *pairwise cost-ordering sign flip* (finding i above), which survives Retraction 4 because it is an intra-family statement about the estimator, not a frontier-membership claim. related_work.citation: Erol, Suzgun, Jurafsky, Zou. "Cost-of-Pass: An Economic Framework for Evaluating Language Models." arXiv:2504.13359
related_work.venue_status: ICLR 2026 Poster -- verified via OpenReview api2 notes/search: venue string "ICLR 2026 Poster", venueid ICLR.cc/2026/Conference, submission 16408, Camera_Ready_Revision invitation present. arXiv citation_online_date 2026/02/26 but citation_date/v1 2025-04-17, so first public is PRE-cutoff.
related_work.what_it_covers: Formalises cost-of-pass = expected monetary cost to produce one correct solution, and frontier cost-of-pass = the minimum over available models plus a human-expert reference. Tracks the frontier over a year, does counterfactual-frontier ablations by removing model classes, and prices inference-time techniques (majority voting, self-refinement, budget-aware TALE-EP). This is the strongest existing statement that cost belongs on the evaluation axis alongside accuracy.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Entirely silent on the estimator used to compute the cost term. Their headline quantity is an expectation over generations that either do or do not produce a correct solution under some cap; nowhere do they state whether cap-exhausting generations contribute their (maximal) cost to the denominator, nor do they report coverage or n-dropped. Because cost-of-pass divides by success rate, a downward-biased numerator and a success-conditioned sample compound. No cost distribution, no percentiles, no termination-reason breakdown.
related_work.known_defects: The framework's own construction is maximally exposed to our hazard: 'expected cost of generating a correct solution' invites averaging over runs that produced a correct solution, which is exactly the survivorship conditioning we quantify, and the failures are the expensive ones. Reported means only -- a heavy-tailed cost distribution is compressed to a point estimate, so the frontier is drawn from statistics that cannot represent it. Frontier and counterfactual-frontier conclusions are stated as robust but are never stress-tested against accounting perturbations; our sign-flip result shows a plausible perturbation of exactly this kind reverses pairwise cost orderings. Monetary cost is taken from provider price lists, which makes truncation invisible by construction (a capped generation is billed, but if the run is discarded from the average the bill vanishes from the report).
related_work.verified_how: arXiv abs page (citation_date 2025/04/17, citation_online_date 2026/02/26) + OpenReview api2 notes/search returning venue "ICLR 2026 Poster" with venueid ICLR.cc/2026/Conference and Camera_Ready_Revision among invitations.

related_work.citation: Kapoor, Stroebl, Siegel, Nadgir, Narayanan. "AI Agents That Matter." arXiv:2407.01502
related_work.venue_status: Accepted at TMLR -- verified via OpenReview api2 notes/search (venue "Accepted by TMLR", venueid TMLR).
related_work.what_it_covers: Audit of agent benchmarking practice. Three findings: narrow focus on accuracy without cost leads to needlessly complex and costly SOTA agents and to mistaken attribution of accuracy gains; model-developer and downstream-developer benchmarking needs are conflated; many agent benchmarks have inadequate or absent holdout sets, producing shortcut-taking and overfitting. Proposes joint accuracy-cost optimisation and demonstrates a cost reduction at fixed accuracy. The canonical 'you must report cost' paper for agents.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Argues for the cost axis but not for how to estimate the cost. Does not treat budget-capped or timed-out trajectories as an estimator problem, does not report coverage or the fraction of trajectories excluded, and does not report cost distributions or tail percentiles. Its own retry/scaffold cost analyses are at the mean.
related_work.known_defects: Prescribes cost reporting without prescribing a denominator convention or a coverage disclosure, so a paper can comply fully with its recommendations and still publish a 3-7x understated mean -- which is exactly what we did before catching it, and what our own AR-baseline script did again afterwards. Uses mean cost throughout despite agent trajectory costs being heavy-tailed by construction (retries, tool loops, step caps). The holdout-set critique is empirical and thorough while the cost critique stays largely normative -- no measurement of how much existing reported costs are wrong, which is the gap we fill quantitatively.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv abs page (citation_date 2024/07/01) + OpenReview api2 notes/search returning venue "Accepted by TMLR", venueid TMLR.

related_work.citation: Anonymous / preprint. "CaRE: Compute-aware Remasking Evaluation Protocol for Masked Diffusion Language Models." arXiv:2607.24763
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (arXiv v1 2026-06-04). I searched OpenReview for this exact title and did NOT find it; a related MDLM-remasking-audit paper, "Re-evaluating Confidence Remasking in Masked Diffusion Language Models", IS on OpenReview at ICML.cc/2026/Workshop/SPIGM (Poster) and ICML.cc/2026/Workshop/AdaptFM (Poster) -- possibly the same work renamed, but I did not confirm the link and do not assert it.
related_work.what_it_covers: The nearest neighbour in both spirit and subfield: a compute-aware evaluation audit of MDLMs. Observes that seven recent remasking papers evaluate under incompatible nominal step counts, metrics and temperatures without jointly controlling them, making their strategy rankings incomparable. Standardises ACTUAL NFE, enforces multi-metric reporting, controls stochasticity; applies it to 7 remasking strategies x LLaDA-8B-Base and Dream-7B-Base x 4 stochasticity levels x 3 step budgets, plus a 12-model leaderboard (150M-8B). Finds temperature explains most MAUVE variance and that compute-matched comparison REVERSES several published rankings.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Standardises the compute budget but not the accounting over requests that exhaust it. Nothing on truncation/step-budget exhaustion as an estimator problem: no coverage reporting, no all-request-vs-completed-only comparison, no per-request cost distribution or tail percentiles. Its ranking reversals come from varying the compute setting; it does not ask whether rankings also reverse at FIXED compute purely from the choice of denominator, which is our result. Evaluated on open-ended text (OpenWebText, LM1B) with MAUVE, not on pass/fail task benchmarks where a request can be unambiguously classified terminated-vs-truncated -- so the hazard is structurally hard to see in their setting.
related_work.known_defects: MAUVE-centric evaluation on OpenWebText/LM1B means the notion of a 'completed' generation is fuzzy and the truncation hazard cannot surface -- a coverage blind spot rather than an error. 'Actual NFE' is still a single scalar mean per configuration; a heavy NFE tail across prompts would be invisible, and their own finding that temperature dominates variance suggests per-prompt heterogeneity is large. One reported effect (high-entropy remasking reduces MAUVE by 0.296 at 256 steps, unmask_temp=0.25) is given at p=0.020 within a large strategy x temperature x budget grid, i.e. borderline under any multiplicity correction. Base models only, no instruct/code models, so the ranking-reversal claim is untested in the regime (code, pass@1, budget caps) where budgets actually bind.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv abs page fetched with cache-busting (citation_date and citation_online_date both 2026/06/04, i.e. AFTER the 2026-05-07 cutoff -> concurrent); OpenReview api2 notes/search on the title (no match) and on the related-title paper (two ICML 2026 workshop venueids confirmed).

related_work.citation: "BlockServe: Block-Grained Continuous Batching for High-Throughput Diffusion LLM Serving." arXiv:2607.08930
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (arXiv v1 2026-07-09); no venue claimed on the abs page.
related_work.what_it_covers: Serving framework for dLLMs built explicitly around convergence heterogeneity: when batching, sequences converge at different rates so fast requests stall behind slow stragglers, creating compute bubbles and tail latency. Combines block-grained scheduling (evict completed requests at block boundaries), mixed-state execution (dual cache + parallel decoding over heterogeneous batches via gather-scatter indexing), and a compute-aware admission controller with token-budgeted refill. 1.9-10.6x throughput over Fast-dLLM on Dream and LLaDA across five benchmarks.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Fixes the tail in the serving layer and takes offline benchmark cost/quality numbers as given. Does not examine how the offline evaluations it is optimising against account for requests that never converge, so the system's gains and the benchmark's costs are denominated in incompatible units -- system-side throughput is measured over all admitted requests, benchmark-side cost over completed ones. Provides no estimator or reporting guidance for the offline side.
related_work.known_defects: 'Comparable generation quality' is asserted against Fast-dLLM without a truncation/coverage accounting: block-grained eviction and token-budgeted admission are precisely mechanisms that can convert a slow request into a truncated one, and a throughput win partly financed by dropping tail requests would be indistinguishable from a real win under the reported metrics. The 1.9-10.6x range is very wide and the abstract does not identify which convergence-heterogeneity regime sits at each end, so the headline number is not reproducible from the abstract. Baseline is Fast-dLLM only (a dLLM-internal comparison) with no matched AR serving stack such as vLLM continuous batching -- the same missing-cross-family-control pattern we hit in our own Retraction 4.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv abs page fetched directly (title and citation_date 2026/07/09 confirmed, full abstract read).

related_work.citation: "DiLaServe: High SLO Attainment Serving for Diffusion Language Models." arXiv:2606.29094
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (arXiv v1 2026-06-27); no venue claimed on the abs page.
related_work.what_it_covers: Cluster-level dLLM serving system targeting latency SLOs. Identifies three dLLM-specific challenges: the speed-quality tradeoff created by confidence-based denoising, choosing parallelisation levels across model instances under fluctuating load, and coordinating approximate KV caching whose per-step costs are non-uniform. Provides deadline-aware scheduling and adaptive load control.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: SLO attainment is a per-request tail statement, so DiLaServe independently confirms that tails, not means, govern real dLLM cost -- but it never connects this to how offline dLLM evaluations report cost. It does not define or measure a request-level cost estimator for benchmark reporting, and does not address deadline-missed / truncated requests as an accounting problem for the quality numbers.
related_work.known_defects: SLO attainment is reported as a rate, which makes the COST of the requests that miss their deadline invisible: a policy that sheds or truncates expensive stragglers improves attainment while worsening true mean cost, and the reported metric cannot separate the two. Non-uniform per-step cost from approximate KV caching is named as a challenge but, per the abstract, not surfaced as a per-request cost distribution. Quality under the speed-quality knob is traded off without a truncation-coverage audit, so quality-neutrality claims under aggressive deadlines are unaudited.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv abs page fetched directly (title and citation_date 2026/06/27 confirmed, full abstract read).

related_work.citation: "Sangam: Efficiently Serving Diffusion LLMs with the AR Stack." arXiv:2607.04206
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (arXiv v1 2026-07-05); no venue claimed on the abs page.
related_work.what_it_covers: Serving system for cached dLLM inference. Observes that bidirectional attention forbids exact AR-style KV caching (committing one position shifts all others), that approximate caching (Fast-dLLM, dKV-Cache) therefore induces a repeated prefill/decode structure, and that AR serving mechanisms are relevant but not directly applicable because dLLM decodes are block-sized, prefills recur, and chunked prefill is precluded. Introduces a deficit token-budget scheduler admitting in-flight decodes.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: A deficit token-budget scheduler is a per-request budget allocator, so Sangam is operationally about exactly the quantity whose offline accounting we correct -- yet it inherits offline benchmark cost figures without questioning their denominator. No treatment of budget-exhausted requests as a measurement problem; no offline reporting guidance.
related_work.known_defects: A deficit scheduler with a token budget mechanically produces requests that exhaust their allocation; the abstract gives no accounting for what happens to those requests' cost and quality in the reported results, which is the serving-side twin of our hazard. Recurring-prefill cost is the paper's central mechanism but is characterised structurally rather than as a measured per-request distribution, so the very heterogeneity that motivates the design is not quantified. Comparisons are against dLLM caching baselines (Fast-dLLM, dKV-Cache) rather than a matched AR serving stack, despite the paper's framing being explicitly about borrowing the AR stack.

related_work.citation: Dehghani, Tay, Arnab, Beyer, Vaswani. "The Efficiency Misnomer." arXiv:2110.12894
related_work.venue_status: Preprint on arXiv (2021-10-25); widely cited as an ICLR 2022 paper but I did NOT verify that via OpenReview or official proceedings, so I record it as preprint-verified only.
related_work.what_it_covers: The canonical efficiency-reporting critique. Enumerates common cost indicators (parameters, FLOPs, speed/latency), shows they are not mutually correlated and can contradict each other, demonstrates that incomplete indicator reporting yields partial or misleading conclusions about which model is more efficient, and gives recommendations for reporting efficiency metrics.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Purely a cross-indicator critique -- it varies WHICH cost is reported while holding the sample fixed. It never considers WHICH REQUESTS are averaged over, so the survivorship-conditioning hazard is outside its scope. Written pre-generative-budget era: no notion of per-request generation budgets, truncation, or termination reasons, and no distributional reporting (its recommendations are about indicator multiplicity, not about percentiles or coverage).
related_work.known_defects: Recommends reporting multiple cost indicators but not the sample definition or coverage behind each, so full compliance is compatible with a 3-7x biased mean on every indicator. Its examples are training/inference on fixed-shape vision and text workloads where per-example cost is nearly constant, so heavy-tailed per-request cost -- the regime where the denominator matters most -- is untested; the paper's conclusions plausibly do not transfer to budgeted generative decoding, which is our setting. Prescriptive rather than quantitative on the size of the error a reader would make.

related_work.citation: Hutter, Bartz-Beielstein et al. "Bayesian Optimization With Censored Response Data." arXiv:1310.1947
related_work.venue_status: Preprint on arXiv (2013-10-07); associated with the NIPS 2011 BayesOpt workshop lineage but I did not verify a venue, so recorded as preprint-verified only.
related_work.what_it_covers: The canonical statistical treatment of exactly our hazard, in a different community. Addresses Bayesian optimisation under partially RIGHT-CENSORED responses, where some evaluations yield only a lower bound on the objective. The motivating application is runtime-minimising algorithm configuration: slow runs are deliberately capped, and correctly handling the resulting right-censored observations substantially improves state-of-the-art model-based configuration versus discarding or naively imputing them.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Entirely within algorithm configuration / solver runtime; nothing about language models, generation budgets, or benchmark cost reporting. It is about OPTIMISING under censoring, not about REPORTING unbiased cost in an evaluation table, and it does not address ranking reversals between methods induced by the reporting convention. The port to LLM generation-with-budget cost accounting -- where the censoring variable is model calls or tokens rather than wall-clock, and where the consumer is a Pareto plot rather than a surrogate model -- is entirely open.
related_work.known_defects: Not a defect in the paper so much as our positioning asset: the SAT/planning community independently converged on PAR10 (penalise capped runs at 10x the cap) precisely because plain means over completed runs are misleading, i.e. the correction is a DEFAULT there and absent in LLM evaluation. Their imputation is tailored to a surrogate-model objective and is not calibrated as an unbiased population-mean estimator, so it is not directly reusable as a reporting standard -- which leaves room for us to specify a reporting convention (union accounting + explicit coverage + percentiles) rather than an imputation. Their empirical scope is solver runtimes, so the magnitude of bias they observe carries no information about the magnitude in LLM generation.

related_work.citation: "AgentSLABench: Evaluating and Benchmarking Agentic Systems Under Resource Constraints." arXiv:2608.00805
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (arXiv v1 2026-08-01, i.e. six days before the concurrency cutoff reference date); no venue claimed.
related_work.what_it_covers: Resource-aware agent evaluation framework measuring correctness alongside latency, cost, compute, memory and network under DECLARED resource budgets -- explicitly analogised to systems profilers (perf, pprof, cProfile) with correctness added as a first-class dimension. 16 task environments across 6 categories, isolated Docker containers with declared CPU/memory/time/network budgets, SHA256-sealed test sets, standardised profiling protocol. Introduces Efficiency-Adjusted Success Rate (EASR) = success weighted by resource consumption relative to declared budgets, arguing high accuracy at unbounded cost is not production-viable.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: The most methodologically adjacent concurrent work and the one whose design most needs our correction: it declares per-task budgets, so budget exhaustion is a first-class event in its protocol, yet the abstract describes no accounting for budget-exhausted tasks in the resource means, no coverage reporting, and no cost percentiles. EASR folds cost into a single scalar per agent-task, which cannot express a heavy tail. Being concurrent (2026-08-01), it does not preempt us; it is the natural venue-mate and the natural first external replication target for our estimator.
related_work.known_defects: EASR weights success by resource consumption relative to declared budgets, which makes a failed-and-budget-exhausted task and a failed-and-cheap task contribute very differently while the abstract specifies no convention for either -- the metric's behaviour under exhaustion is undefined, and it is a compound scalar that conflates the estimator question with the weighting question. Reports per-agent-per-task profiles but no distributional summary, so intra-task variance across trials is invisible. Baselines are 5 general scaffolds (ReAct, PlanAndSolve, Reflexion, CoT, Random) plus 4 task-specialised agents, and the headline '100% success on 3/5 core tasks' for specialised agents on 16 environments is a very small denominator for a benchmark claim. Docker-isolated declared budgets should make the truncation flag trivially recordable, so this is a clean, cheap external setting in which to test whether our bias reproduces.

related_work.citation: "The Coupling Tax: How Shared Token Budgets Undermine Visible Chain-of-Thought Under Fixed Output Limits." arXiv:2605.07686
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (arXiv v1 2026-05-08 -- one day after the 2026-05-07 concurrency cutoff, so concurrent, but only barely; worth re-checking if the cutoff is ever tightened).
related_work.what_it_covers: The closest existing FORMAL treatment of truncation as a measurement effect. Identifies the 'coupling tax': when reasoning traces and final answers share one output-token budget, long traces crowd out the answer. Derives a truncation-waste decomposition Acc_think(b) = alpha_c * F_L(b) + alpha_t * (1 - F_L(b)) that predicts the thinking/non-thinking crossover from chain-length and accuracy statistics, explaining inverse scaling within Qwen3; replicated on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B. Mitigation: split-budget generation (IRIS) reaching 74.0-83.6% on MATH-500 variants.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Crucially, it decomposes ACCURACY as a function of the truncation CDF F_L(b) -- it is a quality-side truncation analysis. It does not decompose COST, and does not observe that the cost average is itself conditioned on non-truncation. So it establishes the mathematical vocabulary (a truncation CDF mixing two regimes) that we need on the quality axis, and leaves the cost axis entirely open. It also has no notion of cost-ordering reversal between methods, and no coverage-reporting prescription.
related_work.known_defects: Their decomposition treats alpha_c and alpha_t (accuracy conditional on completion vs truncation) as arm-level constants, which is exactly the homogeneity assumption our per-arm bias spread (0.95x-7.18x) shows fails on the cost axis; the analogous cost-side quantity is strongly arm-dependent, so importing their two-parameter form for cost would be wrong and we should say so. Restricted to math/BBH text reasoning with Qwen3 plus one DeepSeek replication -- no code generation, no diffusion models, no structural runtime, so the claim that the crossover is predictable from chain-length statistics is untested where budgets bind hardest. The IRIS numbers (74.0 / 78.8 / 83.6%) come from three progressively stronger extraction/gating variants, and the 83.6% 'fixed non-oracle SC+IRIS gate' adds self-consistency, so the headline gain is not attributable to split-budget generation alone -- an unfair-baseline hazard in their own mitigation claim.

related_work.citation: "Quantization Inflates Reasoning: Token Inflation as a Hidden Cost of Low-Bit Reasoning Models." arXiv:2606.25519
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (arXiv v1 2026-06-24, citation_online_date 2026/06/29).
related_work.what_it_covers: Structurally the closest 'hidden cost' paper: shows low-bit PTQ can preserve accuracy while increasing reasoning-token usage, so per-token speedups are offset. Introduces the CoT Token Inflation Ratio (quantized vs full-precision reasoning length, averaged across benchmarks) over math, code, science QA and agentic tool use; links inflation to behavioural changes (more intermediate steps, more semantic repetition) and to end-to-end serving penalties; evaluates prompting, decoding-time sampling and QAT as mitigations. Concludes reasoning-token usage should be reported.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Argues a specific cost is under-reported for a specific intervention (quantization), and their 'even when they still answer correctly' framing shows they DO condition on correctness -- but they never turn this into a general estimator critique, and they do not consider that generations hitting the length cap are excluded or mis-counted. Their inflation ratio is a ratio of means, so it inherits our bias in both numerator and denominator; the biases need not cancel when the two arms have different truncation rates, which is likely precisely when quantization inflates length toward the cap.
related_work.known_defects: The CoT Token Inflation Ratio is defined as a ratio of benchmark-averaged reasoning lengths, which (a) is silent on cap-hitting generations, (b) can cancel or amplify the survivorship bias unpredictably across arms, and (c) averages across benchmarks with different length distributions, so a single heavy-tailed benchmark can dominate. Conditioning on 'still answer correctly' is exactly the survivorship conditioning we critique, applied to length rather than cost, and is unexamined. 'Measurable end-to-end real-world serving penalties' is asserted but the abstract gives no tail/percentile characterisation, only means, despite inflation being a distributional-shift claim. Mitigation findings ('prompting and decoding-time sampling offer inconsistent tradeoffs') are stated qualitatively without a controlled budget-matched comparison.

related_work.citation: "Broken Chains: The Cost of Incomplete Reasoning in LLMs." arXiv:2602.14444
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (arXiv v1 2026-02-16); no venue claimed.
related_work.what_it_covers: The most relevant PRE-cutoff paper on truncation as a first-class phenomenon. Constrains four frontier models (GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Flash, DeepSeek-V3.2, Grok 4.1) to reason via code, comments, both, or neither, then ablates token budgets to 10/30/50/70% of optimal on AIME, GSM8K, HMMT. Finds truncated reasoning can be actively harmful (DeepSeek-V3.2: 53% with no reasoning vs 17% with truncated CoT at 50% budget), code degrades gracefully where comments collapse, hybrid underperforms, and robustness is strongly model-dependent.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Establishes pre-cutoff that budget truncation is consequential and heterogeneous across methods -- useful support for our premise -- but it is purely a QUALITY-side study. It measures accuracy under imposed budgets and never examines the cost estimator: no all-request vs completed-only cost comparison, no coverage reporting, no cost percentiles, no claim about cost-ordering reversal. It therefore does not preempt our claim; it strengthens the motivation for it, and its model-dependent robustness result is the quality-side analogue of our method-dependent bias factor.
related_work.known_defects: Budgets are set as percentages 'of optimal' where optimal is itself estimated from model behaviour, making the x-axis model-dependent and cross-model comparisons at '50% budget' not compute-matched -- a fairness defect our union-accounting protocol would expose. API-only frontier models, so cost is unmeasurable at the token level and the paper reports no cost quantity at all despite 'Cost' in the title (the cost is accuracy loss, not compute). Four models x three benchmarks with no seed/variance reporting, and headline contrasts (53% vs 17%) are single-configuration point estimates. No verification that 'no reasoning' and 'truncated CoT' arms have matched answer-extraction, so part of the 53-vs-17 gap could be parsing failure rather than misleading reasoning -- the same unparseable-output confound we measured directly in our own NFE sweep (94%->1.8%).

related_work.citation: "Diffusion Language Models: An Experimental Analysis." arXiv:2606.19475
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (arXiv v1 2026-06-17, v2 exists); no venue claimed.
related_work.what_it_covers: Large systematic dLLM audit: 8 state-of-the-art DLMs across 8 benchmarks (reasoning, coding, translation, knowledge, structured problem solving), explicitly considering BOTH generation quality and computational efficiency, motivated by exactly the incomparability problem we care about (differing evaluation protocols, datasets, inference budgets, generation hyperparameters). If its efficiency numbers are completed-only means, our correction could reorder its efficiency conclusions -- which is exactly the 'changes method ranking in at least one external setting' bar in the candidate's own kill criterion.

followup_openings.target_paper: Cost-of-Pass: An Economic Framework for Evaluating Language Models (arXiv:2504.13359, ICLR 2026 Poster) -- PRE-cutoff, so this is the highest-value follow-up target
followup_openings.defect: Cost-of-pass is defined as the expected monetary cost of generating a CORRECT solution, and frontier cost-of-pass as the minimum over models. The construction never specifies the sample over which the cost expectation is taken, and never reports coverage or n-dropped. Because the metric divides by success rate, a survivorship-conditioned numerator and a success-conditioned denominator compound. Costs are taken from provider price lists, which structurally hides truncation: a capped generation is billed, but if the run is dropped from the average the bill disappears from the report. Only means are reported, so a heavy-tailed cost distribution is compressed to a point estimate, and the frontier/counterfactual-frontier conclusions are never stress-tested against accounting perturbations.
followup_openings.our_fix: Re-derive cost-of-pass as an explicitly censored estimator. Define cost over the union of terminated and budget-exhausted requests, prove that the completed-only version is E[cost | terminated] and give the condition for downward bias (cost and truncation positively associated, which holds whenever the budget binds on the hardest requests). Then instantiate it on our corpus: 8 arms x 2 benchmarks with per-arm (completed-only mean, union mean, ratio, n dropped, coverage, termination_reason breakdown, p50/p95/p99). Headline the two results that a reviewer cannot dismiss as bookkeeping: (a) the pairwise SIGN FLIP -- completed-only makes scaffold-Large look 0.88x/0.83x the cost of scaffold-Medium while union accounting makes it 2.48x/3.05x, in both benchmarks; (b) the bias GROWS with budget -- 2.85x->5.32x (HE+) and 3.69x->7.18x (MBPP+) when model_call_budget doubles 512->1024, while truncation rate barely moves (17/164 -> 17/164; 35/378 -> 28/333). Then apply the corrected estimator to Cost-of-Pass's own inference-time-technique comparison (majority voting, self-refinement, TALE-EP), where capped/failed generations are exactly the expensive ones, and report whether any frontier or counterfactual-frontier conclusion moves.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This is the single strongest positioning available: it attaches our correction to the pre-cutoff, peer-reviewed, ICLR-2026 framework that the field is adopting as the standard way to report cost, rather than to our own retracted internal result. It converts 'we found a bug in our harness' into 'the community's canonical cost metric is defined in a way that invites a 3-7x error, and here is the estimator that fixes it plus a demonstration that it reverses orderings.' It also directly satisfies the candidate's own kill criterion (frontier membership or ranking must change in at least one external setting), because Cost-of-Pass supplies an external frontier construction to test against.

followup_openings.target_paper: CaRE: Compute-aware Remasking Evaluation Protocol for Masked Diffusion Language Models (arXiv:2607.24763) -- CONCURRENT (2026-06-04), so complement rather than compete
followup_openings.defect: CaRE standardises ACTUAL NFE and shows compute-matched comparison reverses several published remasking rankings -- but it standardises the compute BUDGET while leaving unspecified how to account for generations that exhaust it. It reports no coverage, no all-request vs completed-only comparison, no per-request cost distribution. Its evaluation surface (OpenWebText/LM1B with MAUVE, base models only) makes 'completed' inherently fuzzy, so the truncation hazard structurally cannot appear; and its own finding that temperature dominates MAUVE variance implies large per-prompt heterogeneity that a mean NFE cannot represent. One headline interaction effect is reported at p=0.020 inside a large strategy x temperature x budget grid, i.e. fragile under multiplicity correction.
followup_openings.our_fix: Position our estimator as the missing second axis of CaRE's own thesis and prove the axes are independent. CaRE shows rankings reverse when you vary compute at fixed accounting; we show rankings reverse when you vary accounting at FIXED compute (our sign flip is measured within a single budget setting). Concretely: adopt CaRE's compute-matched protocol, add the union-accounting + coverage layer, and demonstrate on a pass/fail task surface (HumanEval+/MBPP+) where terminated-vs-truncated is unambiguous -- the regime CaRE's MAUVE-on-OpenWebText setting cannot reach. Also port the tail reporting: CaRE's per-configuration mean NFE becomes a p50/p95/p99 NFE profile, which we can motivate empirically since our own arms show a 76x intra-arm wall-clock spread (median 3.42s vs p95 261.27s, max 889.32s on scaffold_large_heplus).
followup_openings.why_it_matters: CaRE is the nearest neighbour in both spirit and subfield and will be the paper a reviewer names first. Framing ours as the orthogonal completion of its programme -- budget standardisation plus denominator standardisation, jointly needed and independently sufficient to flip rankings -- converts the closest competitor into the citation that legitimises the direction, and gives us a concrete, credible venue-mate. It also extends CaRE's claim to instruct/code models and a pass/fail metric, a regime it explicitly does not test.

followup_openings.target_paper: AgentSLABench (arXiv:2608.00805, CONCURRENT 2026-08-01) and AI Agents That Matter (arXiv:2407.01502, TMLR, PRE-cutoff)
followup_openings.defect: AI Agents That Matter prescribes joint accuracy-cost reporting but specifies no denominator convention and no coverage disclosure, so a paper can comply fully and still publish a 3-7x understated mean; it uses means throughout on trajectory costs that are heavy-tailed by construction (retries, tool loops, step caps). AgentSLABench declares per-task CPU/memory/time/network budgets -- making budget exhaustion a first-class protocol event -- yet its Efficiency-Adjusted Success Rate folds cost into one scalar weighted by consumption relative to declared budgets, with no stated behaviour for budget-exhausted tasks, no coverage reporting, and no cost percentiles. Its headline '100% success on 3/5 core tasks' rests on 16 environments, a small denominator.
followup_openings.our_fix: Supply the missing reporting standard as a drop-in and validate it in an external harness. Deliverable 1: a coverage-and-tail reporting spec -- union-of-{terminated, budget-exhausted} accounting, mandatory (n_total, n_truncated, coverage per cost field, termination_reason histogram), and p50/p95/p99 alongside the mean -- concretely instantiated as the proc() accessor and field_coverage() reporter already in scripts/make_pareto_figures.py (commit 8451e93). Deliverable 2: because AgentSLABench runs Docker-isolated tasks under DECLARED budgets, recording a budget-exhausted flag is nearly free there; recompute its resource means and EASR under union accounting and report whether any agent ranking moves. Deliverable 3: define EASR's undefined behaviour under exhaustion and show the two natural conventions give different agent orderings.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This is the cheapest credible path to the external replication our kill criterion demands, and it makes the contribution prescriptive rather than confessional. It also targets the two papers that shape how the agent community reports cost, so the fix has a natural adoption path; and pairing a PRE-cutoff prescriptive paper (AI Agents That Matter) with a CONCURRENT budget-declaring harness (AgentSLABench) lets us argue the hazard is both long-standing and still live.

followup_openings.target_paper: BlockServe (2607.08930), DiLaServe (2606.29094), Sangam (2607.04206) -- all CONCURRENT (2026-06/07)
followup_openings.defect: All three treat the request tail as first-class in the SCHEDULER while inheriting offline benchmark cost/quality numbers computed over completed requests, so system-side gains and benchmark-side costs are denominated in incompatible units. Each also has a specific internal exposure: BlockServe asserts 'comparable generation quality' at 1.9-10.6x throughput over Fast-dLLM without truncation/coverage accounting, even though block-grained eviction and token-budgeted admission are exactly mechanisms that convert slow requests into truncated ones -- a throughput win partly financed by shedding tail requests would be indistinguishable from a real win. DiLaServe reports SLO attainment as a rate, which renders the cost of deadline-missing requests invisible, so a policy that sheds expensive stragglers improves the metric while worsening true mean cost. Sangam's deficit token-budget scheduler mechanically produces allocation-exhausted requests with no stated accounting for their cost or quality. All three benchmark only against dLLM baselines (Fast-dLLM, dKV-Cache) with no matched AR serving stack.
followup_openings.our_fix: Write the unit-reconciliation result: define one request-level cost quantity that is computable both offline (union accounting over model calls / tokens_fed / attended_context_sum) and online (per-request served cost), and show that under completed-only offline accounting a scheduler can report a throughput or SLO win that is partly an artifact of reclassifying expensive requests as truncated. Instantiate the mechanism concretely with our budget-doubling result, which is the clean existence proof: raising the budget 512->1024 barely changes the truncation rate (~1-2pp) yet nearly doubles the accounting bias (2.85->5.32x, 3.69->7.18x), so 'give it more budget' is not a substitute for correct accounting and the hazard is WORST in the generous-budget regime these systems target. Add the audit these papers cannot do for themselves: report our per-task p95/p99 wall-clock (261.27s p95 vs 3.42s median, 889.32s max) to show a straggler distribution in an offline harness of the same shape as the convergence heterogeneity BlockServe designs for.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This supplies the 'why now' with actual teeth rather than assertion: three concurrent serving papers independently discovered the tail dominates real dLLM cost, which is strong external corroboration of our premise and, because all three are concurrent, cannot preempt us. It also upgrades the contribution from an evaluation-hygiene note to a claim about a measurable inconsistency between two active literatures, which is a much better fit for a systems or reproducibility venue than an errata.

followup_openings.target_paper: Our own corpus -- the convergent-default evidence, and the reframing forced by Retraction 4/5 (git 1170ae6, 2026-08-07)
followup_openings.defect: Two things. First, a defect in the CANDIDATE as filed: leg 3 claims the contribution is that corrected accounting moves scaffold Large off the Pareto frontier. That is now obsolete -- Retraction 4 (matched Qwen2.5-Coder-7B AR: HE+ .524 vs scaffold Medium .177 at 70x fewer tokens_fed) removed the entire scaffold family from the frontier first, so 'Large leaves the frontier' is uninteresting. Filing leg 3 as written would be a fourth self-inflicted retraction. The candidate also mis-states two facts: MBPP+ Large@1024 has LANDED (n=333, 28 truncations) so the 'MISSING (a)' flag is stale, and the '10.4%->9.2%' truncation figure is a cross-benchmark blend (correct per-benchmark: HE+ 10.4%->10.4%, MBPP+ 9.3%->8.5%). Second, the real defect worth publishing: this bug is a CONVERGENT DEFAULT, not a one-off. scripts/_summarize_ar_run.py independently reintroduces `ok = [row for row in metrics if row.get("process")]` and computes every cost statistic over `ok` -- written by a different agent, for a different model family, AFTER Retraction 3 had already documented the hazard.
followup_openings.our_fix: Reframe leg 3 from frontier membership to the ESTIMATOR-INTRINSIC sign flip, which survives Retraction 4 because it is an intra-family statement about accounting rather than a claim about who owns the frontier: completed-only puts Large at 0.88x/0.83x Medium's cost, union puts it at 2.48x/3.05x -- a reversal in both benchmarks. Pair it with the budget-monotonicity result (bias rises 2.85->5.32x and 3.69->7.18x under budget doubling) as the counter-intuitive headline. Then add a third leg the candidate does not have: a recurrence audit. Present the `if row.get("process")` filter reappearing independently in the AR summarizer as evidence that the hazard is a design-level attractor in metrics-logging schemas that split success and failure telemetry into separate keys, and propose the schema-level fix (one cost record per request with an explicit termination_reason, never two mutually exclusive keys) rather than a discipline-level exhortation. Also restrict all 1024-budget cross-arm comparisons to the shared 333 MBPP+ task_ids or flag the coverage gap explicitly.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: The recurrence audit is what makes this a methods contribution instead of an errata note: a single self-report is anecdote, but the same error re-emerging independently in a second harness after being documented is evidence about how telemetry schemas cause the bias, which is generalisable and actionable. And the reframing is load-bearing for survival -- as filed, leg 3's central claim was killed hours before this review by our own AR baseline, and the sign-flip framing is strictly stronger anyway because it shows the bias reorders methods rather than merely inflating magnitudes.

blocking_gaps: LEG 4 IS FALSIFIED BY DATA ALREADY ON DISK. The candidate says budget-doubling 'confirm[s] the tail is intrinsic, not a budget artifact.' runs/scaffold_large_mbppplus_budget4096_hit35/ contains the 33 MBPP+ tasks that truncated at 512, re-run at cap 4096: ALL 33 resolve (termination_reason='resolved' for 33/33), at nfe between 1035 and 1077 (median 1049). A cap of 1077 -- 5% above the 1024 cap -- would have resolved every one of them. The tail is NOT intrinsic; the 512 and 1024 caps were placed just below a resolution cliff. Leg 4 as filed asserts the opposite of what our own probe shows.

THE BUDGET-MONOTONICITY HEADLINE IS AN ARITHMETIC IDENTITY, NOT AN EMPIRICAL FINDING. I compared runs/scaffold_large_heplus vs runs/scaffold_large_heplus_budget1024 task-by-task: all 147 resolved tasks have BIT-IDENTICAL cumulative_model_tokens at cap 512 and cap 1024 (147 identical, 0 differing). The decoder is deterministic, so nothing about the resolved set changes; the only thing that moves is that capped runs burn ~2.26x more tokens because they run to a 2x-higher cap. So ratio = 1 + (trunc_total/resolved_total)*(147/164), and raising the cap mechanically raises trunc_total. 'Bias grows with budget (2.85x->5.32x)' is a restatement of 'capped runs cost the cap.' Publishing it as a counter-intuitive empirical result is the same class of error as Retraction 3 and would be retraction #6.

THE MONOTONICITY IS ALSO NON-MONOTONIC. Combining the two gaps above: MBPP+ bias ratio is 3.691x at cap 512, 7.463x at cap 1024, and 1.000x at cap 4096 (zero truncations, so completed-only == union). The sharpened claim's headline (ii) 'the bias GROWS with the compute budget rather than shrinking' is false at the third point we already measured. It rises then collapses, because the cliff is at ~1077.

THE TITLE'S 'SYSTEMATICALLY' IS FALSE, AND OUR OWN ARMS SHOW SIGN REVERSAL. Mean cumulative_model_tokens by termination_reason: scaffold_tiny_heplus resolved=2875.2 (n=112) vs depth_capacity_exhausted=2430.3 (n=52) -- truncated tasks are CHEAPER; same for scaffold_tiny_mbppplus (3860.7 vs 2378.8). So for depth-capacity arms the completed-only mean is UPWARD biased (ratios 0.951x, 0.930x). Only the model_call_budget mechanism makes truncated runs expensive (large HE+ 229250.1 vs 12155.7 = 18.9x; large MBPP+ 175834.7 vs 5848.5 = 30.1x). The bias direction is set by WHICH cap binds -- an early-exit cap biases up, a run-to-cap bias biases down. This is a better finding than the one filed, but it contradicts the filed title.
