related_work.citation: "Constrained Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Efficient Inference over Finite Automata." arXiv:2607.07026.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint. arXiv v1 2026-07-08. OpenReview api2 /notes/search on the exact title returns no matching note, so no verified venue.
related_work.what_it_covers: Exact, tractable sampling from the constrained mean-field posterior for any finite-automaton constraint, treating automata as graphical models; depth reduction cuts sampling depth from O(L) to O(log L). Dream-7B and LLaDA-8B on xLAM, BFCL Live/Non-Live, Sudoku, Countdown, Spider, GSM-Symbolic. BFCL-Live greedy 63.9→71.5, stochastic 22.3→69.0, tree variant +4% wall clock. Figure 4 is exactly an accuracy-vs-denoising-steps plot from 256 down to 16 on BFCL Simple for both models and both JSON/Python formats, with the stated finding that 'baseline performance drops sharply with fewer steps, whereas our method remains much more robust'.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Figure 4 is the candidate's headline claim already demonstrated — but on function calling / planning / SQL, NOT on executable code with tests; no HumanEval+/MBPP+, no EvalPlus, no pass@1+. x-axis is steps, not a cost unit, so it is not a frontier and there is no cost-matched crossover. No trained-structural-prior arm. Finite automata only, not full CFGs.
related_work.known_defects: (1) Figure 4 is a bare plot with no numbers, no CIs, no seed count, and only the BFCL 'Simple' split — the easiest slice — so the strongest form of the low-step-robustness claim rests on the weakest evidence in the paper. (2) Overhead accounting is regime-dependent and the flattering number is highlighted: the chain variant costs +114% wall clock while the tree variant costs +4%; the abstract advertises '<5%'. (3) Table 1 shows the method barely helps where the task is semantically hard — Spider 52.7→53.0, GSM-Symbolic 39.9→40.2 greedy — i.e. constraint value collapses exactly when the deficit is semantic, which is our hypothesis-splitting evidence, but the paper frames it only as 'format gap is structural, not semantic'. (4) Their own Table 2 ablation shows filtering alone is insufficient and remasking under recomputed marginals is needed, meaning 'grammar validity by construction' is not the whole mechanism — a nuance a naive constrained-mask implementation would miss. (5) Concurrent (2026-07-08), so no preemption.

related_work.what_it_covers: A compute-aware evaluation framework for MDLM remasking strategies: standardises ACTUAL NFE, enforces multi-metric reporting, controls stochasticity. related_work.citation: "Is Your Diffusion Sampler Actually Correct? A Sampler-Centric Evaluation of Discrete Diffusion Language Models." arXiv:2602.19619.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (v1 2026-02-23, v2 2026-05-27; comment '30 pages, 10 figures'). No OpenReview venue note found.
related_work.what_it_covers: Sampler-centric oracle framework replacing learned denoisers with an exact HMM posterior to isolate sampler-induced error. Shows few-step discrete diffusion samplers are NOT distributionally correct even under an oracle denoiser, with transition-level mismatch vanishing only as steps approach sequence length; and that NLL/GenPPL/MAUVE improvements do not imply correct sampling.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Synthetic ground-truth Markov chains, no real model, no code, no constraints. Provides the theoretical reason the low-step deficit may be irreducibly distributional (joint-vs-factorised) rather than merely syntactic — directly relevant to our mechanism story, but never connected to grammar enforcement or to executable-code quality.
related_work.known_defects: (1) Oracle-denoiser HMM setting is far from a 7B code model, so the practical magnitude of sampler-induced error at 64 vs 512 steps on Python is unmeasured — an opening for us. (2) Says nothing about whether constraints interact with (or worsen) the factorisation error, even though a per-position legality mask is itself a mean-field object.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list=2602.19619 (v2 record, published 2026-02-23T09:06:13Z, updated 2026-05-27) for title/date/abstract.

related_work.citation: "The Hidden Cost of Structured Generation in LLMs: Draft-Conditioned Constrained Decoding" (DCCD). arXiv:2603.03305.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (v2 record; published 2026-02-08T03:52:24Z). No OpenReview venue note found.
related_work.what_it_covers: Argues constrained decoding distorts generation when the model puts low mass on valid continuations, pushing decoding into locally valid but semantically wrong trajectories; proposes generating an unconstrained draft first, then constrained decoding conditioned on it. KL-projection analysis of a cumulative 'projection tax'. Up to +24 points strict structured accuracy (15.2%→39.0% on GSM8K with a 1B model), and enables smaller models to match larger constrained baselines.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Autoregressive LLMs only — no diffusion, no parallel/mean-field commit, no step budget, no code-execution benchmark. Its 'projection tax' framing is the best available theory for why constraints can fail to help (or hurt), and it has never been tested in the dLLM low-step regime where the mean-field is most misaligned.
related_work.known_defects: (1) AR-only, so the joint-vs-factorised pathology specific to parallel commit is absent. (2) Two-pass draft-then-constrain doubles compute and the gains are not reported at matched total compute against a single-pass baseline with more sampling. (3) 'Parameter efficiency' claim (small pairs matching larger models) compares across model sizes without equal-FLOP accounting.

diff.differentiation_statement: The candidate's stated novelty claim — "nobody has swept constraint benefit against compute" — is false and must be dropped before a reviewer does it for us. Four of the five dLLM constrained-decoding papers already sweep denoising steps: DINGO (2505.23061, NeurIPS 2025) Appendices J/K sweep {16,32,64,128} with Acc/Parse/Time; Mündler et al. (2508.10111, ICLR 2026 Poster) Appendix D.4 Tables 5/6 sweep {16,...,256} on Dream-7B reporting syntactic AND functional correctness plus per-step overhead; EPIC (2606.00722, concurrent) sweeps {16,...,256} for relative inference time; and 2607.07026 (concurrent) Figure 4 plots accuracy-vs-denoising-steps 256→16 for Dream and LLaDA with exactly the claimed qualitative finding ("baseline drops sharply with fewer steps, ours remains robust"). Worse, those tables largely FALSIFY the candidate's central claim: at 16 steps, 2508.10111 lifts C++ syntactic correctness 8.1%→99.2% while functional correctness moves only 1.4%→4.9% — near-perfect legality recovers under 5 of the 34.8 points available at 256 steps — and DINGO holds Parse at 100% across all step counts while accuracy still climbs 18%→33% from 16 to 128 steps. So what survives is not the claim but its negation, and four differentiators no prior paper closes. (1) Cost unit: every one of the four prices constraints in seconds or relative time AT THE SAME step count, never against MORE STEPS of unconstrained decoding; none plots a quality-versus-cost frontier. We price everything in cumulative_model_tokens with the truncation-inclusive proc() accessor (our own Retraction 3 fix, commit 8451e93) and report CPU-side constraint overhead separately, which makes "constrained-at-64 versus unconstrained-at-256 at equal token cost" askable for the first time. (2) Language and grader: all four dLLM CFG papers use C++/JSON/SMILES and none uses Python, EvalPlus, HumanEval+ or MBPP+; Python's off-side rule forces INDENT/DEDENT into the grammar, the hardest and most practically relevant case, and evalplus untrusted_check with extra tests is a stricter functional grader than HumanEval-X pass@1. (3) A three-way error decomposition — unparseable / parses-but-unbound-name / parses-and-binds-but-fails-tests — that splits grammar cost from scope cost from semantic cost; every prior paper stops at the binary syntactic-versus-functional split, which is precisely why none of them noticed that their own low-step tables show legality is necessary but nearly worthless. (4) A trained-structural-prior arm: the TreeDiff/AnCoder line puts AST structure into TRAINING and never asks whether a free inference-time CFG mask substitutes for it, while the constrained-decoding line never trains anything; we run both plus a matched plain-SFT control against a common token-cost axis, so "is a learned grammar redundant with an enforced one at equal cost" gets its first direct answer. Reframed this way the paper is a compute-aware audit of the constrained-decoding-for-dLLMs literature — the CaRE (2607.24763) move applied to constraints instead of remasking, in a token-normalised rather than NFE-normalised cost unit, on executable Python.

followup_openings.target_paper: Mündler, Dekoninck, Vechev, arXiv:2508.10111 (ICLR 2026 Poster), Appendix D.4 Tables 5/6
followup_openings.defect: Steps are swept but never converted into a cost axis: overhead is measured in seconds against unconstrained decoding at the SAME step count, so constrained-at-16-steps is never priced against unconstrained-at-256-steps. Consequently the paper cannot see, and never states, what its own Table 5 implies — that at 16 steps constraining takes C++ syntactic correctness 8.1%→99.2% while functional correctness moves only 1.4%→4.9%, and that at 128 steps Con.- is actually worse than vanilla (23.9 vs 24.5).
followup_openings.our_fix: Re-run the constraint-versus-no-constraint contrast with cumulative_model_tokens as the x-axis (truncation-inclusive proc() accessor, CPU constraint overhead reported separately), and read off the iso-cost comparison the original could not: does constrained decoding at N/4 the step budget beat unconstrained at N? Then state the non-monotonicity and the near-zero absolute functional ceiling at low steps as findings, with the three-way unparseable/unbound-name/semantic decomposition explaining why legality is necessary but nearly worthless — plus per-cell bootstrap CIs, which the original ablation lacks entirely.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It converts a buried appendix table into a headline result of the opposite sign, and gives the field the constraint-vs-compute accounting convention it currently lacks. It also cleanly re-scopes our candidate: we are not the first to sweep, we are the first to price, and the pricing reverses the reading.

followup_openings.defect: None evaluates on Python, and none uses EvalPlus. The constrained languages are C++, JSON-Schema and SMILES — all bracket-delimited grammars where a CFG needs no whitespace sensitivity. Python's off-side rule requires INDENT/DEDENT lexing inside the grammar, which is where a CFG mask over parallel mask positions is most likely to break, and it is the language of essentially every code-LM benchmark.
followup_openings.our_fix: Port the incremental-legality mask to a Python subset with explicit INDENT/DEDENT handling (tree_sitter_python is already installed) on HumanEval+ and MBPP+ graded by evalplus untrusted_check with extra tests, and report the mask's own failure modes: rate at which a jointly-illegal commit slips through a per-position mean-field mask, and rate at which the mask paints the sampler into a dead end (the failure LAVE identifies in C++). Implement following 2607.07026's exact constrained mean-field posterior or EPIC's Earley-based check rather than a weaker hand-rolled mask, and cite them for it.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It is a genuine untested regime, not a cosmetic swap: whitespace-sensitive grammars are the case the whole line has avoided, and a negative result there (mask helps syntax, cannot help pass@1+) is a substantive limit on the literature's central promise. It also makes our numbers directly comparable to the code-LM mainstream instead of to HumanEval-X C++.

followup_openings.target_paper: Zhang et al., LAVE, arXiv:2602.00612
followup_openings.defect: Denoising steps are fixed at T=128 and justified only as 'a balanced trade-off between model performance and inference cost', with no sweep anywhere in the paper. Separately, its headline functional gains are best-of-k (functional@10 28.1%→41.4% on Dream-7B CPP-Bench), so a 10x sampling budget is compared against numbers that do not pay for it — there is no unconstrained best-of-10 or unconstrained-at-10x-steps control.
followup_openings.our_fix: Two matched controls at equal total token cost: (a) sweep LAVE-style lookahead constraining across step budgets to test whether T=128 is anywhere near the optimum, and (b) price functional@k honestly by comparing constrained@k against unconstrained with the SAME total model-token spend reallocated as either more samples or more steps. Report whether the constrained curve dominates once the sampling budget is charged for.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This is the cleanest repair available: LAVE is the one CFG paper with no step sweep at all, and its best-of-k accounting is exactly the family of error our project already retracted twice (NFE-as-cost-unit, truncation-dropping averages). A reviewer will accept 'the strongest reported gain in this line is a sampling-budget artifact' if we show it at matched cost.

followup_openings.target_paper: arXiv:2607.07026, Figure 4 and Table 1
followup_openings.defect: The accuracy-vs-steps evidence is a bare four-panel plot on the BFCL 'Simple' split with no numbers, no CIs and no stated seed count, while Table 1 quietly shows the method barely moves the needle where the task is semantically hard (Spider 52.7→53.0, GSM-Symbolic 39.9→40.2 under greedy). The paper frames everything as 'the format gap is structural, not semantic' and never confronts the cases where its own gains vanish.
followup_openings.our_fix: Turn the qualitative plot into a quantitative, seeded, CI-bearing measurement on executable code, and use the three-way error decomposition to predict WHEN constraints buy compute: our hypothesis becomes 'constraint value scales with the illegality share of the residual error, and collapses once residual error is scope/semantic', which their Spider and GSM-Symbolic rows already corroborate. Also test their Table 2 finding that filtering alone is insufficient and remasking under recomputed constrained marginals is required — i.e. verify that a naive legality mask underperforms the exact posterior in the low-step regime specifically.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It supplies the missing quantitative and mechanistic layer under a concurrent paper's most-cited figure, and yields a predictive rule rather than a benchmark delta. Because 2607.07026 is concurrent (2026-07-08) we can cite it as convergent evidence while owning the code setting, the cost axis and the decomposition.

followup_openings.target_paper: TreeDiff arXiv:2508.01473 and AnCoder arXiv:2602.17688 versus the constrained-decoding line
followup_openings.defect: The two lines never meet. TreeDiff/AnCoder pay training compute to install an AST/structural prior and never ask whether a zero-training inference-time CFG mask obtains the same benefit; the four constrained-decoding papers never compare against any trained structural prior. So 'is a learned grammar redundant with an enforced grammar?' is unanswered in both directions, and neither line reports training cost and inference cost on a common axis.
followup_openings.our_fix: Put four arms on one token-cost frontier: unconstrained Dream-Coder-Instruct, grammar-constrained Dream-Coder, our trained structural runtime (scaffold Medium: HE+ .177 at 13.98k tok, MBPP+ .354 at 7.08k tok), and the matched plain-SFT control (HE+ nfe512 .2195, MBPP+ .2434) that already fails to reach the frontier at any point. If the constrained curve reaches scaffold Medium's cost band, the learned prior is substantially redundant and our own Pareto claim must be rewritten to say the low-cost segment belongs to grammar enforcement generally; if it does not, the trained runtime is doing something a CFG cannot express, and both the scaffold claim and the AST-training line are strengthened.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This is the only part of the candidate with no prior-art overlap at all, it is the load-bearing falsification test for our own surviving claim, and it is the arm that makes the paper a contribution rather than an audit. It also uses assets already on disk with no training.

followup_openings.target_paper: CaRE arXiv:2607.24763 (concurrent) and the compute-accounting convention across the dLLM literature
followup_openings.defect: CaRE establishes compute-aware MDLM evaluation but standardises on NFE as the compute unit and restricts itself to remasking strategies on OpenWebText/LM1B with MAUVE-family metrics. NFE is not comparable across decoders with different per-step sequence lengths — our own measurements show flat-canvas decoding costs 685 tok/step (HE+) and 604 (MBPP+) because prompt+512 canvas is re-attended every step, versus roughly 181 tok/call for a short tree serialisation — and constrained decoding adds CPU-side work that no NFE count sees at all.
followup_openings.our_fix: Extend compute-aware evaluation from remasking to CONSTRAINTS, in a token/FLOP-normalised unit rather than NFE, on an executable-code task with a hard grader, with CPU constraint overhead reported as a separate column so it is neither hidden nor double-counted, and with truncated/budget-capped tasks included via the proc() accessor. Note explicitly that early-exit effects (which EPIC shows can drive relative time below 100%) make same-step-count time ratios an unreliable cost proxy.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It positions the paper as a protocol contribution the community is visibly converging on, with a strictly better cost unit than the concurrent state of the art, and it is backed by two accounting errors we already found and retracted in our own work — which is exactly the credibility a methodological audit needs.

LAVE (2602.00612) and TreeDiff (2508.01473) are confirmed CoRR-only via OpenReview's DBLP-mirrored notes (venueid dblp.org/journals/CORR/* and OpenReview.net/Public_Article), which is weaker evidence of NON-acceptance than of acceptance — DBLP lags 2026 venues badly per project experience. Venue claims I do consider firm: 2508.10111 = ICLR 2026 Poster (OpenReview forum 7Sph4KyeYO, venueid ICLR.cc/2026/Conference, Camera_Ready_Revision invitation present) and DINGO 2505.23061 = NeurIPS 2025 poster (venueid NeurIPS.cc/2025/Conference). CaRE's arXiv record is internally odd: id prefix 2607.* with published date 2026-06-04 and comment 'updated version'; I recorded first-public as 2026-06 and it is concurrent either way, but the exact v1 date is uncertain. I read 2508.10111, 2602.00612, 2606.00722, 2607.07026 and 2505.23061 as full PDFs via pdftotext, so the step-sweep tables and numbers quoted from them are first-hand; for 2602.17688, 2508.01473, 2607.24763, 2602.19619 and 2603.03305 I read only API abstracts, so my "known_defects" for those five are inferences from abstract-level claims and should be re-checked against the PDFs before appearing in a rebuttal. I could not extract arXiv comment/version-history fields reliably (the abs-page scrape returned only v1 lines and empty comment cells), so I cannot rule out that 2508.10111 has a post-v1 revision adding cost-normalised analysis — worth one direct check of the ICLR camera-ready before we commit to the "never priced" framing, since that framing is our main differentiator. arXiv API rate-limited repeatedly (HTTP 429) and Semantic Scholar returned 429 on most queries, so my search coverage leans on arXiv full-text search plus OpenReview; ACL Anthology was not queried directly. Two claims in the candidate that I verified as FALSE and that must not be repeated: "every one of them evaluates at a single standard step budget" (false for 2508.10111, 2606.00722, 2607.07026, and for DINGO which the candidate does not cite at all — only LAVE fixes T=128), and "my arXiv probes ... return 0 hits: nobody has swept constraint benefit AGAINST compute" (the sweeps exist; what is missing is cost-normalisation, Python/EvalPlus, the error decomposition, and the trained-prior arm). The candidate also omits DINGO (2505.23061, NeurIPS 2025) and LAVE (2602.00612), both genuinely prior, both of which a reviewer in this area would know.
diff.sharpened_claim: Constrained decoding for diffusion LLMs is evaluated at the wrong exchange rate, and correcting it reverses the field's implicit story about what low-step decoding is missing. Prior work prices a grammar mask against unconstrained decoding at the SAME step count and reports near-perfect syntactic correctness; when we instead price it in cumulative model tokens — so that constrained-at-64-steps competes against unconstrained-at-256-steps, with CPU-side constraint overhead reported separately and budget-truncated tasks included — the low-compute deficit of masked diffusion code generation turns out NOT to be dominated by structural illegality. On HumanEval+ and MBPP+ in Python (the whitespace-sensitive grammar the entire dLLM constrained-decoding line has avoided in favour of C++/JSON/SMILES), graded by evalplus with extra tests, we decompose the residual error at each budget into unparseable / parses-but-unbound-name / parses-and-binds-but-fails-tests, and show that legality is necessary but nearly worthless: enforcing it recovers only a small fraction of the pass@1+ gap, exactly as prior work's own unread appendix tables already imply (2508.10111 Table 5: at 16 steps C++ syntax 8.1%→99.2% but functional 1.4%→4.9% against a 34.8% ceiling; DINGO Appendix J: Parse pinned at 100% across all step counts while accuracy still climbs 18%→33% from 16 to 128 steps). We further show constraint value tracks the illegality share of the residual error and collapses once that residual is scope- or semantics-bound, which predicts the otherwise unexplained flat rows in concurrent work (Spider 52.7→53.0, GSM-Symbolic 39.9→40.2). Finally, on a single token-cost frontier with four arms — unconstrained, grammar-constrained, our trained structural runtime, and a matched plain-SFT control — we adjudicate a question neither the constrained-decoding line nor the AST-training line (TreeDiff, AnCoder) has posed: whether a learned grammar is redundant with an enforced one at equal cost. Either the constrained curve reaches the trained runtime's cost band, and our own Pareto segmentation must be rewritten to credit grammar enforcement generally rather than a trained structural runtime; or it does not, and the trained prior is provably doing something no CFG expresses. The deliverable is a compute-aware evaluation protocol for constraints — CaRE's move applied to constraints instead of remasking, in a token-normalised rather than NFE-normalised unit, on executable Python — plus the negative result that grammar validity is the cheap part of the low-compute gap.

blocking_gaps: THE CENTRAL CLAIM IS ALREADY FALSIFIED, ON OUR OWN DISK, WITH ZERO GPU. I built a 100%-legality oracle (bracket/quote repair, else longest-parseable-prefix; empty program is legal) over the existing solutions and graded with real `evalplus.evaluate`. Verified residual_illegal=0/164 and 0/378 on all six arms, i.e. this is a strict UPPER BOUND on what ANY grammar mask, CFG, or automaton can buy. Result (raw -> 100%-legal): HE+ nfe64 .018->.018 (+.000), nfe128 .140->.152 (+.012), nfe256 .555->.561 (+.006); MBPP+ nfe64 .029->.040 (+.011), nfe128 .233->.275 (+.042), nfe256 .545->.569 (+.024). As a share of the gap to the .707/.680 ceiling that is 0.0% / 2.1% / 3.9% and 1.7% / 9.4% / 17.8%. Constrained nfe64 lands at .018 (HE+) and .040 (MBPP+) -- INSIDE the candidate's own stated kill band of .00-.05 on BOTH benchmarks. Artifacts: /apdcephfs_wzc1/share_304376610/pighzliu_code/dllm_draft/runs/_AUDIT_legal_dream_instruct_{heplus,mbppplus}_nfe{64,128,256}/solutions.jsonl

THE MECHANISM IS NOT ILLEGALITY, IT IS DEGENERATE REPETITION -- so the candidate misdiagnoses its own motivating measurement. Measured on raw_output in runs/dream_instruct_heplus_nfe*: immediate duplicate-bigram rate ('the the', '-------.') is 43.70% at nfe64, 7.03% at nfe128, 0.45% at nfe256, 0.17% at nfe512. Prose-only outputs with ZERO code-like lines: 25.6% at nfe64 -> 1.8% -> 0.0%. Fraction of the canvas inside a ``` fence: 10.4% at nfe64 -> 33.8% -> 39.1%. So at nfe64 the model has not written an illegal program; it has not written a program. A legality mask over mask positions cannot fix a canvas that is 90% English prose and half-filled with repeated tokens -- it would only make the prose grammatical Python, which is what the +0.000 measures.

P(pass | already parseable) does not collapse at low NFE, which kills the 'legality is the binding constraint' reading directly. Measured from solutions_eval_results.json: HE+ nfe64 8 parseable, .375 pass|parse; nfe128 48, .479; nfe256 131, .695; nfe512 161, .720. MBPP+ nfe128 167, .527; nfe256 325, .634; nfe512 372, .691. P(pass | unparseable) = 0.000 in all 7 runs. So the low-NFE arms are not producing near-correct programs blocked by a syntax error -- they are producing FEWER programs, and the ones they produce are also semantically worse. Legality is necessary and nearly worthless, which is exactly the differentiation_statement's own reading; the candidate's `claim` field still asserts the opposite and would have to be inverted.

IMPLEMENTATION COST IS UNDERSTATED AND THE ONE ENV DEPENDENCY IS MISSING. `tree_sitter` 0.26.0 + `tree_sitter_python` ARE installed (claim verified), but lark / outlines / llguidance / xgrammar are ALL absent from /opt/conda/envs/dllm-env -- so there is no off-the-shelf CFG-mask engine to lean on and the 'follow 2607.07026 or EPIC rather than inventing a weaker mask' plan means implementing an Earley/automaton intersection engine from scratch. Measured tree_sitter throughput is 5,167 full parses/sec on 2KB source (193 us each). A naive per-position mask needs 512 positions x 152,064 vocab = 77.9M legality checks PER STEP; at measured speed that is ~251 minutes per diffusion step. A usable mask therefore requires incremental lexer-level pruning + vocabulary bucketing, not a parse-per-candidate loop. That is the real build, and it is the multi-week part.

PYTHON'S OFF-SIDE RULE IS WORSE HERE THAN THE POSITIONING ADMITS. The positioning correctly notes no prior dLLM CFG paper does Python. But measured syntax-error messages at nfe64/nfe128 are dominated by errors a per-position CFG mask structurally CANNOT prevent under parallel commit: 'invalid syntax' 68/56, 'unmatched )' 22/9, 'unindent does not match any outer indentation level' 4/8, 'unexpected indent' 5/6, 'unterminated string literal' 13+4/6. INDENT/DEDENT legality at position i depends on tokens committed at other positions in the SAME step, which is precisely the jointly-illegal-though-individually-legal failure the candidate flags as an 'honest subtlety'. It is not a subtlety, it is the dominant error class.

THE FOUR-ARM PARETO FRAMING IS DEAD, INDEPENDENTLY, VIA RETRACTIONS 4 AND 5 (commit 1170ae6, dated TODAY, and NOT in the task brief given to me). The brief says the 'surviving claim' is that scaffold and flat diffusion own different frontier segments. That claim was retracted hours ago: a matched AR baseline (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, architecturally identical to Dream-Coder-v0-Base -- same hidden 3584 / 28 layers / 28 heads / 4 KV / intermediate 18944 / vocab 152064 / rope_theta 1e6, differing only by mask_token_id 151666) scores HE+ .524 / MBPP+ .648 at 204/101 tokens_fed, vs scaffold Medium .177/.354 at 13,980/7,080. AR strictly dominates scaffold Medium on BOTH cost axes AND quality (+.30). Retraction 5: AR also wins on infilling, diffusion's supposed home turf (qwen_fim .7638 @239 tok vs dreamon_fim .7018 @4923). So followup_opening #5 -- billed as 'the only part with no prior-art overlap' and 'the load-bearing falsification test for our own surviving claim' -- is adjudicating a frontier that no longer exists. Any 4-arm plot MUST carry the AR arm as a fifth, and the AR arm dominates the whole low-cost region the candidate wants to contest.

prior-art overlap is genuine and the positioning's own verification_notes concede the novelty claim is false. Mundler et al. 2508.10111 (ICLR 2026 Poster) App D.4 Tables 5/6 already sweep steps {16..256} with syntax AND functional correctness plus per-step overhead; DINGO 2505.23061 (NeurIPS 2025) App J/K sweep {16..128}; EPIC and 2607.07026 both sweep. What is left after removing the false novelty claim is cost-normalisation + Python/EvalPlus + the 3-way decomposition -- and my oracle bound shows the headline finding those would support is a NEGATIVE result whose magnitude (+0.000 to +0.042) is available with no GPU at all.

PHASE 2 -- ONLY IF PHASE 1 REVIEW DEMANDS A REAL SAMPLER (~12-18 GPU-hours, plus 1-2 weeks CPU-side build; NOT 45 and NOT recommended)
2a. Build the incremental legality mask against models/Dream-Coder-v0-Instruct-7B via the EXISTING hook: models/Dream-Coder-v0-Instruct-7B/generation_utils.py line 416 `logits = generation_logits_hook_func(i, x, logits)` and line 455 `x = generation_tokens_hook_func(i, x, logits)`. scripts/generate_evalplus_dream.py already threads `generation_logits_hook_func` (used today for --suppress-scaffold-tokens), so the plumbing exists and needs no model edit. Note the sampler is `alg='entropy'`, alg_temp=0.0, and commits `int(num_mask_token*(1-s/t))` positions per step by top-k confidence -- so a mask must be applied to `mask_logits` BEFORE the top-k transfer selection, and must handle the multi-position joint commit.
2b. Mandatory: bucket the 152,064-entry vocab by lexical class ONCE (offline), then mask at bucket granularity; a parse-per-candidate loop is 251 min/step at measured tree_sitter speed (5,167 parses/sec) and is a non-starter.
2c. GPU cost, measured not estimated, from runs/*/metrics.rank*.jsonl elapsed_seconds summed: unconstrained HE+ nfe{16,32,64,128,256,512,1024} = 0.055/0.070/0.100/0.160/0.278/0.515/1.104 GPU-h; MBPP+ = 0.102/0.133/0.197/0.329/0.591/1.110/2.418 GPU-h. Both benchmarks, all of {32,64,128,256,512} = 3.03 GPU-h unconstrained. One constrained arm at a 3-4x CPU-bound slowdown = ~10-12 GPU-h. Everything else in the candidate's 4-arm design is ALREADY MEASURED and must be reused, not re-run.
2d. Run on LOCAL GPUs 2,4,6,7 (verified idle: nvidia-smi shows 1 MiB used; GPUs 0/1/3/5 hold ~34 GB each from the in-flight MBPP+ Large@1024 job -- do not touch). Protocol must match the existing sweep exactly or the reuse is void: --steps N --max-new-tokens 512 --temperature 0.1 --top-p 0.95, CHAT template (I verified scripts/_run_nfe_sweep_wzc1.sh and _run_nfe_lowend_wzc1.sh pass NEITHER --no-chat NOR --base-continuation, so all published NFE numbers are chat-template), 8-way shard by `index % world_size == rank`.

DO NOT DUPLICATE: AR baseline is done (.104, Retraction 4). Infilling/FIM is done (.73, Retraction 5). Sampler-protocol audit is live on .82 -- and since top_p 1.0->0.95 alone moved HumanEval +14.6 points, i.e. 3-350x the entire oracle legality effect I measured, that audit is where the real variance is. MBPP+ Large@1024 is live on .252 and LOCAL.
feas.risk:
The most likely failure is no longer a null -- I already got the null, so the risk has inverted: the risk is spending weeks building a CFG-constrained sampler to re-derive a +0.000-to-+0.042 effect that a 20-line post-hoc oracle establishes as an upper bound today, and then reporting the null as if the implementation were load-bearing. A reviewer will ask "why did you need a sampler to show that legality does not help, when repairing your existing outputs to 100% legality shows the same thing?" and there is no answer.

The second, subtler confound is the one that would actually make a built sampler WORSE than my oracle and produce a misleading negative: a real per-position mask is applied to `mask_logits` before the top-k confidence transfer, so it changes WHICH tokens get committed and in what order, and it can paint the sampler into a dead end (the LAVE failure) or push it into the DCCD "projection tax" regime. It can therefore score BELOW the unconstrained arm -- exactly as 2508.10111 Con.- does at 128 steps (23.9 vs 24.5) and as DINGO's Greedy-Constrained does on JSON-Mode (54->32 at 16 steps). If that happens we would report "constraints hurt", which is a claim about our mask's quality, not about grammar enforcement, and we would have no way to separate the two. My oracle has no such confound because it is post-hoc and monotone by construction: it can only add legality, never remove information.

Third: the three-way decomposition's middle tier is soft. My unbound-name pass uses a crude single-pass AST walk that unions all Store/arg/alias names irrespective of scope, so it under-reports (10/164 at nfe128, 6/164 at nfe256). Publishing "scope cost" off that would be a fourth accounting error of the same family as the three retractions.
feas.required_control:
THE PAIRED POST-HOC LEGALITY-ORACLE CEILING, RUN BEFORE ANY SAMPLER IS BUILT, AND ASSERTED TO BE 100% LEGAL.

The mechanism: take the EXISTING unconstrained solutions, force them to 100% parseability post-hoc (repair, else longest-parseable-prefix, else empty program -- all legal), assert residual_illegal == 0 with `ast.parse` on every task, and grade with the same `evalplus.evaluate` on the same n. Because the oracle only adds legality and costs zero extra model tokens, its score is a strict upper bound on any constrained sampler at equal token cost. If the oracle does not move the number, no CFG, automaton, Earley parser, or exact mean-field posterior can. Publish the ceiling next to any constrained-arm result, always at matched token cost.

Why this specific control, tied to each retraction:
- Retraction 1 (verifier compared nothing; empty solutions scored full marks): the oracle's fallback output is literally the empty program, so if the grader were still broken the oracle would score ~1.0. It scores .018 on HE+ nfe64. The oracle IS a negative control on the grader, every time it runs. I used `evalplus.evaluate` (n=164/378), never a hand-rolled check.
- Retraction 2 (restart policy silently discarded the scaffold draft, so the pipeline measured a different model than claimed): the oracle is a pure function of the SPECIFIC solution string for the SAME task_id, so it is structurally incapable of substituting a different arm's output. The paired task_id join is the anti-discard invariant, and it must be asserted (identical task_id sets, both directions) rather than assumed. A constrained sampler has no such guarantee -- if the mask silently no-ops for any reason (wrong hook, mask applied after top-k selection, dtype/min-value clamp swallowed), it reports the UNCONSTRAINED number under a constrained label, and that is Retraction 2 exactly. Hence the second mandatory assertion for Phase 2: log per-step how many vocabulary entries the mask actually suppressed and assert it is non-zero on every step of every task, plus assert final legality is ~100%; a constrained run whose measured final unparseable rate matches the unconstrained run's is a no-op mask, not a null result.
- Retraction 3 (cost average dropped the truncated, most expensive tasks): the oracle arm is priced at its twin's cost via the `proc()` accessor in scripts/make_pareto_figures.py, with `field_coverage()` printed so the have/total ratio is visible; and the oracle is defined over ALL n tasks including the ones that produced pure prose, which are precisely the tasks a "constrained-only-where-it-parsed" analysis would drop.

Report alongside it, mandatorily: P(pass | parseable) and P(pass | unparseable) per arm (the latter must be 0.000 -- it is, in all 7 runs I checked -- otherwise the grader is accepting non-programs), the paired per-task flip counts with McNemar, and the degenerate-repetition rate, so the reader can see whether the residual error is legality, scope, semantics, or the model failing to emit code at all.

lens.title: Coupled Multi-Site Repair: parallel commits where an autoregressive editor must serialize
lens.claim: On bugs whose fix requires mutually consistent changes at two or more disjoint sites (rename at definition and all uses; signature change and all call sites), a masked diffusion model that commits all sites in one denoising pass achieves higher consistency and test pass rate than the same model editing site-by-site, and than a matched AR code model editing site-by-site -- but we test it against the strongest AR arm, whole-function rewrite, which sees every site at once.
lens.why_now: Multi-site consistency is where parallel commits plus bidirectional conditioning should pay off most, and the surface is empty for diffusion. The only systematic multi-hunk repair study, 2511.11012, uses AR coding AGENTS (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini-cli, Qwen Code) on 404 PolyHunk bugs and finds repair accuracy declines with hunk dispersion and spatial proximity -- exactly the axis a bidirectional joint editor should attack -- with no diffusion model anywhere. The only diffusion-beats-AR-on-repair claim, 2510.04605, is CoRR-only and our own audit found it compares commercial Mercury-Diffusion-7B against general-purpose AR Llama3-8B with no code-model control, plus two garbled self-citations and a fabricated LLaDA reference (cited as arXiv:2309.12401, which is an astrophysics paper). My probes return 0 hits for diffusion crossed with rename, def-use, or coordinated/coupled code edits. And the benchmarks exist and are Python-only, which matters because our node has no docker, java, go, or rustc, making SWE-bench, Defects4J, and non-Python HumanEvalPack infeasible -- so this is the strongest repair claim that is actually runnable here.
lens.experiment: Build a consistency-coupled edit suite from three sources: HumanEvalPack-Python (164 buggy solutions with bug_type and failure_symptoms) and CanItEdit (105 before/after pairs with tests plus descriptive and lazy instructions), both of which I downloaded to data/edit/, plus synthetic rename and signature-change mutations of HE+ canonical solutions generated by the same def-use carver I validated (113/164 tasks have coupled pairs). Retain only instances where a correct fix demands >=2 coordinated sites. Four arms: (a) Dream-Coder-Instruct JOINT -- remask all coupled sites, one denoising pass, every site conditioned on every other; (b) Dream-Coder-Instruct SEQUENTIAL site-by-site (isolates jointness within one model); (c) Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct AR site-by-site; (d) Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct AR WHOLE-FUNCTION rewrite -- mandatory, because a rewriting AR model also sees all sites, and this is the arm most likely to beat us. Metrics: test pass via the benchmarks' own suites; a consistency metric (all coupled sites changed compatibly, computed by def-use re-analysis); Excision Score (2510.21537), which removes content shared with the ground truth before comparing, so reviewers cannot object that BLEU-style scores are dominated by unchanged code; and cumulative_model_tokens.
lens.assets_needed: HAVE (newly put on disk by me): data/edit/humanevalpack_python.parquet (164 rows, 15 columns including buggy_solution, bug_type, test, instruction) and data/edit/canitedit.parquet (105 rows with before/after/tests/instruction_descriptive/instruction_lazy/taxonomy) -- both verified loadable with pandas in the dllm-env. HAVE: Dream-Coder-Instruct; ast + tree_sitter_python for the mutation generator and the consistency metric; the fixed evalplus-based execution harness. MISSING -- FLAG: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct for arms (c) and (d), same download as capability-1, and again coordinate with the AR baseline already running on .104. HARD LOCAL BLOCKERS RESPECTED: no docker/podman so SWE-bench is out; no javac/go/rustc so HumanEvalPack java/cpp/go/rust are out -- the design is deliberately Python-only. CAVEAT TO HEED: 2604.05100 audits CanItEdit and EDIT-Bench and reports modest test counts (CanItEdit median 13 tests) and shared codebases across 6% of CanItEdit problems, which is exactly why we add our own mutation-generated instances with full HE+ test suites rather than relying on CanItEdit alone.
lens.kill_criterion: Two independent kills. (1) If arm (a) JOINT is within noise of arm (b) SEQUENTIAL, the parallel-commit capability is not realized and the claim dies. (2) If arm (d), AR whole-function rewrite, matches or beats (a) at equal token cost, then diffusion's joint commit confers no advantage over simply letting an AR model see and rewrite everything -- and I expect this to be a real risk, since whole-function rewrite gives AR full visibility too. This must be stated up front, not discovered late; if (d) wins, the paper becomes a negative result bounding where multi-site parallel commits help.
lens.builds_on: Follow-up on 2511.11012 (multi-hunk repair behavioural study, 2025-11-14) whose defect is that it evaluates only AR agents and never tests the paradigm whose structural affordance is simultaneous multi-site commitment, and a direct replacement for 2510.04605 whose diffusion-vs-AR repair comparison is confounded (no code-model AR control) and whose citations we verified to be partly fabricated. Adopts the evaluation instrument from Excision Score (2510.21537) and the benchmark caveats from Edit-But-Verify (2604.05100).

diff.differentiation_statement: No pre-2026-05-07 paper makes this claim with this method in this setting, and the intersection of {masked diffusion model} x {multi-site coupled repair} x {joint-vs-sequential commit ablation within one model} is empty. The three closest bodies of work each miss a different leg. (1) The multi-hunk repair literature (2506.04418 HUNK4J, 2511.11012, 2607.26591 MultiFixer, 2605.06209 SiblingRepair) is entirely autoregressive -- agents, spectrum-based localization, multi-agent coordinators -- and is Java-centric (Defects4J/GHRB/VUL4J). It establishes the phenomenon we attack (repair accuracy declines monotonically with hunk divergence and spatial dispersion; no model succeeds in the most dispersed Fragment class) but never tests the paradigm whose architectural affordance is simultaneous multi-site commitment. Its notion of "joint" repair is prompt-level (put all sites in one LLM context) not decode-level (commit all sites in one denoising pass conditioned bidirectionally on each other). (2) The one diffusion-vs-AR repair claim, 2510.04605, is confounded and unusable as prior art: it compares commercial Mercury-Diffusion-7B against general-purpose AR-Llama3-8B with no code-model AR control, and I independently verified its reference [6] cites "LLaDA: A Large Language and Denoising Assistant, arXiv:2309.12401" -- arXiv:2309.12401 is in fact "The dependence of assembly bias on the cosmic web," an MNRAS astrophysics submission -- and its reference [2] is literally "Anonymous Author(s). 2025." Our arm (c) Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct is exactly the code-model control it lacks, and our arm (d) whole-function rewrite is the AR-favouring ceiling it never gave AR. (3) The diffusion parallel-decoding literature (2510.21961 PUNT, 2509.22738 approximate joint sampling, 2601.15593, 2606.14620) has established -- theoretically and empirically -- that parallel unmasking *degrades* joint-distribution fidelity because simultaneously committed tokens are assumed conditionally independent, and that shipped checkpoints commit with a partial left-to-right bias rather than genuinely in parallel. That literature is about generic sequence quality and speed-quality tradeoffs, never about whether joint commitment buys *semantic consistency across coupled program sites*. It is in fact an argument that our arm (a) may lose, which makes our design a genuine test rather than a demo: we are the first to ask whether parallel commitment helps precisely where the coupling is semantic and long-range, and to price it against an AR rewriter that also sees every site. The setting differences are also independently sufficient: Python-only with executable HE+/CanItEdit test suites versus their Java compile-and-test; def-use-verified consistency metric versus their hunk-count metrics; and cumulative_model_tokens cost accounting versus their token-count-free accuracy reporting.
diff.sharpened_claim: Reframe from "diffusion wins" to "we measure whether decode-level joint commitment is a real capability, and locate its boundary." Primary claim: on Python bugs requiring mutually consistent changes at >=2 disjoint sites, we decompose consistency failure into (i) a paradigm effect and (ii) a visibility effect, by crossing {diffusion, AR} x {sees-all-sites, sees-one-site-at-a-time} into a 2x2 -- arms (a)/(b) isolate jointness within one model, (c)/(d) isolate it within the other -- and report at equal cumulative_model_tokens. The falsifiable, publication-worthy result in every branch: if (a)>(b) but (d)>=(a), the advantage is *visibility, not parallel commitment*, which directly contradicts the architectural motivation offered by 2510.04605 and by diffusion-for-code papers generally, and is the negative result the field needs. Secondary claim, and the one I'd make load-bearing because it is measurement rather than a horse race: parallel commitment and semantic coupling are in tension. Instrument the denoising trajectory (following the honest-order methodology of 2606.14620) to measure, per instance, how many of the coupled sites Dream-Coder actually commits in the *same* accept step versus in separated steps, and regress consistency success on that observed simultaneity. This converts the kill criterion into a finding: if joint commits are rare (as 2601.15593's AFP and 2606.14620's left-to-right commit bias predict), we show the affordance is nominal rather than realized in shipped checkpoints -- a mechanism-level explanation for why diffusion code models do not beat AR on coupled repair, which no existing paper provides. Strengthen the coupling axis by porting the HUNK4J divergence and spatial-proximity variables (2506.04418) onto Python instances, so results are directly comparable to the AR-agent dispersion curves and the paper reads as the missing paradigm column of that study rather than a standalone diffusion demo.
diff.verification_notes: Could not verify: (1) Semantic Scholar Graph API and DBLP were unreachable through the available proxy (empty responses on all attempts), so cross-checking rests on arXiv listing pages plus the OpenReview API, both of which did work. (2) arXiv's Atom API returns a 301 through this proxy and silently empties on many quoted-phrase queries; I therefore used the arXiv HTML search endpoint, which returned sane totals, but recall on that endpoint is imperfect -- several plausible queries ("diffusion model code infilling fill-in-the-middle", "multi-span infilling language model code", "variable rename consistency code LLM benchmark") returned zero-total pages that I read as low-recall rather than as proof of absence. The "surface is empty" conclusion is therefore high-confidence but not exhaustive; a targeted ACL Anthology and ICSE/FSE/ASE proceedings sweep is still worth doing before camera-ready, since multi-hunk repair is an SE-venue topic and SE proceedings are poorly indexed by arXiv search. (3) SiblingRepair (2605.06209) v1 is dated exactly 2026-05-07, i.e. exactly on the concurrency cutoff -- I mark it concurrent=true, but note the call is knife-edge and depends on the cutoff being inclusive. I could not find a venue for it (no comments/journal-ref field; OpenReview search returned only unrelated APR records), so I record it as preprint. (4) I did NOT verify SiblingRepair's internals beyond its abstract; its "simultaneous repair, which jointly repairs siblings" vs "iterative repair" pair is the single closest thing in the literature to our (a)-vs-(b) contrast, and if its paper contains a head-to-head ablation of those two strategies then our within-model jointness comparison is a Java/AR-side precedent that we must cite and differentiate from (we differ by paradigm, language, and by having the diffusion arm at all). Someone should read that PDF before the related-work section is written. (5) The claim in the proposal that its def-use carver found "113/164 tasks have coupled pairs" is unverified by me; I could not locate the carver output on disk. What I did measure directly from data/edit/humanevalpack_python.parquet is a hard feasibility problem stated in the follow-up openings below: only 12/164 HumanEvalPack-Python instances have >=2 line-level diff hunks and only 37/164 have >=2 token-level changed regions, so HumanEvalPack cannot carry a multi-site suite and the synthetic mutations must do the heavy lifting. CanItEdit is healthier: 72/105 instances have >=2 line-level hunks. (6) Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct is genuinely absent from both disks -- I checked /apdcephfs_wzc1/.../models/ and dllm_draft/models/ on wzc1, and /apdcephfs_zwfy6/.../models/ returned empty -- so the MISSING flag is correct and download is a real prerequisite. (7) Excision Score's venue status is worse than the proposal assumes; see openings.

related_work.citation: Nashid, Ding, Gallaba, Hassan, Mesbah. "Beyond Accuracy: Behavioral Dynamics of Agentic Multi-Hunk Repair." arXiv:2511.11012
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (v1 2025-11-14, v2 2026-06-05). No journal-ref or comments field on the arXiv abs page; OpenReview search returned no submission record. Verified via arXiv abs page metadata.
related_work.what_it_covers: First systematic study of LLM coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini-cli, Qwen Code) on 404 multi-hunk bugs from PolyHunk; 1,616 trajectories. Fine-grained localization, repair accuracy, regression behavior, operational dynamics. Key finding: repair accuracy declines consistently with hunk divergence and spatial proximity. Also contributes Maple for repository-level context (+~21% for Gemini-cli).
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Entirely autoregressive agents; no diffusion model anywhere. 'Coordinated edits' are measured as an outcome, never as a decode-time mechanism -- no arm where multiple sites are committed simultaneously. Agent-level confounds (tool use, retries, localization) are entangled with the model's editing ability, so it cannot isolate whether the failure is localization or joint generation. Java/PolyHunk only.
related_work.known_defects: Agentic setup confounds localization with repair: Codex localizes at 75.3% and Qwen Code at 40.4%, so the reported repair-accuracy spread (26.98%-92.82%) is partly a localization spread, and the paper cannot attribute dispersion-driven decline to joint-generation difficulty. Four proprietary/closed agents means no controlled model-family comparison and no reproducibility at fixed weights. No token-cost-matched comparison across agents -- it reports that failures consume 33-440% more input tokens but does not equalize budget when comparing accuracy. The dispersion metrics it uses are inherited from 2506.04418 rather than validated independently.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv abs page fetched directly via proxy; citation_date, dateline, and full abstract read from page metadata. Confirmed v1 2025-11-14 (pre-cutoff), v2 2026-06-05.

related_work.citation: Anonymous/unclear authorship. "Exploring the Power of Diffusion Large Language Models for Software Engineering: An Empirical Investigation." arXiv:2510.04605
related_work.venue_status: Preprint only. OpenReview/DBLP record shows 'CoRR 2025' (dblp.org/journals/CORR/2025) -- i.e. no peer-reviewed venue. Verified via OpenReview API search returning only the DBLP CoRR record.
related_work.what_it_covers: Claims first comprehensive DLLM evaluation across the SDLC (code generation, defect detection, program repair, cross-file maintenance) on 52,937 tasks across Devign/Defects4J/Bears/SWE-bench/Mercury/HumanEval. Headline: 7B DLLMs beat AR-LLMs by ~30% average accuracy, 113% on cross-file repair, with lower latency. This is the only extant diffusion-beats-AR-on-repair claim.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: No code-specialized AR control, no diffusion code model (uses commercial Mercury-Diffusion-7B, not Dream-Coder/DiffuCoder/LLaDA), no multi-site or coupled-edit analysis, no per-site consistency metric, no token-cost matching. Program repair is scored as first-patch compile-and-pass (PR rate), which conflates localization with editing.
related_work.known_defects: Severe and independently verified by me from the PDF. (i) The entire diffusion-vs-AR claim rests on Diff-Mercury-7B vs AR-Llama3-8B -- a commercial diffusion model versus a general-purpose AR chat model with no code pretraining. Code Llama and CodeT5+ are cited in the intro but never used as baselines, so the 'DLLMs are a superior paradigm' conclusion could be entirely explained by code-domain pretraining rather than paradigm. (ii) Reference [6] reads 'Chen Gong, Zheng Li, Ziyi Lin. 2023. LLaDA: A Large Language and Denoising Assistant. arXiv:2309.12401' -- I fetched arXiv:2309.12401 and it is 'The dependence of assembly bias on the cosmic web,' an MNRAS astrophysics submission. The citation is fabricated. (iii) Reference [2] is 'Anonymous Author(s). 2025. Beyond Autoregression: An Empirical Study of...' -- an unresolved anonymous self-citation left in the bibliography. (iv) Latency claims are internally strange: Table 6 shows Diff-Mercury-7B at 1598-9329 tokens/s vs AR-Llama3-8B at 305-460 tokens/s, a 3-20x throughput gap far outside any published diffusion speedup, with no hardware or batching disclosure. (v) SWE-bench is scored with self-invented MDVR/PRR metrics rather than the standard resolved rate, making the '113% cross-file gain' non-comparable to any SWE-bench leaderboard.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv abs page + full PDF downloaded and converted with pdftotext; grepped the model/baseline tables and the reference list. Separately fetched arXiv:2309.12401 abs page to confirm it is an astrophysics paper. Venue checked via OpenReview API (returns DBLP CoRR 2025 record only).

related_work.citation: "SiblingRepair: Sibling-Based Multi-Hunk Repair with Large Language Models." arXiv:2605.06209
related_work.venue_status: Preprint; cs.SE; no comments, journal-ref, or DOI field on the arXiv abs page. OpenReview search returned no matching submission. Verified via arXiv abs page metadata scrape.
related_work.what_it_covers: THE closest work on the jointness axis. LLM-based multi-hunk APR specialized for 'sibling' locations (code locations implementing related functionality that share an issue and need the same fix -- semantically our 'coupled sites'). Uses spectrum-based fault localization plus token/embedding sibling matching, then generates consistent patches via two explicitly contrasted strategies: simultaneous repair (jointly repairs siblings) and iterative repair (progressively analyzes candidates). Evaluated on Defects4J and GHRB against Hercules; includes a data-leakage check.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Autoregressive LLM only -- no diffusion arm, so 'simultaneous' means all siblings in one prompt/one generation, never one denoising pass with bidirectional cross-site conditioning. Java (Defects4J/GHRB) only, so infeasible on our node and non-overlapping with our Python suite. Combines the two strategies as complementary components of one system rather than isolating simultaneous-vs-iterative as a controlled single-variable ablation of a fixed model. No token-cost accounting for the two strategies. No whole-function-rewrite ceiling arm.
related_work.known_defects: Component-level, not paradigm-level: because simultaneous and iterative repair are fused into one pipeline together with sibling detection and patch carry-over, the reported gain over Hercules cannot be attributed to jointness. Relies on spectrum-based fault localization, so results are confounded by localization quality exactly as in 2511.11012. Defects4J is heavily contaminated for modern LLMs; the paper acknowledges leakage but 'limited impact' claims on Defects4J are hard to sustain. Our fix: we hold localization fixed by *giving* all arms the ground-truth coupled site set, which removes the localization confound entirely, and we run on Python instances with mutation-generated (hence uncontaminated) coupled bugs.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv abs page fetched via proxy; dateline confirmed '[Submitted on 7 May 2026]', subjects/comments/jref/doi fields scraped (all empty except cs.SE). OpenReview API searched for the title -- no record. NOTE: first-public date is exactly the 2026-05-07 cutoff, so the concurrency call is knife-edge.

related_work.citation: Nashid et al. "Characterizing Multi-Hunk Patches: Divergence, Proximity, and LLM Repair Challenges." arXiv:2506.04418
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (v1 2025-06-04, v2 2025-11-17); no journal-ref on arXiv abs page. Verified via arXiv abs page metadata.
related_work.what_it_covers: The actual origin of the metrics 2511.11012 uses, and arguably the more important prior work for us. Introduces HUNK4J (multi-hunk patches from 372 real defects), defines *hunk divergence* (lexical/structural/file-level variation among edits within a patch, scaled by hunk count) and *spatial proximity* (how hunks distribute across the program hierarchy). Empirical study over six LLMs: success declines with divergence and dispersion; with the LLM alone, NO model succeeds in the most dispersed 'Fragment' class.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Six AR LLMs, no diffusion. Reports only whether the patch succeeds -- no per-site consistency measure, so it cannot say whether failures are inconsistent-across-sites versus wrong-at-one-site. No cost accounting. Its divergence/proximity axes have never been ported to Python or to a paradigm comparison.
related_work.known_defects: Hunk divergence is a composite of lexical, structural and file-level differences with hunk count folded in; the paper does not show the composite predicts difficulty better than the simple hunk count, so the construct validity of the headline axis is unestablished -- a cheap, high-value follow-up. 'No model succeeds in the most dispersed Fragment class' is a zero-cell claim whose sample size in that stratum is not made salient, so it may be an n-too-small artifact. Real-world defect provenance means contamination is uncontrolled for LLMs trained on GitHub.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv abs page fetched via proxy; dateline and full abstract read from metadata; surfaced through arXiv HTML search on 'multi-hunk program repair' (11 total results, full list reviewed).

related_work.citation: "MultiFixer: A Coordinator-Proposer Based Multi-Agent Framework For Fixing Multi-Hunk Bugs." arXiv:2607.26591
related_work.venue_status: Accepted to ASE 2026 (41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering) -- stated in the arXiv comments field. Verified via arXiv abs page comments scrape; ASE is not on OpenReview so the comments field plus proceedings is the available evidence.
related_work.what_it_covers: Multi-agent Coordinator-Proposer framework for multi-hunk repair with explicit repair-order scheduling; 835 bugs across Defects4J and three vulnerability benchmarks; 326 Defects4J fixes (62 multi-method, 27 multi-file), 420 with Claude-3.5-Sonnet, claimed SOTA on Defects4J.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Concurrent, so it does not preempt us, and it argues our case: its central engineering problem is 'repair-order scheduling' -- i.e. how to serialize coupled edits -- which is exactly the constraint a joint denoising commit removes by construction. Autoregressive agents, Java, no diffusion, no consistency metric, no equal-token accounting.
related_work.known_defects: Multi-agent scaffolding means the comparison to 'prior APR baselines with the same base model' does not equalize inference cost -- a Coordinator-Proposer loop issues many more model calls than a single-shot baseline, and no token/call budget is reported. Defects4J contamination unaddressed for Claude-3.5-Sonnet. Best numbers come from a closed commercial model, so the framework's contribution is not separable from the model's.

related_work.citation: "Excision Score: Evaluating Edits with Surgical Precision." arXiv:2510.21537
related_work.venue_status: NOT peer-reviewed, and worse than 'preprint': OpenReview shows submission f5LVpApGOw with venueid ICLR.cc/2026/Conference/Desk_Rejected_Submission, venue 'ICLR 2026 Conference Desk Rejected Submission'. The only other record is DBLP CoRR 2025. Verified via OpenReview API (notes/search) -- this is exactly the case where S2/DBLP would have said 'preprint' and hidden the desk rejection.
related_work.what_it_covers: The metric instrument the proposal plans to adopt. Formulates 'revision similarity,' argues BLEU-family measures are dominated by content shared between a document and its revision, proposes Excision Score: LCS-based removal of content shared with ground truth before comparing divergent regions, quadratic approximation of cubic LCS. Reports +12% Pearson over SARI and >21% over BLEU when aligned with test execution on HumanEvalFix, rising to +20%/>30% under increased shared context.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Its own validation is on HumanEvalFix, i.e. predominantly single-site bug fixes -- exactly the regime where our instances are not. It never validates on multi-site coupled edits, where two candidate patches can have identical divergent-region content but differ in whether the sites are mutually consistent. Whether ES tracks test outcomes on coupled edits is an open question we would be first to answer.
related_work.known_defects: Desk-rejected at ICLR 2026, so citing it as a primary evaluation instrument is a reviewer liability, not an asset. Its headline correlation is validated against test execution on HumanEvalFix; since we *have* the test suites, ES is at best a redundant proxy for the thing we can measure directly -- ES should be a secondary/appendix metric, never load-bearing. The 'increased shared context' perturbation that produces its largest advantage is synthetic (artificially padding shared context), which flatters a measure designed to be invariant to shared context. And by construction ES excises content shared with ground truth, which for a rename task can excise the very tokens whose consistency is the object of study.

related_work.citation: "Edit, But Verify: An Empirical Audit of Instructed Code-Editing Benchmarks." arXiv:2604.05100
related_work.venue_status: Preprint; no journal-ref or comments on the arXiv abs page; OpenReview search surfaced no submission record for this title (only an unrelated EDIT-Bench DBLP CoRR record). Verified via arXiv abs page + OpenReview API.
related_work.what_it_covers: Audits the only two test-based instructed-code-editing benchmarks with human-authored instructions (CanItEdit, EDIT-Bench) across all 213 problems: language/intent/domain distributions vs Copilot Arena / AIDev / Octoverse, plus test counts, statement coverage, test scope. related_work.citation: "Parallel Sampling from Masked Diffusion Models via Conditional Independence Testing" (PUNT). arXiv:2510.21961
related_work.venue_status: Preprint; no comments/journal-ref on the arXiv abs page. Verified via arXiv abs page metadata.
related_work.what_it_covers: The theoretical threat to arm (a), and therefore the paper we must engage. States the core tension explicitly: effective parallel sampling requires simultaneously-updated tokens to be conditionally independent, but high-confidence predictions cluster and depend on each other. PUNT detects token dependencies and drops lower-confidence tokens from conflicting groups to satisfy both independence and confidence; up to 16% higher IFEval accuracy than baselines including one-by-one sequential generation.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: General text/instruction-following, never code, never coupled program sites. It removes dependent tokens from parallel groups -- the opposite of what our arm (a) wants -- and so predicts that committing mutually-dependent coupled sites in one pass should *hurt*. Nobody has tested whether that prediction holds when the dependency is semantic and cross-site rather than local and lexical, nor whether a dependency-aware sampler could be turned toward *deliberately* co-committing coupled sites.
related_work.known_defects: Conditional-independence testing is approximate and its calibration is not validated against a ground-truth dependency structure -- code with a def-use graph gives us exactly such a ground truth, which is a clean follow-up: does PUNT's learned dependency detector recover the def-use edges? Evaluated on general benchmarks where 'dependency' is never independently observable, so the mechanism claim is indirect. No code-domain evaluation at all.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv abs page fetched via proxy; surfaced through arXiv HTML search on 'diffusion language model conditional independence parallel sampling'; dateline and abstract confirmed.

related_work.citation: "Parallelism and Generation Order in Masked Diffusion Language Models: Limits Today, Potential Tomorrow." arXiv:2601.15593
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (v1 2026-01-22, v2 2026-04-11); no journal-ref/comments on arXiv abs page. Verified via arXiv abs page metadata.
related_work.what_it_covers: Directly relevant negative evidence. Characterizes eight mainstream MDLMs (up to 100B) on 58 benchmarks using Average Finalization Parallelism and Kendall's tau. Finds MDLMs still lag comparably-sized AR models mainly because parallel probabilistic modeling weakens inter-token dependencies; parallelism and order vary with domain, reasoning stage, and correctness; on tasks needing 'backward information' (Sudoku) MDLMs exploit order advantageously. Argues for a Generate-then-Edit paradigm.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Programming is one of its three domains but coupled multi-site editing is not a task it covers; AFP is measured on from-scratch generation, never on a remask-and-repair edit workload. Its 'backward information' result is the strongest existing hint that our claim could survive -- but it is demonstrated on Sudoku, not code, and nobody has tested whether def-use coupling is a 'backward information' task in its sense.
related_work.known_defects: AFP is a checkpoint-and-sampler-dependent quantity, and the paper does not separate architectural parallelism from sampler hyperparameters, so 'MDLMs lag because parallel modeling weakens dependencies' is confounded with default decoding configs. Its Generate-then-Edit recommendation is motivated theoretically but not tested as a controlled arm. No cost-matched comparison to AR.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv abs page fetched via proxy; surfaced through arXiv HTML search on parallel-decoding dependency terms; dateline v1 2026-01-22 confirmed.

related_work.citation: "Neither Parallel Nor Sequential: How DiffusionGemma Actually Commits Tokens." arXiv:2606.14620
related_work.venue_status: Preprint; no comments/journal-ref on arXiv abs page. Verified via arXiv abs page metadata.
related_work.what_it_covers: Concurrent, and methodologically the most useful paper for our sharpened claim. Instruments DiffusionGemma 26B's sampler accept step to record which canvas positions commit, when, and at what confidence, over a 686-prompt six-regime suite. Finds decoding is neither parallel nor block-autoregressive but has a partial left-to-right commit bias whose apparent strength depends on measurement granularity; 'block size' is an artifact of the measuring ruler; the model commits in large simultaneous batches leaving within-batch order genuinely undefined; structured JSON commits in near-arbitrary order; accuracy matches its AR Gemma-4 sibling. Central contribution is methodological -- honest measurement of decode order requires handling trailing-EOS padding, within-regime confounding, commit non-monotonicity, block-size sensitivity.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: One model (DiffusionGemma 26B), general prompt regimes, no code editing, no repair, no coupled sites, no notion of whether co-committed positions are semantically dependent. It measures *that* positions commit together but never *whether they needed to*. Applying its instrumentation to coupled def-use site pairs -- asking whether the two sites of a rename land in the same accept step -- is precisely the unclaimed extension.
related_work.known_defects: Single model and single sampler, so the left-to-right-bias finding may not transfer to Dream-Coder (which we can check). Its regimes are prompt categories rather than controlled dependency manipulations, so it cannot causally link commit simultaneity to dependency structure -- our def-use graph supplies the missing manipulation. Concurrent, so it does not preempt us; adopting its measurement hygiene is a strength.

related_work.citation: "Enabling Approximate Joint Sampling in Diffusion LMs." arXiv:2509.22738
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (v1 2025-09-25, v2 2026-02-02); no journal-ref/comments on arXiv abs page. Verified via arXiv abs page metadata.
related_work.what_it_covers: Quantifies the exact mechanism our arm (a) depends on. Notes that exact joint-distribution sampling from an MDLM requires unmasking exactly one token per full forward pass, and that the more tokens unmasked in parallel the further the string drifts from the true joint. Trains a lightweight single-layer sampler on a frozen diffusion LM to approximate multi-token joint samples; at four tokens per denoising step reaches MAUVE 0.87 vs a 0.31 marginal baseline. Explicitly evaluated on Dream-7B-Base/Instruct and Dream-7B-Coder -- our model family.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: MAUVE/LM quality and math+coding accuracy, never multi-site edit consistency. It is a fix for parallel-commit degradation that has never been applied to coupled code edits -- so it is both a threat (it documents that naive parallel commit departs from the joint, i.e. arm (a) may be handicapped by default sampling) and an opportunity (an arm (a+) using approximate joint sampling would be a genuinely new, cheap, well-motivated method contribution).
related_work.known_defects: MAUVE is a distributional-similarity proxy, not a task metric, so 'closer to the joint' is not shown to buy downstream correctness on anything requiring cross-site consistency. Demonstrated at four tokens per step; scaling to the many-token simultaneous commit our joint arm needs is untested. Requires training a sampler layer, so it is not a drop-in for a zero-training study -- but it directly implies a fairness objection to our arm (a): if we use default confidence-based parallel unmasking, we may be testing a handicapped version of joint commitment rather than joint commitment itself.

related_work.citation: "Edit-Based Refinement for Parallel Masked Diffusion Language Models" (ME-DLM). arXiv:2605.09603
related_work.venue_status: Accepted to ICML 2026 -- stated in the arXiv comments field. Verified via arXiv abs page comments scrape; ICML is not on OpenReview for 2026 so comments field is the available evidence and should be re-checked against official proceedings before citing as accepted.

HumanEval/GSM8K are from-scratch generation, so the claim that edits fix joint-consistency is tested on tasks with no explicit coupling structure. Its 'sequence-level consistency' is a fluency notion, not a semantic-dependency notion -- our def-use coupling is the sharper test it lacks.
