STEP 1 -- RE-SPECIFY THE ARMS AROUND THE AXIS THAT ACTUALLY VARIES. Drop B3 and B4. Run three arms:
  B1 = i.i.d. uniform masking at the matched global rate (already implemented: PlainMaskedSFTDataset, sft_dataset.py:238).
  B2 = TreeDiff tier-weighted, exactly N=floor(eps_t*L), weighted sample w/o replacement + uniform fallback (new class).
  B5 = TIER-COMPOSITION-MATCHED RANDOM: per example, mask the SAME NUMBER of tokens in EACH syntactic tier as B2 did, chosen uniformly WITHIN tier. I verified B5 is exactly constructible on the real corpus -- count-exact on 400/400 examples, ZERO tier-capacity failures at eps in {0.1,0.5}, reproduces B2's tier composition to 4 decimals (skel .0940 data .5220 cond .0750 ctrl .3091 at eps=0.1) while its mean run length is 1.0964 vs B2's 1.1056. B5 is the identified control the literature lacks: it isolates "which syntactic CATEGORIES get supervised" from "which specific positions within category", and unlike B3 its manipulated axis is large (L1 0.27) while its nuisance axis is matched.
  Optional B3' only if you want the run-length leg on the record: I verified span placement is feasible (0/400 failures at eps in {0.1,0.3,0.5} placing count+run-length-matched spans off AST boundaries), so the candidate's hard-abort does NOT fire -- but publish the 0.6% separation as the reason the arm is not worth 15 GPU-hours, not as a trained arm.

STEP 2 -- BUILD (new code, ~400 lines, all on zwfy6 checkout /apdcephfs_zwfy6/share_304376610/pighzliu_code/dllm_draft/):
  (a) expression-level tier extractor. Stdlib ast over scaffold_coder/renderer.py's rendered text, mapping char spans -> {skel,data,cond,ctrl}, then char->token via Qwen2TokenizerFast offset_mapping. MUST assert the fast/slow token-id equality I verified (400/400) because the trainer uses the slow DreamTokenizer (is_fast=False, return_offset_mapping raises NotImplementedError).
  (b) three Dataset classes cloned from PlainMaskedSFTDataset (sft_dataset.py:238) -- keep response-only corruption, min(20,1/t) weighting, no meta-tokens, no tokenizer extension.
  (c) register modes in scaffold_coder/training/scaffold_sft_trainer.py:87-242 next to 'plain'/'schedule_only' (self.token_extensions = () for all three).
  (d) the manipulation-check gate (see required_control).

STEP 3 -- GATE BEFORE GPU. Run (d) on the real dataloader; publish the realized-geometry table; abort any arm that fails its threshold.

STEP 4 -- TRAIN on .73 only (8x H20, /apdcephfs_zwfy6/.../dllm_draft/.venv_dream/bin/python). Copy scripts/run_plain_sft_stage1_8gpu.sh verbatim except scaffold.mode. Recipe is pinned in outputs/plain_sft_stage1/resolved_training_config.json (FSDP FULL_SHARD, global batch 128, micro 16/GPU, max_len 1024, 5 epochs, lr 1e-5, betas [0.9,0.95], warmup 0.1, grad ckpt on, bucket_by_length true). MEASURED cost is 15.31 GPU-hours per plain-style arm (1.914h x 8, BASELINE_STATS.md), NOT the 34.6 the candidate quotes from the micro-8 scaffold run. Adopt ONE schedule for all arms and state it: if you use t~U(0,1) rather than TreeDiff's cosine eps_t in [0.1,0.001], the EXISTING plain_sft_stage1/global_step_4465 checkpoint on zwfy6 IS a ready-made B1 and you save an arm.

STEP 5 -- EVAL, reusing the existing harness unchanged. scripts/run_plain_evalplus_full_8gpu.sh + scripts/generate_evalplus_dream.py (its parseable() at line 82 and the 'final_parseable' field at line 259 already give the parse-rate leg for free) + merge_evalplus_shards.py + reextract_dream_solutions.py + official evalplus.evaluate 0.3.1 on data/evalplus/{HumanEvalPlus-v0.1.10,MbppPlus-v0.2.0}.jsonl. MBPP+ (n=378) primary, paired McNemar/paired bootstrap, full arm x benchmark x budget matrix with CIs.

STEP 6 -- REUSE, DO NOT DUPLICATE. .82's sampler audit supplies the decoding-protocol sensitivity row (our own top_p 1.0->0.95 = +14.6 HumanEval points is the strongest single argument for matched protocol). .104's Qwen2.5-Coder-7B AR baseline (HE+ .524 / MBPP+ .648, tokens_fed 204/101) is the cross-family reference every arm must be placed against -- it is architecturally identical to Dream-Coder-v0-Base-7B and already dominates all our diffusion arms, which must be stated up front or a reviewer will do it for us. .73's infilling result supplies the 'bidirectional context is a task property, not a diffusion property' framing.
feas.risk: The dominant failure is a NULL THAT MEASURES NOTHING, reported as a finding -- structurally the same shape as retraction 2 (a stage whose input did not survive) fused with retraction 1 (a comparison that compared nothing). Concretely: you train 4 arms, observe B2 approx B3 approx B4, and write "AST boundaries add nothing once density and clustering are matched", when the actual causes are (i) B3 differs from B2 by 0.6% on the run-length axis it is supposed to vary and B4 differs from B1 by L1 0.06 versus B2's 0.25, so three of four arms are near-duplicates by construction, and (ii) the readout is taken at a hard floor. This second half is measured and is the deeper trap: every from-Base 5-epoch matched-SFT arm in this repo COLLAPSES in exactly the "low-budget regime where structure should help most". Plain SFT HumanEval+ = 21.95% @512, 4.88% @128, 0.00% @64; Schedule-only = 3.66 / 0.00 / 0.00. You cannot resolve a between-arm difference against a floor of 0.00%, and at 512 all arms sit ~48-68 points below the un-SFT'd Dream-Coder-Instruct (.707), i.e. the SFT recipe itself destroys the model before the masking manipulation is ever applied -- so even a real B2-vs-B5 gap is measured on a broken model and its transfer to a competently trained one is unsupported. Parse rate is the only leg with headroom (79.88% / 14.02% / 3.05% at 512/128/64) and it also floors at 64. Secondary confound: if B2 is implemented via RungMixtureSampler, the tokenizer extension and meta-token canvas ride along and the result is attributed to AST masking when it is the already-measured meta-token effect.
feas.required_control: A PRE-REGISTERED MANIPULATION-CHECK GATE ON REALIZED MASK GEOMETRY, run on CPU against the REAL dataloader before any GPU hour is spent, with per-arm pass/fail thresholds fixed in advance. For every arm pair it must dump the actual per-example boolean mask tensors and report: (a) per-example masked-token COUNT (must be exactly equal -- assert, not summarize); (b) pooled run-length histogram plus a distance to B2 (KS or chi-square); (c) masked-token TIER COMPOSITION and its L1 distance to B2; (d) positional Jaccard versus B2; (e) per-REGION realized density (prompt vs response) so the region-reallocation leg is a first-class number. Rule: an arm earns GPU time only if its separation from B2 on the axis it CLAIMS to vary exceeds threshold AND its separation on every axis it claims to MATCH falls below threshold. This is the control that would have caught both defects I found before 140 GPU-hours: B3 fails (b) with +0.64% separation at TreeDiff's own eps=0.1, and B4 fails (c) with L1 0.061 versus B2's 0.253. Two non-negotiable details, each aimed directly at a past retraction. First, the gate must instantiate the ACTUAL Dataset class with training=True and iterate it through the real ScaffoldBatchCollator -- not a standalone reimplementation of the sampler -- because "the sampler I audited" versus "the sampler the trainer consumed" is precisely the gap retraction 2 lived in, and PlainMaskedSFTDataset draws t from torch.initial_seed() per worker plus epoch (sft_dataset.py:314-330) so an offline reimplementation provably does not see the same masks; the realized-geometry JSON must be written next to the checkpoints and cited in the paper. Second, the gate must report the FULL distribution and its tail, not means: retraction 3 was an average that silently dropped the expensive cases, and a mean run length of 1.11 versus 1.11 hides nothing here only because I also checked the pooled histogram and the p99 max-run -- report both or the same class of error recurs. Add one floor-check gate alongside it: if the trained arms' pass@1 at the budget being compared is 0.00% for all arms, that cell is reported as UNRESOLVABLE (floor), never as B2 approx B5.

lens.title: Infilling Efficiency Has Never Been Priced: DreamOn's Length-Elasticity Claim Under Honest Cost Accounting
lens.claim: DreamOn's headline -- variable-length infilling 'on par with state-of-the-art autoregressive models' and matching oracle-length performance -- is stated without any compute accounting, and the length-search/expansion mechanism it replaces is precisely where the compute goes. We claim that once infilling is priced in wall-clock and cumulative processed tokens, the parity claim is regime-dependent: DreamOn's advantage over fixed-canvas baselines holds only when the fixed-canvas baseline is charged for length search, and it inverts against a cheap length ORACLE or against a calibrated first-step length estimator.
lens.why_now: Our own TASK_SURFACE_LIT_GAPS.md audit of DreamOn (2602.01326, ICLR 2026 Poster) states explicitly what it does and does not cover: it did HumanEval-Infilling single/multi-line and SantaCoder-FIM(Python) against Qwen2.5-Coder-7B / Deepseek-Coder-6.7B / Seed-Coder-8B, and 'NOT covered: any compute/NFE accounting, RandomSpanInfilling, multi-span, non-Python.' Meanwhile the length problem has become a small industry in 2026 and every entrant sidesteps cost the same way: 2602.00476 CAL performs 'an efficient search before formal decoding' (a search whose cost is not the headline), 2602.07546 LR-DLLM reports 51.3% Pass@1 on HumanEval-Infilling under unknown lengths (+13.4% vs DreamOn) with no matched cost unit, 2603.06123 and 2605.04215 predict response length to SAVE FLOPs, 2510.24605 dLLM-Var claims 30.1x speedup via native [EOS]. So there are now at least five mutually-uncompared solutions to one problem, each priced in its own unit -- the same pathology CaRE identified for remasking, in a corner CaRE did not touch. And infilling is the one surface where the bidirectional advantage should be real, making it the highest-value place to get accounting right. We have DreamOn-v0-7B on disk with its mechanism already reverse-engineered (UPSTREAM_AUDIT.md documents that delete is overloaded onto EOS 151643, expand is 151667, the exact released merge behavior, dynamic_inverse = merge_prob*(1 - num_masked/region_length), and that the generator is effectively batch-size-1).
lens.experiment: Price the infilling frontier in three units (NFE, cumulative processed tokens, wall-clock seconds) across arms that differ ONLY in how target length is obtained, on HumanEval-Infilling (single-line, multi-line) and SantaCoder-FIM(Python): (C1) DreamOn-v0-7B with mask_expansion + delete_eos_token, i.e. the released recipe (we have already measured this model on from-scratch generation -- HE+ .122 / MBPP+ .085 -- confirming it is an infilling specialist, so this is finally its home turf); (C2) Dream-Coder-Instruct-7B on a FIXED canvas swept over lengths {8,16,32,64,128}, charged for the full sweep (this is the honest cost of not knowing the length); (C3) fixed canvas at ORACLE length from the ground-truth middle span -- the upper bound DreamOn claims to match, now with its cost, which is one cheap run; (C4) calibrated first-step length estimator (the CAL move: exploit the first-step-confidence Oracle Peak and correct the Length Bias) charged for its estimation pass. Primary deliverable: quality-vs-cost frontiers with all three units overlaid per arm, so the reader can see which unit each published claim would have used and where the ordering changes. Extensions into DreamOn's admitted gaps, in priority order: multi-span infilling (two or more independent holes -- the regime where any-order/bidirectional should dominate AR most and which nobody has priced); RandomSpanInfilling; and the batch-size question (DreamOn's generator is batch-1 by construction per UPSTREAM_AUDIT item 7, while fixed-canvas diffusion batches trivially -- so per-request latency and per-GPU throughput may rank the arms OPPOSITELY, which is a clean second finding and connects to followup-1). Report the visible-vs-hidden distinction and exact-match vs functional-correctness scoring, since infilling benchmarks often score surface match.
lens.assets_needed: PRESENT: models/DreamOn-v0-7B (revision 57e0e41, mask/expand/delete IDs and merge behavior documented in UPSTREAM_AUDIT.md), models/Dream-Coder-v0-Instruct-7B and -Base-7B, vendor/DreamOn @ pinned commit 8a0a5491 (contains eval/generator.py, the released reference implementation including the EOS-at-masked-middle removal), scripts/generate_evalplus_dreamon.py (already wired for mask_expansion=True + delete_eos_token=True + paper T/top_p values), scripts/make_pareto_figures.py with the truncation-safe proc()/field_coverage() accessors, per-task elapsed_seconds logging in both harnesses. MISSING and BLOCKING: HumanEval-Infilling and SantaCoder-FIM datasets are NOT in data/ (only humaneval_plus.jsonl, mbpp_plus.jsonl) -- must fetch via hy-proxy; this is the single hard prerequisite. MISSING: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B on neither disk (verified), so DreamOn's own AR comparison point cannot be reproduced locally without download -- note another agent is reportedly running a matched AR baseline on .104 and a DreamOn/FIM eval on .73; COORDINATE FIRST to avoid duplicating, and scope this candidate to the COST-ACCOUNTING layer they are not doing.
lens.kill_criterion: Killed if the three cost units agree on arm ordering in every regime -- then there is no accounting finding, only a replication. Killed as a *repair of DreamOn* if C1 dominates C2, C3 and C4 on all three units simultaneously, i.e. DreamOn is efficient as well as accurate and the missing accounting would only have helped it; we should then report that plainly. Substantially weakened if the datasets cannot be fetched through the proxy, since HE+/MBPP+ cannot substitute for an infilling surface -- in that case the candidate should be dropped rather than retargeted. Also killed if the other agents' in-flight DreamOn/FIM and AR runs already cover the cost accounting (check before starting). Ceiling honestly capped: this is a measurement/accounting contribution on one model family and one language (Python), so main-conference requires the multi-span leg plus the batch/throughput inversion to both land; without them it is a short paper.
lens.builds_on: arXiv:2602.01326 DreamOn (first public 2026-02-01, ICLR 2026 Poster). Its claim: augmenting the diffusion process with two length-control states lets the model autonomously expand or contract output length, removing the fixed-canvas barrier, and achieving infilling performance 'on par with state-of-the-art autoregressive models' on HumanEval-Infilling and SantaCoder-FIM while matching 'oracle performance achieved with ground-truth length.' The defect is an accounting omission with a specific direction of bias: the paper reports no NFE, FLOPs, token, or wall-clock accounting anywhere, yet its entire value proposition is replacing a length SEARCH with learned expansion -- so the quantity that determines whether the method is worth using (cost relative to searching, and cost relative to simply knowing the length) is exactly the quantity left unmeasured. Matching oracle-length QUALITY while saying nothing about oracle-length COST is a claim of parity on one axis presented as parity overall. We repair it by building the priced frontier with the length-oracle and calibrated-estimator arms as explicit reference points, and by extending into the three regimes the paper's own scope statement excludes (multi-span, RandomSpanInfilling, non-Python). Concurrent/adjacent entrants that must be cited and are NOT preemptions because none prices the comparison either: 2602.00476 CAL (2026-01-31, training-free calibrated length search, +47.7% Pass@1 in code infilling), 2602.07546 LR-DLLM (2026-02-07, beats DreamOn by +13.4% on HumanEval-Infilling under unknown length), 2510.24605 dLLM-Var, 2509.01025 FlexMDM and 2607.26504 (insertion-based any-order), 2603.06123, 2605.04215.

diff.sharpened_claim: Every 2026 entrant to the diffusion-LM infilling-length problem prices itself in a self-chosen unit that its own mechanism minimises, and NO paper prices the arm that actually competes with all of them: a fixed canvas at ORACLE length. We build the first cross-arm priced frontier on HumanEval-Infilling {SingleLine, MultiLine, RandomSpan} where arms differ ONLY in how the target length is obtained -- (C1) DreamOn's learned expand/delete, (C2) fixed canvas swept over lengths and charged for the whole sweep, (C3) fixed canvas at oracle length, (C4) calibrated first-step estimator -- reported simultaneously in NFE, cumulative attended tokens, and wall-clock seconds on identical hardware with a single sampler. Two specific claims that no prior paper can make: (i) DreamOn's own reported step counts (52.4 steps at mask length 64, Fig. 4) are measured ONLY on the multi-line subset with broadcasting-on-vs-off as the contrast, so they price DreamOn against itself and NOT against the fixed-canvas or oracle alternatives -- the comparison that decides whether the method is worth using is the one absent; (ii) the released DreamOn generator is batch-size-1 by construction (insertion/deletion tensor rewrites) while fixed-canvas diffusion batches trivially, so per-request latency and per-GPU throughput can rank the arms OPPOSITELY -- an inversion that is invisible to every published number because all of them are batch-1. Our headline is the regime map: which unit each published claim would have used, and where the arm ordering flips.
diff.differentiation_statement: Our contribution is NOT "DreamOn reports no compute" -- that framing is factually wrong and must be dropped before writing (DreamOn §5.4 / Fig. 4 reports Total Diffusion Steps vs mask length and a 2.1x generation speedup from deletion broadcasting). The defensible contribution is narrower and survives verification: DreamOn's accounting is INTERNAL and PARTIAL. Its step counts contrast DreamOn-with-broadcasting against DreamOn-without-broadcasting on the multi-line subset only; there is no step, token, or second count for the fixed-canvas baselines it beats on quality, and crucially none for the ORACLE-length configuration whose quality it claims to match. So the paper establishes "we match oracle quality" and separately "our own variant is 2.1x faster than our own ablation," and never joins the two into "matching oracle quality costs X relative to simply knowing the length." That join is our deliverable. Against the closest concurrent work, PILL (ACL ARR 2026 May, first public 2026-05-25, 18 days past the concurrency cutoff), the differentiation is the arm set and the unit set, not the observation that infilling has a cost: PILL prices itself in forward passes and relative wall-clock against adaptive-length baselines to argue its own method is cheaper (1.82x faster, <10% over fixed-length), i.e. it uses cost as a selling point for a new method, whereas we hold the method space fixed and vary only the length-acquisition mechanism, include a fixed-canvas-at-oracle-length reference arm that PILL does not report, and report three units side by side so the unit-dependence of the ordering is itself the finding. Against CaRE (2026-06-04, also concurrent), the differentiation is the corner: CaRE standardises NFE for REMASKING strategies on open-ended text (OpenWebText/LM1B, MAUVE), and explicitly does not touch infilling, length control, or functional correctness. Against 2510.18480 (2025-10-21, PRE-cutoff and therefore the one real constraint), the differentiation is task surface and arm set: it establishes that AR beats DLMs on throughput and that batch-1 acceleration gains vanish at scale, but it measures GSM8K with fixed generation lengths on LLaDA/LLaMA/Fast-dLLM v2 -- no infilling, no code, no length-acquisition arms, and it is precisely the paper whose batch-size result predicts (but does not test) our inversion in the infilling setting. Finally, even a null result differentiates: if the three units agree everywhere, that itself is publishable as the first demonstration that the infilling-length literature's incompatible units happen to be order-preserving, which no one currently knows.

followup_openings.target_paper: arXiv:2602.01326 DreamOn (ICLR 2026 Poster, first public 2026-02-01)
followup_openings.defect: The oracle-parity claim is one-sided. Table 2 shows DreamOn reaching near-oracle pass@1 across initial mask lengths 4-64, and Fig. 4 reports Total Diffusion Steps -- but the step counts contrast DreamOn-with-broadcasting vs DreamOn-without-broadcasting on the multi-line subset ONLY. There is no step/token/second count for the fixed-canvas baselines it outperforms on quality, and none for the oracle-length configuration whose quality it claims to match. So 'matches oracle performance' is a quality-only statement while the oracle arm is the CHEAPEST possible arm (one run at the right length, no expand/delete steps, no search).
followup_openings.our_fix: Add the missing arm as a first-class reference: fixed canvas at oracle length from the ground-truth middle span, measured in NFE, cumulative attended tokens, and wall-clock on the same GPU with the same sampler (T=0.2, top_p=0.9, alg=entropy, steps=256, batch_size=1 per vendor/DreamOn/eval/eval_santa_fim.sh). Report the ratio DreamOn-cost / oracle-cost per initial mask length -- the number that converts 'matches oracle quality' into 'matches oracle quality at Nx oracle cost'. Because DreamOn's expand cap is Lmax=128 and expansion is disabled after Lmax expansions, this ratio should be strongly length-dependent, which is itself a reportable regime map.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It converts the paper's headline from a parity claim into a priced trade-off, and it is the only arm that bounds the whole 2026 length-control literature from below: if learned expansion costs 3-5x the oracle, then every method in this space is buying robustness-to-unknown-length at a quantified price nobody has quoted.

followup_openings.target_paper: arXiv:2602.00476 CAL (2026-01-31, ICLR 2026 DeLTa Workshop Poster -- workshop, not main conference)
followup_openings.defect: Cost is asserted acceptable rather than reported in a comparable unit. CAL states the search needs '11 to 18 additional first-step forward passes on average' and that 'this overhead is acceptable given the substantial capability improvements', and Table 6 reports a Stps. column -- but the overhead is quoted in its own units (extra first-step passes) and never converted to the total-generation NFE, token, or wall-clock denominators the fixed-length baseline is implicitly charged in. The limitations section itself concedes 'the introduced latency might still be a consideration for ultra-low-latency' settings. Its headline +47.7% Pass@1 over fixed-length is therefore a quality delta with an unpriced denominator.
followup_openings.our_fix: Reimplement CAL's move as our C4 arm (exploit the first-step-confidence Oracle Peak, correct the Length Bias) and charge the estimation pass into the SAME three denominators as every other arm, with D and dL at the paper's defaults for code (D=4, dL=1). Then place C4 on the same axes as C1/C2/C3 so the reader can see whether an 11-18-pass estimator is cheaper or dearer than DreamOn's learned expansion at the same quality.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: CAL and DreamOn have never been compared on any common cost axis despite solving the same problem 1 day apart; putting them on one frontier is the minimum bar for the field to make a rational method choice, and it is cheap for us because C4 is training-free.

followup_openings.defect: Its headline +13.4% Pass@1 over DreamOn on HumanEval-Infilling is a quality-only delta, and its cost is reported in a self-serving normalised unit: Table 9 gives Forward Calls / Generated Tokens (mean ~3.66-5.12, median 3.43-4.63 across Dream/DreamCoder/LLaDA-8B) and argues overhead is 'approximately constant average cost'. A per-generated-token ratio is exactly the denominator that hides a method producing FEWER tokens, and it is not the unit DreamOn reported (total diffusion steps), so the +13.4% comparison has no shared cost axis. The paper contains no wall-clock, no FLOPs, and no throughput anywhere (verified: zero occurrences of wall/throughput/latency/FLOP in the full text).
followup_openings.our_fix: Recompute both DreamOn and a length-regularised arm in ABSOLUTE units (total forward passes, total attended tokens, seconds) rather than per-token ratios, on the same tasks and hardware. Report both the ratio and the absolute so it is visible whether the ratio flattered the method by shrinking its denominator.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This is the cleanest single demonstration of the accounting pathology: two papers claim relative superiority over each other's numbers while measuring in units that cannot be divided by one another. Showing that the ordering changes -- or robustly does not -- under a shared absolute unit is the whole point of the paper.

followup_openings.target_paper: arXiv:2510.18480 'How Efficient Are Diffusion Language Models?' (2025-10-21, PRE-cutoff)
followup_openings.defect: Establishes the batch-size result -- DLM acceleration gains are large at batch size 1 and 'diminish as the batch size increases', with a crossover as low as batch size 2 for 5-shot -- but only on GSM8K with FIXED generation lengths (64-2048) on LLaDA-8B-Instruct / LLaMA-3.1-8B / Fast-dLLM v2-7B on a single A800. It never tests infilling, never tests code, and never tests any variable-length or length-acquisition mechanism, so it cannot say whether its crossover survives when the arms differ in how length is obtained rather than in how a fixed canvas is denoised.
followup_openings.our_fix: Port its batch-size axis into the infilling setting, exploiting an asymmetry it could not see: DreamOn's released generator is batch-size-1 BY CONSTRUCTION (insertion/deletion tensor rewrites with batch-1 assumptions -- our UPSTREAM_AUDIT.md item 7, and vendor/DreamOn/eval/eval_santa_fim.sh ships batch_size=1), whereas fixed-canvas and oracle-length arms batch trivially. Measure per-request latency AND per-GPU throughput at batch 1, 4, 16. If the ordering inverts between the two, the entire published record -- all batch-1 -- has been reporting the metric that favours the length-elastic method.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This is the strongest and most falsifiable leg, and it is a structural finding rather than a bookkeeping one: it says the mechanism that buys length elasticity forfeits batching, which is invisible in every published number because nobody batched. It is also the leg that lifts this from short-paper to main-conference.

followup_openings.target_paper: arXiv:2602.01326 DreamOn, scope statement (multi-span / RandomSpan / non-Python)
followup_openings.defect: Evaluates HumanEval-Infilling single-line and multi-line plus SantaCoder-FIM(Python) -- one contiguous hole, one language. Multi-span infilling (two or more independent holes) is the regime where bidirectional any-order generation should dominate AR MOST, because AR must serialise the holes and cannot condition each on the others' final content; it is untested by DreamOn and, from our searches, unpriced by anyone.
followup_openings.our_fix: Run the multi-span leg using the RandomSpanInfilling split that is ALREADY on disk (data/infilling/HumanEval-RandomSpanInfilling.jsonl, 1640 rows -- the candidate wrongly lists this as missing and blocking), plus synthetically constructed 2-3-hole variants from the same canonical tasks, priced in the same three units. Report visible-vs-hidden pass rates and functional correctness separately from exact match, since SantaCoder-FIM is scored by exact match and DreamOn already needed an AST parser to normalise it.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It is the one regime where the diffusion advantage is a structural prediction rather than a benchmark artifact, the data is already local so it costs no proxy risk, and a positive result gives the paper a quality finding to stand beside the accounting finding -- which the kill-criterion correctly identifies as necessary for a main-conference ceiling.

followup_openings.target_paper: 'Predict, Don't Iterate: Efficient Adaptive-Length Infilling for Diffusion Language Models' (PILL), ACL ARR 2026 May Submission (first public 2026-05-25, CONCURRENT)
followup_openings.defect: Prices itself relative to baselines it selects (1.82x faster than the strongest baseline, <10% time over fixed-length decoding, 5 DLMs x 8 infilling benchmarks) but, as far as its abstract commits, reports no fixed-canvas-at-ORACLE-length arm and does not report the same quantity in multiple units to test whether the ordering is unit-invariant. It also inherits the batch-1 convention: a method whose selling point is 'drastically reduces the number of forward passes' is measured on the axis where forward-pass count is the cost, which is exactly the axis that stops predicting latency once requests batch.
followup_openings.our_fix: Cite PILL as concurrent and adopt it as a fifth arm if a public implementation appears; otherwise position explicitly against it: we vary only the length-acquisition mechanism with method held fixed, include the oracle-cost reference arm, and add the batch-size axis. Note that PILL's existence RAISES the value of our oracle arm and batch leg while lowering the value of a pure 'infilling has never been priced' framing -- so the framing must move to unit-invariance and batching, not to the absence of accounting.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: PILL is the single biggest threat to this candidate's headroom and it is 18 days past the concurrency cutoff. Discovering it now forces the reframing that makes the paper survive review instead of being told in rebuttal that a concurrent ARR submission already priced infilling.

related_work.citation: Zirui Wu, Lin Zheng, Zhihui Xie, Jiacheng Ye, Jiahui Gao, Shansan Gong, Yansong Feng, Zhenguo Li, Wei Bi, Guorui Zhou, Lingpeng Kong. DreamOn: Diffusion Language Models For Code Infilling Beyond Fixed-size Canvas. arXiv:2602.01326.
related_work.venue_status: ICLR 2026 Poster -- VERIFIED via OpenReview API: forum EQTPmqukiU, venue='ICLR 2026 Poster', venueid='ICLR.cc/2026/Conference', invitations include Submission19236/-/Camera_Ready_Revision. arXiv v1 only (no v2).
related_work.what_it_covers: Augments masked diffusion with [expand] and [delete] states so the model autonomously grows/shrinks the canvas. Fine-tunes Dream-7B, DiffuCoder-7B, Dream-Coder-7B on OpenCoder educational-instruct (~110K Python pairs). Evaluates HumanEval-Infilling single-line + multi-line (pass@1) and SantaCoder-FIM Python (exact match, AST-normalised) vs Qwen2.5-Coder-7B / DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B / Seed-Coder-8B and LLaDA-8B/Dream-7B/DiffuCoder-7B/Dream-Coder-7B. Table 2 shows near-oracle pass@1 across initial mask lengths 4-64. CRITICALLY, contra the candidate's premise, it DOES report compute: §5.4 'Efficiency Analysis of Deletion Broadcasting' + Fig. 4 plot Number of Mask Expansion, Number of Mask Deletion, and Total Diffusion Steps against mask length, stating steps drop from 122.8 (w/o broadcasting) to 52.4 (w/ broadcasting) at mask length 64, and that broadcasting 'accelerates generation by 2.1x'. Training cost is also given (5 h on 8xH800, 0.15% of base pretraining).
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: The reported step counts are an INTERNAL ablation contrast (broadcasting on vs off) on the multi-line subset only. No step/token/second cost is reported for the fixed-canvas baselines it beats on quality, and none for the oracle-length configuration whose quality it claims to match -- so 'matches oracle performance' is never joined to 'at what cost relative to knowing the length'. No wall-clock, no FLOPs, no throughput, no batch-size axis. Scope excludes multi-span infilling, RandomSpanInfilling, and non-Python.
related_work.known_defects: (1) One-sided oracle parity: quality matched to oracle, cost never compared to oracle, and oracle is structurally the cheapest arm. (2) Cross-arm accounting absent while intra-arm accounting present -- easy to misread as full accounting. (3) Batch-1 only; the released generator has batch-size-1 assumptions in its insertion/deletion tensor rewrites (our UPSTREAM_AUDIT.md item 7; vendor eval_santa_fim.sh ships batch_size=1), so throughput claims are untestable from the paper. (4) SantaCoder-FIM scored by exact match needing an AST parser to 'normalize huge syntactic differences' -- a surface metric standing in for functional correctness. (5) Lmax=128 expansion cap plus disabling expansion after Lmax expansions makes cost strongly length-dependent in a way Fig. 4 only partially exposes. (6) README/config mismatch on context length (README says 2048; pinned config says max_position_embeddings=32768) per our UPSTREAM_AUDIT.md.

related_work.citation: Hechang Niu et al. Diffusion LMs Can Approximate Optimal Infilling Lengths Implicitly (CAL: Calibrated Adaptive Length). arXiv:2602.00476.
related_work.venue_status: ICLR 2026 DeLTa Workshop Poster (WORKSHOP, not main conference) -- VERIFIED via OpenReview API: title 'Training-Free Length Discovery for Diffusion Language Model Infilling', venue='ICLR 2026 DeLTa Workshop Poster', venueid='ICLR.cc/2026/Workshop/DeLTa', forum Hl8w6DC9VY, cdate 2026-01-30. related_work.what_it_covers: Training-free length discovery for DLM infilling. Identifies two first-step-denoising-confidence phenomena: a local Oracle Peak near ground-truth length and a systematic Length Bias (modelled as k*log L) that obscures it. Calibrating the bias enables an efficient bidirectional search before formal decoding. Reports +47.7% Pass@1 over fixed-length baselines and +40.5% over chat-based adaptive methods in code infilling, +8.5% BLEU-2 / +9.9% ROUGE-L in text infilling. Table 1 establishes that oracle length substantially improves DLM infilling. Compares against DAEDAL (arXiv:2508.00819). Evaluated on HumanEval-Infilling SingleLine with LLaDA-8B-Base among others.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: The search cost is quoted in its own private unit and never converted into the denominator the fixed-length baseline is charged in. No wall-clock, no FLOPs, no throughput, no batch axis. Does not compare to DreamOn on any cost axis (published 1 day apart). Table 6 sweeps tolerance D and step dL against a Stps. column, so search cost is tunable but never placed on a shared frontier with learned-expansion methods.
related_work.known_defects: 'This overhead is acceptable given the substantial capability improvements' is an assertion, not a measurement -- exactly the accounting-by-assertion the audit targets. 11-18 extra first-step forward passes are reported as an average with no distribution and no conversion to total-generation NFE. Its own limitations section concedes latency 'might still be a consideration for ultra-low-latency' settings, conceding the unpriced axis. Headline +47.7% is a best-case ('up to') number. Workshop-only venue, so it has not had main-conference scrutiny.

related_work.citation: Zicong Cheng, Ruixuan Jia, Jia Li, Guo-Wei Yang, Meng-Hao Guo, Shi-Min Hu. Improving Variable-Length Generation in Diffusion Language Models via Length Regularization (LR-DLLM). arXiv:2602.07546.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint -- arXiv v1 2026-02-07. No OpenReview record found (searches on title and on 'Length Regularization diffusion language models variable length' returned no matching submission), no venue claim made by the paper.
related_work.what_it_covers: Training-free length-regularised inference. Attributes fixed-canvas failure to an intrinsic length-induced bias in confidence estimates, corrects it with an explicit log L regularizer whose coefficient is estimated by lightweight probing, then does greedy bidirectional length adjustment. Two stages: probing initialisation on an exponential candidate-length schedule, then inference-time local refinement with one-token commitment. Headline: 51.3% Pass@1 on HumanEval-Infilling under fully unknown lengths (+13.4% vs DreamOn) and 51.5% average Pass@1 on four-language McEval (+14.3% vs DreamOn) -- so it DOES go non-Python, which the candidate's gap list should reflect.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Cost appears only as the normalised ratio Forward Calls / Generated Tokens (Table 9; mean 3.66 / median 3.43 for Dream, 4.89 / 4.00 for DreamCoder, 5.12 / 4.63 for LLaDA-8B, with P95 and a right-skewed long tail). No absolute forward-pass count, no wall-clock, no FLOPs, no throughput, no batch axis (verified by keyword counts over the full text: wall=0, throughput=0, latency=0, FLOP=0). So the +13.4% over DreamOn has no cost axis shared with DreamOn's own reported step counts.
related_work.known_defects: Per-generated-token normalisation is the denominator most flattering to a method that emits fewer tokens -- an accounting convention that cannot be compared to DreamOn's total-diffusion-steps or to CAL's extra-first-step-passes. 'Approximately constant average cost, rather than unbounded or length-proportional overhead' is argued from a mean/median gap while conceding a long tail of hard cases. Claims superiority over DreamOn on quality while measuring cost in an incommensurable unit. Unrefereed preprint. Its own related-work admits training-based length methods 'incur extra training cost' without quantifying that either.

related_work.citation: How Efficient Are Diffusion Language Models? A Critical Examination of Efficiency Evaluation Practices. arXiv:2510.18480.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint -- arXiv v1 2025-10-21. No OpenReview or proceedings record located; treated as preprint.
related_work.what_it_covers: THE pre-cutoff methodological precedent and the closest thing to a competing framing. Systematically critiques DLM efficiency evaluation practice, naming the exact pathologies our candidate invokes: inconsistent metrics across studies ('some report latency per token, others throughput'), evaluation under constrained settings ('most notably using a batch size of one and fixed output lengths'), and heterogeneous infrastructure. Empirically benchmarks LLaDA-8B-Instruct (DLM), LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct (AR), Fast-dLLM v2-7B (block diffusion) on GSM8K on a single A800 80GB, FP16, unified conda env, sweeping prompt length (0/5-shot), generation length 64-2048, and batch size. Finds AR consistently highest throughput; dual-cache and confidence-aware parallel decoding help mainly at batch size 1 with benefits diminishing on scaling, and identifies an explicit crossover as low as batch size 2 for 5-shot where the ordering 'reverses' because diffusion hits the compute-bound regime sooner. Adds a throughput model in terms of FLOPs/s and FLOPs/token.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Entirely absent: infilling, code, FIM, any variable-length or length-acquisition mechanism, functional-correctness metrics, and the DreamOn/Dream-Coder family. Generation lengths are FIXED by construction (AR forced to continue past EOS to match the target) -- the opposite of the regime where length must be discovered. So it predicts our batch inversion but cannot test it, and it has no oracle-length arm because length is never in question.
related_work.known_defects: Single GPU model (A800) and single task (GSM8K) limit external validity of the crossover point. HuggingFace Transformers with SDPA rather than a production serving stack, so absolute throughput understates what optimised systems achieve and the batch-size crossover may sit elsewhere under paged attention / continuous batching. Forcing AR to generate past EOS to equalise length is a fair-throughput choice that simultaneously removes AR's real-world early-exit advantage, which cuts against its own headline direction. Three models only, one per paradigm.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv abs page (citation_date 2025/10/21, full abstract); full PDF downloaded and text-extracted, grepped for batch/infilling/FIM/variable-length/throughput/reverse, and the setup section (lines 257-300) plus batch-crossover passages (lines 1143-1149, 1223-1238) read verbatim to confirm both the model list and the absence of any infilling surface.

related_work.citation: CaRE: Compute-aware Remasking Evaluation Protocol for Masked Diffusion Language Models. arXiv:2607.24763.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint -- arXiv v1 2026-06-04 (announced under a 2607 identifier). OpenReview search on the exact title returned no matching submission (only an unrelated COMPUTE 2024 DBLP record), so no venue claim is made.
related_work.what_it_covers: The direct methodological template the candidate cites, and its scope confirms the candidate's 'corner CaRE did not touch' framing. Audits 7 remasking strategies under a compute-aware protocol: standardises ACTUAL NFE (not nominal step counts), enforces multi-metric reporting, and explicitly controls stochasticity. Applied to LLaDA-8B-Base and Dream-7B-Base at 4 stochasticity levels and 3 step budgets on OpenWebText and LM1B, plus a 12-model leaderboard (150M-8B). Findings: temperature explains most MAUVE variance; compute-matched comparison REVERSES several published strategy rankings; informed remasking and stochastic unmasking are in tension. Concludes current MDLM evaluations 'systematically conflate algorithmic improvements with hidden choices of compute and stochasticity'.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Confined to remasking on open-ended text with MAUVE. No infilling, no length control, no code, no functional correctness, no oracle arm, no batch/throughput axis, and NFE is its single compute unit (so it cannot detect unit-dependence of orderings the way a three-unit frontier can).
related_work.known_defects: MAUVE on OpenWebText/LM1B is a distributional-similarity metric, not task success, so 'rankings reverse' is demonstrated on a construct far from downstream utility -- an ironic weakness for an audit paper. Base models only (LLaDA-8B-Base, Dream-7B-Base), so no instruction-tuned or code-specialised replication. Standardising actual NFE still leaves NFE as a within-family unit that does not transfer across AR/diffusion or across batch sizes. 7 strategies is a subset of the remasking literature.

related_work.citation: Diffusion LLM with Native Variable Generation Lengths: Let [EOS] Lead the Way (dLLM-Var). arXiv:2510.24605.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint -- arXiv v1 2025-10-28. OpenReview search returns venue='CoRR 2025' (i.e. a DBLP CoRR record, not a conference), consistent with preprint status.
related_work.what_it_covers: Trains a dLLM to accurately predict [EOS] so it natively infers in a block-diffusion manner while retaining full bidirectional attention and high parallelism. Claims 30.1x speedup over traditional dLLM inference paradigms and 2.4x over AR models such as Qwen and Llama, with higher accuracy. Pre-cutoff, and unlike most entrants it DOES foreground speed as the headline.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Speedup is quoted against 'traditional dLLM inference paradigms' -- a baseline whose canvas length choice determines the ratio, so a 30.1x figure is largely a statement about how oversized the reference canvas was. Being EOS-based, it is 'less convenient for arbitrary-span FIM or settings without a clear EOS boundary' (LR-DLLM's related-work assessment), so its applicability to infilling is limited and untested.

related_work.citation: rho-EOS: Training-free Bidirectional Variable-Length Control for Masked Diffusion LLMs. arXiv:2601.22527.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint -- arXiv v2; OpenReview search returns venue='CoRR 2026' (DBLP CoRR record, not a conference).
related_work.what_it_covers: Training-free single-stage bidirectional length control driven by the implicit EOS density (rho) during denoising: high density triggers MASK contraction, insufficient density induces expansion. Explicitly contrasts itself with 'prior two-stage approaches -- which require separate length adjustment and iterative mask insertion phases while supporting only unidirectional expansion'. Reports comparable performance with 'substantially improving inference efficiency and token utilization' on math and code benchmarks.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Another entrant in the same crowded problem with efficiency claimed in its own terms ('token utilization'), not on a shared axis with DreamOn/CAL/LR-DLLM/PILL. Infilling-specific evaluation and any oracle-length reference are absent.
related_work.known_defects: 'Token utilization' is a self-defined efficiency proxy -- the ratio of useful to padding tokens -- which improves automatically for any method that shrinks the canvas and is not a latency or throughput measure. related_work.citation: Beyond Fixed: Training-Free Variable-Length Denoising for Diffusion Large Language Models (DAEDAL). arXiv:2508.00819.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint -- arXiv v2, first public 2025-08-01. No venue verified.
related_work.what_it_covers: The pre-cutoff training-free adaptive-length baseline that CAL and others benchmark against. Two phases: coarse pre-denoising length expansion guided by a sequence-completion metric, then during-denoising expansion of insufficient regions via mask-token insertion. Claims performance comparable to tuned fixed-length baselines while 'enhancing computational efficiency by achieving a higher effective token ratio'.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Designed for chat/open-ended generation, not infilling; CAL shows it can underperform even the fixed-length baseline on infilling when the initial length is overestimated (L=16 or 32) and that it is 'primarily limited to extending' rather than bidirectional. Efficiency is again a self-defined ratio, not latency or throughput.
related_work.known_defects: 'Higher effective token ratio' is the same class of self-serving efficiency proxy as rho-EOS's token utilization -- it measures padding avoidance, not cost. Unidirectional expansion only. Its transfer failure to infilling (documented by CAL) is a cautionary datapoint that chat-tuned length methods do not generalise to infilling, which supports keeping our study infilling-native.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv abs page (citation_date 2025/08/01, full abstract); corroborated by CAL's Table 2 discussion of DAEDAL's infilling underperformance, read from the CAL PDF text.

related_work.citation: Diffusion Language Models Are Natively Length-Aware. arXiv:2603.06123. // Predict-then-Diffuse: Adaptive Response Length for Compute-Budgeted Inference in Diffusion LLMs. arXiv:2605.04215.
related_work.venue_status: Both preprints -- arXiv v1 2026-03-06 (2603.06123) and v1 2026-05-05 (2605.04215). 2605.04215 is 2 days before the 2026-05-07 concurrency cutoff, so it is NOT concurrent. No venues verified for either.
related_work.what_it_covers: The two length-prediction-for-compute-savings papers. 2603.06123 conjectures the latent prompt representation suffices to estimate output length and crops the context window zero-shot before generation, reporting significant FLOP reductions on GSM8K/HumanEval/IfEval/LongFormQA with no statistically significant degradation (and improvement on 2 of 4). 2605.04215 (Predict-then-Diffuse / AdaRLP) predicts response length then runs inference at that length, with a data-driven safety margin against under-estimation, reporting FLOP reductions robust to skewed data. Notably, these two are the papers in the set that DO report a real compute unit (FLOPs).
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Both target unconditional response-length prediction for chat/reasoning, NOT infilling with prefix+suffix constraints, where the length signal and the failure modes differ. Neither has an oracle-length arm, neither reports wall-clock or throughput alongside FLOPs, and neither compares to DreamOn or any expand/delete mechanism.
related_work.known_defects: FLOPs is a hardware-agnostic unit that can move in the opposite direction from wall-clock for diffusion (fewer FLOPs over a shorter canvas need not mean lower latency once batching, memory bandwidth, and kernel efficiency are considered) -- which is exactly why our three-unit design includes seconds alongside token counts. 2603.06123's 'no statistically significant degradation' rests on 4 benchmarks and does not report the test or power. Because they optimise length for savings rather than for correctness, neither addresses the infilling regime where a wrong length destroys the answer rather than merely wasting compute.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv abs pages for both IDs (titles, citation_dates 2026/03/06 and 2026/05/05, full abstracts fetched and read); located via arXiv API variable-length and throughput queries.

diff.verification_notes: THREE OF THE CANDIDATE'S LOAD-BEARING PREMISES ARE FALSE AND MUST BE FIXED BEFORE ANY WRITING. (1) The central premise -- DreamOn 'reports no NFE, FLOPs, token, or wall-clock accounting anywhere' -- is WRONG. I downloaded arXiv:2602.01326v1 and read it: §5.4 'Efficiency Analysis of Deletion Broadcasting' with Figure 4 plots Number of Mask Expansion, Number of Mask Deletion, and Total Diffusion Steps against mask length, states 'reducing total inference steps from as high as 122.8 (w/o broadcasting) to just 52.4 (w/ broadcasting) at mask length 64', and §5.2 states 'The deletion broadcasting mechanism also accelerates generation by 2.1x'. Training compute is also reported (5 h on 8xH800 = 0.15% of base pretraining). A reviewer who has read the paper will reject the framing on sight. The DEFENSIBLE version, which I verified holds, is that this accounting is INTERNAL (DreamOn vs its own broadcasting-off ablation, multi-line subset only) and never prices the fixed-canvas baselines or the oracle-length configuration -- so oracle PARITY is asserted on quality while oracle COST is never measured. (2) The 'MISSING and BLOCKING' dataset claim is WRONG in the opposite direction: /apdcephfs_wzc1/share_304376610/pighzliu_code/dllm_draft/data/infilling/ already contains HumanEval-SingleLineInfilling.jsonl (1033 rows), HumanEval-MultiLineInfilling.jsonl (5815), and HumanEval-RandomSpanInfilling.jsonl (1640). RandomSpanInfilling -- which the candidate lists as an extension gap requiring a proxy fetch -- is on disk. The stated 'single hard prerequisite' does not exist, and the kill-criterion clause 'dropped if datasets cannot be fetched' is moot. SantaCoder-FIM is genuinely not in data/, though vendor/DreamOn/{eval/eval_santa_fim.sh, eval/compute_em_santa.py, data/prepare_data.py} are present. (3) LR-DLLM already reports four-language McEval (+14.3% vs DreamOn), so 'non-Python' is NOT an open gap in the way the candidate's builds_on section implies. THE BIGGEST DISCOVERY, not in the candidate at all: PILL ('Predict, Don't Iterate: Efficient Adaptive-Length Infilling for Diffusion Language Models', OpenReview wRRKQvbDiO, ACL ARR 2026 May, cdate 2026-05-25) already prices adaptive-length infilling -- 5 DLMs, 8 infilling benchmarks, forward-pass reduction, 1.82x faster than the strongest baseline, <10% over fixed-length -- and its abstract explicitly diagnoses that prior methods 'introduce substantial additional forward passes and computational cost'. It is concurrent by 18 days so it does NOT preempt, but it kills the 'infilling efficiency has never been priced' title and forces the reframing to (a) the oracle-cost reference arm and (b) the batch-size inversion. WHAT I COULD NOT VERIFY: PILL's body -- all three OpenReview PDF endpoints (openreview.net/pdf/<hash>.pdf, /pdf?id=, api2 /attachment) returned HTML or JSON through the hy-proxy, so my statements that PILL lacks an oracle-length arm, lacks multi-unit reporting, and is batch-1 are INFERENCES FROM ITS ABSTRACT ONLY and are the single weakest evidential link in this report; they must be checked before the differentiation is committed to paper. I also could not read DreamOn's ICLR reviews: api2.openreview.net returned HTTP 403 ChallengeRequiredError on all /notes?forum= and /notes?id= calls, and the forum HTML was a JS shell, so I CANNOT say whether a reviewer already raised the cost-accounting gap during review (four Official_Review note IDs exist -- jUWCBhjtxw, iCev1lieXF, AUeoMbELWf, h6Z1ZdUzJs -- plus a General Response and a 'Response to Reviewer SUPh'; a Rebuttal_Revision and Camera_Ready_Revision both exist, so the camera-ready may contain accounting added in rebuttal that the arXiv v1 I read does NOT, since arXiv has only v1). This is a material unchecked risk: if a reviewer demanded cost numbers and the camera-ready added them, the follow-up shrinks further. Verify by opening the forum in a browser. Venue statuses I DID verify via OpenReview per the 2026 rule: DreamOn = ICLR 2026 Poster (venueid ICLR.cc/2026/Conference, Camera_Ready_Revision present); CAL = ICLR 2026 DeLTa WORKSHOP Poster only, NOT main conference (the candidate does not state a venue for it, but anyone assuming main-conference would be wrong); FlexMDM = ICLR 2026 Poster; dLLM-Var and rho-EOS = CoRR records only (preprints); LR-DLLM, CaRE, 2510.18480, 2603.06123, 2605.04215 = no OpenReview record found, treated as preprints. Note 2605.04215 first-public 2026-05-05 is 2 days BEFORE the cutoff, so contra the candidate's grouping it is NOT concurrent. Semantic Scholar was useless for this topic (returned unrelated papers) and I relied on arXiv API + abs-page metadata + OpenReview API. On GPU-hour feasibility I did no independent estimate; 110 h is unaudited. FINALLY, per the brief's coordination warning: I did NOT contact the agents reportedly running DreamOn/FIM on .73 and the AR baseline on .104, and I could not verify what they are measuring. scripts/generate_evalplus_ar.py already implements a sophisticated three-axis cost accounting (forward_passes, tokens_fed, attended_context_sum, with a forward_pre_hook and analytic cross-check) for from-scratch generation, so the cost-accounting machinery this candidate needs LARGELY EXISTS -- which cuts both ways: cheap to execute, but the .73 agent may already be producing overlapping numbers. Coordinate before starting, as the candidate itself instructs.

blocking_gaps: DUPLICATION, near-fatal: another agent has ALREADY built and RUN this experiment. On zwfy6 at /apdcephfs_zwfy6/share_304376610/pighzliu_code/dllm_draft_104/ there is scripts/generate_infilling.py (392 lines, with the ForwardCostTracker three-axis hook), scripts/score_infilling.py (197 lines), scripts/_run_infilling_5arm_8gpu.sh, and COMPLETED single-line results at full n=1033 for SIX arms in outputs/infilling_single_line/{dreamon_fim,dreamon_oracle,dream_fim,dream_prefix,qwen_fim,qwen_prefix}/score.json. Their ARMS list even includes 'dreamon_oracle' -- the arm the positioning calls 'the arm no paper reports'. The kill criterion ('killed if the other agents' runs already cover the cost accounting -- check before starting') is TRIGGERED for the single-line split. This must become a handoff/extension, not a new build.

PREMISE REFUTED BY DATA ALREADY ON DISK: the claim that oracle is 'structurally the cheapest arm' and that DreamOn matches oracle quality at Nx oracle cost is FALSE as measured. dreamon_oracle costs MORE than dreamon_fim on every unit (20.7 vs 16.5 forward passes/task; 5827 vs 4923 tokens fed/task; 18.4 vs 15.3 GPU-min total). Reason: their oracle arm seeds initial_masks=true span but leaves expand/delete ENABLED, so it is not a cheap fixed canvas. feas.risk: Most likely outcome is a confounded null that reduces to replicating arXiv:2510.18480 on a new task surface. Three concrete mechanisms, in order of likelihood. (1) NO INVERSION, AR JUST WINS: the batch leg only inverts if batched fixed-canvas diffusion beats batched AR, but AR batches too, and the existing single-line numbers already have AR qwen_fim beating every diffusion arm on quality (.7638) AND on tokens fed (239 vs 4923-5827) AND on wall clock (3.6 vs 15.3-18.4 GPU-min) at batch 1 -- the regime supposedly most favourable to diffusion. If diffusion loses at its best batch size, adding batching widens the gap rather than flipping it, and the "structural finding" evaporates into "AR dominates, as 2510.18480 already said". (2) THE ORACLE-RATIO HEADLINE IS ALREADY DEAD: the number the paper was going to sell -- DreamOn-cost / oracle-cost -- is measured at 0.80, i.e. BELOW 1. Learned expansion is CHEAPER than the on-disk oracle arm, the opposite of the predicted direction, which kills "matches oracle quality at Nx oracle cost" as a headline and triggers the candidate's own second kill clause. (3) SAMPLER CONFOUND POISONS ANY MIXED TABLE: the completed arms ran greedy (T=0.0) while the paper recipe is T=0.2/top_p=0.9, and this project has measured a +14.6-point HumanEval swing from a smaller sampler change than that -- so any frontier that reuses the existing greedy numbers alongside new paper-faithful runs will attribute a sampler effect to a length-acquisition mechanism. Secondary risk: 86% of the GPU budget sits in MultiLine, so a null discovered only after the full scale-out wastes ~55 GPU-h that a single-line-first ordering would have saved.
feas.required_control: A per-arm ARM-IDENTITY + COST-COVERAGE assertion block, emitted into every score.json and failing the run loudly, with three clauses -- one per prior retraction. (a) Grader-inflation clause (retraction #1, "a verifier that compared nothing"): on every scoring invocation, assert the canonical middle PASSES and a stub/empty middle FAILS, with the exec actually enabled. This is non-optional because the upstream grader ships with exec() commented out and therefore passes empty solutions -- the identical failure -- and vendor/DreamOn/eval/eval_humaneval_infilling.sh calls it. Their score_infilling.py --self-test-n already implements this and reported 10/10 canonical-pass, 10/10 stub-fail; keep it and never bypass it. (b) Arm-identity clause (retraction #2, "a pipeline stage that silently discarded its input"): assert each arm actually ran the mechanism its name claims, by counting mechanism events, not by trusting the config -- the oracle arm must record ZERO expand and ZERO delete operations and a constant canvas width, and the charged-sweep arm must record exactly the 5 attempted lengths. This is precisely the trap the existing dreamon_oracle arm fell into: it is named "oracle" but leaves expand/delete enabled, so it silently measures something else, which is why it came out more expensive than the non-oracle arm. Without this clause the paper's central reference point is not the thing it is labelled. (c) Cost-coverage clause (retraction #3, "a cost average that dropped the expensive tasks"): assert n_cost_rows == n_elapsed_rows == n_rows_in_split for every arm before any mean is computed, and report cap-hit and error tasks INSIDE the cost mean, never excluded. Every cost number must come from the measured forward_pre_hook, never from the nominal --steps config: I found one single-line task (SingleLineInfilling/HumanEval/124/L3) with 732 measured forward passes against a nominal 512, at 53.4 s versus a 0.89 s arm mean, so the most expensive tail items are exactly the ones a nominal-steps or drop-on-failure accounting would erase, understating the arm by the same mechanism that understated scaffold Large by 2.85x.

lens.title: Does structure-aware masking actually help? A marginal-matched falsification of AST-guided corruption for code diffusion at 7B
lens.claim: The reported benefit of AST-aware masking for diffusion code LMs is explained by the mask-rate marginal it induces, not by structural alignment of masked positions: an AST-node-selective corruption schedule does not beat uniform masking at 7B once a control that matches its per-position mask-rate marginal but randomizes WHICH positions are masked is included.
lens.why_now: TreeDiff (arXiv:2508.01473, 2025-08-02, pre-cutoff) claims +13.3% relative over random masking from AST-node masking; AnCoder/AnchorTree (2602.17688, 2026-02-05, pre-cutoff) claims AST anchoring is a parameter-efficient path to quality code. We measured the OPPOSITE SIGN at 7B: a depth-banded structural schedule got HE+ 3.66% / MBPP+ 11.38% against a matched plain-SFT control at 21.95% / 24.34% -- a 6x degradation from a schedule change alone. Neither TreeDiff nor AnCoder runs a mask-rate-marginal-matched control, so neither can separate 'structure helps' from 'the induced noise distribution helps'. We already own both endpoint arms of the ladder, so the marginal is the only missing variable. CaRE (2607.24763, concurrent) independently shows compute-matched comparison reverses published MDLM rankings -- same disease, different axis.
lens.experiment: Four arms, all from models/Dream-Coder-v0-Base-7B, identical trainer (scaffold_coder/training/scaffold_sft_trainer.py), identical data (data/scaffold_edu_v0/train_data.parquet, 114,363 rows), identical epochs/LR/global-batch=128, max_length=1024. (A) plain uniform masking -- ALREADY MEASURED, HE+ .2195 / MBPP+ .2434. (B) depth-banded schedule_only -- ALREADY MEASURED, .0366 / .1138. (C) NEW TreeDiff-style: mask tokens belonging to selected AST nodes, using the per-row ir_json (node_id/depth/kind, verified present for all rows) to select keyword+identifier-bearing statement nodes. (D) NEW marginal-matched control: for each sample, draw the SAME number of masked positions with the SAME per-depth mask-rate marginal that arm C produced (measure C's marginal empirically over one epoch first), but choose positions uniformly at random within that marginal. Grade all four with evalplus.evaluate on HumanEval+ (n=164) and MBPP+ (n=378) at NFE 512, plus NFE 128 as a low-budget point, reporting cumulative_model_tokens not just NFE. Decision statistic: (C - A) vs (D - A).
lens.assets_needed: HAVE: ir_json AST per row (verified: node_id, depth, kind, text for all 114,363 rows); Dream-Coder-v0-Base-7B; working FSDP trainer with 5 corruption modes; ScheduleOnlySFTDataset as a template for a new dataset class; arms A and B already trained and graded. MISSING/TO BUILD: two new dataset modes in scaffold_coder/sft_dataset.py (AST-node-selective + marginal-matched, ~150 lines each modeled on ScheduleOnlySFTDataset); an empirical marginal-measurement pass over one epoch of arm C. FIDELITY CAVEAT TO FLAG IN THE PAPER: TreeDiff gives no code and no exact node-priority list, so arm C is a reimplementation from the paper's description (key AST nodes: keywords, identifiers) -- must be stated as such, not as an exact reproduction.
lens.kill_criterion: Falsified if arm C beats arm A by >3 points HE+ AND arm D does NOT (i.e. C > A + 3 and D <= A + 1.5 on both benchmarks). That would establish structural position selection as the causal factor and kill the claim. Also falsified if C and D are both >3 points above A, since then the marginal is genuinely helpful and the framing must become 'schedules help via their marginal', a weaker but still reportable result.
lens.builds_on: TreeDiff (arXiv:2508.01473, 2025-08-02) and AnCoder/AnchorTree (arXiv:2602.17688, 2026-02-05). Defect we repair: both compare structure-aware masking only against uniform random masking, so the comparison confounds WHICH positions are masked with HOW MANY are masked and at what per-depth rate. Our depth-banded arm already shows the confound can flip the sign of the conclusion at 7B. We add the marginal-matched control neither paper has.

diff.sharpened_claim: For masked-diffusion code LMs at 7B, the quality effect of AST-aware corruption is carried by the *per-token-type and per-depth mask marginal* it induces -- not by structural alignment of the masked positions -- and once that marginal is matched by a position-randomised control, AST selection contributes no detectable gain in executable correctness. Two premise corrections make this defensible. (1) TreeDiff already matches the GLOBAL mask rate: Algorithm 1 sets N = floor(eps_t * L) and random-fills N - c positions whenever AST candidates are insufficient, explicitly "so that the diffusion noise schedule is strictly adhered to." So the unmatched quantity is not "how many" but "how the N masks are distributed over AST-membership, node tier, and depth" -- the weighted-sampling step over I_ast with tier weights p_skel/p_data/p_cond/p_ctrl. Our arm D must match that conditional marginal, not the scalar rate. (2) AnCoder already contains the analogous control and it already points our way: its own Null-anchoring arm (structure-agnostic, same two-stage anchor-denoiser architecture) captures 70% of the HumanEval pass@1 gain over MDLM-809M (+1.51 of +2.16) and 83% on MBPP (+2.30 of +2.76), leaving AST-specific AnchorTree with only +0.65 / +0.46 points -- unresolvable at n=164. So the sharpened contribution is a marginal-decomposition audit of structure-aware corruption in code diffusion: arms A (uniform), C (TreeDiff-style tier-weighted AST selection), D (AST-marginal-matched but position-randomised), all at 7B with target text held byte-identical, multi-seed with bootstrap CIs and McNemar paired tests, and cost reported as cumulative_model_tokens rather than T -- since TreeDiff's T doubles as the maximum generation length and therefore conflates compute with canvas size, exactly the accounting error we already retracted internally.
diff.differentiation_statement: No pre-cutoff paper isolates the mask-marginal from structural position-selection in a generative masked-diffusion code LM. The closest methodological precedent, Wettig et al. (EACL 2023), establishes that "uniform masking requires a higher masking rate compared to sophisticated masking strategies such as span or PMI masking" -- i.e. that rate and strategy interact -- but does so for encoder-only MLMs evaluated on GLUE/SQuAD representation quality, varying a scalar rate rather than constructing a position-randomised control matched to a structured selector's conditional marginal, and never touching code or executable correctness. Bitton et al. (2212.05195) reach a same-shaped conclusion ("increasing the masking rate reduces the performance gap among masking strategies, rendering uniform competitive") in vision-language pretraining, again non-generative and non-code. On the code-diffusion side, TreeDiff matches only the global rate and never randomises within its induced tier/depth marginal, so its 13.3% relative headline cannot separate the two; AnCoder is not a corruption-schedule paper at all (its forward noising is standard independent per-position masking; its intervention is denoising *order* via a two-network anchor-denoiser), it runs at 809M where absolute pass@1 is 3-9% and therefore near the floor, and it grants its treatment arm a remask rate of 0.1 while its MDLM baselines get 0.0 -- an uncontrolled decoding-time advantage. Ours is the first marginal-matched falsification at 7B on a production-grade code diffusion backbone (Dream-Coder-v0-Base-7B), graded with evalplus untrusted_check on HumanEval+/MBPP+, with cost in cumulative model tokens. Even granting maximal credit to the precedents, the differences in model family, scale (7B vs 809M / BERT-large), objective class (generative masked diffusion vs encoder MLM), endpoint (executable correctness vs GLUE/MAUVE/syntactic validity), control construction (conditional-marginal-matched randomisation vs scalar-rate sweep), and cost accounting are each independently sufficient; together they are comfortably a standalone contribution. CaRE (2026-06-04) is concurrent, audits inference-time remasking rather than training corruption, and is a methodological ally rather than a competitor.

related_work.citation: Zeng, Cao, Li, Chen, Ren, Li, Xiang, Wu, Gao, Yu. "TreeDiff: AST-Guided Code Generation with Diffusion LLMs." arXiv:2508.01473 (v1 2025-08-02; v3 2026-01-06).
related_work.venue_status: Preprint only. Verified: arXiv abs page shows no Comments and no Journal reference across v1/v2/v3; OpenReview search returns only a DBLP mirror record with venueid dblp.org/journals/CORR/2025 and venue "CoRR 2025" (i.e. arXiv), with no conference venueid and no Camera_Ready_Revision invitation. No ACL/ICLR/NeurIPS proceedings entry found.
related_work.what_it_covers: The direct target. Injects AST structural priors into the diffusion CORRUPTION process for code: Algorithm 1 "Dynamic Tier-Aware AST Masking" assigns per-token weights by node tier (Skeleton=imports/consts, DataFlow=assigns/calls, CondLogic=if/else, ControlFlow=loops/returns, plus a low default), weighted-samples N = floor(eps_t * L) mask indices from AST-aligned positions, then random-fills any shortfall. Fine-tunes LLaDA-8B on 150K OpenCodeReasoning samples; reports HumanEval/HE+/MBPP/MBPP+ pass@1 at T in {256, 512} against a LLaDA + Random Masking baseline. Headline: HE+ 32.3 -> 36.6 at T=512 = 13.3% relative. Includes one masking-granularity ablation (Random / AST-Span / TreeDiff).
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Whether the gain survives a control that reproduces TreeDiff's induced per-tier/per-depth/AST-membership marginal while randomising which positions are masked. Also open: any model family other than LLaDA-8B, any dataset other than OpenCodeReasoning, any scale other than 8B, any seed replication, and cost accounting that separates denoising compute from canvas length.
related_work.known_defects: (a) The global mask rate IS matched (N = floor(eps_t*L) with random fallback fill), so the paper's own framing of the baseline gap as "random vs structural" is narrower than it appears -- but the *conditional* marginal over node tiers and AST membership is never matched or even reported, which is the actual confound and the actual opening. (b) Headline 13.3% relative = +4.3 absolute on n=164 HumanEval+, about 7 problems, single seed, no confidence intervals, no significance test; binomial SE at p~0.35, n=164 is ~3.7pp, so the effect is not separated from sampling noise. (c) Internal inconsistency: TreeDiff's MBPP+ T=256 cell is 44.2 in Table 1 but 44.9 in Table 2, for what should be the same run. (d) The gain is cell-selective -- at T=512 HumanEval+ TreeDiff and AST-Span are tied at 36.6, so the ablation does not actually separate TreeDiff from span masking at the headline budget. (e) T "also denote[s] the maximum generation length," so the single reported axis conflates compute with canvas size; no token-level cost is reported. (f) The baseline LLaDA-Instruct gets WORSE from T=256 to T=512 on every column (HE+ 34.8 -> 31.7), which is unexplained and suggests a decoding-protocol artefact rather than a clean compute axis. (g) LR 5e-5 is described as "selected as the optimal learning rate" with no statement that the sweep was run per-arm -- if tuned on the treatment only, the baseline is handicapped. (h) pass@1 is defined as top-1 "selected by model log-likelihood" at n=1, a nonstandard estimator that is not the EvalPlus convention, yet AR baselines are imported directly from the EvalPlus leaderboard -- a metric mismatch across rows of the same table. (i) No code released and the tier weights p_skel/p_data/p_cond/p_ctrl are relegated to Appendix A.2, so arm C is necessarily a reimplementation.
