related_work.citation: Kim et al. (Dream/DreamOn team), "DreamOn: Diffusion Language Models For Code Infilling Beyond Fixed-size Canvas", arXiv:2602.01326 — ICLR 2026 Poster
related_work.venue_status: Published, ICLR 2026 Poster. Verified via OpenReview: notes/search returns venue='ICLR 2026 Poster', venueid='ICLR.cc/2026/Conference'. Semantic Scholar still reports venue='arXiv.org' (28 cites) — another S2 lag on a 2026 venue.
related_work.what_it_covers: The variable-length / mask-expansion diffusion model we have on disk. Relevant here because it is the same model family and the same benchmark surface, and because our own .73 measurement (HumanEval-SingleLineInfilling n=1033) puts DreamOn at .702 (post-bugfix) against a matched Qwen2.5-Coder-7B native-FIM AR at .7638 using 8.5x fewer tokens-fed.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: No compute/token accounting in the paper; no matched-cost AR comparison; multi-span, non-Python, and RandomSpanInfilling untested (recorded in our own TASK_SURFACE_LIT_GAPS.md).
related_work.known_defects: Its published comparisons against Qwen2.5-Coder-7B/DeepSeek-Coder are quality-only, with no token or step cost, so the efficiency reading the field takes from it is unsupported. Separately, our own audit found that in the released code `mask_expansion=True` and `delete_eos_token=True` are silently swallowed by **kwargs and are not real parameters — a reproducibility defect in the artifact, independent of the paper's claims.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list; OpenReview api2 notes/search -> 'ICLR 2026 Poster', ICLR.cc/2026/Conference; Semantic Scholar graph batch (stale). The kwargs defect and the .702/.7638 numbers are from our own repo: /apdcephfs_wzc1/share_304376610/pighzliu_code/dllm_draft/DLLM_RESULTS_20260807.md (Retraction 5), commit eedd0075 in the zwfy6 checkout.

diff.differentiation_statement: Three axes separate this from everything I found, but only if the claim is rebuilt (see below), because the premise it cites has already been falsified in our own repo. (1) TEACHER TYPE. Every order-learning paper derives its order from a signal internal to the denoiser — Gt-Margin from ground-truth-token logit margins (2602.09501), SAS from the model's own pathwise log-likelihood (2606.23567), TraceLock from the model's own completed trace (2605.24697), Adaptive Order Policies from denoiser correctness (2606.00295) — and the one paper using an external teacher, TRIMS (2604.00666), uses an AR LM emitting a scalar per-token difficulty. Nobody distills orders from an EXECUTABLE SYMBOLIC DECODER that emits multi-token commit sets with typed holes, rule fixed-points and backtracking. The structural-prior code papers are the other half of the gap: TreeDiff (SURGeLLM 2026) and AnCoder (2602.17688) use AST NODE IDENTITY as a masking/priority prior over stochastic corruption — static tree labels, no generated trajectory, no fixed order at all. Our teacher is a running program, and its output is a sequence of commit SETS, not a ranking. (2) THE COMPILATION QUESTION. Every one of these systems keeps its ordering apparatus at inference: PAPL (ICLR 2026 Oral) aligns training to a planner that is still used at sampling time; Adaptive Order Policies has a joint-training mode but never evaluates the denoiser with the policy removed; Where-to-Unmask ships a planner module. Nobody asks whether the mechanism can be DELETED and the model priced like vanilla. (3) COST UNIT AND CONTROL. Where-to-Unmask fixes exactly L one-token steps so all orders are compute-identical by construction; TreeDiff prices in denoising steps T and conflates T with canvas length; TRIMS prices in TPS (tokens predicted per step), which is not compute. We price in measured cumulative_model_tokens with a verified forward_pre_hook, and we run a random-permutation control matched on BOTH step count and the per-step commit-count histogram — a control no paper I found runs (TRIMS randomises bucket assignment, which is not histogram-matched to a specific external trajectory). Honest caveats a reviewer will raise, which we should pre-empt rather than hide: 'Train for the Worst, Plan for the Best' (ICML 2025, 200 cites) already argues conceptually that inference-time order is where the leverage is and training cannot cheaply absorb it, so our contribution is the empirical test with the matched control, not the conceptual insight; and PAPL's theorem says plain masked-CE on a non-uniform path is a mis-specified objective, so arm A trained with vanilla SFT risks measuring 'wrong loss' rather than 'orders do not transfer' — we must add a P-ELBO arm or scope the claim to plain-SFT transferability.

followup_openings.target_paper: SELF (blocking, must be read first): our own /apdcephfs_wzc1/share_304376610/pighzliu_code/dllm_draft/DLLM_RESULTS_20260807.md, Retractions 4 and 5, commit 1170ae6
followup_openings.defect: The candidate's why_now rests on 'structural runtime and flat diffusion own disjoint segments of the quality-compute frontier with NO crossover' and on scaffold Medium 'holding the frontier' at 13.98k/7.08k tokens. That finding was RETRACTED on 2026-08-07, hours before this candidate was written. Retraction 4: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B base (verified architecture-identical to Dream-Coder-v0-Base-7B: hidden 3584 / 28 layers / 28 heads / 4 KV heads / intermediate 18944 / vocab 152064 / rope_theta 1e6, differing only by mask_token_id 151666) scores HE+ .524 and MBPP+ .648 at 204 / 101 mean tokens_fed. That is ~70x cheaper than scaffold Medium AND +.341 / +.294 higher quality — strict Pareto dominance on tokens_fed, and still ~+0.30 quality on attended_context_sum. Retraction 5: the same AR model with native FIM sentinels scores .7638 on HumanEval-SingleLineInfilling vs DreamOn .702, at 8.5x fewer tokens. So scaffold Medium does not hold any frontier, and the segmentation the candidate proposes to 'upgrade' does not exist. Running Phase 1-3 as written would spend 50 GPU-hours to explain the source of a non-existent advantage.
followup_openings.our_fix: Do NOT run the experiment to upgrade the segmentation claim. Re-aim the same machinery at a claim that survives Retraction 4. The trajectory dumper, the flat-canvas converter, arm A, and the histogram-matched arm B are all still exactly the right apparatus — only the headline changes. Sharpened target: 'Is a structure-derived generation order learnable at all by a flat-canvas diffusion student, and does teaching it buy anything over a step-and-histogram-matched random order?' Both outcomes remain publishable, and neither depends on scaffold beating AR. Add a third arm trained with PAPL's P-ELBO so a null result cannot be dismissed as a mis-specified objective, and report every arm against BOTH the matched AR point (.524 / .648 at 204/101 tokens_fed) and the vanilla NFE curve so the frontier is honest from the first figure.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This is the single highest-value finding of this review. It converts a 50-GPU-hour experiment whose headline is already dead into the same experiment with a live headline, and it prevents a fifth retraction of exactly the class the project has already suffered four times (a claim built on a missing baseline).

followup_openings.target_paper: TreeDiff (arXiv:2508.01473, SURGeLLM 2026 workshop)
followup_openings.defect: Two separable defects. (a) Cost is reported only as denoising steps T, and T doubles as the max generation length, so the T=256 vs T=512 columns confound compute with canvas size; the claim 'structural priors accelerate convergence' is about steps, not tokens. (b) The structural control is uniform random masking, not a mask-budget-matched-but-structure-shuffled control: TreeDiff explicitly allocates a budget N with per-token weights W[i], so the ablation that isolates 'AST node identity' from 'any non-uniform weighting with the same per-step budget' is missing. Its AR comparison is also leaderboard-copied (CodeLlama/CodeQwen/DeepSeek-Coder), not lineage- or cost-matched.
followup_openings.our_fix: We already have the three things TreeDiff lacks: a measured token-cost instrument (forward_pre_hook, verified against closed-form on 1084 task-runs), a matched-lineage AR control (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, architecture-identical to Dream-Coder-Base), and the histogram-matched shuffle control from arm B. Re-run the TreeDiff claim on Dream-Coder rather than LLaDA, replacing steps with cumulative_model_tokens and replacing uniform-random with budget-and-histogram-matched structure-shuffled masking. Predicted publishable outcomes either way: if the AST gain survives the matched control on a token axis, TreeDiff's result is strengthened and generalised to a second backbone; if it does not, we have shown that a workshop result attributing gains to AST structure was attributing them to non-uniform mask scheduling.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This is the cleanest single-paper repair available, it reuses infrastructure we have already built and debugged, it needs no new training beyond two SFT arms, and it lands on the exact axis (token cost vs steps) where our project already has a defensible methodological contribution.

followup_openings.target_paper: TRIMS (arXiv:2604.00666, preprint under review)
followup_openings.defect: The headline axis is TPS = tokens predicted per step, which is not a compute unit: a diffusion step attending a 512-token canvas is not comparable to an AR step. We have measured this concretely — flat-canvas cost is 685 tok/step on HE+ and 604 on MBPP+, versus 204 / 101 TOTAL tokens_fed for matched AR. TRIMS therefore reports a parallelism ratio as if it were efficiency. Compounding this, TRIMS uses an AR teacher for supervision yet never reports that AR teacher as a quality/cost Pareto point, so the reader cannot see that the teacher may dominate the student. Its random control randomises bucket assignment, not the per-step commit-count histogram of a specific external trajectory.
followup_openings.our_fix: Reprice TRIMS-style trajectory supervision in measured cumulative tokens on Dream-Coder, and plot the AR teacher itself on the same axes. Then strengthen the control from 'random bucket assignment' to 'random permutation with identical step count AND identical tokens-committed-per-step histogram', which is the control our arm B already specifies. This yields a general methodological claim — 'TPS is not a cost unit for cross-family comparison; trajectory-supervision gains shrink or invert when repriced' — that is independent of whether our own structural student works.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It generalises beyond one paper: TPS/NFE-as-cost is endemic in the dLLM acceleration literature, and we have already independently established the 685-vs-181 tok/step and 70x/1719x tokens_fed gaps needed to make the argument quantitatively. This is the audit contribution our own results file already flags as our most defensible direction.

followup_openings.target_paper: Where-to-Unmask / Gt-Margin (arXiv:2602.09501, preprint)
followup_openings.defect: Its controlled protocol performs exactly L unmasking steps, one token per step, for every ordering strategy. This makes all orders compute-identical BY CONSTRUCTION, so the paper structurally cannot say anything about quality-per-token — and it also excludes multi-token commit sets entirely, which is precisely what any real structural or parallel decoder emits. Separately, the oracle requires ground-truth tokens, and the paper never quantifies how much of the Gt-Margin gain (e.g. GSM8K 0.605 -> 0.845) survives imitation by the deployable planner.
followup_openings.our_fix: Extend the Gt-Margin framework from one-token-per-step to multi-token commit SETS, and re-measure on the token-cost axis rather than the fixed-L axis. Our runtime already emits multi-token commit sets natively (decoder_runtime.commit_many), so we can construct the k-token-per-step generalisation of Gt-Margin and compare: oracle-margin commit sets, structural commit sets, and histogram-matched random commit sets, all at equal measured tokens. Also report the oracle-to-imitation retention ratio that 2602.09501 omits.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It turns a real limitation of the closest order-learning paper into a positive result on a strictly more general decoding regime, and it makes our runtime an asset (it is the only multi-token commit-set generator we have) rather than a liability under Retraction 4.

followup_openings.target_paper: PAPL (arXiv:2509.23405, ICLR 2026 Oral) and Adaptive Order Policies (arXiv:2606.00295, ICLR 2026 Workshop, concurrent)
followup_openings.defect: Both are the closest thing to 'training absorbs the order', and both stop one ablation short. PAPL aligns training to a planner that REMAINS at inference, so it cannot distinguish 'training absorbed the path' from 'training became compatible with a path it still needs'. Adaptive Order Policies has a joint policy+denoiser training mode — the one configuration where absorption could show — but evaluates it with the policy still attached; the decisive ablation (joint-trained denoiser evaluated alone under plain confidence sampling) is absent from both.
followup_openings.our_fix: Run exactly that missing ablation as the core of our study, with the mechanism REMOVED at eval and the student priced like vanilla. Concretely: train the student on external commit trajectories, then evaluate with no planner, no meta-tokens, no typed holes; report quality at matched cumulative tokens against (i) the runtime teacher, (ii) the histogram-matched random-order student, (iii) plain-SFT, and (iv) matched AR. Adopt P-ELBO for one arm so that a null result is attributable to non-transferability rather than to the objective mis-specification PAPL proved. Framed as 'can an ordering mechanism be compiled away?', this is a question an ICLR Oral raised and did not answer.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It converts our study from 'another order-learning paper' into the mechanism-removal ablation that two order-learning papers (one an ICLR Oral) both omitted, and the P-ELBO arm closes the one methodological hole that would otherwise let a reviewer dismiss a negative result.

followup_openings.target_paper: Neither Parallel Nor Sequential / DiffusionGemma (arXiv:2606.14620, concurrent) — a design threat, not a target
followup_openings.defect: It reports that shipped dLLMs commit in large simultaneous batches leaving within-batch order GENUINELY UNDEFINED, and that structured output (JSON) is committed in essentially arbitrary order. This is a direct threat to our Phase-2 conversion, which assumes 'the set of tokens committed at runtime step k' is a well-defined and learnable supervision target. If within-step order is undefined and models do not spontaneously adopt structural orders even on structured output, our student may be being asked to fit a target that carries less information than we assume.
followup_openings.our_fix: Add a cheap pre-registration gate before spending the 50 GPU-hours: measure order-fidelity, not just quality. Log the student's own commit trajectory at eval (the same accept-step hook DiffusionGemma used) and compute Kendall's tau between the student's realised commit order and the teacher's runtime order, for arm A, arm B, and plain-SFT. If arm A's tau is not measurably above arm B's, the students never learned the order and a quality null result is uninterpretable — that gate is a ~2 GPU-hour check that decides whether the rest of the budget is worth spending. Report tau alongside pass@1 either way.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It is the difference between 'orders do not transfer' (a real finding) and 'our supervision signal was degenerate' (a fifth retraction). It costs almost nothing and it directly answers the first question a reviewer will ask about a negative result.

diff.sharpened_claim: Reframed to survive our own Retraction 4 and to maximise follow-up value: "Can an external symbolic decoder's generation order be compiled into flat-canvas diffusion weights, and does it buy anything over a matched random order? We dump multi-token commit trajectories from an executable typed-AST decoder runtime and supervise a flat-canvas Dream-Coder student on them, then evaluate with the runtime REMOVED so the student is priced exactly like vanilla. Against two controls no prior order-learning paper runs together -- a random permutation matched on both step count and the per-step commit-count histogram, and a matched-lineage autoregressive model (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, architecture-identical to Dream-Coder-Base) placed on the same measured cumulative-token axis -- we report both quality at matched token cost and ORDER FIDELITY (Kendall's tau between the student's realised commit order and the teacher's), so that a null result distinguishes 'the order was not learned' from 'the order was learned and did not help'. A third arm trained with PAPL's P-ELBO rules out objective mis-specification. Secondary and independently publishable: repricing TreeDiff-style AST-masking and TRIMS-style trajectory supervision from denoising steps and tokens-per-step onto measured cumulative tokens, where our instrumented flat canvas costs 685 tok/step (HE+) against 204 total tokens_fed for the matched AR model." Note that the original claim's premise -- that scaffold Medium holds a low-cost segment of the frontier -- must be dropped: the matched AR baseline dominates it by ~70x in tokens_fed at +.34 quality.

feas.risk: The overwhelmingly likely outcome is a VACUOUS null that looks like a finding. Because the flat-canvas projection of the oracle trajectory is exactly document order (1000/1000) and the runtime commits one token per step (transfer_tokens=1 in every graded row), arm A's supervision order IS left-to-right AR order. So arm A vs arm B is "AR order vs random order on a flat canvas" — and arm A will very likely beat arm B, which the team would be tempted to write up as "structure-derived orders DO transfer," when the measured content is only the long-known easy fact that left-to-right beats random for code. The mirror risk is equally bad: if the conversion drops the 44.5% SPECIAL commits ([expand]/[delete]/[STMT]/[FUNC]) and arm A then fails, the team writes "orders do not transfer" when the true cause is that the supervision target was missing nearly half the teacher's decisions — i.e. Retraction 2 (a stage that silently discarded its input) recommitted at 44% instead of 100%. A third, quieter confound: cost. Both arms are flat-canvas, so they must be priced at nfe x (prompt + canvas) = 685 tok/step (HE+) / 604 (MBPP+); if anyone prices them by NFE, or reads only `process` and not `failure_process` (Retraction 3), the "matched cumulative_model_tokens" brackets around scaffold Medium's 13.98k/7.08k are wrong by 2.85-3.69x — and those brackets are themselves anchored to a retracted frontier that AR dominates ~70x.
feas.required_control:
TEACHER-SIGNAL NON-DEGENERACY GATE, run BEFORE any training, and it must be a two-sided gate — this is the control that prevents a fourth instance of "the pipeline measured something other than what the claim names."

Concretely, on the exact trajectories that will be used as labels, and reported in the paper whatever the outcome:
  (1) ORDER NON-TRIVIALITY. Kendall tau between the teacher's realised LEXICAL commit order and plain document (left-to-right) order. PRE-REGISTER the kill: if tau >= 0.95, the "structural order" is AR order, arm A is an AR-order arm, and the study is CANCELLED — not reframed. I have already measured this for the CPU oracle path: 1000/1000 exact match, tau = 1.0. It must be re-measured for the model-driven path (Step 1) because that is the only path where confidence ranking and `_defer_structural_commit` could produce a non-trivial order.
  (2) LABEL COVERAGE, reported as a number in the paper. Fraction of the teacher's commit decisions that survive conversion to flat-canvas supervision. Measured: 55.5% LEXICAL survive, 44.5% SPECIAL (meta-token) are dropped. Any claim of form "training on the runtime's orders" is false unless that 44.5% is either represented or the claim is explicitly narrowed to "the lexical projection of the runtime's orders, discarding 44% of its decisions."
  (3) ADOPTION FIDELITY at eval, with the mechanism removed. Log the STUDENT's own commit trajectory (the `prediction_provider` hook at `model_sampler.py:233` already supports this) and report tau(student, teacher) for arm A, arm B, and plain-SFT. A quality null is uninterpretable unless arm A's tau is measurably above arm B's — that separates "the order was not learned" from "the order was learned and did not help."

Why this is the analogue of the three prior retractions: Retraction 1 shipped a verifier that compared nothing — gate (1) forces the comparison to have a non-degenerate reference (document order) instead of assuming the teacher order is special. Retraction 2 shipped a stage that silently discarded its input — gate (2) makes the discarded fraction a reported number rather than an invisible 44%. Retraction 3 averaged away the expensive tasks — gate (3), plus mandatory `proc()`-accessor costing over ALL tasks including `failure_process`, keeps the cost axis honest. Gates (1) and (2) together cost ~1 GPU-h and, on the evidence I already gathered, will terminate this candidate before it consumes 50.

lens.title: Why depth-banded corruption destroys code diffusion: a three-factor decomposition of a 6x training regression
lens.claim: The 6x quality regression from our depth-banded structural schedule is attributable to the mask-rate marginal and the loss weighting it induces rather than to structural position selection, and swapping either factor back to the uniform setting recovers most of the gap to matched plain SFT.
lens.why_now: We hold an unusually large, clean, single-variable negative result -- schedule-only HE+ 3.66% / MBPP+ 11.38% against matched plain SFT 21.95% / 24.34%, same base checkpoint, same split, same trainer, same 5 epochs, only the corruption schedule differing -- and we have not diagnosed it. Nobody has published a mechanism for WHEN structure-aware noising hurts; the literature (TreeDiff, AnCoder) only reports when it helps. We also already measured the confound: schedule-only produces 61.4 supervised masks per sample against plain's 42.1, and normalized loss mass p99 of 14.07 against a maximum_weight cap of 20.0, so the two arms differ in at least three separable ways at once. Decomposing this both explains our own result and de-risks candidate training-1 by telling us in advance which factor to hold fixed. This is the cheapest high-information experiment in the set and needs no new asset.
lens.experiment: Three single-factor arms, each identical to the schedule_only configuration except one factor reverted to the plain setting, all from Dream-Coder-v0-Base-7B on data/scaffold_edu_v0 at matched epochs/LR/batch. (i) POSITIONS: keep the depth-banded mask-rate marginal and band weighting, but choose masked positions uniformly at random. (ii) MARGINAL: keep depth-banded position selection and band weighting, but rescale so the per-sample masked-count distribution matches plain's measured mean of 42.1. (iii) WEIGHTING: keep depth-banded positions and marginal, but switch loss weighting from the band derivative/u form to plain's min(maximum_weight, 1/t) -- corruption.py already exposes weighting in {unit, mdlm, dreamon_linear} plus maximum_weight, so this arm is a config change with no new code. Grade all three on HumanEval+ and MBPP+ at NFE 512 plus NFE 128, and report the recovered fraction of the 18.3-point HE+ gap (3.66 -> 21.95) attributable to each factor, with the two endpoint arms we already own anchoring the decomposition. Also report parseable-rate and syntax-error rate per arm, since our sweeps show the low-NFE regime is governed by structural legality (syntax errors fall 94%->1.8% over the NFE range).
lens.assets_needed: HAVE EVERYTHING: both endpoint arms already trained and graded on both benchmarks; corruption.py with HierarchicalBandConfig, the weighting switch (verified: unit/mdlm/dreamon_linear) and maximum_weight; ScheduleOnlySFTDataset and PlainMaskedSFTDataset side by side in sft_dataset.py; per-arm mask-count statistics already computed (schedule-only 61.4 vs plain 42.1 vs meta-token 16.3). MISSING: only two small dataset-mode flags for arms (i) and (ii); arm (iii) is pure config. This is the lowest-risk candidate to execute first.
lens.kill_criterion: The additive decomposition is falsified if no single-factor swap recovers more than 4 of the 18.3 HE+ points (all three arms stay below 8% HE+), which would mean the regression is irreducibly interactive and the factor story is wrong. The specific claim is falsified if the POSITIONS swap (i) recovers the most -- that would make structural position selection the dominant cause, contradicting the claim and, notably, also contradicting TreeDiff's positive result in the opposite direction.
lens.builds_on: Our own schedule-only arm (SCHEDULE_ONLY_STATS.md) versus our own matched Plain-SFT control. Also positions against TreeDiff (2508.01473) and AnCoder (2602.17688): if factor (ii) or (iii) dominates, our negative result and their positive results are RECONCILED rather than contradictory, which is a more useful contribution than a bare disagreement and is the outcome I would bet on.

related_work.citation: Yiming Zeng, Jinghan Cao, Zexin Li, Yiming Chen, Tao Ren, Zhuochun Li, Dawei Xiang, Xidong Wu, Shangqian Gao, Tingting Yu. "TreeDiff: AST-Guided Code Generation with Diffusion LLMs." arXiv:2508.01473 (v1 2025-08-02, v3 2026-01-06).
related_work.venue_status: Preprint. Verified via arXiv API (v1 2025-08-02, v2 2025-08-07, v3 2026-01-06; no journal_ref, no arxiv:comment) and OpenReview api2 term search, which returns only the DBLP-mirrored record venueid=dblp.org/journals/CORR/2025, venue='CoRR 2025'. No conference venueid or camera-ready found on OpenReview.
related_work.what_it_covers: The single closest positive-result paper. AST-guided (not random) selection of masked positions during MDM corruption, on LLaDA-8B-Instruct + LoRA, 150K OpenCodeReasoning samples, 3 epochs, LR 5e-5, 8xA100. Region-specific: random masking in the reasoning region, AST-node-level masking in the code region. Reports +13.3% relative on HE+ vs a LLaDA+Random-Masking control that shares data and hyperparameters. Ablates masking GRANULARITY (token-level AST vs span-level AST vs random). Crucially, TreeDiff explicitly holds the mask BUDGET fixed: 'Following the corruption rate eps_t we first set a mask budget of N = floor(eps_t * L) tokens', with a fallback that randomly samples the remaining N-c tokens 'to guarantee that the diffusion noise schedule is strictly adhered to'.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Because TreeDiff pins N = floor(eps_t*L) by construction, it only ever varies our factor (i) POSITIONS, never our factors (ii) MARGINAL or (iii) WEIGHTING. It therefore cannot say what happens when a structural schedule also changes the per-sample masked-count distribution and the loss mass -- which is exactly the regime our schedule-only arm sits in. Its loss (Eq. 1) is a plain sum over masked positions with no 1/t or band-derivative weighting, so it has zero evidence on weighting. It never explains why its own span-level arm falls BELOW the random baseline on MBPP (39.7 vs 41.5 at T=512), which is a small structural-masking regression of the same sign as ours and is left as prose speculation about 'loss of local information'.
related_work.known_defects: (1) LoRA-only adaptation (admitted: full FT of LLaDA-8B at 4096 exceeded their 8xA100 memory), so the result is about adapter-level plasticity, not full-parameter training -- ours is full-parameter and may not replicate. (2) Non-standard forward process: base noise eps_t cosine-annealed from 0.1 to 0.001 over TRAINING STEPS, then P_mask ~ U(eps_t, 1) per sample. This couples the corruption level to training progress (a curriculum) and is never compared against standard MDLM t~U(0,1); the headline is thus confounded by a curriculum they do not ablate. (3) Zero loss-weighting ablation. (4) Single backbone, single dataset, no seeds, no CIs, no significance test; differences are 1-4 points on n=164/378. (5) T is simultaneously the denoising-step count AND the max generation length ('the denoising steps T also denote the maximum generation length'), so their test-time scaling axis conflates compute budget with canvas size. (6) AR baselines are copied from the EvalPlus leaderboard rather than re-run under their protocol. (7) The MBPP span-level regression contradicts their own thesis and is unresolved.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API metadata + full HTML text of v3 (fetched and parsed: abstract, Sec 3.4 mask-budget formula, Sec 4.1 baselines/setup, Sec 4.2 ablation table, Appendix A.1/A.2 hyperparameters); OpenReview api2 /notes/search (both ?query= and ?term=); Semantic Scholar.

related_work.citation: "AnCoder: Anchored Code Generation via Discrete Diffusion Models." arXiv:2602.17688 (v1 2026-02-05).
related_work.venue_status: Preprint. Verified via arXiv API (v1 2026-02-05) and Semantic Scholar (publicationVenue = arXiv.org, DBLP journals/corr/abs-2602-17688, citationCount 0). OpenReview api2 term search on the exact title returns no note with a matching title, i.e. no conference record found.
related_work.what_it_covers: The second closest positive-result paper, and the one that most sharply frames the design axis we are decomposing. AnchorTree adds SOFT hierarchical anchoring: an auxiliary anchor-supervision term with weight gamma (Eq. 9: NELBO term + mu * anchor term) on a two-stage anchor-denoiser architecture, with AST-informed depth weighting over keyword and identifier anchors. Models are 809M, initialised from Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B (494M). HumanEval Syntax 65.58 -> 74.72, Pass@1 3.29 -> 5.45; MBPP Syntax 74.46 -> 80.12, Pass@1 6.34 -> 9.10 at T=2048. Explicitly separates itself from TreeDiff: 'TreeDiff modifies this by introducing a forward noising schedule that is not position-wise independent and also depends on AST depth. However, TreeDiff leaves the denoising process unchanged.' AnCoder therefore keeps the standard position-wise-independent MDLM forward process and intervenes on the LOSS/architecture instead.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: AnCoder is the mirror image of our experiment: it moves the structural prior OUT of the corruption process and INTO an auxiliary loss term, and gets a positive result. It never runs the structural-corruption arm (no TreeDiff baseline, despite critiquing TreeDiff by name), so the literature still has no head-to-head of structure-in-corruption vs structure-in-loss under matched supervision. Its only ablation is the scalar gamma; no mask-count, no mask-rate marginal, no timestep-weighting ablation. It also never tests whether the depth weighting or the anchor supervision is doing the work (Null anchoring already gets 72.24/4.80 vs AnchorTree 74.72/5.45, so most of the syntax gain is attributable to the two-stage architecture, not to the AST hierarchy -- they do not say this).
related_work.known_defects: (1) The Null-anchoring row is the buried lede: 809M MDLM 65.58 -> Null 72.24 -> AnchorTree 74.72 on HumanEval Syntax means the two-stage anchor-denoiser ARCHITECTURE contributes ~6.7 points and the AST hierarchy only ~2.5. The abstract's 'structurally anchored diffusion' claim is over-attributed. (2) Absolute pass@1 is 3-9%, i.e. roughly 5-15 solved tasks; +2.16 absolute on HumanEval is ~4 tasks with no CI or significance test. (3) 809M only -- no evidence the effect survives at 7B, where the pretrained code prior is far stronger and structural scaffolding has less headroom (this is precisely the scale at which our negative result lives). (4) The 494M MDLM row does NOT use the two-stage architecture while all 809M rows do, so the size comparison is architecture-confounded. (5) gamma ablation trained for only 2 epochs / 12K steps on the annealing set while headline models are trained longer, so the selected gamma may not be optimal at full budget.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API metadata; full HTML text of v1 fetched and parsed (Table 1 with the Null/Keyword/Identifier/AnchorTree rows, Table 2 test-time scaling, Sec 2 Structure-Aware Diffusion related work, Sec 3.1 forward process, Eq. 9 anchor objective, Sec 5.3 ablation); Semantic Scholar graph API; OpenReview api2 search.

related_work.citation: Alexander Wettig, Tianyu Gao, Zexuan Zhong, Danqi Chen. "Should You Mask 15% in Masked Language Modeling?" arXiv:2202.08005 (v1 2022-02-16). EACL 2023.
related_work.venue_status: Published, EACL 2023. Verified via arXiv API arxiv:comment field: 'Accepted to EACL 2023. The code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/princeton-nlp/DinkyTrain'.
related_work.what_it_covers: The conceptual prior art for our exact decomposition. It argues masking rate has TWO separable effects -- 'it leads to more corruption, which makes the prediction task more difficult; it also enables more predictions, which benefits optimization' -- and uses that framework to reinterpret BERT's 80-10-10 corruption. Most directly relevant to our claim: it finds that 'uniform masking requires a higher masking rate compared to sophisticated masking strategies such as span or PMI masking', i.e. the optimal mask-rate marginal is COUPLED to the masking strategy. That is the mechanism our claim asserts for a code diffusion model.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Encoder-only MLM evaluated by GLUE/SQuAD fine-tuning and linguistic probes; not a generative masked diffusion model, not code, not executable correctness, no iterative-denoising inference axis (no NFE), no per-timestep loss weighting (MLM uses a single fixed rate, not t~U(0,1) with a 1/t-style weight). It establishes rate-strategy coupling but cannot tell us the sign or magnitude in a 7B code dLLM, nor separate a third factor (loss weighting) that only exists in the diffusion formulation.
related_work.known_defects: Largest model is BERT-large scale; conclusions about optimal rate are known to be architecture- and objective-specific. 'Preserves 95% of fine-tuning performance at 80% masking' is measured on discriminative transfer, which is far more forgiving than executable code generation -- so the paper's headline robustness to high mask rates should NOT be assumed to carry to our setting, and our result is a natural place to test that.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API metadata including the arxiv:comment venue string.

related_work.citation: Zitian Gao, Haoming Luo, Lynx Chen, Jason Klein Liu, Ran Tao, Joey Zhou. "What Makes Diffusion Language Models Super Data Learners?" arXiv:2510.04071 (v1 2025-10-05).
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (arXiv arxiv:comment: 'Technical report, work in progress'). No venue claimed.
related_work.what_it_covers: The closest METHODOLOGICAL prior art: an extensive single-factor ablation campaign to 'disentangle the sources' of dLLM behaviour, concluding that random masking of input tokens is the dominant factor and that comparable gains come from MLP dropout and weight decay, i.e. the mechanism is generic stochastic regularization rather than anything diffusion-specific.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Framed on data efficiency in multi-epoch pretraining under limited data, with no code benchmark, no executable-correctness metric, and no structural/non-uniform masking arm at all. Its regularization interpretation predicts that changing WHICH positions are masked should matter little relative to HOW MANY -- a prediction that directly supports our claim's direction but has never been tested in a structured domain where syntactic legality gates the metric.
related_work.known_defects: Self-labelled work-in-progress technical report; no venue review. Ablations are at small scale in a data-constrained regime, so the 'stochastic regularization' explanation may be an artifact of multi-epoch overfitting pressure and need not hold for a single 5-epoch SFT on 114K code samples from a strong 7B code prior. No code, no syntax metric, no seeds reported.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API metadata + abstract.

related_work.citation: Jaeyeon Kim, Jonathan Geuter, David Alvarez-Melis, Sham Kakade, Sitan Chen. "Stop Training for the Worst: Progressive Unmasking Accelerates Masked Diffusion Training." arXiv:2602.10314 (v1 2026-02-10).
related_work.venue_status: ICML 2026. Verified via OpenReview api2 term search: venue 'ICML 2026 regular', venueid ICML.cc/2026/Conference (also ICLR 2026 Workshop MM Intelligence Poster, and CoRR 2026 mirror).
related_work.what_it_covers: The strongest existing evidence that a NON-UNIFORM forward masking process HELPS, and thus the key paper our negative result must be reconciled against. PUMA modifies the forward masking process so that training-time mask patterns match the highly structured masks that inference-time unmasking actually produces, giving ~2.5x pretraining speedup at 125M and stacking with AR initialisation.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: PUMA's non-uniformity is INFERENCE-ALIGNED (progressive prefix-like unmasking), not SYNTAX-ALIGNED. Our depth-banded schedule is non-uniform in a way that is orthogonal to (and possibly anti-correlated with) inference-time unmasking order, which gives a clean testable explanation for why ours regressed and theirs sped up. PUMA is 125M pretraining on text, with perplexity/likelihood metrics; no 7B, no SFT, no code, no executable metric, no syntax-error accounting.
related_work.known_defects: Progressive unmasking changes BOTH the mask pattern and the per-sample masked-count distribution simultaneously, and the paper attributes the speedup to pattern alignment without a mask-count-matched control -- exactly the confound our arm (ii) is designed to isolate. The 2.5x figure is a pretraining-speed claim at one scale (125M) with no scaling ladder, so it is a prime replication target. Train-test-mismatch framing also predicts a downside PUMA does not test: narrowing training to inference-aligned masks should degrade arbitrary-position infilling, which is masked diffusion's actual structural advantage.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API metadata; OpenReview api2 /notes/search?term= returning venueid ICML.cc/2026/Conference.

related_work.citation: Jaeyeon Kim, Kulin Shah, Vasilis Kontonis, Sham Kakade, Sitan Chen. "Train for the Worst, Plan for the Best: Understanding Token Ordering in Masked Diffusions." arXiv:2502.06768 (v1 2025-02-10). ICML 2025 (oral).
related_work.venue_status: ICML 2025 oral. Verified via OpenReview api2 term search: venue 'ICML 2025 oral', venueid ICML.cc/2025/Conference (also FPI-ICLR2025 Poster).
related_work.what_it_covers: Theory plus experiment that MDMs must learn an exponentially large set of infilling subproblems, some computationally intractable, and that adaptive decode ORDER lets inference sidestep the hard ones (Sudoku <7% -> ~90%). Provides the mechanism by which a corruption schedule that concentrates probability mass on structurally correlated, hard-to-infill mask patterns could hurt.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: All of the intervention is on the INFERENCE side (decode order); the paper does not modify the training-time forward process to avoid hard subproblems. It also works on logic puzzles and small models, so it never touches code, syntax legality, or 7B SFT. Our factor (i) POSITIONS arm is effectively the training-side test of its thesis, which the paper itself does not run.
related_work.known_defects: Hardness results are for stylised distributions (Sudoku, planted problems); the leap to natural code is unargued. No cost accounting for adaptive-order inference against the NFE budget it consumes, so the <7% -> 90% headline is not compute-matched against simply running more denoising steps.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API metadata; OpenReview api2 /notes/search?term= returning venueid ICML.cc/2025/Conference with venue 'ICML 2025 oral'.

related_work.citation: Bowen Sun, Yujun Cai, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Yiwei Wang. "Blockwise SFT for Diffusion Language Models: Reconciling Bidirectional Attention and Autoregressive Decoding." arXiv:2508.19529 (v1 2025-08-27).
related_work.venue_status: Preprint; rejected at ICLR 2026. Verified via OpenReview api2 term search returning venue 'Submitted to ICLR 2026' with venueid ICLR.cc/2026/Conference/Rejected_Submission, plus a CoRR 2025 DBLP mirror.
related_work.what_it_covers: The closest CONTROL-DESIGN prior art for what we are proposing. It changes the SFT masking scheme for a dLLM and then defends the attribution with exactly the machinery our candidate needs: matched compute AND matched token budgets, a normalised 'traversal' unit tau so that arms supervising different numbers of tokens per step are compared at equal total supervision (it notes Classical supervises 96 tokens/step while Blockwise supervises 32, so Blockwise runs 3x more epochs), a factorial B_train x B_infer grid to remove compute confounds, and an explicit claim that gains 'stem from faithful training-inference alignment rather than incidental masking effects'. Also uses per-sequence Bernoulli pi ~ Uniform(1e-3, 1) with a mask-at-least-one-token fallback, the same construction as our plain control.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Math reasoning (GSM8K/MATH/MetaMathQA), not code; no executable-correctness or syntax-legality metric; no structural/AST prior; and although it matches token budgets it never decomposes the LOSS WEIGHTING factor -- its ablations vary prefix noise and block size, not the timestep weight. Its epoch-renormalisation trick is nonetheless the fairness convention our arm (ii) should adopt rather than reinvent.
related_work.known_defects: Single A100 with per-device batch size 1 and gradient accumulation, so its 'equal compute' matching is wall-clock at one very small configuration and may not hold under 8-GPU DDP. Rejected at ICLR 2026, so its claims have not survived review -- worth reading the reviews for the objections a reviewer will also raise against us. The 'rather than incidental masking effects' claim rests on the block-size factorial, which controls for block size but not for the number of supervised tokens per gradient step within a fixed tau.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API metadata; full HTML text of v2 fetched and parsed (abstract, implementation details with the tau traversal convention and the 96-vs-32 tokens/step example, Sec 4.3 factorial design, Sec 4.4 prefix-noise ablation); OpenReview api2 /notes/search?term= returning ICLR.cc/2026/Conference/Rejected_Submission.

related_work.citation: Subham Sekhar Sahoo, Jean-Marie Lemercier, Zhihan Yang, Justin Deschenaux, Jingyu Liu, John Thickstun. "Scaling Beyond Masked Diffusion Language Models." arXiv:2602.15014 (v1 2026-02-16). ICML 2026.
related_work.venue_status: ICML 2026. Verified via OpenReview api2 term search: venue 'ICML 2026 regular', venueid ICML.cc/2026/Conference.
related_work.what_it_covers: Directly load-bearing for our factor (iii). It shows masked diffusion becomes ~12% more FLOPs-efficient when the NELBO weighting alpha'_t/(1-alpha_t) (the 1/t-family weight our plain control implements as min(maximum_weight, 1/t)) is replaced by a simple cross-entropy objective, describing this as a low-variance objective that also shifts compute-optimal checkpoints toward smaller models. So the literature already establishes that the timestep loss weight materially changes MDLM training efficiency -- which is exactly the prior a reviewer will bring to our factor (iii).
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: The finding is in from-scratch IsoFLOP pretraining measured by validation perplexity plus GSM8K after SFT; it never crosses the weighting choice with a NON-UNIFORM masking marginal, and never evaluates on executable code. Our factor (iii) is the interaction term this paper leaves untested: our schedule-only arm uses a band derivative/u weight normalised within-sample, which is a third weighting family beyond both NELBO 1/t and plain CE.
related_work.known_defects: Cross-family comparisons rest on their own criticism that perplexity misleads across families, yet the 12% MDLM efficiency claim is itself a perplexity/FLOPs claim. No code benchmark. Scaling to 1.7B, so the 7B regime is extrapolation. The paper's own message -- that the loss weight is worth ~12% of compute efficiency -- implies that a weighting swap alone is unlikely to move a 7B SFT arm by 18 points, which is a real prior against our claim that factor (iii) can dominate; we should say so rather than be caught by it.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API metadata; full HTML text of v1 fetched and parsed (abstract, contribution list, NELBO Eq. 7 with the alpha'_t/(1-alpha_t) weight, optimizer/IsoFLOP setup); OpenReview api2 /notes/search?term= returning ICML.cc/2026/Conference.

related_work.citation: Despoina Kosmopoulou, Efthymios Georgiou, Vaggelis Dorovatas, Georgios Paraskevopoulos, Alexandros Potamianos. "Masked Diffusion Language Models with Frequency-Informed Training." arXiv:2509.05056 (v1 2025-09-05).
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (arXiv arxiv:comment 'Preprint'; BabyLM 2025 Challenge submission). OpenReview api2 returns only a Public_Article 'CoRR 2025' mirror, no conference venueid.
related_work.what_it_covers: The only paper we found that varies BOTH axes we call (ii) and (iii) in the same study: it applies non-uniform, frequency-informed masking that prioritises rare tokens, explores multiple noise scheduling strategies including two-mode approaches, AND investigates different noise weighting schemes within the NELBO objective, while claiming to maintain theoretical validity.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: BabyLM data-constrained regime with linguistic-competence/world-knowledge/human-likeness metrics; no code, no execution, no 7B, no AST. It reports competitive-with-baseline results rather than a factor decomposition, and does not report a matched masked-count control, so it cannot say whether its frequency-informed marginal or its weighting scheme is responsible for anything.
related_work.known_defects: Results are 'competitive to hybrid autoregressive-masked baselines', i.e. no clear win, and the paper does not disentangle its own three simultaneous changes (frequency-informed selection, two-mode schedule, NELBO weighting) -- the same three-way confound we are proposing to break, in a different setting. The 'maintaining theoretical validity' claim is asserted rather than empirically checked against a matched-mask-count arm.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API metadata + abstract; OpenReview api2 /notes/search?term= returning only a Public_Article CoRR 2025 record.

related_work.citation: Shansan Gong, Ruixiang Zhang, Huangjie Zheng, Jiatao Gu, Navdeep Jaitly, Lingpeng Kong. "DiffuCoder: Understanding and Improving Masked Diffusion Models for Code Generation." arXiv:2506.20639 (v1 2025-06-25). ICLR 2026.
related_work.venue_status: ICLR 2026 Poster. Verified via OpenReview api2 term search: venue 'ICLR 2026 Poster', venueid ICLR.cc/2026/Conference (plus CoRR 2025 DBLP mirror).
related_work.what_it_covers: The reference 'understanding' paper for masked diffusion in code: a 7B dLLM trained on 130B code tokens, systematic analysis of denoising behaviour, the finding that sampling temperature diversifies generation ORDER as well as token choice, and coupled-GRPO, an RL scheme that constructs complementary mask noise to reduce log-likelihood variance. Establishes the 7B-code-dLLM setting our work sits in.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Its training-side contribution is RL (coupled-GRPO), not the SFT corruption schedule; it never varies the masking marginal, position selection, or timestep weighting during supervised training, and reports no negative result about structural noising. Its complementary-mask insight (variance reduction via how masks are drawn) is nonetheless mechanistically adjacent to our factor (ii)/(iii) story and should be cited as such.
related_work.known_defects: The +4.4% EvalPlus gain from coupled-GRPO is reported without a mask-noise-matched non-coupled control at equal sample count, so the variance-reduction attribution is partly assumed. Analysis of 'how causal generation should be' rests on an AR-ness metric of the authors' own construction with no external validation.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API metadata; OpenReview api2 /notes/search?term= returning ICLR.cc/2026/Conference, venue 'ICLR 2026 Poster'.

related_work.citation: Mengyu Ye, Keito Kudo, Ryosuke Takahashi, Jun Suzuki. "Reconsidering Positional Supervision in Masked Diffusion Language Model Training." arXiv:2601.22947 (v1 2026-01-30).
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (arXiv arxiv:comment 'preprint, WIP').
related_work.what_it_covers: A loss-side intervention in MDLM SFT that is a fourth candidate factor we do not currently control: it shows LLaDA-8B-Instruct is highly sensitive to small positional shifts under iterative parallel decoding (displacing 1% of generated tokens by one position substantially reduces win rates), attributes this to position-wise cross-entropy penalising shifts harshly, and replaces CE with a CTC-style alignment-flexible objective plus a <slack> token, beating a matched CE-trained baseline on four benchmarks.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Open-ended generation with win-rate/LLM-judge metrics, not code or execution. But it flags a real hazard for our decomposition: our schedule-only arm supervises 61.4 positions per sample under a band-derivative weight, and if position-wise CE is shift-brittle then a schedule that changes WHICH positions carry loss mass may degrade quality through an alignment channel that none of our three arms isolates.
related_work.known_defects: Self-labelled WIP; the 1%-displacement intervention is synthetic and may overstate real decoding shift rates. CTC adaptation introduces a <slack> token and a modified collapse map, i.e. two changes at once, with no ablation separating them.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API metadata + abstract.

related_work.citation: Zirui Wu, Lin Zheng, Zhihui Xie, Jiacheng Ye, Jiahui Gao, Shansan Gong. "DreamOn: Diffusion Language Models For Code Infilling Beyond Fixed-size Canvas." arXiv:2602.01326 (v1 2026-02-01). ICLR 2026.
related_work.venue_status: ICLR 2026 Poster. Verified via OpenReview api2 term search: venue 'ICLR 2026 Poster', venueid ICLR.cc/2026/Conference. arXiv arxiv:comment also states 'ICLR 2026'.
related_work.what_it_covers: Modifies the diffusion training objective with two length-control states to allow variable-length generation, built on Dream-Coder-7B and DiffuCoder-7B, matching AR models on HumanEval-Infilling and SantaCoder-FIM. Relevant here only as the closest example of a minimal-change objective modification on our exact backbone family, and because our repo already exposes a dreamon_linear weighting mode -- so it anchors what a legitimate weighting variant looks like.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: No structural/AST prior, no mask-rate decomposition, and its evaluation is infilling (its home turf), not from-scratch generation, so it says nothing about the HE+/MBPP+ regression regime.
related_work.known_defects: 'Matches oracle performance achieved with ground-truth length' is the headline, but oracle-length is a favourable reference point that hides how often the length controller over- or under-shoots; no distributional analysis of final lengths reported in the abstract.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API metadata including arxiv:comment 'ICLR 2026'; OpenReview api2 /notes/search?term= returning ICLR.cc/2026/Conference.

related_work.citation: Qing Wang, Jacob Devasier, Chengkai Li. "What Gets Unmasked First? Trajectory Analysis of Diffusion Models for Graph-to-Text Generation." arXiv:2605.31564 (v1 2026-05-29).
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (no arxiv:comment, no venue claimed). First public 2026-05-29, i.e. on/after the 2026-05-07 concurrency cutoff.
related_work.what_it_covers: CONCURRENT. Identifies 'a previously undocumented failure mode of supervised fine-tuning: SFT disrupts this strategy by prematurely anchoring structural sentence-ending tokens early in the decoding trajectory', and fixes it at inference by downweighting structural-token confidence (+9.4 BLEU-4). This is a same-family finding to ours -- SFT interacting badly with STRUCTURAL tokens -- discovered independently and in a different modality.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Graph-to-text with BLEU, not code with execution; the intervention is training-free and inference-side, so it does not touch the corruption schedule or loss weighting. It offers a competing explanation for our regression (structural tokens being resolved at the wrong point in the trajectory) that our three arms would not distinguish from a marginal/weighting story, so it should be cited and, ideally, addressed with a trajectory diagnostic.
related_work.known_defects: Concurrent, so not preemptive. Single task family; lambda-scaled structural decoding is a hand-tuned inference hack with no principled selection of lambda; BLEU-4 as the construct for structural correctness is weak compared to a parser.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API search + metadata; first-public date checked against the 2026-05-07 cutoff.

related_work.citation: Chengze Li, Yitong Zhang, Jia Li, Liyi Cai, Ge Li. "Beyond Autoregression: An Empirical Study of Diffusion Large Language Models for Code Generation." arXiv:2509.11252 (v1 2025-09-14).
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (no arxiv:comment venue).
related_work.what_it_covers: First broad empirical study of dLLMs for code: 9 diffusion LLMs, 4 benchmarks, findings that dLLMs are competitive with similar-size AR models, extrapolate length better, and an exploration of 'factors impacting the effectiveness and efficiency of diffusion LLMs' with practical guidance. Sets the reference numbers and the factor-study framing for our benchmark surface.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Entirely inference-side factors (decoding steps, block size, remasking, temperature) on off-the-shelf checkpoints; no training runs at all, so no corruption-schedule, mask-marginal, or loss-weighting evidence. The training-side factor study is exactly the gap our candidate fills.
related_work.known_defects: Survey-style breadth with shallow per-model tuning; sampler settings are known to move HumanEval by double-digit points (our own top_p 1.0 -> 0.95 moved HE by +14.6), so cross-model rankings from lightly tuned samplers are fragile.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API metadata + abstract.

diff.differentiation_statement: Nothing in the literature decomposes a structure-aware corruption schedule into separable factors, and nothing reports a mechanism for when such a schedule HURTS. TreeDiff (2508.01473) and AnCoder (2602.17688) are both positive-result papers, and each one holds fixed exactly the factors we vary: TreeDiff pins the mask budget by construction (N = floor(eps_t * L), with a random fallback explicitly justified so that "the diffusion noise schedule is strictly adhered to"), so it varies only position selection and has literally no evidence on the mask-count marginal or on loss weighting; AnCoder deliberately keeps the standard position-wise-independent MDLM forward process and moves the structural prior into an auxiliary anchor loss with weight gamma, so it varies only the weighting of an added term, never the corruption. Our schedule-only arm perturbs position selection, the masked-count marginal (61.4 vs 42.1 supervised masks per sample) and the loss-mass convention (within-sample-normalised band derivative/u, p99 14.07, cap 20.0, versus plain's min(20, 1/t) total-mass convention) simultaneously, at 7B full-parameter rather than LoRA (TreeDiff) or 809M from-scratch (AnCoder), and it produced an 18.3-point HE+ regression against a matched plain-SFT control that shares base checkpoint, split, trainer, epochs and LR. The conceptual decomposition we would supply -- that rate and strategy are coupled, and that raising the mask count trades "more corruption" against "more predictions" -- exists only for encoder MLM on GLUE/SQuAD (Wettig et al., EACL 2023) and only for pretraining data efficiency in text dLLMs (2510.04071); neither touches executable code, iterative-denoising NFE budgets, syntax legality, or a diffusion timestep weight. And the two papers that do vary a non-uniform forward process at scale are aligned to the wrong axis for us: PUMA (ICML 2026) makes masks inference-aligned and gets a 2.5x speedup, while Scaling Beyond MDLM (ICML 2026) shows the timestep weight is worth about 12% of compute efficiency. Both are cited as the priors we must beat, and both leave the interaction of a non-uniform masking marginal with the loss weighting completely untested -- which is our contribution. A reviewer accepts this as the first mechanistic account of when structure-aware noising fails, run at a scale (7B, full-parameter, executable metric, syntax-error accounting) where neither positive-result paper operates.

followup_openings.defect: The headline +13.3% relative HE+ gain is confounded by an unablated training curriculum. Appendix A.2 reveals the forward process is not standard MDLM t~U(0,1): the base noise eps_t is cosine-annealed from 0.1 down to 0.001 as a function of the TRAINING STEP, and the per-sample mask probability is then P_mask = (1-eps_t)*lambda + eps_t with lambda ~ U(0,1). So all arms, including the Random-Masking control, are trained under a step-dependent noise curriculum that is never compared against a standard uniform-t forward process. The paper attributes its gain to AST-guided position selection while a second, larger design change sits underneath every arm.
followup_openings.our_fix: Run our arm (i) POSITIONS as a direct replication test: keep the depth-banded mask-rate marginal and band weighting, choose masked positions uniformly at random, and hold everything else at the schedule-only configuration. That gives the first clean measurement of the position-selection factor in isolation, on a 7B backbone under full-parameter training and standard t~U(0,1), with no curriculum underneath. If POSITIONS recovers little, TreeDiff's structural-selection story does not carry to 7B full-parameter SFT and its gain is more plausibly the curriculum plus LoRA-scale plasticity.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: TreeDiff is the paper every reviewer will cite against a negative structural-masking result. Showing that its one varied factor (position selection) is not the one that governs quality at 7B, and that its unablated curriculum is a live alternative explanation, converts our regression from an embarrassing disagreement into a scope correction on the field's reference positive result.

followup_openings.target_paper: TreeDiff (arXiv:2508.01473)
followup_openings.defect: TreeDiff reports, but never explains, a structural-masking regression of the same sign as ours: its span-level AST arm drops BELOW the random baseline on MBPP (39.7 vs 41.5 at T=512; 51.6 vs 52.9 at T=256) while beating it on HumanEval. The paper's explanation is prose -- span masking causes 'a significant loss of local information' -- with no measurement of masked-count, loss mass, or syntax-error rate per arm to support it.
followup_openings.our_fix: Our three arms plus the two endpoints we already own give a quantitative account of exactly this phenomenon, and we can report the diagnostic TreeDiff never did: parseable-rate and syntax-error rate per arm at both NFE 512 and NFE 128. Our own data already show these are the governing quantities (schedule-only sits at 41.46% HE+ syntax errors and 58.54% parseable at 512 NFE, versus a 94%->1.8% unparseable decline across the NFE range for a healthy model), so we can test whether contiguous/structurally correlated masking degrades legality rather than semantics.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This is a reconciliation rather than a contradiction, which is a far stronger contribution than a bare disagreement: TreeDiff's own span-level MBPP regression becomes a data point in our decomposition, and the mechanism we supply explains both signs of their result at once.

followup_openings.defect: The paper over-attributes its gain to the AST hierarchy. Its own Table 1 shows that on HumanEval the 809M MDLM baseline gets 65.58 Syntax / 3.29 Pass@1, Null anchoring (gamma = 0) already gets 72.24 / 4.80, and AnchorTree gets 74.72 / 5.45. So roughly 6.7 of the 9.14 syntax points come from the two-stage anchor-denoiser ARCHITECTURE with no structural prior at all, and only ~2.5 from AnchorTree's AST depth weighting. The abstract nonetheless claims 'structurally anchored diffusion offers a parameter-efficient path to high-quality code generation'. Separately, the 494M MDLM row does not use the two-stage architecture while every 809M row does, so the size comparison is architecture-confounded.
followup_openings.our_fix: Report the Null-vs-structural split explicitly in related work, and design our decomposition so the same trap is impossible for us: because both our endpoints share one architecture and one backbone, every point of our 18.3-point gap is attributable to the corruption schedule alone. Then use AnCoder's own framing to sharpen the comparison -- AnCoder puts the structural prior in the LOSS and wins; we put it in the CORRUPTION and lose -- and test whether our factor (iii) WEIGHTING arm recovers the gap, which would say the structural prior is fine but its delivery vehicle (corruption vs auxiliary loss) is what matters.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It reframes our negative result as the missing half of AnCoder's positive one, and yields a crisp, quotable design rule for the field: deliver structural priors through the loss, not through the forward process. That rule is testable, actionable, and currently unstated in the literature.

followup_openings.target_paper: AnCoder (arXiv:2602.17688)
followup_openings.defect: Untested at scale and untested against the method it critiques. All AnCoder models are 809M, initialised from a 494M AR coder, with absolute pass@1 of 3.29-9.10 -- roughly 5-15 solved tasks -- reported with no confidence intervals or significance tests. And although Section 2 names TreeDiff and criticises it for modifying the forward process, TreeDiff is never run as a baseline, so the field has no head-to-head between structure-in-corruption and structure-in-loss.
followup_openings.our_fix: Provide the 7B data point AnCoder's claim needs and the head-to-head it skipped. Our arms (i) and (iii) together bracket the two delivery vehicles at 7B on the same backbone, split and trainer: (i) isolates structural POSITION selection in the corruption process (TreeDiff's axis) and (iii) isolates the structural LOSS weighting (AnCoder's axis). Report per-arm bootstrap CIs on HE+ (n=164) and MBPP+ (n=378) at both NFE points, since with 6/164 passes the schedule-only arm has a CI wide enough to matter and the literature routinely omits this.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: Structural anchoring gains at 809M from a weak code prior may simply not survive at 7B, where the pretrained prior already supplies syntax -- our HE+ 3.66 vs matched-plain 21.95 vs Dream-Coder-Instruct 70.7 ladder is direct evidence that headroom depends violently on the strength of the starting prior. Testing the scale-dependence of a fresh positive result is a clean, cheap, high-credibility follow-up.

followup_openings.target_paper: PUMA / Stop Training for the Worst (arXiv:2602.10314, ICML 2026)
followup_openings.defect: PUMA changes the forward process so training masks match inference-time unmasking patterns, and attributes a 2.5x pretraining speedup to that alignment -- but progressive unmasking simultaneously changes the per-sample masked-COUNT distribution, and no mask-count-matched control is reported. It is also demonstrated only at 125M, on text, with likelihood metrics.
followup_openings.our_fix: Our arm (ii) MARGINAL is precisely the missing control, transplanted to a setting where it can be decisive: rescale the depth-banded schedule so the per-sample masked-count distribution matches plain's measured mean of 42.1 while keeping depth-banded position selection and band weighting. Adopt Blockwise SFT's traversal-normalisation convention (tau, equal total supervision) rather than equal epochs, so a reviewer cannot object that the arms saw different total supervision. Then state the resulting general claim: whether a non-uniform forward process helps or hurts depends on whether it is aligned with the inference-time unmasking distribution (PUMA: aligned, helps) or with a syntax hierarchy orthogonal to it (ours: not aligned, hurts).
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This turns three separate results -- PUMA's speedup, TreeDiff's gain, our regression -- into one predictive rule about forward-process design, and supplies the mask-count control that two of the three papers omit. It is also the arm most likely to actually explain our 18.3 points, given that the two arms differ by 61.4 vs 42.1 supervised masks per sample.

followup_openings.target_paper: Scaling Beyond Masked Diffusion Language Models (arXiv:2602.15014, ICML 2026)
followup_openings.defect: It establishes that swapping the NELBO alpha'_t/(1-alpha_t) weight for plain cross-entropy buys ~12% FLOPs efficiency in from-scratch pretraining, measured by validation perplexity plus post-SFT GSM8K. It never crosses the weighting choice with a non-uniform masking marginal, never evaluates executable code, and stops at 1.7B.
followup_openings.our_fix: Our arm (iii) WEIGHTING supplies the missing interaction term at 7B with an execution metric: hold depth-banded positions and marginal fixed and switch the loss weight from the band derivative/u form (within-sample normalised) to plain's min(maximum_weight, 1/t). corruption.py already exposes weighting in {unit, mdlm, dreamon_linear} plus maximum_weight, so this is a config change. Critically, use their result as a stated prior AGAINST our own hypothesis: if a weighting family is worth ~12% of compute efficiency in pretraining, a weighting swap alone recovering 18.3 points of HE+ in SFT would be surprising and demands the interaction explanation, not a main-effect one. Report the recovered fraction with that prior made explicit.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: Pre-empting the strongest reviewer objection -- that loss weighting is a second-order knob and cannot plausibly carry an 18-point gap -- is worth more than the arm itself. Either we recover the points and show weighting is first-order once the masking marginal is non-uniform (a genuinely new interaction result), or we do not, and the decomposition correctly localises the cause elsewhere.

followup_openings.target_paper: Blockwise SFT (arXiv:2508.19529) and What Makes Diffusion LMs Super Data Learners (arXiv:2510.04071)
followup_openings.defect: Both papers do what we propose -- ablate a masking design to attribute an effect -- and both stop short in the same way. Blockwise SFT matches compute and token budgets and runs a factorial design, and explicitly claims its gains come from alignment 'rather than incidental masking effects', but its ablations vary prefix noise and block size, never the timestep loss weight, and its setting is math not code. Super Data Learners concludes random masking is the dominant factor and is interchangeable with MLP dropout and weight decay, but does so in data-constrained multi-epoch pretraining with no structural masking arm and no executable metric.
followup_openings.our_fix: Import Blockwise SFT's fairness machinery wholesale (tau traversal normalisation for equal total supervision; a factorial rather than one-factor-at-a-time reading where affordable) and extend Super Data Learners' disentangling method to the one regime it skipped: a structured domain with a hard legality gate, at 7B, on a strong pretrained prior, with syntax-error rate reported alongside pass@1 so the corruption-versus-optimization trade-off Wettig et al. describe becomes directly observable rather than inferred.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: It positions our paper as the method these two established, and gives us their controls for free, which is the difference between an anecdote about one failed run and a decomposition a reviewer will accept as identifying a mechanism.

MATERIAL PROBLEM FOUND IN THE CANDIDATE'S OWN DESIGN -- a FOURTH confound that the proposed three arms cannot detect, verified empirically on disk, not from literature:

/apdcephfs_wzc1/share_304376610/pighzliu_code/dllm_draft/scaffold_coder/sft_dataset.py builds the two endpoint arms with DIFFERENT TOKENIZATIONS of byte-identical text. PlainMaskedSFTDataset (line 304) does a single `tokenizer.encode(str(row["response"]))`. ScheduleOnlySFTDataset (line 462) calls `_segmented_schedule_only_response` (line 842), which encodes each IR span SEPARATELY in a loop (`tokenizer.encode(rendered.text[span.start:span.end])`) and concatenates. Measured with the Dream-Coder-v0-Base-7B tokenizer over the first 300 rows of data/scaffold_edu_v0/train_data.parquet: the rendered IR text equals `response` exactly (200/200 checked, zero mismatches), yet the token sequences differ on 300/300 rows, with mean 96.5 vs 83.9 tokens and a mean inflation ratio of 1.168x. This independently reproduces the canvas-length gap already recorded in SCHEDULE_ONLY_STATS.md (schedule-only 149.8 vs plain 137.6).

Consequences the candidate must absorb before execution: (a) the schedule-only arm was trained on off-BPE-manifold token sequences, which is a strong independent candidate cause of its 41.46% HE+ / 34.13% MBPP+ syntax-error rate, and is a more parsimonious explanation than any of the three proposed factors; (b) all three proposed arms inherit the segmented tokenizer, so the decomposition would attribute tokenizer damage to whichever factor happens to correlate with it, and the stated kill criterion (no arm recovers >4 of 18.3 points) would very likely fire for the wrong reason; (c) the 61.4-vs-42.1 mask-count gap is itself partly a tokenization artifact, since ~1.17x more tokens at the same mask probability yields ~1.17x more masks, so arm (ii) as specified would be partly re-normalising a tokenizer effect. Minimum fix: re-run the plain control on the segmented tokenization (cheap, re-anchors the 18.3-point gap to a like-for-like baseline), or add a fourth TOKENIZER arm. Either way the claim should be stated as a four-factor decomposition.

Also flag a cost discrepancy: est_gpu_hours is 45, but SCHEDULE_ONLY_STATS.md records 40.93 allocated GPU-hours for ONE five-epoch arm (5.116 h wall on 8 GPUs). Three arms is roughly 123 GPU-hours of training, plus EvalPlus generation at 50.23 s/sample (HE+, n=164) and 43.92 s/sample (MBPP+, n=378) across two NFE points per arm, roughly another 40 GPU-hours. Realistic total is 160-200 GPU-hours, not 45. With the tokenizer arm or the re-anchored plain control it is higher still. The "cheapest high-information experiment in the set" framing survives on information-per-hour, but the hour count in the proposal is off by roughly 4x.
diff.sharpened_claim: When a structure-aware corruption schedule is added to masked-diffusion SFT of a 7B code model, quality is governed not by which positions the structure selects but by the collateral changes the schedule makes to the supervision distribution -- the masked-count marginal, the loss-mass convention, and (in our implementation) the tokenization the structural spans induce. We demonstrate this by decomposing an 18.3-point HumanEval+ regression (3.66% vs 21.95% for a matched plain-SFT control sharing base checkpoint, split, trainer, epochs and LR) into single-factor arms from Dream-Coder-v0-Base-7B, and we report the recovered fraction of the gap per factor at NFE 512 and 128, with parseable-rate and syntax-error rate alongside pass@1 so that the corruption-versus-optimization trade-off is directly observable rather than inferred. The result reconciles rather than contradicts the field's positive structural results: TreeDiff pins the mask budget by construction (N = floor(eps_t*L)) and so varies only position selection, and AnCoder deliberately preserves the position-wise-independent forward process and moves the structural prior into an auxiliary anchor loss -- meaning both papers, by design, avoid exactly the factors we show are decisive. The resulting design rule is that structural priors should be delivered through the loss or through inference-aligned masks (cf. PUMA), not by reshaping the corruption marginal, and it is the first mechanistic account in the literature of WHEN structure-aware noising hurts. Two amendments to the original plan are load-bearing: add a fourth arm (or re-anchor the plain control) for the span-segmented tokenization confound we verified on disk -- 300/300 rows differ in token sequence at a 1.168x mean inflation despite byte-identical text -- and normalise arms by total supervision (Blockwise SFT's traversal convention) rather than by epochs, so that no arm can be dismissed as having simply seen more supervised tokens.

blocking_gaps: ARM (iii) IS NOT A CONFIG CHANGE -- the proposal's central 'lowest-risk' claim is FALSE. The weighting enum {unit, mdlm, dreamon_linear} + maximum_weight lives on RungMixtureConfig (/apdcephfs_wzc1/.../dllm_draft/scaffold_coder/corruption.py:43-74), which is used ONLY by scaffold.mode=rung_mixture. scaffold.mode=schedule_only builds HierarchicalBandConfig (scaffold_sft_trainer.py:193-211), which has NO weighting field (corruption.py:367-383, verified field list). `grep -n weighting scaffold_coder/sft_dataset.py` returns ZERO hits: ScheduleOnlySFTDataset accepts no weighting parameter at all. Arm (iii) requires plumbing a new field through HierarchicalBandConfig + the hydra band block + ScheduleOnlySFTDataset.__getitem__.

THE PROPOSAL MISDESCRIBES ITS OWN BASELINE ARM'S WEIGHTING. The claim says schedule-only uses 'the band derivative/u form'. It does NOT. `min(maximum_weight, derivative/u)` appears at corruption.py:205 inside _per_position_band_weights, whose ONLY caller is corruption.py:619 in GlobalBandSampler -- i.e. scaffold.mode=hierarchical (the meta-token Scaffold arm), not schedule_only. ScheduleOnlySFTDataset (sft_dataset.py:518-527) uses min(maximum_weight, 1.0/u) where u = band.clock(t). `grep -c derivative scaffold_coder/sft_dataset.py` = 0. So the actual schedule-only weight is the SAME 1/x functional family as plain's min(maximum_weight, 1.0/t) (sft_dataset.py:368); the only differences are (a) the argument is a per-position band clock u instead of a global t, and (b) plain divides by supervised count (line 370: base_weight/supervised = total-mass convention) while schedule-only rescales to a within-sample mean (lines 556-568). Factor (iii) as written is therefore not the swap the proposal thinks it is, and its 'is worth ~12% of compute efficiency' prior from 2602.15014 does not apply.

ARM (ii) MARGINAL IS NOT SEPARABLE FROM ARM (iii) IN THIS CODE. sft_dataset.py:518-527 uses the SAME u for both the mask probability (probabilities.append(u)) and the loss-weight base (1.0/max(u,1e-6)). Rescaling the marginal to hit plain's 42.1 masks necessarily changes every loss weight. There is no code path that changes the masked-count distribution while holding the weight base fixed. Arms (ii) and (iii) as specified are not orthogonal single-factor swaps; a strict one-factor-at-a-time reading requires decoupling the mask-probability clock from the weight clock, which is new code.

TWO PREVIOUSLY UNDOCUMENTED CONFOUNDS BETWEEN THE ENDPOINT ARMS, found by reading the on-disk training telemetry (neither is in SCHEDULE_ONLY_STATS.md nor in the positioning report). THE PROPOSAL'S OWN 4TH CONFOUND (segmented tokenization) IS REAL AND I REPRODUCED IT INDEPENDENTLY, but at a slightly different magnitude than reported. MEASURED LOSS-MASS DIRECTION IS OPPOSITE TO THE PROPOSAL'S IMPLICATION. The proposal cites schedule-only's 'p99 of 14.07 against a maximum_weight cap of 20.0' as evidence schedule-only has anomalous loss mass; in fact schedule-only carries LESS than half the total per-sample loss mass of plain. Any claim about 'the loss weighting it induces' must be restated with the correct sign or it will be a third mis-stated premise.
