blocking_gaps: NO SEED ANYWHERE in the diffusion harness, and the sampler is genuinely stochastic. scripts/generate_evalplus_dream.py has no --seed and never calls torch.manual_seed (grep for seed/manual_seed/deterministic returns nothing); by contrast scripts/generate_evalplus_ar.py:212 HAS --seed default 1234. Meanwhile models/Dream-Coder-v0-Instruct-7B/generation_utils.py:58-73 sample_tokens does `if temperature > 0: x0 = dists.Categorical(probs=probs).sample()`, and every NFE run used T=0.1 > 0. I confirmed torch.initial_seed() differs across processes (7704390826431647482 / 14105703864843390214 / 14999765917596774336). So EVERY existing number in the 6-point sweep is from an unseeded stochastic decode, and the 512-vs-1024 'fixed point' compares two runs differing in TWO variables (schedule flush + desynchronized RNG stream), not one. This is the blocking gap; it is a ~5-line fix (--seed + torch.manual_seed/cuda.manual_seed_all) plus reruns.

THE DETERMINISM BASELINE DOES NOT EXIST, AND THE RUN THE POSITIONING USED AS ONE IS A DIFFERENT SAMPLER CONFIG. The positioning treats runs/dream_coder_instruct_heplus.r1 as a same-setting replicate of _r2 and concludes 'run-to-run nondeterminism is large (1/164 byte-identical)'. That is wrong: scripts/_run_baselines_wzc1_8gpu.sh:81 launches r1 with `--steps 512 --max-new-tokens 512 --temperature 0.1` and NO --top-p, so it takes the argparse default top_p=1.0 (line 109), whereas scripts/_run_baselines_r2_wzc1.sh:55 passes --top-p 0.95. r1 scores .585 plus / .616 base vs r2 .707/.762 -- that 12.2-point gap is the already-known top_p sensitivity result, not noise. So the true run-to-run noise floor at fixed config is UNMEASURED, and it is the one number the whole paper rests on.

THE BYTE-IDENTITY NUMBER IS AMBIGUOUS AND BOTH THE CANDIDATE AND THE POSITIONING QUOTE IT WITHOUT SAYING WHICH FIELD. I recomputed both. On the extracted `solution` field (solutions.jsonl): 163/164 HE+ and 376/378 MBPP+ -- the CANDIDATE's numbers are right. On the raw model output (`raw_output` in metrics.rank*.jsonl): 150/164 HE+ and 335/378 MBPP+ -- the POSITIONING's numbers are right. The gap is entirely scripts/generate_evalplus_dream.py extract_python(), which strips prose/fences and therefore MASKS real generation differences. Quoting 163/164 without saying 'post-extraction' is the same class of error as Retraction 3 (a post-processing step that silently hides the disagreements). The defensible headline is the raw 150/164 with the extraction effect reported alongside.

THE CANVAS x STEPS GRID IS CONFOUNDED BY RAW-OUTPUT TRUNCATION, WHICH WILL FIRE THE KILL CRITERION FOR THE WRONG REASON. I tokenized the actual outputs. Raw output length (prose + fences + code) at canvas 512: median 499 (HE+) / 475 (MBPP+), max = 512 = canvas, i.e. the model FILLS the canvas. Fraction of raw outputs longer than a candidate canvas: 96.3%/97.4% at 128, 89.0%/80.4% at 256, 79.9%/67.7% at 384. Extracted code is far shorter (median 189/131; only 22.0%/2.9% exceed 256). So running canvas=256 does not 'test whether the long canvas carries information' -- it TRUNCATES 89% of raw generations before extract_python can find the code fence. The kill_criterion says the candidate dies if canvas256/steps256 scores >3pts below canvas512/steps512; that will almost certainly happen from truncation, killing a valid paper for a harness reason.

KILL CRITERION IS UNDERPOWERED BY ~2x. '>3 pts on HE+ n=164' = 4.9 tasks. Binomial SE at p=.707, n=164 is 0.0355, so 3 pts = 0.84 SE, and an unpaired 95% CI half-width is 7.0 pts. The stated threshold is inside noise. Needs a paired design (McNemar / paired bootstrap on per-task outcomes, which solutions_eval_results.json supports) plus multi-seed, or the criterion cannot fire correctly in either direction.

feas.risk: The most likely failure is a CONFOUNDED result on the canvas grid that trips the kill criterion for a harness reason, compounded by an uninterpretable fixed point. Two mechanisms, both measured on disk today. (1) Truncation, not information: the model fills the canvas with prose+fences (raw median 499/475 tokens against a 512 canvas, max exactly 512), while the extracted code is only median 189/131. So 89.0% of HE+ raw outputs and 80.4% of MBPP+ exceed a 256 canvas. Running canvas=256 truncates the raw generation before extract_python can locate the code fence, pass@1 falls by far more than 3 points, and the stated kill_criterion fires -- concluding "the long canvas carries information" when the true cause is that the harness prints an explanation before the code. That is a false kill of a valid paper, and it is the same shape as Retraction 2 (a stage that silently discarded its input). (2) Two variables at once: I found the 14 HE+ / 43 MBPP+ differing raw outputs diverge at median 99.6%/99.5% through -- consistent with the flush -- BUT the minimum is 33.0% (HE+) and 20.6% (MBPP+), i.e. some diverge in the MIDDLE, which the final-flush difference cannot explain. The only remaining explanation is RNG desynchronization: at T=0.1 Categorical.sample() draws per masked position per step, so a 1024-step run consumes ~2x the RNG stream of a 512-step run, and with no seed the streams are unrelated from the start. Therefore today's 512-vs-1024 pair differs in schedule AND in random stream, and NOTHING in it is attributable -- exactly Retraction 1, a comparison that controls nothing. Secondary risk: because the nonzero-commit subsequences are provably identical except the flush, a reviewer can dismiss the whole fixed point as arithmetic tautology ("you proved zero-commit steps commit zero tokens"); the surviving empirical content is the 2.14x wall clock and the flush perturbation, which is a workshop-sized result unless the grid and cost-unit legs land cleanly.
feas.required_control: SEEDED THREE-PART DETERMINISM CONTROL, run BEFORE any grid cell and reported in the paper as a table, plus truncation accounting on every cost/quality cell. Part A (determinism floor): after adding --seed, run steps=512/canvas=512/seed=1234 TWICE in separate processes and assert 164/164 HE+ raw byte-identical. If this fails the harness is nondeterministic and every byte-identity claim in the paper is void -- this is the gate. Part B (noise ceiling): steps=512/canvas=512 at seeds {1234,2026,42}, giving the run-to-run pass@1 spread; the kill threshold must then be restated as a multiple of THAT spread rather than the arbitrary 3 points (which I measured at only 0.84 binomial SE, versus a 7.0-point unpaired 95% CI half-width), and the 512-vs-1024 comparison must be paired McNemar on per-task outcomes, not a difference of two aggregates. Part C (single-variable attribution): steps=512 vs steps=1024 at the SAME seed with RNG-consumption discipline documented, so the residual difference is attributable to the schedule flush alone. Only Part C licenses the sentence "514 of 1024 forward passes are paid for and provably discarded." WHY THIS IS THE CONTROL THAT PREVENTS THE ANALOGOUS RETRACTION: retraction 1 was a verifier that compared nothing -- the current 512-vs-1024 pair is exactly that, two runs differing in schedule AND in an unseeded RNG stream, presented as a controlled comparison; the proof it is uncontrolled is already on disk in the mid-output divergences at 33.0%/20.6% that the flush cannot explain. Bolted on, and preventing the Retraction-3 analogue: report TRUNCATION RATE (fraction of raw outputs hitting the canvas) and raw-vs-extracted length as first-class columns of every grid cell, and run the primary analysis on the paired subset whose canvas-512 solution fits the smaller canvas -- because averaging pass@1 over a small canvas silently drops the long generations, which are precisely the expensive tasks that Retraction 3 dropped. Finally, always state which field a byte-identity number refers to: 163/164 is post-extract_python, 150/164 is raw, and quoting the former alone lets a post-processing step hide the disagreements.

lens.title: A Two-Line Post-Processing Fix Moves Diffusion Code-LM Scores by up to 10 Points: Output-Extraction Artifacts Dominate the Low-Step Regime
lens.claim: The canonical finding that low-step diffusion decoding buys mostly syntactic validity (unparseable rate ~90% at 64 steps falling to ~2% at 512) is substantially an artifact of fixed-canvas truncation interacting with regex-based code extraction, not of denoising. Because the canvas is fixed while the model appends trailing prose and self-generated tests, the final lines are cut mid-token; a repair that drops trailing lines until the buffer parses recovers a complete correct function in a large fraction of cases, worth +7.3 (HE+) and +10.3 (MBPP+) pass@1+ at 128 steps and +2.4/+3.2 at 256 steps.
lens.why_now: Low-step quality is the headline metric of the entire dLLM acceleration literature, and essentially every paper reports it through a bespoke extract_python-style regex plus fixed max_new_tokens. Our measured effect at 128 steps (+10.3 MBPP+) is larger than the reported gains of most published decoding methods, so published low-NFE rankings may be measuring post-processing hygiene rather than algorithms. This is the same defect class as the two retractions already in this repo, so we have both the instinct and tooling to audit it credibly, and no paper found audits extraction artifacts for dLLMs.
lens.experiment: (1) ALREADY MEASURED on our runs, evalplus-graded via official untrusted_check: at HE+ nfe128, 56 of 112 unparseable outputs recover a parseable complete def by dropping trailing lines -> +12 base/+12 plus (.140 -> .213); MBPP+ nfe128 100 repaired -> +42 base/+39 plus (.233 -> .336); nfe256 +2.4/+3.2. At nfe512 ALL 9 residual unparseable cases recover a def (+2 base HE+, +3 base/plus MBPP+); inspection confirms complete correct functions followed by truncated assert-spam (HumanEval/64,/83,/124; Mbpp/3,/245,/296,/286,/300,/468). (2) TO RUN: factor the repair into one documented post-processor and re-score the full 6-point sweep on both benchmarks under three extraction policies -- raw regex (status quo), truncate-to-last-parseable, EOS/stop-sequence-aware decode -- reporting delta at every NFE so budget-dependence is explicit. (3) Generalize: same three-policy audit on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and DiffuCoder-7B, plus the AR Qwen2.5-Coder control where we predict a much smaller delta because AR emits a real EOS -- establishing whether this is a dLLM-specific hazard of fixed-canvas decoding having no natural stopping signal. (4) Publish the post-processor + per-task provenance table so others can re-score their runs.
lens.assets_needed: runs/dream_instruct_{heplus,mbppplus}_nfe* plus both r2 runs (have, 12 runs); scripts/generate_evalplus_dream.py:53-79 extract_python (have, is the object of study); evalplus 0.3.1 grader with get_groundtruth (have, already produced the numbers above). MISSING: LLaDA-8B-Instruct and DiffuCoder-7B weights (hy-proxy download) for generalization; the AR control overlaps the Qwen2.5-Coder run in flight on .104 -- reuse its solutions.jsonl.
lens.kill_criterion: Dies if the repair delta is not benchmark-general -- specifically if the AR control shows a comparable delta (>5 pts at matched output length), because then it is generic code-extraction hygiene already known in the AR literature rather than a fixed-canvas dLLM hazard, and the framing collapses to a bug report. Also dies if the repair leaks information: if truncate-to-last-parseable ever selects among multiple candidate functions rather than deterministically dropping a suffix, the gains are invalid -- must verify it is a pure suffix-drop with no oracle access.
lens.builds_on: Not a follow-up to a method paper but an audit of a shared measurement convention, in the spirit of CaRE (2607.24763) for remasking and ParallelBench (2510.04767) for parallelism, neither of which touches output extraction or canvas truncation. It externalizes this repo's own retraction pattern (hand-rolled verifier; process-only cost averaging) applied to a convention the whole subfield shares. DreamOn (2602.01326, ICLR 2026) treats fixed-canvas length mismatch as a generation-capability problem for infilling; we address the downstream measurement consequence in from-scratch generation -- a different defect at a different layer.

related_work.citation: Liu, Xia, Wang, Zhang. "Is Your Code Generated by ChatGPT Really Correct? Rigorous Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code Generation." arXiv:2305.01210; NeurIPS 2023.
related_work.venue_status: NeurIPS 2023 (OpenReview forum id=1qvx610Cu7, linked from official EvalPlus README line 74). Verified via arXiv API + README fetch.
related_work.what_it_covers: The EvalPlus benchmark itself -- HumanEval+/MBPP+, untrusted_check grader, and (in the v0.3.1 codebase we have on disk) an OFFICIAL tree-sitter post-processor `evalplus/sanitize.py`. `sanitize()` calls `code_extract()`, which searches all (i,j) line spans for the longest syntax-checking span, then keeps only imports plus entry-point-reachable defs. `evalplus/codegen.py:89` calls `sanitize()` on every sample, so the canonical end-to-end EvalPlus path (`evalplus.evaluate --model ...`, README line 86) already ships syntax-aware trailing-garbage removal. The v0.3.1 release note (README line 38) advertises 'one command to run all: generation + post-processing + evaluation'.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: The sanitizer is documented as a convenience, never as a measurement-validity control. EvalPlus never reports sanitized-vs-raw deltas, never characterises WHICH generation regimes it rescues, and was designed for AR models emitting prose after a complete function -- not for fixed-canvas dLLM decoding where the canvas is cut mid-token. Whether the sanitizer's effect is budget-dependent, and whether it is adequate at low NFE, is entirely unstudied.
related_work.known_defects: `code_extract` is O(n^2) over line spans and picks the span with the most non-blank lines, so on a mid-token-truncated dLLM canvas it can prefer a long syntactically-valid span that does NOT contain the entry point. We measured this directly: on HE+ nfe128 the entry-point `def` is absent in 36/164 raw outputs but 65/164 AFTER official sanitize -- sanitization nearly doubles entry-point loss. And it leaves 110/164 (nfe64) and 32/164 (nfe128) still unparseable. So the official sanitizer is simultaneously (a) strong enough to capture most of the candidate's claimed effect and (b) demonstrably mis-specified for the low-step dLLM regime. That asymmetry is the real opening.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API metadata; fetched official README from raw.githubusercontent.com/evalplus/evalplus/master; read the installed evalplus 0.3.1 source at /opt/conda/envs/dllm-env/lib/python3.11/site-packages/evalplus/{sanitize.py,codegen.py}; executed sanitize() over our own 12 runs and rescored with evalplus.evaluate.

related_work.citation: Eniser et al. (as indexed). "Output Format Biases in the Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code Translation." arXiv:2403.17214; Forge 2024 (v2 = journal extension).
related_work.venue_status: Conference version accepted at 2024 IEEE/ACM Intl. Conf. on AI Foundation Models and Software Engineering (Forge 2024) per arXiv comment field; v2 is a journal extension. Verified via arXiv API comment.
related_work.what_it_covers: This is the closest paper to the candidate's *claim shape*, and it is pre-cutoff. It establishes exactly the thesis that non-code elements in LLM output interfere with evaluation metrics and bias assessments; finds 26.4%-73.7% of outputs from 11 instruct models require post-processing; proposes prompt-engineering + regex extraction reaching 92.73% code-extraction success rate; and empirically confirms output-format bias affects execution-based metrics (Computational Accuracy) and text metrics (BLEU/CodeBLEU) across 5 languages.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Autoregressive models only, and code TRANSLATION not from-scratch generation. Their failure mode is 'model appended prose after a complete program' -- the model chose to stop and then kept talking. It cannot cover the dLLM failure mode, where a fixed canvas is exhausted and the buffer is cut mid-token with no stopping signal ever emitted. Crucially, they have no compute-budget axis: there is no notion of denoising steps, so the interaction 'extraction-policy delta shrinks monotonically as NFE grows' is outside their design space entirely.
related_work.known_defects: Their remedy is a regex + prompt-engineering combination benchmarked by Code Extraction Success Rate, a proxy metric -- CSR measures whether extraction produced something code-shaped, not whether the extracted program is the one the model meant. They never report per-task pass/fail flips or check that extraction cannot LOSE a previously-passing solution. Our fix: report signed per-task flips (gained/lost) under each policy and audit entry-point preservation, which is precisely how we caught the official EvalPlus sanitizer silently increasing entry-point loss from 36 to 65 of 164.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API: title, v1 date 2024-03-25, v2 date 2025-10-13, comment field naming Forge 2024, full abstract with the 26.4%-73.7% and 92.73% CSR figures.

related_work.citation: "CaRE: Compute-aware Remasking Evaluation Protocol for Masked Diffusion Language Models." arXiv:2607.24763.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint; no venue in arXiv comment (comment reads only 'updated version'). Not found as an accepted paper on OpenReview.
related_work.what_it_covers: The candidate's stated sibling-in-spirit. Audits 7 remasking strategies over LLaDA-8B-Base and Dream-7B-Base by standardising actual NFE, enforcing multi-metric reporting, controlling stochasticity; finds temperature explains most MAUVE variance and that compute-matched comparison REVERSES several published rankings. Establishes the genre 'published dLLM gains may be evaluation artifacts'.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Open-ended generation metrics (MAUVE, GenPPL) on OpenWebText and LM1B -- no execution-based code benchmark, no output extraction, no fixed-canvas truncation. Their artifact is on the sampling/compute-accounting side; the extraction/stopping side of the pipeline is untouched. They also stop at 8B base models and never test instruct models where padding/EOS pathologies live.
related_work.known_defects: MAUVE is itself sensitive to detokenisation and truncation, so an unparseable/truncated-tail artifact could be confounding their own headline temperature effect -- they do not control for it. Our fix: run the extraction/stopping-policy axis as a second factor inside a CaRE-style compute-matched design, showing whether their ranking reversals survive when the output-extraction policy is also held fixed.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list fetch (title, v1 2026-06-04, abstract with the 0.296 MAUVE / p=0.020 figures); OpenReview search returned no accepted-paper record.

related_work.citation: "ParallelBench: Understanding the Trade-offs of Parallel Decoding in Diffusion LLMs." arXiv:2510.04767; ICLR 2026 Poster.
related_work.venue_status: ICLR 2026 Poster -- CONFIRMED via OpenReview API: venue='ICLR 2026 Poster', venueid='ICLR.cc/2026/Conference'. (Semantic Scholar/DBLP still show 'CoRR 2025', exactly the 2026-venue lag documented in project memory.)
related_work.what_it_covers: The candidate's other cited sibling. First benchmark purpose-built for dLLMs; information-theoretic analysis of parallel decoding plus synthetic list-operation case studies; shows standard math/coding benchmarks are insufficient to expose quality loss from parallel decoding, and that dLLMs degrade dramatically under parallel decoding where AR models do not.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: The artifact studied is conditional-independence error from parallel token commitment, measured on tasks chosen to be analytically tractable. Output extraction, canvas truncation, and pass@1 post-processing policy are not part of the analysis. Their AR-vs-dLLM contrast is on task accuracy, not on measurement-pipeline sensitivity -- which is the axis we would add.
related_work.known_defects: Their claim 'standard code/math benchmarks fail to capture degradation' is asserted against raw benchmark scores; if those raw scores are themselves depressed by extraction artifacts (as we measure: +7.4 MBPP+ from post-processing alone at nfe128), part of the insensitivity they attribute to benchmark design is instead pipeline hygiene. Our fix: re-run their dLLM-vs-AR contrast under a fixed, audited extraction policy to separate 'benchmark cannot see it' from 'harness threw it away'.

related_work.citation: "DreamOn: Diffusion Language Models For Code Infilling Beyond Fixed-size Canvas." arXiv:2602.01326; ICLR 2026 Poster.
related_work.venue_status: ICLR 2026 Poster -- CONFIRMED via OpenReview API: venue='ICLR 2026 Poster', venueid='ICLR.cc/2026/Conference'.
related_work.what_it_covers: Names the fixed-canvas length-mismatch problem for code and fixes it at the generation layer: two length-control states let the model expand/contract output length from its own predictions. Built on Dream-Coder-7B and DiffuCoder. Establishes 'fixed canvas is the bottleneck for code dLLMs' as accepted, citable framing.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Infilling, and a generation-capability remedy. It never asks what the canvas mismatch does to MEASUREMENT in from-scratch generation, and never reports an extraction-policy ablation. So the downstream-measurement consequence is genuinely open -- the candidate's positioning here is correct.
related_work.known_defects: Because DreamOn changes output length, comparisons against fixed-canvas baselines confound 'better length control' with 'less truncation garbage for the extractor to trip on'. Their reported gains are not decomposed into these two channels. Our fix: rescore DreamOn vs its fixed-canvas baseline under raw / official-sanitize / stop-aware extraction; the fraction of DreamOn's advantage that evaporates under a strong extractor is the share that was measurement, not capability. This is the single highest-value follow-up available.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API (v1 2026-02-01, comment 'ICLR 2026'); OpenReview api2 notes/search returning venueid ICLR.cc/2026/Conference plus visible reviewer-response threads.

related_work.citation: "Rainbow Padding: Mitigating Early Termination in Instruction-Tuned Diffusion LLMs." arXiv:2510.03680.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (25 pages, project page ai-isl.github.io/rainbow-padding). No accepted-venue record found.
related_work.what_it_covers: Diagnoses '<eos> overflow' in instruction-tuned dLLMs: as allocated sequence length grows, responses paradoxically shorten and collapse into <eos> streams. Root-causes it to <eos>'s dual role as terminator and padding, and fixes it with a cycle of distinct padding tokens plus one epoch of LoRA.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Establishes that dLLM stopping behaviour is pathological and length-budget-dependent -- the mechanism underneath the candidate's hypothesis -- but treats it as a generation-quality problem measured by response length and output quality. No execution-based code benchmark under multiple extraction policies, and no claim about pass@1 accounting.
related_work.known_defects: The pathology is defined on generated length, and 'output quality' is reported without stating the extraction policy. If their evaluation used a permissive extractor, part of the reported improvement is recovered post-processing headroom rather than better termination. Our fix: replicate their length-robustness result under the three-policy extraction grid so the termination effect is separated from the extraction effect.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list fetch: title, v1 2025-10-04, abstract.

related_work.citation: "VoidPadding: Let [VOID] Handle Padding in Masked Diffusion Language Models so that [EOS] Can Focus on Semantic Termination." arXiv:2606.17999.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (v2 comment: 'Minor related-work revisions; results unchanged'). No accepted-venue record found.
related_work.what_it_covers: Same family as Rainbow Padding, post-cutoff: separates padding ([VOID]) from termination ([EOS]) so a learned [EOS] enables early stopping and [VOID] guides adaptive canvas expansion. Directly targets 'a dLLM has no natural stopping signal', which is the candidate's proposed mechanism.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Training-side remedy (instruction tuning with a new padding token). Says nothing about how existing published fixed-canvas numbers should be re-scored, nor about extraction policy. Concurrent, so it cannot preempt us; it does supply a strong citation that our diagnosed mechanism is real and independently recognised.
related_work.known_defects: Requires retraining/instruction-tuning, so it cannot repair the existing literature's reported numbers -- exactly the niche a post-hoc, zero-training extraction audit fills. They also do not report whether their early stopping changes measured code pass@1 net of post-processing.

related_work.citation: "rho-EOS: Training-free Bidirectional Variable-Length Control for Masked Diffusion LLMs." arXiv:2601.22527.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (comment: '11 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables'). No accepted-venue record found.
related_work.what_it_covers: Pre-cutoff and training-free, so the closest thing to a preemption of the mechanism: uses implicit EOS density during denoising as a signal of generation sufficiency, adjusting generation length. Explicitly frames fixed generation length as forcing a trade-off between output quality and compute -- the same quality-vs-budget framing as the candidate.

related_work.citation: "Diffusion Language Models Are Natively Length-Aware." arXiv:2603.06123.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint; no comment field, no accepted-venue record found.
related_work.what_it_covers: Pre-cutoff. States plainly that DLMs operate over a fixed max-length window for a predetermined number of denoising steps independent of required response length; shows the latent prompt representation suffices to estimate needed output length; proposes zero-shot pre-generation context cropping. Evaluates on HumanEval among four benchmarks and reports large FLOP reductions with no statistically significant degradation.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Cropping the canvas BEFORE generation to save compute -- an efficiency intervention. It does not measure how the uncropped fixed-canvas convention distorts reported pass@1, and reports no extraction-policy ablation. Notably it overlaps our HumanEval + fixed-canvas + compute-budget setting most closely of any pre-cutoff paper, so it must be cited and distinguished carefully.
related_work.known_defects: 'No statistically significant performance degradation' is the weakest form of the claim and is reported under a single unstated extraction policy; a permissive extractor can mask real degradation, and their own mechanism (shorter canvas) mechanically reduces truncated-tail garbage, which would flatter the cropped arm. Our fix: re-run their crop-vs-no-crop comparison under all three extraction policies; if the no-degradation result only holds under one policy, their headline is policy-dependent.

related_work.citation: "Speculative Refinement: A Hybrid Autoregressive Diffusion Decoding Strategy and Its Behavior Across Benchmarks." arXiv:2606.27474.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint ('7 pages + 2 pages References'). No accepted-venue record found.
related_work.what_it_covers: Concurrent, and the single most threatening finding to the candidate's headline: reports that 'code benchmarks conflate structural discovery with logical correctness -- providing a syntactic scaffold lifts accuracy from near zero to over 20% WITHOUT CHANGING THE MODEL, indicating much of the baseline failure is structural.' That is the same qualitative discovery as ours (low-step code scores are dominated by structure/syntax, not logic), on the same benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP), with an AR-vs-diffusion protocol comparison.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Their lever is a syntactic SCAFFOLD supplied at generation time, not a post-hoc extraction policy, and the near-zero-to-20% jump is attributed to structural discovery in general rather than isolated to canvas truncation plus extraction. They do not run a three-policy extraction grid, do not report per-NFE deltas, and do not audit entry-point preservation or per-task pass/fail flips. Because it is concurrent (2026-06-25 >= 2026-05-07) it does not preempt us, but it substantially reduces the novelty of 'low-step code scores are mostly structural'.
related_work.known_defects: 'Near zero to over 20%' from a supplied scaffold is exactly the kind of number that needs an oracle-leak audit: a scaffold can encode task information. They report no control establishing the scaffold is task-independent. Our fix: our repair is a deterministic pure suffix-drop with zero task information, verified by signed per-task flips (we measured gained=3, lost=0 at HE+ nfe128), giving a leak-free lower bound on the structural share they estimate with a possibly-leaky intervention.

related_work.venue_status: Preprint; no comment field, no accepted-venue record found.

related_work.citation: "Is Your Diffusion Sampler Actually Correct? A Sampler-Centric Evaluation of Discrete Diffusion Language Models." arXiv:2602.19619.
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (30 pages, 10 figures; code at luhantang.github.io/dllm_sampler). No accepted-venue record found.
related_work.what_it_covers: Pre-cutoff dLLM measurement-validity audit: separates denoiser approximation error from sampler-induced error using an exact HMM-posterior oracle denoiser; shows few-step samplers are not distributionally correct even with a perfect denoiser, with mismatch vanishing only as steps approach sequence length; and that NLL/GenPPL/MAUVE improvements do not imply correct sampling.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: The strongest pre-cutoff statement that few-step dLLM decoding is broken in a step-count-dependent way, but entirely in distributional terms on synthetic chains -- no code benchmark, no pass@1, no extraction. It is a competing EXPLANATION for low-step degradation that our design must rule out rather than a preemption. This is a genuine risk to the candidate: some of the low-step deficit is real sampler incorrectness.
related_work.known_defects: Confined to an oracle-denoiser synthetic setting, so it cannot say how much real-model low-step degradation on real benchmarks is sampler error versus pipeline artifact. Our fix: our per-NFE extraction-delta curve upper-bounds the pipeline-artifact share, and the residual after strong extraction is attributable to genuine sampler/denoiser error -- decomposing exactly what they leave unquantified. Framing our paper as this decomposition, rather than as 'the canonical finding is an artifact', is both more defensible and more useful.

diff.differentiation_statement: The candidate as written rests on a factual premise that I falsified by execution, so it must be reframed before it is pursued -- but a strong paper survives the reframing. The premise "essentially every paper reports low-step quality through a bespoke extract_python-style regex" is wrong for the benchmark in question: EvalPlus 0.3.1 ships an official tree-sitter post-processor (`evalplus/sanitize.py`), and `evalplus/codegen.py:89` applies it to every sample, so the canonical `evalplus.evaluate --model ...` path already performs syntax-aware trailing-garbage removal. I ran it over our own 12 runs and rescored with the official grader: on HE+ nfe128 the official sanitizer recovers 41 of 112 unparseable outputs and moves plus-pass@1 from .140 to .159 (+1.9), whereas the candidate claims +7.3 for its own repair -- and the candidate's repair, implemented as a pure suffix-drop, yields only +1.5 (.152) and is thus WORSE than the tool EvalPlus already ships. On MBPP+ nfe128 the official sanitizer gives +7.4 (.233->.307) against the candidate's claimed +10.3, again beating the proposed repair (+4.5). So "a two-line fix moves scores by up to 10 points" is not defensible: most of the effect is already captured by the standard tool, our numbers do not reproduce the claimed HE+ magnitude, and Speculative Refinement (arXiv:2606.27474, concurrent) has independently reported the qualitative version of the headline. What survives, and is genuinely unoccupied, is a sharper and more interesting finding that the same runs support: the official sanitizer is mis-specified for the low-step fixed-canvas regime and its failure is systematic and budget-dependent. Measured: raw unparseable rate on HE+ falls 93.9%/68.3%/20.1%/1.2% across nfe 64/128/256/1024, and even after official sanitization it is still 67.1%/19.5%/2.4%/0.0% -- so at low NFE the standard post-processor leaves two thirds of outputs unparseable. More damning, because `code_extract` selects the syntactically-valid line span with the most non-blank lines, on a mid-token-truncated canvas it can prefer a long valid span that omits the required function: entry-point `def` is absent in 36/164 raw outputs but 65/164 AFTER official sanitization, i.e. the field-standard sanitizer nearly doubles entry-point loss precisely in the regime the acceleration literature reports as its headline. No paper I found audits this. Against the closest prior work the position is clean: arXiv:2403.17214 (pre-cutoff) established output-format bias but for autoregressive code translation with no compute-budget axis and no dLLM truncation mode, and validated its remedy by Code Extraction Success Rate -- a proxy that cannot detect the entry-point loss we measure; CaRE audits compute accounting and ParallelBench audits parallel commitment, neither touching extraction; DreamOn (ICLR 2026) and the EOS/padding line (Rainbow Padding, VoidPadding, rho-EOS, Natively Length-Aware) fix stopping at the generation or training layer and so cannot re-score the existing literature. And arXiv:2602.19619 supplies the competing explanation -- few-step samplers are genuinely distributionally incorrect -- which turns our contribution into a decomposition of the low-step deficit into pipeline-artifact and true-sampler-error shares rather than a debunking. The differentiator a reviewer will accept: we are the first to treat the code-eval post-processor as a budget-dependent measurement instrument, to show the field-standard sanitizer degrades entry-point recovery exactly where dLLM papers make their claims, and to bound how much of the reported low-step deficit is instrument rather than model.

It also still leaves 110/164 (nfe64) and 32/164 (nfe128) unparseable, i.e. it fails hardest exactly in the low-step regime dLLM acceleration papers headline. The tool is documented as convenience post-processing and has never been characterised as a measurement instrument with a regime of validity.
followup_openings.our_fix: Characterise the sanitizer as an instrument: report, per NFE and per benchmark, (a) unparseable rate before/after, (b) entry-point-preservation rate before/after, (c) signed per-task pass/fail flips. Then ship an entry-point-anchored suffix-drop that is provably monotone -- it never removes the entry point and never selects among candidate functions, so it cannot leak oracle information. Contribute it upstream as a `--sanitize-policy` option so dLLM papers can report under a policy validated for truncated canvases.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: Every EvalPlus-reported dLLM number inherits this instrument. Showing the community's default post-processor has a known-bad regime, and supplying a drop-in replacement plus a re-scoring table, repairs a shared measurement convention at zero GPU cost and gives the paper a concrete artifact.

followup_openings.target_paper: DreamOn (arXiv:2602.01326, ICLR 2026 Poster)
followup_openings.defect: DreamOn's variable-length canvas mechanically produces less mid-token truncation than its fixed-canvas baselines, so its reported infilling gains conflate two channels: genuinely better length control, and simply handing the extractor cleaner text. The paper reports no extraction-policy ablation, so the decomposition is unavailable.
followup_openings.our_fix: Rescore DreamOn and its fixed-canvas baseline under the three-policy grid (raw / official sanitize / entry-point-anchored suffix-drop). The share of DreamOn's advantage that disappears under the strongest extractor is the share that was measurement rather than capability. Weights are already on disk (models/DreamOn-v0-7B, models/Dream-Coder-v0-Instruct-7B), so this is a rescoring plus one generation pass on its home turf -- infilling, which this repo has never evaluated DreamOn on.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: Highest-value opening available: it audits an ICLR 2026 paper on the exact mechanism (fixed canvas) our finding concerns, is cheap, and simultaneously fixes this repo's self-diagnosed failure of never evaluating DreamOn on its home turf.

followup_openings.target_paper: Is Your Diffusion Sampler Actually Correct? (arXiv:2602.19619)
followup_openings.defect: Establishes that few-step samplers are distributionally incorrect even under an oracle denoiser, with mismatch vanishing only as steps approach sequence length -- but only in a synthetic HMM setting with no real benchmark, so it cannot say how much real low-step degradation on HumanEval/MBPP is sampler error versus measurement artifact.
followup_openings.our_fix: Publish the decomposition they leave open: the per-NFE extraction-policy delta upper-bounds the pipeline-artifact share, and the residual after the strongest validated extractor is attributable to genuine sampler/denoiser error. Our measurements already sketch the curve (HE+ sanitize delta +0.6/+1.2/+1.9 at nfe 1024/256/128; MBPP+ +0.5/+4.0/+7.4), showing the artifact share grows monotonically as budget shrinks while remaining far smaller than the total deficit.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: Converts the paper from a debunking (fragile, and partly scooped by concurrent arXiv:2606.27474) into a decomposition (defensible, additive, and citable by both the sampler-correctness and acceleration literatures). This should be the paper's spine.

followup_openings.target_paper: Output Format Biases in Code Translation (arXiv:2403.17214, Forge 2024)
followup_openings.defect: Validates its extraction remedy with Code Extraction Success Rate -- whether extraction produced something code-shaped -- rather than with signed per-task correctness flips. CSR cannot detect an extractor that produces valid-looking code while discarding the required function, which is exactly the failure we measured in the official EvalPlus sanitizer (36 -> 65 entry-point losses out of 164).
followup_openings.our_fix: Replace CSR with a signed flip audit (gained / lost / net per task) plus entry-point preservation, and demonstrate it catches a real failure CSR would score as success. Our HE+ nfe128 audit shows the official sanitizer gains 3 and loses 0 tasks -- a pure-gain, leak-free result that CSR could not have certified.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: Upgrades the metric of the closest pre-cutoff paper and extends its thesis from autoregressive code translation to fixed-canvas diffusion generation with a compute-budget axis they had no notion of. This is the clean 'we fix the prior work's metric' contribution.

followup_openings.target_paper: Diffusion Language Models Are Natively Length-Aware (arXiv:2603.06123)
followup_openings.defect: Claims 'no statistically significant performance degradation' from pre-generation canvas cropping on HumanEval among four benchmarks, under a single unstated extraction policy. Cropping mechanically reduces truncated-tail garbage, which flatters the cropped arm through the extractor rather than through the model -- an uncontrolled confound in a paper that overlaps our HumanEval + fixed-canvas + compute-budget setting most closely of any pre-cutoff work.
followup_openings.our_fix: Re-run crop-vs-no-crop under all three extraction policies. If the no-degradation headline holds only under the permissive policy, it is policy-dependent and must be restated; if it survives the strongest extractor, that strengthens their claim and still yields a reusable control.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: This is the pre-cutoff paper nearest our setting, so a reviewer will ask about it. Turning it from a positioning threat into a target we audit converts the closest-prior-work risk into a result.

followup_openings.target_paper: CaRE (arXiv:2607.24763, concurrent) and ParallelBench (arXiv:2510.04767, ICLR 2026)
followup_openings.defect: Both audit dLLM evaluation but hold the output-extraction stage fixed and unstated. CaRE's headline is that compute-matched comparison reverses published remasking rankings; ParallelBench's is that standard code/math benchmarks cannot capture parallel-decoding degradation. Neither controls for the extraction artifact, so part of CaRE's ranking reversals and part of ParallelBench's diagnosed benchmark insensitivity may be pipeline hygiene -- we measure +7.4 MBPP+ from post-processing alone at nfe128.
followup_openings.our_fix: Add extraction policy as a second factor to a CaRE-style compute-matched design and test whether their ranking reversals survive; separately, re-run ParallelBench's dLLM-vs-AR contrast under a fixed audited extractor to split 'benchmark cannot see it' from 'harness threw it away'. Includes the candidate's own AR control (Qwen2.5-Coder on .104), where we predict a much smaller delta because AR emits a real EOS.
followup_openings.why_it_matters: Positions our factor as orthogonal and composable with the two established dLLM audit frameworks rather than competing with them, and the AR control is the load-bearing test that this is a fixed-canvas hazard rather than generic code-extraction hygiene.

lens.title: Structure at the Wrong Granularity: Typed-AST Decoding Guarantees Statement Topology and Still Emits Unbalanced Brackets
lens.claim: A typed-AST decoding runtime that guarantees well-formed statement topology by construction does not deliver syntactic validity, because 100% of its residual parse failures are intra-leaf lexical errors (unbalanced parens/brackets, unterminated strings) inside token cells the tree does not constrain; structural priors and lexical constraints are therefore non-substitutable, and a leaf-level bracket/string automaton at the single token-commit choke point should eliminate the entire residual syntax-error class without touching the structural prior.
lens.why_now: 'Structure helps code diffusion' is asserted by structural/anchored approaches (AnCoder/AnchorTree 2602.17688; Diffusion on Syntax Trees 2405.20519) and separately 'grammar constraints help dLLMs' by CFG-constrained decoding work (2508.10111; LAVE 2602.00612; EPIC 2606.00722; automata 2607.07026). Nobody has measured that these operate at different granularities and that the structural one leaves a specific, fully characterizable lexical residue. We have a working runtime plus SFT checkpoint, so we can decompose 'validity' into topology vs lexis empirically -- and the fix localizes to one function.
lens.experiment: (1) ALREADY MEASURED: across four scaffold runs EVERY final_parseable=False output fails on a lexical, never topological, error. HE+ Medium 16/164 and MBPP+ Medium 28/378 decompose as unmatched ')', "'(' was never closed", unmatched ']', unterminated string literal, invalid decimal literal -- concrete instances `for i in range(len(numbers):` (HumanEval/0) and `if char == '<:` (HumanEval/56). Statement/clause structure is always well-formed, exactly as the runtime promises. (2) TO RUN, decisive intervention: add a leaf-level lexical automaton (bracket-depth counter + string-literal state) as a logit mask inside DecoderRuntime._commit_token, reached from commit/commit_many in scaffold_coder/decoder_runtime.py:407-465 -- the single choke point all lexical tokens pass through. Run the 2x2 {scaffold, scaffold+leaf-automaton} x {HE+ n=164, MBPP+ n=378} at Medium, reporting final_parseable rate, pass@1+, and cumulative_model_tokens via a proc() accessor reading process OR failure_process so truncated tasks are not silently dropped. (3) Separation control that makes it a granularity claim rather than a bug fix: apply a whole-sequence CFG constraint (Python grammar, LAVE/EPIC-style) to flat Dream decoding at matched token cost, showing it fixes lexis but not the semantic plateau, while the leaf automaton fixes lexis without touching topology -- the two constraint types are orthogonal and neither alone closes the gap (scaffold Medium peaks .177/.354 with parse rate already 0.90/0.93).
lens.assets_needed: scaffold_coder/decoder_runtime.py with commit/commit_many/_commit_token/rule_fixed_point/unresolved_masks (have, working); models/Scaffold-v0-stage1-7B 29GB SFT ckpt (have on LOCAL -- verify presence before dispatch per the two-disk rule); runs/scaffold_{tiny,small,medium,large}_{heplus,mbppplus} for the before-side (have, 8 runs with telemetry); evalplus grader (have). MISSING: no leaf-level lexical automaton exists -- must be written (bracket-depth + string-state tracker over the tokenizer vocabulary; the only real implementation work); for the CFG control, reuse EPIC's public implementation (github.com/hyundong98/EPIC-Decoding) or write a Python-subset Earley checker.
lens.kill_criterion: Dies if the leaf automaton drives final_parseable to 1.000 but pass@1+ does not move beyond noise (<2 pts, MBPP+ n=378), proving the lexical residue was never the binding constraint and the granularity framing, while true, is inconsequential -- a real risk since scaffold Medium's parse rate is already 0.90/0.93 against a .177/.354 ceiling, so honest upside is bounded at ~10 HE+ / 28 MBPP+ tasks. Also dies if any residual parse failure turns out topological after all, falsifying the clean 100%-lexical decomposition.
lens.builds_on: Repairs an untested assumption shared by AnCoder/AnchorTree (2602.17688, 2026-02-05), which anchors diffusion on AST-salient tokens and asserts existing approaches 'often produce broken programs' without decomposing which layer of structure causes the breakage. Complements rather than duplicates the CFG-constrained-dLLM line (2508.10111 2025-08-13; LAVE 2602.00612; EPIC 2606.00722; 2607.07026), all of which enforce a whole-sequence grammar and none of which asks what a structural prior leaves unconstrained -- our claim is precisely that these mechanisms are complementary, which their papers cannot state having no structural runtime to compare against.

diff.differentiation_statement: No prior paper makes this candidate's claim, so it is not preempted -- but I executed the candidate's own pre-registered kill criterion as a zero-GPU oracle experiment during this review, and IT FIRED, so the claim as written must be replaced before dispatch. Two things are true simultaneously. (1) The positioning gap is real and defensible: the structural-diffusion line (TreeDiff 2508.01473, 2025-08-02; AnCoder/AnchorTree 2602.17688, 2026-02-05; Diffusion-on-Syntax-Trees 2405.20519, 2024-05-30) asserts that AST priors reduce "broken programs" and the CFG-constrained-dLLM line (2508.10111, ICLR 2026 Poster, first public 2025-08-13; LAVE 2602.00612, 2026-01-31; DINGO 2505.23061, 2025-05-29; EPIC 2606.00722 and automata 2607.07026, both concurrent) enforces whole-sequence grammars, and no paper in either line measures that these operate at different granularities or characterises what a structural prior leaves unconstrained. Targeted arXiv queries for granularity/structural-vs-lexical decomposition and for structural-prior-complementary-to-grammar-constraint return zero hits. We uniquely hold a runtime that guarantees statement topology by construction, so we are the only party who can measure the residue a structural prior leaves. (2) But the specific mechanism claim -- "100% of residual parse failures are intra-leaf lexical errors" and "a leaf-level bracket/string automaton should eliminate the entire residual syntax-error class" -- is falsified by the candidate's own artifacts. Re-deriving from runs/scaffold_{medium,large}_{heplus,mbppplus}/solutions.rank*.jsonl (71 pooled parse failures): only 52.1% are bracket/string errors, 42.3% are intra-leaf expression-grammar errors that a bracket/string automaton cannot express (HumanEval/131 `while n > 0 and product != 0: n, product *= 1 - n % 10:`; HumanEval/160 `result % (operand[i+1] == 0 else ...`; Mbpp/751 `and if: if ... return False`), and 5.6% ARE indentation/topology-surfacing errors ("unindent does not match any outer indentation level" on HumanEval/135, "unexpected indent" on Mbpp/751 and Mbpp/223) -- which the candidate itself names as an independent kill condition. A tokenize()-based test shows only 63.4% of failures are even reachable by a bracket-depth + string-state tracker. Decisively, I built an oracle upper bound (bracket-balancing + string-closing + maximal parseable truncation) and graded it with evalplus: parse rate rises 0.902 -> 0.994 (HE+) and 0.926 -> 0.979 (MBPP+), while pass@1+ moves 0.1768 -> 0.1768 on HE+ (0 tasks gained, 0 lost) and 0.3651 -> 0.3783 on MBPP+ (+1.3 pts, 5 tasks gained, 0 lost). Both legs land inside the candidate's own "<2 pts on MBPP+ n=378" kill band, at an oracle ceiling no real logit-mask automaton can exceed. So the differentiated version is not "add an automaton and win"; it is the null result itself, which is stronger and already 90% collected: we can state, with a matched oracle ceiling rather than a weaker method, that driving a structural runtime's syntactic validity to ~1.0 buys essentially nothing in functional correctness -- making us the empirical counterexample to the premise shared by AnCoder, TreeDiff and 2508.10111 that syntactic validity is the operative lever for code quality. That premise is exactly what 2606.21619 (2026-06-19, concurrent) attacks from the opposite direction, and CRANE (2502.09061, 2025-02-13) attacks theoretically for over-restrictive grammars; we supply the missing third case -- a perfectly sound, non-distorting, topology-guaranteeing constrainer whose validity gains still do not convert.
diff.sharpened_claim: Syntactic validity is not the binding constraint on structural code-diffusion quality, and we show this with an oracle ceiling rather than a weaker method. (1) DECOMPOSITION (measured, corrected): a typed-AST runtime that guarantees statement/clause topology by construction still emits unparseable programs, and the residue is NOT purely bracket/string as first believed: across 71 pooled failures from four scaffold runs it splits 52.1% bracket/string, 42.3% intra-leaf expression-grammar (misplaced `else`, augmented-assignment on a tuple, keyword salad inside one leaf cell), 5.6% indentation errors that surface as topology violations in the rendered text despite a well-formed tree -- so structural priors and lexical constraints are non-substitutable AND the leaf-cell abstraction itself leaks. A bracket-depth+string-state automaton is expressive enough for only 63.4% of failures (tokenize() test). (2) NON-CONVERSION (measured, decisive): an ORACLE lexical repair -- bracket balancing, string closing, plus maximal parseable truncation, an upper bound strictly above any real logit-mask automaton -- lifts final_parseable 0.902->0.994 (HE+ n=164) and 0.926->0.979 (MBPP+ n=378) while pass@1+ goes 0.1768->0.1768 (HE+, 0 tasks flipped either way) and 0.3651->0.3783 (MBPP+, +1.3 pts, 5 gained, 0 lost). Validity and functional correctness are decoupled at the ~0.90->~0.99 margin: the last 10 points of parse rate are worth <=1.3 points of pass@1+. (3) POSITIONING CONSEQUENCE: this is a counterexample to the premise that structural/grammar machinery improves code generation *through* validity. Unlike CRANE (over-restrictive grammar hurts reasoning) and 2606.21619 (incomplete/unsound constrainers distort the model distribution), our constrainer is sound, complete-by-construction for topology, and distortion-free -- and its validity gains still do not convert. Therefore reviewers should read reported validity/compilability improvements in the structural-diffusion line as not evidencing quality gains, and the real gap at scaffold Medium's .177/.354 ceiling is semantic, not syntactic. Cost accounting throughout uses a proc() accessor reading process OR failure_process so budget-truncated tasks are not dropped.

related_work.citation: TreeDiff: AST-Guided Code Generation with Diffusion LLMs, arXiv:2508.01473
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (v1 2025-08-02, v3 2026-01-06). OpenReview search surfaces it only as 'CoRR 2025' via the DBLP.org mirror domain, i.e. no accepted venue found; no ICLR/NeurIPS/ACL venueid.
related_work.what_it_covers: The closest PRE-CUTOFF structural-diffusion-for-code paper. Injects AST structural priors into the diffusion CORRUPTION process: instead of random token masking, selectively masks tokens belonging to key AST nodes, so the model internalises syntactic boundaries and long-range hierarchical dependencies. Reports 13.3% relative improvement over random masking. Directly asserts the premise our candidate targets: 'code requires syntactic precision; even minor structural inconsistencies can render a program non-executable.'
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Structure enters only as a training-time masking schedule -- it gives no decode-time guarantee, so it cannot say what a structural prior leaves unconstrained. It never decomposes residual failures into topological vs lexical, never measures parse rate as a separate axis from pass@1, and never asks whether the parse-rate gains are what produced the 13.3%. It has no leaf/terminal abstraction at all, so the granularity question is unaskable within its framework.
related_work.known_defects: The headline 13.3% is relative, on a single comparison (AST-masking vs random-masking) with no grammar-constrained-decoding baseline and no oracle-repair control -- so the causal chain 'AST prior -> better syntax -> better functional correctness' is asserted, not decomposed. Our oracle result attacks exactly the untested middle link: we show at the 0.90->0.99 parse-rate margin the link carries <=1.3 pts of pass@1+. Follow-up: rerun TreeDiff's own comparison with parse rate and pass@1 reported separately plus an oracle lexical repair applied to both arms; if the random-masking arm's deficit is mostly repairable-syntax, the 13.3% is a validity artifact, not a capability gain.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list=2508.01473v3 (HTTP 200, full abstract, published 2025-08-02, updated 2026-01-06); OpenReview api2 /notes/search returned it under venue 'CoRR 2025' domain DBLP.org with no conference venueid.

related_work.citation: AnCoder: Anchored Code Generation via Discrete Diffusion Models (AnchorTree framework), arXiv:2602.17688
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (v1 2026-02-05, no later version). OpenReview term search for 'AnCoder' returns 0 titled hits; 'AnchorTree' search returns only unrelated AST papers. Anonymous ICLR.cc/2026/Conference blind submissions appear in generic searches but cannot be resolved to this title (api2 /notes?id= is challenge-gated, HTTP 403), so no venue claim is supportable.
related_work.what_it_covers: The paper the candidate names as its primary repair target. Uses the AST to prioritise resolving 'syntactically and semantically salient tokens' (keywords if/while, identifiers) to establish a structural scaffold guiding remaining generation. Explicitly motivates itself with 'existing approaches fail to respect the rigid structure of programming languages and, as a result, often produce broken programs that fail to execute.'
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Never decomposes 'broken programs' into which layer of structure broke. Anchoring is a token-ORDERING prior over a flat sequence, not a construction-time topology guarantee, so it cannot isolate a leaf-level residue. Provides no parse-rate-vs-pass@1 decomposition and no evidence that its quality gains flow through validity rather than through better global planning.
related_work.known_defects: (a) The load-bearing motivational claim 'often produce broken programs that fail to execute' is stated without an error taxonomy -- no breakdown of what fraction of failures are topological vs lexical vs semantic. (b) It is a family of models ('a family of models showing that structurally anchored diffusion offers a parameter-efficient path'), so quality gains are confounded between the structural prior and the training/parameter regime; no ablation isolates the anchoring from the training recipe. (c) No grammar-constrained-decoding baseline, despite 2508.10111 being available since 2025-08. Our fix: supply the missing taxonomy on a runtime with an actual construction-time guarantee, and show via oracle repair that the executability axis they invoke is nearly decoupled from pass@1+ at high parse rates -- so 'produces fewer broken programs' cannot be cited as evidence of better code.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list=2602.17688 (HTTP 200, full abstract, published 2026-02-05). OpenReview api2 /notes/search with term='AnCoder' -> 0 titled hits; with 'AnchorTree anchored diffusion abstract syntax tree code generation' -> only unrelated AST retrieval/summarisation papers.

related_work.citation: Constrained Decoding of Diffusion LLMs with Context-Free Grammars, arXiv:2508.10111
related_work.venue_status: ICLR 2026 Poster (OpenReview venue string 'ICLR 2026 Poster', venueid ICLR.cc/2026/Conference, note 7Sph4KyeYO); ALSO DL4C @ NeurIPS 2025 Oral (venueid NeurIPS.cc/2025/Workshop/DL4C, note fwH661m0Kq). Verified via OpenReview per the 2026-venue rule -- arXiv alone would have shown preprint.
related_work.what_it_covers: The strongest pre-cutoff CFG-constrained-dLLM paper and the natural comparator for the candidate's 'separation control'. First constrained decoding method for diffusion models handling context-free grammars; reduces constrained decoding to additive infilling, then to CFG-vs-regular-language intersection emptiness. Evaluated on C++ code infilling and JSON extraction; reports near-perfect syntactic correctness while 'consistently preserving or improving functional correctness'.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Enforces a WHOLE-SEQUENCE grammar and never asks what a structural prior leaves unconstrained -- it has no structural runtime to compare against, so it cannot state the complementarity claim. Its code evaluation is C++ infilling and JSON, not Python from-scratch generation on EvalPlus, and it never separates a topology axis from a lexical axis.
related_work.known_defects: (a) 'Preserving or improving functional correctness' is the weakest possible framing of the quality axis and is exactly the claim our oracle result bounds: at a 0.90->0.99 validity margin the functional payoff is <=1.3 pts, so near-perfect syntactic correctness is not evidence of a quality win. Follow-up: rerun their pipeline reporting the paired flip counts (tasks gained / tasks lost) rather than aggregate pass rates -- our HE+ leg gained 0 and lost 0 out of 16 repaired programs, a pattern invisible in aggregates. (b) No oracle-repair ceiling, so readers cannot tell how much of the reported functional gain is attainable by trivial post-hoc syntax fixing versus genuinely requiring in-loop constraints. (c) Overhead is reported as 'practical' but EPIC (2606.00722) later measures existing CFG-constrained dLLM decoding as up to 4x slower and destroying parallel decoding -- so the cost accounting in the original flatters the method.

OpenReview api2 /notes/search query='Constrained Decoding of Diffusion LLMs with Context-Free Grammars' returned venue='ICLR 2026 Poster' venueid=ICLR.cc/2026/Conference and venue='DL4C @ NeurIPS 2025 Oral'.

related_work.citation: Lookahead-then-Verify (LAVE): Reliable Constrained Decoding for Diffusion LLMs under Context-Free Grammars, arXiv:2602.00612
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (v1 2026-01-31, v2 2026-02-08). OpenReview search surfaces it as venue 'CoRR 2026' via OpenReview.net/Public_Article (note zdjJSK2NRn) -- i.e. indexed preprint, no accepted venue found. NOTE: the candidate's write-up cites this ID; it does exist but arXiv id_list=2602.00612 alone returned 0 entries in my first pass and was only recoverable via keyword search, so the ID should be double-checked at citation time.
related_work.what_it_covers: Improves reliability of CFG-constrained dLLM decoding by using the model's parallel all-position distributions to look ahead and verify that a proposed token keeps the partial output completable to a valid sentence -- fixing the failure mode where prior dLLM-specific methods permit dead-end intermediate outputs.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Purely whole-sequence grammar; no structural/AST runtime, no granularity decomposition, no leaf-vs-topology separation. Says nothing about whether validity gains convert to functional correctness on Python EvalPlus.
related_work.known_defects: Framed entirely around reliability of constraint satisfaction, with functional correctness secondary -- the same construct-validity gap our oracle experiment exposes: satisfying the grammar is measured, mattering is assumed. Follow-up: apply their lookahead machinery to a structural runtime's leaf cells (a much smaller lookahead horizon than whole-sequence, hence cheaper) and report paired task flips; our data predicts near-zero flips, which would be a clean negative result for the whole line.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv keyword search (abs:'constrained decoding' AND abs:diffusion) returned 2602.00612v2 with published 2026-01-31; abstract retrieved from that result set. OpenReview api2 /notes/search returned venue 'CoRR 2026', domain OpenReview.net/Public_Article.

related_work.citation: DINGO: Constrained Inference for Diffusion LLMs, arXiv:2505.23061
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (v1 2025-05-29, only version); no accepted venue found in OpenReview searches.
related_work.what_it_covers: Earliest pre-cutoff constrained-decoding-for-dLLM work I found. Dynamic-programming, provably distribution-preserving constrained decoding enforcing regular expressions on dLLMs, motivated by the fact that dLLMs predict blocks in parallel so AR constrained-decoding algorithms fail to preserve the true output distribution. Up to 68pp improvement on symbolic math and JSON.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Regular expressions only (weaker than CFG, and weaker than our topology guarantee); JSON/symbolic-math surfaces, not Python EvalPlus; no structural prior, so no granularity claim possible. Importantly, a bracket-matching automaton is NOT expressible as a regex over unbounded nesting depth, which DINGO never flags as a limitation for code.
related_work.known_defects: Reports constraint-satisfaction deltas (up to 68pp) as the headline with functional-correctness impact underexplored -- the recurring pattern across this line. Also, the regular-language restriction is exactly the expressiveness ceiling our tokenize() test quantifies from the other side: we measure that even a bracket-depth+string-state tracker (a strict superset of what a regex can do here) reaches only 63.4% of a structural runtime's residual failures. Follow-up: publish that expressiveness-coverage number as a design guide -- it tells constrained-decoding authors what fraction of real code failures their constraint class can even in principle address.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv keyword search result set (abs:'constrained decoding' AND abs:diffusion), entry 2505.23061v1 published 2025-05-29, abstract retrieved.

related_work.citation: EPIC: Efficient and Parallel Inference under CFG Constraints for Diffusion Language Models, arXiv:2606.00722
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (v1 2026-05-30). CONCURRENT (>= 2026-05-07), does not preempt. OpenReview term searches returned no titled hits. Public code at github.com/hyundong98/EPIC-Decoding.git per abstract -- the candidate proposes reusing it, which is viable.
related_work.what_it_covers: Efficiency-focused CFG-constrained decoding for dLLMs: lexing memoization, Earley-style parsing instead of DFAs, relaxed compatible-subset selection for parallel commit. Reduces inference time up to 67.5% and overhead up to 90.5% vs existing CFG-constrained dLLM decoding.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Purely an efficiency contribution; explicitly does not revisit whether the enforced validity buys quality. No structural prior, no granularity decomposition, no Python EvalPlus from-scratch pass@1+ analysis.
related_work.known_defects: Its own framing supplies the accounting critique of the earlier CFG line: it documents that prior methods are 'up to four times slower than unconstrained decoding' and 'substantially diminish... parallel decoding', which those papers under-reported. But EPIC in turn optimises a mechanism whose quality payoff is unestablished -- our oracle result says at high parse rates that payoff is <=1.3 pts, so a 67.5% speedup on it may be optimising a near-null intervention. Follow-up: pair EPIC's speed table with a paired-flip quality table and an oracle-repair ceiling on the same benchmarks; that is a cheap, high-value addition its authors omitted. Their 'lexing memoization' also implicitly concedes the lexical layer is a distinct stage from the grammar layer -- an engineering acknowledgement of our granularity claim that they never elevate to a scientific finding.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv keyword search (abs:'constrained decoding' AND abs:diffusion) returned 2606.00722v1 published 2026-05-30 with full abstract. Note direct arXiv id_list=2606.00722 returned 0 entries on first attempt (flaky API), recovered via search.

related_work.citation: Constrained Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Efficient Inference over Finite Automata, arXiv:2607.07026
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (v1 2026-07-08). CONCURRENT, does not preempt.
related_work.what_it_covers: Exact, tractable sampling from the constrained mean-field posterior for any finite-automaton constraint on dLLMs; treats automata as graphical models, guarantees satisfaction by construction, compatible with parallel/block-wise decoding and arbitrary remasking. Evaluated on Dream-7B and LLaDA-8B (our exact model family) across function calling, planning, text-to-SQL, math.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Notably does NOT evaluate Python code generation / EvalPlus despite using Dream-7B, and has no structural prior to compare against. Its 'finite automaton' constraint class is precisely the expressiveness level of the candidate's proposed leaf-level bracket/string automaton, which makes it the correct technical reference for the fix -- and its restriction to automata is what our 63.4% coverage number bounds.
related_work.known_defects: Reports accuracy gains on tasks with short, highly-schematised outputs (BFCL, Sudoku, Spider) where format compliance IS most of the metric -- so the gains may be format-repair rather than capability, a construct-validity confound it does not control for. Follow-up: run their method on Dream-7B EvalPlus HumanEval+/MBPP+ (they have the model, they skipped the benchmark) with parse rate and pass@1+ reported separately; we already know Dream-Coder-Instruct's unparseable rate falls 94%->1.8% across the NFE sweep with pass@1+ saturating at .707, and our oracle result predicts near-zero conversion at the top of the validity range -- so this is a directly testable, cheap negative prediction about a concurrent paper's untested regime.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list=2607.07026 (HTTP 200, abstract, published 2026-07-08).

related_work.citation: The Alignment Problem in Constrained Code Generation, arXiv:2606.21619
related_work.venue_status: Preprint (v1 2026-06-19). CONCURRENT, does not preempt -- and it is the nearest neighbour to our sharpened (null-result) claim, so it must be cited and distinguished.
related_work.what_it_covers: Attacks the same premise from the opposite direction: constrained decoding is proposed to remove compilation errors by construction 'improving functional correctness as a byproduct', but if the constrainer is incomplete (rejects valid target programs) or unsound, it distorts the LM distribution. Across seven models, two target languages, two constrainers, three benchmarks: when the constrainer is incomplete, UNCONSTRAINED decoding significantly outperforms constrained decoding on functional correctness -- up to 97% reduction, via pushing the model into low-probability regions and causing timeouts.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Its mechanism is constrainer MISALIGNMENT (incompleteness/unsoundness distorting the distribution). It therefore leaves entirely open the case of a SOUND, distortion-free, complete-by-construction constrainer: does validity convert then? That is exactly our case -- a typed-AST runtime whose topology guarantee is constructive, plus an ORACLE post-hoc repair that cannot distort the model distribution at all (it edits finished outputs, so incompleteness bias is definitionally absent). We show non-conversion even with zero distortion, which is a strictly different and complementary mechanism.
related_work.known_defects: Studies AR LLMs and type/syntax constrainers, not dLLMs and not structural runtimes; its explanation is confined to distribution distortion, so it cannot distinguish 'constraints hurt because they distort' from 'validity was never the binding constraint'. Our oracle design separates these two for the first time: post-hoc repair has no distortion channel, so a null result there isolates the second mechanism. Follow-up: add an oracle post-hoc repair arm to their three benchmarks as the distortion-free control they lack -- it converts their finding from 'bad constrainers hurt' into a decomposition of how much of the validity axis matters at all.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list=2606.21619 (HTTP 200, full abstract, published 2026-06-19).

related_work.citation: CRANE: Reasoning with constrained LLM generation, arXiv:2502.09061
related_work.venue_status: Preprint per arXiv (v1 2025-02-13, v4). I did not obtain an OpenReview/proceedings confirmation, so I make no venue claim beyond preprint.
related_work.what_it_covers: The canonical pre-cutoff statement that strict grammar enforcement diminishes LLM reasoning, with a theoretical explanation (restrictive grammars that only permit syntactically valid final answers reduce expressivity/reasoning) plus a fix (augment the output grammar with extra rules to preserve reasoning while ensuring syntactic and semantic correctness).
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: About over-restrictiveness of whole-sequence grammars in AR models. Says nothing about structural priors, about granularity of constraint, or about whether validity gains from a non-restrictive constraint convert to functional correctness. Its remedy assumes validity is worth having and just needs headroom.
related_work.known_defects: Its theory explains why constraints can HURT but not the case where constraints neither hurt nor help -- our measured regime (0 tasks gained and 0 lost on HE+ across 16 repaired programs). Follow-up: our data supplies the missing third cell of the 2x2 (constraint restrictive? x validity converts?), which CRANE's framework predicts should not exist and 2606.21619 also does not cover.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv keyword search (all:'grammar' AND all:'syntactic validity' AND all:'code generation') surfaced 2502.09061v4 published 2025-02-13; abstract retrieved via id_list.

related_work.citation: Diffusion On Syntax Trees For Program Synthesis, arXiv:2405.20519
related_work.venue_status: Preprint per arXiv (v1 2024-05-30, only version; project page tree-diffusion.github.io). No accepted-venue confirmation obtained; no venue claim made.
related_work.what_it_covers: The origin of the 'diffusion that preserves syntactic validity by construction' idea the candidate builds on: neural diffusion over syntax trees of any CFG, iteratively editing programs while preserving syntactic validity, combined with search and execution feedback. Applied to inverse graphics (image -> program).
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: Domain is tiny graphics DSLs, not Python; the DSLs have shallow/trivial lexical structure, so the leaf-level residue we observe cannot arise there. This is precisely why the granularity question is new: 'preserves syntactic validity by construction' is TRUE for a DSL with no rich terminals and FALSE for Python, where the tree does not constrain intra-leaf token content.
related_work.known_defects: The 'preserves syntactic validity' guarantee is stated generally ('any context-free grammar') but demonstrated only where terminals are trivial -- an untested-regime generalisation gap. Our fix names the boundary condition explicitly and measures it: on Python, a tree-preserving runtime still yields 9.8%/7.4% unparseable at Medium, with 42.3% of failures being intra-leaf expression grammar the tree abstraction does not reach and 5.6% surfacing as indentation errors. That is a concrete, quantified scope correction to a widely-cited guarantee.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API id_list=2405.20519 (HTTP 200, full abstract, published 2024-05-30, single version, comment lists project page).

related_work.citation: TRANX: A Transition-based Neural Abstract Syntax Parser for Semantic Parsing and Code Generation, arXiv:1810.02720 (and A Syntactic Neural Model for General-Purpose Code Generation, arXiv:1704.01696)
related_work.venue_status: Long-established prior art (TRANX arXiv v1 2018-10-05; the syntactic neural model arXiv v1 2017-04-06). I did not re-verify their proceedings entries; both are pre-2020 so concurrency is not at issue.
related_work.what_it_covers: The classical grammar/AST-constrained decoder line that our runtime descends from: decoding via a transition system over an abstract syntax description, using target-MR syntax to constrain the output space. Establishes the architecture where non-terminal expansion is grammar-constrained.
related_work.what_it_leaves_open: In this family, terminal/leaf token generation is handled by a separate copy/generate mechanism outside the grammar -- structurally the same split our candidate rediscovers -- but the literature treats this as an implementation detail and never measures the resulting error residue, and never asks whether closing it would improve task metrics. No modern paper connects this classical split to dLLM constrained decoding.
related_work.known_defects: The split between grammar-constrained non-terminals and unconstrained terminals is never audited: no paper in this line reports what fraction of its residual failures are terminal-level. Our contribution is to supply that audit in the modern dLLM setting AND to show it does not matter for task metrics -- which retroactively justifies the classical line's decision to leave terminals unconstrained. Framing this as vindication of a 2017-2018 design choice makes the null result more publishable, not less.
related_work.verified_how: arXiv API keyword searches (all:'TranX' AND all:'semantic parsing'; all:'syntactic neural model' AND all:'code generation') returned both with published dates 2018-10-05 and 2017-04-06; TRANX abstract retrieved via id_list.

followup_openings.target_paper: The candidate's OWN pre-registered kill criterion (self-audit, highest priority)
followup_openings.defect: The claim 'ALREADY MEASURED: across four scaffold runs EVERY final_parseable=False output fails on a lexical, never topological, error' is false on the candidate's own artifacts, and the proposed intervention fails the candidate's own kill test. Re-deriving from runs/scaffold_{medium,large}_{heplus,mbppplus}/solutions.rank*.jsonl: 71 pooled failures split 52.1% bracket/string, 42.3% intra-leaf expression-grammar (NOT reachable by a bracket/string automaton), 5.6% indentation/topology (HumanEval/135 'unindent does not match any outer indentation level'; Mbpp/751 and Mbpp/223 'unexpected indent') -- the last bucket alone triggers the candidate's second stated kill condition ('dies if any residual parse failure turns out topological after all'). A tokenize()-based expressiveness test puts automaton-reachable failures at 63.4%, not 100%. Separately, the metrics JSONL nests final_parseable under process/failure_process, so a naive top-level read returns 0 failures -- the same silent-drop class as retraction #3.
followup_openings.our_fix: Do NOT dispatch the 50-GPU-hour 2x2. I already ran the decisive experiment at zero GPU cost: an ORACLE lexical repair (bracket balancing + string closing + maximal parseable truncation), a strict upper bound on any real logit-mask automaton, graded with evalplus. Parse rate 0.902->0.994 (HE+) and 0.926->0.979 (MBPP+); pass@1+ 0.1768->0.1768 (HE+, 0 gained / 0 lost of 16 repaired) and 0.3651->0.3783 (MBPP+, +1.3 pts, 5 gained / 0 lost). Artifacts persisted at /apdcephfs_wzc1/share_304376610/pighzliu_code/dllm_draft/runs/_oracle_lexrepair_medium/ (heplus_repaired_samples.jsonl, heplus_repaired_eval_results.json, mbppplus_repaired_samples.jsonl, mbppplus_repaired_eval_results.json, oracle_repair_grade.py).
